q: Which type of law covers legally enforceable agreements between two or more parties?

options.t: Contract law
options.why: Contract law covers legally enforceable agreements. A contract needs an offer, acceptance and an exchange of value, and courts can make the parties keep their promises or pay damages.

options.t: Criminal law
options.why: Criminal law deals with offences against the public, such as theft, and is enforced by the state through prosecution. It does not govern private agreements between two parties.

options.t: Property law
options.why: Property law covers who owns and may use land and belongings. It can touch a contract about a sale, but it is not the body of law that makes agreements enforceable.

options.t: Tort law
options.why: Tort law covers civil wrongs, such as negligence or defamation, where someone is harmed without a contract being broken. It is about injury and fault, not agreements.

q: Sol's Sandwich Shack registers the name of its signature sandwich so rivals cannot sell something confusingly similar under that name. Which protection did Sol's most likely use?

options.t: Franchise
options.why: A franchise is a license to run a business under another firm's brand and system. It does not protect a sandwich name from being copied by rivals.

options.t: Copyright
options.why: Copyright protects original creative works such as books, songs and artwork. A short product name is not covered by copyright, so Sol's would not use it here.

options.t: Trademark
options.why: A trademark protects names, logos and slogans that identify a brand. Registering the sandwich name stops rivals from using a confusingly similar one, which is exactly what Sol's wants.

options.t: Patent
options.why: A patent protects a new invention or process for a set number of years. It does not protect a name, only how something works.

q: A customer slips on a freshly mopped floor in a store that put out no warning sign. The customer's claim that the store failed to take reasonable care is based on which concept?

options.t: Fraud claim
options.why: Fraud means knowingly deceiving someone to gain something. The store did not lie to the customer; it simply failed to warn about a hazard, so fraud does not fit.

options.t: Negligence
options.why: Negligence means failing to take the care a reasonable person would, causing harm. Skipping a warning sign on a wet floor is a classic example, and the injured customer can seek damages.

options.t: Defamation
options.why: Defamation is a false statement that harms someone's reputation. Nothing was said about the customer, so it does not apply to a slip on a floor.

options.t: Breach claim
options.why: A breach claim comes from breaking a contract term. The customer and store had no promise about the floor, so the claim rests on a failure of care, not a contract.

q: Dana, who is 15, signs a contract to buy a used scooter on credit. Which statement is generally true?

options.t: The contract is void unless the seller agrees to cancel it, since she is a minor
options.why: This is wrong because a minor's contract is not void automatically. It is voidable, meaning Dana can choose to cancel it, and the seller's agreement is not needed.

options.t: The contract is fully binding because Dana signed her name to it, whatever her age
options.why: Signing does not make it fully binding. Courts protect minors, so most contracts they sign can be cancelled, even when the signature is genuine and the price fair.

options.t: Dana loses the right to cancel the contract after one day, since the scooter is used
options.why: There is no one-day limit. A minor can generally cancel, and the right usually lasts until a reasonable time after turning 18, whether or not the item was used.

options.t: Dana can usually cancel the contract, because minors may void most contracts
options.why: Minors generally lack full capacity to contract, so they may void most agreements, apart from necessities such as food. Dana can usually cancel, though she may need to return the scooter.

q: What is the purpose of a statute of limitations?

options.t: To make some contracts be put in writing
options.why: Requiring some contracts to be written is the job of the statute of frauds. A statute of limitations is about time limits, not the form a contract takes.

options.t: To list which crimes count as felonies
options.why: Lists of which crimes are felonies come from criminal codes. A statute of limitations may limit how long prosecutors have, but it does not define crime categories.

options.t: To cap the damages that a court may award
options.why: Caps on damages are separate laws that limit the amount awarded. A statute of limitations limits when a case can be filed, not how much is won.

options.t: To set a deadline for filing a lawsuit
options.why: A statute of limitations sets the deadline for filing a lawsuit. It keeps evidence fresh and stops people from being sued over events from long ago.

q: In the communication process, which element is the person who creates and sends the message?

options.t: Channel
options.why: The channel is the medium that carries the message, such as email, a phone call or a face-to-face talk. It is the route, not the person who sends.

options.t: Sender
options.why: The sender is the person who creates, encodes and sends the message. Everything else in the process depends on the sender choosing clear words and a suitable channel.

options.t: Feedback
options.why: Feedback is the receiver's response that shows the message was understood. It travels back to the sender, so it is not the one who starts the message.

options.t: Receiver
options.why: The receiver is the person who gets and interprets the message. The receiver is on the other end, so cannot be the one who creates and sends it.

q: A manager emails a 400-word update to a team that only needs to know a meeting moved to 3 p.m. Which communication principle did the manager ignore?

options.t: Correctness
options.why: Correctness means the facts, grammar and spelling are right. The manager's email may have been accurate, so the problem was its length, not errors.

options.t: Completeness
options.why: Completeness means giving all the facts the reader needs. The email contained too much, not too little, so it was complete but not focused.

options.t: Conciseness
options.why: Conciseness means saying what is needed in as few words as possible. A 400-word email for a simple time change buries the key point and wastes the team's time.

options.t: Courtesy
options.why: Courtesy means being polite and considerate. Nothing suggests rudeness here; the problem was the amount of text, so courtesy is not the principle that was ignored.

q: During a live presentation, a speaker avoids eye contact and talks in a flat, quiet voice. Which area of communication is the main weakness?

options.t: Delivery and nonverbal communication
options.why: Delivery covers voice, eye contact, posture and gestures. Avoiding eye contact and speaking flat and quiet are delivery problems, so this is the main weakness shown.

options.t: Document formatting and layout style
options.why: Document formatting concerns how a written page looks, such as headings and spacing. The scenario is a live talk, so layout is not the problem.

options.t: Word choice and grammar skills used
options.why: Word choice and grammar are about the language used. The speaker's words are not described as weak; the trouble is how they are said, not what is said.

options.t: Accuracy of the facts that were given
options.why: Accuracy concerns whether the facts are right. The scene does not suggest wrong facts, only poor eye contact and a flat voice, which are delivery issues.

q: A team member says, 'I hear that the deadline is worrying you. Let's look at what is realistic.' Which skill is being shown?

options.t: Delegating work
options.why: Delegating means giving a task to someone else. Nothing is being handed off here; the speaker is acknowledging a concern, so delegating is not the skill shown.

options.t: Proofreading text
options.why: Proofreading is checking written text for mistakes. This is a spoken exchange, so no document is being checked.

options.t: Persuasive selling
options.why: Persuasive selling aims to convince someone to buy. The speaker is trying to understand a worry, not to win a sale, so this is not selling.

options.t: Active listening
options.why: Active listening means paying full attention, reflecting back what was heard and responding to feelings. Restating the worry and moving to what is realistic shows it clearly.

q: Which is the best way to share one employee's confidential salary details?

options.t: A private one-on-one meeting
options.why: A private one-on-one meeting keeps sensitive pay details between the people who need to know. It respects confidentiality and lets the employee ask questions in comfort.

options.t: A group text to the whole team
options.why: A group text reaches the whole team at once, so anyone could see the salary. That breaks confidentiality and could embarrass the employee.

options.t: A notice on the break room wall
options.why: A notice on the break room wall is visible to everyone who walks by. Posting private pay details like this defeats the point of keeping them confidential.

options.t: A company-wide chat channel
options.why: A company-wide chat channel is seen by many people and can be copied or shared. Confidential salary details should never be posted in a public channel.

q: Which action is an example of customer service after a sale?

options.t: Closing the store early on weekends each week
options.why: Closing early on weekends is a scheduling choice that affects shoppers before and after the sale. It is not service given to a customer after buying.

options.t: Removing the return policy from the store website
options.why: Removing the return policy takes away a service that customers rely on. It is the opposite of good after-sale service and tends to lose trust.

options.t: Following up to check the customer is satisfied
options.why: Following up to check satisfaction is after-sale service. It shows care, catches problems early and encourages repeat business and good word of mouth.

options.t: Raising prices for repeat buyers every year
options.why: Raising prices for repeat buyers is a pricing decision that punishes loyalty. It is not a service, and it would likely drive regular customers away.

q: A customer brings back a blender with a cracked lid seven days after buying it. Which response best builds goodwill?

options.t: Suggest buying a second blender at a discount and keeping the first
options.why: Pushing a second blender ignores the customer's actual problem, a broken lid. It treats a complaint as a sales chance and is unlikely to build goodwill.

options.t: Apologize, check the return policy, and offer a replacement or refund
options.why: Apologizing, checking the policy and offering a replacement or refund solves the problem fairly. The customer feels heard, and goodwill is built through a quick, courteous fix.

options.t: Explain that cracked lids are normal wear and decline to give help
options.why: Telling the customer a cracked lid is normal wear dismisses the complaint after only a week. It shows no care and risks losing the customer for good.

options.t: Ask the customer to submit a written complaint before any help is offered
options.why: Demanding a written complaint first adds needless steps to a simple return. Slow, bureaucratic handling frustrates customers instead of building goodwill.

q: Which measure best shows how many customers keep buying from a business over time?

options.t: Customer retention rate
options.why: Customer retention rate measures the share of customers who keep buying over a period. A higher rate shows loyalty and is often cheaper to maintain than finding new buyers.

options.t: Break-even point of a firm
options.why: Break-even point is the sales level where revenue equals costs. It tells a firm how much it must sell, not how many customers return.

options.t: Inventory turnover rate
options.why: Inventory turnover shows how quickly stock sells and is replaced. It measures goods moving, not whether customers come back.

options.t: Gross margin of sales
options.why: Gross margin is sales minus the cost of goods sold, shown as a share of sales. It measures profit on products, not customer loyalty.

q: A customer calls in angry about a late order. What should the representative do first?

options.t: Offer a discount before hearing what the problem is
options.why: Offering a discount before hearing the problem is premature. The rep may fix the wrong thing, and the customer still feels unheard and angry.

options.t: Explain the company shipping policy in complete detail
options.why: Explaining policy in detail first sounds defensive. An angry customer needs to be heard before listening to rules and explanations.

options.t: Listen without interrupting and acknowledge the concern
options.why: Listening without interrupting and acknowledging the concern calms the customer. It shows respect and lets the rep learn the real problem before offering a solution.

options.t: Transfer the call to a supervisor without comment or help
options.why: Transferring the call without comment passes the problem on and leaves the customer feeling brushed off. Handing off should come after listening, and with an explanation.

q: Which person is an external customer of a shoe store?

options.t: A store manager reading sales
options.why: A store manager is an employee, so an internal customer at most. External customers are outsiders who pay for goods, not people who work for the store.

options.t: A stockroom worker with boxes
options.why: A stockroom worker is part of the business, so is internal. An external customer is someone outside the firm who buys its products.

options.t: A cashier employed by the store
options.why: A cashier works for the store, so is not an external customer. External customers come from outside and pay for what the shop sells.

options.t: A shopper buying running shoes
options.why: A shopper buying running shoes is outside the firm and pays for its product. That makes them an external customer, the people the store exists to serve.

q: When the price of a product rises and everything else stays the same, what usually happens to the quantity demanded?

options.t: No change
options.why: Price changes do affect demand, so no change is unlikely. The law of demand says that with other things equal, a higher price lowers the quantity people want to buy.

options.t: It falls
options.why: The law of demand says that when price rises, with everything else equal, quantity demanded falls. Buyers cut back or switch because the product costs more.

options.t: It rises
options.why: A rising quantity demanded at a higher price goes against the law of demand. People usually buy less, not more, when the price goes up.

options.t: It doubles
options.why: Quantity demanded does not double when price rises. Demand responds to price in the opposite direction, and a doubling would be an extreme and unrealistic reaction.

q: Which good is the best example of a substitute for tea?

options.t: Teapots
options.why: Teapots are a complement to tea, since they are used with it. A substitute is something that can replace tea, not something that goes along with it.

options.t: Coffee
options.why: Coffee is a substitute for tea, as people can choose it instead. If tea gets more expensive, some buyers switch to coffee, so demand for coffee rises.

options.t: Tea bags
options.why: Tea bags are a form of tea, not a replacement for it. A buyer who wants tea would still need tea bags, so they are not a substitute.

options.t: Honey
options.why: Honey is usually added to tea, so it is a complement. It does not take tea's place as a drink, so it is not a substitute.

q: Mia can work a Saturday shift that pays $80 or attend a free workshop. She attends the workshop. What is her opportunity cost?

options.t: The $80 she gave up
options.why: Opportunity cost is the value of the next best alternative given up. Mia gave up the $80 shift to attend the workshop, so $80 is her cost.

options.t: Nothing, as no cash
options.why: The workshop was free, but time has value. Mia gave up $80 of pay, so the opportunity cost is not zero just because no money was spent.

options.t: Value of other plans
options.why: Vague other plans are not what she gave up. Opportunity cost counts the single best alternative forgone, which here is the $80 shift.

options.t: The workshop fee paid
options.why: The workshop was free, so there was no fee. The cost she bears is the pay she gave up, not a charge for attending.

q: Prices across the economy rise by 4 percent over a year while a worker's wages stay the same. What happens to the worker's purchasing power?

options.t: It doubles
options.why: Purchasing power would not double, because prices rose while wages stayed flat. Doubling would need wages to rise far faster than prices, which did not happen.

options.t: No change
options.why: Purchasing power does change. With prices up 4 percent and pay the same, the worker can afford less than before, so it did not stay constant.

options.t: It rises
options.why: It would rise only if wages grew faster than prices. Here prices rose and pay stayed flat, so the worker can buy less, not more.

options.t: It falls
options.why: Purchasing power falls when prices rise faster than income. The same wages now buy about 4 percent less, so the worker is effectively poorer.

q: Which item would be counted in this year's gross domestic product (GDP) of the country where it was made?

options.t: A pension payment to a retiree from the government this year
options.why: A pension payment is a transfer payment. It moves money without producing a good or service, so it is not counted in GDP.

options.t: A used bicycle resold between two neighbors this year, not new
options.why: A used bicycle resold between neighbors was counted when it was first made. Reselling it does not create new production, so it is not part of this year's GDP.

options.t: A new bicycle produced and sold by a local manufacturer this year
options.why: A new bicycle made and sold this year is a final good produced domestically. GDP counts the value of goods and services produced in the year, so this is included.

options.t: Shares of stock bought and sold on a stock exchange this year
options.why: Buying and selling shares is a financial transfer of ownership. No new goods or services are produced, so stock trading is not counted in GDP.

q: Which term describes recognizing and managing your own emotions and understanding the emotions of others?

options.t: Emotional intelligence
options.why: Emotional intelligence is the ability to recognize and manage your own emotions and to understand those of others. It supports teamwork, leadership and handling conflict.

options.t: Cognitive biases at work
options.why: Cognitive biases are mental shortcuts that can distort thinking. They describe errors in judgment, not skill at handling emotions.

options.t: Market research on needs
options.why: Market research collects information on customer needs. It is a business activity and has nothing to do with managing emotions.

options.t: Technical skill at work
options.why: Technical skill is know-how for specific tasks, such as using software. It is a different ability from reading and managing feelings.

q: Before replying to a harsh email, Kai takes a short walk to cool down. Which skill is Kai using?

options.t: Procrastination
options.why: Procrastination means putting a task off. Kai walks to calm down before replying, which is a thoughtful pause rather than avoiding the task.

options.t: Task delegation
options.why: Task delegation means handing work to someone else. Kai is still writing the reply, only after cooling down, so nothing is delegated.

options.t: Self-regulation
options.why: Self-regulation is controlling emotions and impulses before acting. Taking a walk to cool off before answering a harsh email prevents a reply written in anger.

options.t: Empathy for others
options.why: Empathy is understanding others' feelings. Kai's pause is about managing his own emotion, so self-regulation fits better than empathy.

q: A coworker is quiet after receiving criticism in a meeting. Which response best shows empathy?

options.t: Ignore it so they do not feel singled out
options.why: Ignoring it might seem kind, but it leaves the coworker alone. Empathy means noticing how they feel and showing care, not pretending nothing happened.

options.t: Ask privately how they are doing and listen
options.why: Asking privately how they are doing and listening shows empathy. It acknowledges their feelings without embarrassing them in front of others.

options.t: Joke about it to lighten the mood in the team
options.why: Joking can feel dismissive to someone who is hurting. It treats their feelings as unimportant instead of showing understanding.

options.t: Tell them criticism is part of every job
options.why: Telling them criticism is normal may be true, but it brushes aside their feelings. Empathy first listens and acknowledges, and only then offers advice.

q: Which is the best example of self-awareness at work?

options.t: Blaming teammates whenever a deadline is missed on the project at work
options.why: Blaming teammates avoids looking at your own part. Self-awareness means honestly seeing your own role, strengths and weaknesses.

options.t: Hiding a mistake so that the team stays confident in the plan at work
options.why: Hiding a mistake is avoidance, not insight. A self-aware person admits errors so they can be fixed and learned from.

options.t: Copying the habits of the most confident teammate in order to look good
options.why: Copying a confident teammate is about appearances. Self-awareness is knowing your own traits and habits, not imitating someone else.

options.t: Noticing that tight deadlines make you short-tempered and planning around it
options.why: Noticing that tight deadlines make you short-tempered, and planning around it, shows self-awareness. You recognize your own reaction and manage it before it harms others.

q: Which behaviour best shows a positive attitude at work?

options.t: Avoiding tasks that look difficult to do
options.why: Avoiding difficult tasks is a negative habit. A positive attitude means taking on challenges instead of dodging them.

options.t: Complaining about every change that comes
options.why: Complaining about every change shows resistance and spreads negativity. A positive attitude welcomes change and looks for how to adapt.

options.t: Waiting to be told what to do next each day
options.why: Waiting to be told what to do shows a lack of initiative. A positive attitude looks for useful work without being prompted.

options.t: Looking for solutions when a problem appears
options.why: Looking for solutions when a problem appears shows a positive attitude. It focuses on moving forward and helps the whole team keep going.

q: Which person starts a business and accepts the financial risk for its success?

options.t: Consumers
options.why: Consumers buy goods and services but do not start the business or carry its risk. They are the customers the entrepreneur hopes to attract.

options.t: Auditors
options.why: Auditors examine a firm's financial records for accuracy. They are hired to check books, and they do not start a business or risk their own money.

options.t: Entrepreneur
options.why: An entrepreneur starts a business, organizes resources and accepts the financial risk. Profit or loss falls on them, which is what separates them from employees.

options.t: Wholesaler
options.why: A wholesaler buys in bulk and sells to retailers. It is a link in the supply chain, not the person who starts a business and bears its risk.

q: Priya runs a tutoring business alone and is personally responsible for all of its debts. Which form of ownership is this?

options.t: Limited liability firm
options.why: A limited liability company protects the owners' personal assets from business debts. Priya is personally responsible for all debts, so this form does not fit.

options.t: Sole proprietorship
options.why: A sole proprietorship is owned and run by one person with unlimited personal liability. That matches Priya's tutoring business exactly, as she and the business are legally one.

options.t: Cooperative society
options.why: A cooperative is owned and run by its members for shared benefit. Priya runs her business alone, so it is not a cooperative.

options.t: Corporate entity
options.why: A corporation is a separate legal entity, so owners are not personally liable for its debts. Priya's personal liability means she is not a corporation.

q: Which part of a business plan describes the target market, the competition and the customers?

options.t: Market analysis
options.why: Market analysis describes the target market, customers and competitors. It shows that demand exists and how the business will compete.

options.t: Executive summary
options.why: The executive summary is a short overview of the whole plan, written to grab attention. It sums up the plan instead of analysing the market in detail.

options.t: Operations plan
options.why: The operations plan explains how the business will run day to day, such as location, equipment and staff. It does not analyse customers and competitors.

options.t: Financial plan
options.why: The financial plan shows expected revenue, costs and funding needs. It deals with money, not with studying customers and competition.

q: Two friends open a bike repair shop. They want their personal assets protected from business debts without the formal rules of a corporation. Which structure fits best?

options.t: C corporation company
options.why: A C corporation protects owners but comes with formal rules, such as boards, meetings and double taxation. The friends want protection without that formality.

options.t: Sole proprietorship firm
options.why: A sole proprietorship has one owner with unlimited personal liability. It would not protect either friend, and it is a one-person form, not a partnership.

options.t: General partnership of two
options.why: In a general partnership, each partner is personally responsible for the business's debts. That leaves their personal assets exposed, which they want to avoid.

options.t: Limited liability company
options.why: A limited liability company protects owners' personal assets from business debts while being simpler than a corporation. This gives the friends the protection and flexibility they want.

q: What is the name for the money needed to launch a new business?

options.t: Accounts payable
options.why: Accounts payable are bills a business owes to suppliers. They are money owed, not money gathered to launch the business.

options.t: Startup capital
options.why: Startup capital is the money needed to launch a business, covering equipment, inventory, rent and early costs. It can come from savings, loans or investors.

options.t: Retained earnings
options.why: Retained earnings are profits kept in the business after it has been running. A brand-new business has none yet, so they cannot fund the launch.

options.t: Net income total
options.why: Net income is profit after expenses over a period. It is a result of operating, not the funds needed to begin.

q: Which financial statement reports revenue, expenses and net income for a period of time?

options.t: Balance sheet
options.why: The balance sheet shows assets, liabilities and equity on one date. It is a snapshot, not a report of revenue and expenses over a period.

options.t: Budget plan report
options.why: A budget plan is a forecast of planned income and spending. It looks ahead, while the income statement reports actual results for a past period.

options.t: Income statement
options.why: The income statement reports revenue, expenses and net income for a period, such as a month or year. It shows whether the business made a profit or a loss.

options.t: Cash flow report
options.why: A cash flow report tracks cash coming in and going out. It shows the movement of cash, not revenue, expenses and net income as measured on an income statement.

q: Bright Bean Cafe had $90,000 in sales and $36,000 in cost of goods sold. What is its gross profit?

options.why: Gross profit equals sales minus cost of goods sold. Here $90,000 minus $36,000 is $54,000, which is what is left to cover other expenses.
$126,000 adds the cost of goods sold to sales instead of subtracting it. Gross profit takes the cost away from sales, so the figure must be smaller than sales.
$40,000 does not follow from the numbers. Gross profit is sales of $90,000 less $36,000 in cost of goods sold, which gives $54,000.
$36,000 is just the cost of goods sold. Gross profit is what remains after subtracting that cost from sales, so it is $54,000.

q: A business has $50,000 in current assets and $25,000 in current liabilities. What is its current ratio?

options.why: The current ratio is current assets divided by current liabilities. Here $50,000 divided by $25,000 equals 2.0, meaning $2 of assets for each $1 owed soon.
25.0 does not come from the formula. The ratio divides assets by liabilities, so $50,000 over $25,000 gives 2.0, not a number this large.
0.5 has the numbers upside down, liabilities over assets. The current ratio divides current assets by current liabilities, so the right answer is 2.0.
75.0 would come from nothing sensible here. The ratio divides assets by liabilities, so $50,000 over $25,000 is 2.0.

q: Net income was $18,000 on sales of $240,000. What is the net profit margin?

options.t: 75 percent
options.why: 75 percent is far too high. Net profit margin is net income divided by sales, so $18,000 over $240,000 is only 7.5 percent.

options.t: 13.3 percent
options.why: 13.3 percent comes from dividing sales by net income the wrong way round. Margin divides net income by sales, which gives 7.5 percent.

options.t: 18 percent
options.why: 18 percent confuses the dollar figure with a percentage. The margin is $18,000 divided by $240,000, which is 7.5 percent.

options.t: 7.5 percent
options.why: Net profit margin is net income divided by sales. $18,000 divided by $240,000 is 0.075, or 7.5 percent, meaning 7.5 cents of profit for each dollar sold.

q: Which type of cost stays the same no matter how many units a business produces?

options.t: Marginal
options.why: Marginal cost is the extra cost of making one more unit. It changes with output, so it is not a cost that stays the same.

options.t: Variable
options.why: Variable costs, such as materials, rise and fall with the number of units made. They change with output, so they are not the cost that stays fixed.

options.t: Fixed cost
options.why: A fixed cost, such as rent or insurance, stays the same however many units are produced. It is paid even if output is zero, within a normal range.

options.t: Sunk revenue
options.why: Sunk revenue is not a standard cost type. Sunk costs are past spending that cannot be recovered, and revenue is income, not a cost.

q: What is the process of finding and attracting qualified candidates for a job?

options.t: Termination
options.why: Termination is ending someone's employment. It is the opposite of attracting new people, so it is not part of finding candidates.

options.t: Recruitment
options.why: Recruitment is finding and attracting qualified candidates through ads, referrals and job boards. It builds the pool of people from whom a hire can be chosen.

options.t: Orientation
options.why: Orientation introduces new hires to the company, rules and team. It happens after hiring, so it is not the search for candidates.

options.t: Appraisal
options.why: Appraisal reviews how well a current employee performs. It is about existing staff, not about finding new applicants.

q: Which HR document lists a position's duties, responsibilities and reporting relationship?

options.t: Job description
options.why: A job description lists a position's duties, responsibilities and reporting line. It tells applicants what to expect and helps managers set clear standards.

options.t: Resume of a person
options.why: A resume describes one person's own skills and history. It belongs to the applicant and does not describe what a job requires.

options.t: Performance review
options.why: A performance review evaluates how well an employee did the job. It looks at results, not at listing the duties and reporting lines of a role.

options.t: Employee handbook
options.why: An employee handbook covers company-wide rules and benefits for all staff. It is not specific to one position's duties and reporting relationship.

q: Which U.S. law prohibits employment discrimination based on race, color, religion, sex or national origin?

options.t: Fair Labor Standards Act of 1938
options.why: The Fair Labor Standards Act sets minimum wage, overtime and child labor rules. It is about pay and hours, not discrimination.

options.t: Title VII of the Civil Rights Act
options.why: Title VII of the Civil Rights Act prohibits employment discrimination based on race, color, religion, sex or national origin. It covers hiring, firing and workplace treatment.

options.t: Family and Medical Leave Act of 1993
options.why: The Family and Medical Leave Act allows unpaid, job-protected leave for family and medical reasons. It does not deal with discrimination on these grounds.

options.t: Occupational Safety and Health Act
options.why: The Occupational Safety and Health Act sets workplace safety standards. It protects workers from hazards and does not address discrimination.

q: A supervisor gives a new hire written feedback every 90 days, measured against agreed goals. This process is best called:

options.t: Exit interview for staff
options.why: An exit interview is held when an employee leaves, to learn why. It does not happen every 90 days, and it is not feedback measured against goals.

options.t: Onboarding of a new hire
options.why: Onboarding is helping a new hire settle in during the first weeks. It is not the repeated evaluation of performance against agreed goals.

options.t: Job analysis of a role
options.why: Job analysis studies what a job involves, in order to write a description. It looks at the role, not at how a person is performing in it.

options.t: Performance appraisal
options.why: A performance appraisal is a regular evaluation of an employee's work against goals. Written feedback every 90 days fits the process of reviewing and guiding performance.

q: Which benefit is an example of non-monetary compensation?

options.t: Overtime pay for staff
options.why: Overtime pay is money paid for extra hours. It is monetary compensation, so it is not the example asked for.

options.t: An hourly wage rate paid
options.why: An hourly wage is money paid for time worked. It is direct monetary compensation, not a non-monetary benefit.

options.t: A flexible work schedule
options.why: A flexible work schedule is a benefit with no direct cash value. It improves work-life balance, which makes it non-monetary compensation.

options.t: An annual bonus payment
options.why: An annual bonus is a payment of money. It is monetary compensation, so it does not fit a question about non-monetary benefits.

q: What do we call raw facts and figures before they have been organized or analyzed?

options.t: Cash
options.why: Cash is money in coin or notes. It is not a name for raw facts and figures, which are collected before they are organized.

options.t: Tool
options.why: A tool is something used to do a job. Raw facts and figures are not tools; they are what a tool might later process.

options.t: News
options.why: News is information that has been reported or interpreted. Raw facts are the unprocessed pieces before they are made into a story.

options.t: Data
options.why: Data means raw facts and figures before they are organized or analyzed. Once data is processed and given meaning, it becomes information that people can use.

q: A shop stores customer names, orders and addresses in one organized, searchable electronic system. What is this system called?

options.t: A database
options.why: A database is an organized, searchable electronic collection of information. It lets a shop store, find and update customer names, orders and addresses quickly.

options.t: A firewall
options.why: A firewall is security software or hardware that blocks unwanted network traffic. It protects a system but does not store customer records.

options.t: A spreadsheet
options.why: A spreadsheet can hold data, but it is a grid for calculations. A searchable system that links customers and orders is more precisely called a database.

options.t: A router
options.why: A router directs data between networks, such as to the internet. It moves traffic but does not store and organize customer records.

q: Which practice best protects customer data held by a business?

options.t: Sharing one login among all staff members at work
options.why: Sharing one login makes it impossible to tell who did what. It also means everyone can see all data, which puts customer information at risk.

options.t: Emailing customer files to personal accounts at home
options.why: Emailing files to personal accounts moves customer data outside company control. If the personal account is hacked, the customers' details could leak.

options.t: Limiting access by job role and using strong passwords
options.why: Limiting access by job role means people see only the data they need, and strong passwords make accounts harder to break into. Together they reduce the chance of a leak.

options.t: Keeping the files on an open public network drive
options.why: An open public network drive lets anyone find and read the files. Customer data stored there is exposed to theft or misuse.

q: A company wants to find which products sell best by region and season. Which tool is best for turning raw sales data into trends?

options.t: A word processor for writing letters and reports
options.why: A word processor is for writing documents. It cannot easily summarize large sales tables to show trends by region and season.

options.t: Data analysis software such as a pivot table
options.why: Data analysis software, such as a pivot table, groups and summarizes large sets of data. It lets the company see sales by region and season to find top products.

options.t: An email client for sending and getting messages
options.why: An email client sends and receives messages. It does not analyze sales numbers or reveal trends.

options.t: A slide template used to design a presentation
options.why: A slide template helps present information. It displays results but cannot calculate trends from raw sales data.

q: What does regularly backing up data protect against?

options.t: Complaints from unhappy customers at the store
options.why: Backups do not affect customer satisfaction. They copy files so they can be restored, so they do not deal with complaints.

options.t: Rising prices from the company's suppliers
options.why: Backups have no effect on supplier prices. They are an IT safeguard for company files, not a way to control costs from suppliers.

options.t: Loss of data from failure, error or attack
options.why: Regular backups protect against data loss from hardware failure, human error or cyberattack. With a recent copy, the business can restore files and keep operating.

options.t: Slow internet speeds at the company's office
options.why: Backups do not speed up the internet. They copy data for safekeeping, so connection speed is a separate issue.

q: Which of the four Ps describes where and how customers can buy a product?

options.t: Product
options.why: Product is what a business sells, including its features and quality. It is not about where and how customers buy it.

options.t: Place
options.why: Place covers where and how customers can buy a product, including stores, websites and distribution. It makes the product available at the right time and spot.

options.t: Price
options.why: Price is how much customers pay. It is about cost to the buyer, not the location or method of purchase.

options.t: Promos
options.why: Promotion is how a business tells customers about its product, such as ads and sales. It is about communication, not where it is sold.

q: A company divides its market into groups by age, income and lifestyle. This is called:

options.t: Brand extension plan
options.why: A brand extension uses an existing brand name on a new product. It is about product strategy, not splitting a market into groups.

options.t: Cost-plus pricing
options.why: Cost-plus pricing sets a price by adding a markup to cost. It is a pricing method and has nothing to do with grouping customers.

options.t: Product positioning
options.why: Product positioning is how a brand is placed in customers' minds compared with rivals. It follows segmentation but is not the act of dividing the market.

options.t: Market segmentation
options.why: Market segmentation divides a market into groups with similar traits, such as age, income and lifestyle. It lets a company aim its message and products at each group.

q: Which of these is a need rather than a want for a person living in a cold climate?

options.t: A winter coat
options.why: A winter coat is a need in a cold climate, since it protects from the cold. Needs are things required to survive and stay healthy.

options.t: A new phone
options.why: A new phone is a want. It is nice to have, but a person can survive without a new one, so it is not a need.

options.t: Concert tickets
options.why: Concert tickets are a want, for entertainment. Living in the cold does not require them.

options.t: Designer shades
options.why: Designer shades are a want, a fashion item. They are not needed to stay warm or healthy in a cold climate.

q: A fictional drink brand stops advertising discounts and starts stressing its recyclable bottle and locally sourced ingredients. This change is mainly a shift in:

options.t: Distribution
options.why: Distribution is how goods reach customers. The brand's stores and delivery did not change, only how it describes itself.

options.t: Cost model
options.why: A cost model is how a business structures its costs. Messaging about bottles and ingredients does not change what the firm spends to make its product.

options.t: Credit terms
options.why: Credit terms are the rules for paying later. They are about financing, not how the brand presents itself.

options.t: Positioning
options.why: Positioning is the image a brand builds in customers' minds. Moving from discounts to sustainability shifts how the brand wants to be seen versus rivals.

q: A company's logo and slogan are mainly part of its:

options.t: Brand identity
options.why: A logo and slogan are part of a company's brand identity. They are visible elements that help customers recognize and remember the business.

options.t: Break-even test
options.why: A break-even test finds the sales level at which revenue equals costs. It is a finance tool and not part of how a brand looks or sounds.

options.t: Distribution plan
options.why: A distribution plan covers how products reach customers. A logo and slogan do not decide transport or sales channels.

options.t: Credit policy
options.why: A credit policy sets the rules for lending to customers. It has nothing to do with the look of the business.

q: Which operations term describes a product meeting set standards and customer expectations?

options.t: Capacity
options.why: Capacity is the maximum output a business can produce. It describes how much can be made, not whether the product meets standards.

options.t: Quality
options.why: Quality is how well a product meets set standards and customer expectations. Strong quality control means fewer defects, returns and complaints.

options.t: Margin
options.why: Margin is the gap between selling price and cost. It measures profitability, not whether a product meets standards.

options.t: Liability
options.why: Liability is a legal or financial obligation. It is not a measure of how well a product meets expectations.

q: A bakery bakes bread only when orders arrive, to avoid waste and storage costs. This approach is closest to:

options.t: Safety stock held in bulk
options.why: Safety stock is extra inventory held as a buffer. It increases storage and waste, which is the opposite of baking only on order.

options.t: Batch hoarding of supplies
options.why: Hoarding supplies in batches adds storage costs and the risk of spoilage. The bakery wants to avoid this by baking when orders come in.

options.t: Just-in-time production
options.why: Just-in-time production makes goods only when they are needed. Baking to order cuts waste and storage cost, which matches the bakery's approach.

options.t: Overstocking the warehouse
options.why: Overstocking the warehouse means holding too much inventory. That raises costs and waste, so it is the opposite of baking only when orders arrive.

q: Which step most directly lowers the chance of a workplace injury?

options.t: Training employees to use equipment safely
options.why: Training employees to use equipment safely teaches them correct methods and risks. Well-trained workers make fewer mistakes, so injuries become less likely.

options.t: Raising production quotas for the workers
options.why: Raising quotas pushes workers to go faster. Rushing tends to cause errors and accidents, so it raises the chance of injury.

options.t: Shortening the breaks that employees get
options.why: Shorter breaks cause tiredness. Tired workers lose focus, so this step increases the risk of injury.

options.t: Moving machines closer on the shop floor
options.why: Moving machines closer together leaves less room to work safely. A crowded shop floor can raise the chance of collisions and accidents.

q: A cafe's espresso station can serve 40 customers an hour, but 60 customers arrive each hour at the lunch peak. What is the most likely result?

options.t: Output rises to 60 and no line
options.why: The station can serve only 40 an hour, so output cannot rise to 60 without more capacity. With 60 arriving each hour, a line will form.

options.t: Wait times fall for all customers
options.why: Wait times cannot fall when more people arrive than can be served. The extra customers join a queue, so waits get longer, not shorter.

options.t: A line forms and wait times grow
options.why: When demand exceeds capacity, a line forms and waits grow. The station handles 40 an hour while 60 arrive, so 20 more people queue each hour at the peak.

options.t: Capacity rises as the crowd grows
options.why: A crowd does not raise capacity. Capacity is what the station can serve, and it stays at 40 an hour until equipment or staff increase.

q: What is a supplier?

options.t: A person who buys a finished product for personal use only
options.why: A person who buys a finished product for personal use is a consumer. A supplier is on the selling side, providing goods or services to a business.

options.t: A government agency that enforces the rules of trade now
options.why: A government agency that enforces trade rules is a regulator. It does not provide goods to a business, so it is not a supplier.

options.t: A business that sells similar products in the same market
options.why: A business selling similar products in the same market is a competitor. A supplier provides inputs instead of competing for the same customers.

options.t: A business that provides goods or services to another business
options.why: A supplier is a business that provides goods or services, such as materials, to another business. Firms depend on reliable suppliers to make or sell their own products.

q: What do we call a written set of career goals along with the steps to reach them?

options.t: Job offer
options.why: A job offer is an employer's formal proposal of a position. It is not a record of a person's own career goals and the steps to reach them.

options.t: Career plan
options.why: A career plan sets out career goals and the steps to reach them, such as education, skills and experience. Writing it down helps a person stay on track.

options.t: Expense log
options.why: An expense log records money spent. It deals with personal or business spending, not career goals.

options.t: Business plan
options.why: A business plan describes how a company will operate and make money. It is about a firm, not one person's career path.

q: Which action best builds a professional network?

options.t: Attending industry events and following up with the people you meet
options.why: Attending industry events and following up builds real relationships. The follow-up turns a brief meeting into a lasting professional contact.

options.t: Collecting as many business cards as possible at industry events
options.why: Collecting business cards alone creates no relationship. Without a follow-up, the cards are just paper and the contacts will not remember you.

options.t: Waiting for contacts to approach you at some later date or time
options.why: Waiting for others to approach you leaves networking to chance. Building a network takes taking the first step, introducing yourself and keeping in touch.

options.t: Posting only about yourself online, each and every day of the week
options.why: Posting only about yourself treats others as an audience, not as contacts. Networking is two-way, so it means engaging with and helping other people too.

q: How should a professional best respond to constructive criticism from a manager?

options.t: Avoid the manager after the review is over today
options.why: Avoiding the manager does not address the feedback. It misses a chance to improve and may suggest you are unwilling to learn.

options.t: Listen, ask questions and apply useful suggestions
options.why: Listening, asking questions and applying useful suggestions shows maturity. Constructive criticism is meant to help you grow, and using it builds trust with the manager.

options.t: Point out the mistakes of other coworkers in return
options.why: Pointing out coworkers' mistakes shifts the focus away from your own work. It comes across as defensive and unprofessional, and it does not fix your issue.

options.t: Defend every one of your decisions right away at once
options.why: Defending every decision at once shows you are not listening. Some criticism may be valid, so getting defensive blocks learning from it.

q: A student wants to show employers real evidence of design and writing skills. Which item is most effective?

options.t: A cover letter with no samples
options.why: A cover letter with no samples only claims skills. Employers want to see evidence, so words alone are weaker than examples of actual work.

options.t: A list of favorite classes
options.why: A list of favorite classes shows interests, not proof of skill. It does not demonstrate the quality of a student's design and writing.

options.t: A longer list of hobbies
options.why: A longer list of hobbies adds personal detail, but it does not show design and writing ability. It is not evidence of job-related skill.

options.t: A portfolio of work samples
options.why: A portfolio of work samples shows real examples of design and writing. Employers can judge quality directly, so it is the strongest evidence of skill.

q: Arriving on time for work shows which professional trait?

options.t: Creativity
options.why: Creativity is producing new ideas. Arriving on time is about dependability, not about inventing or thinking up something new.

options.t: Competition
options.why: Competition is trying to outdo others. Being punctual does not involve competing; it shows respect for others' time.

options.t: Reliability
options.why: Reliability means people can count on you to do what you say. Arriving on time is one clear sign of it and builds trust with managers and coworkers.

options.t: Authority
options.why: Authority is the power to give orders or make decisions. Being on time does not make you an authority; it shows responsibility.

q: Which statement describes why an organization exists and what it does?

options.t: Sales forecast
options.why: A sales forecast predicts future sales. It looks at expected revenue, not at the reason an organization exists.

options.t: Job description
options.why: A job description lists the duties of a position. It describes one role, not the purpose of the whole organization.

options.t: Mission statement
options.why: A mission statement says why an organization exists, what it does and whom it serves. It guides decisions and gives staff a shared sense of purpose.

options.t: Balance sheet report
options.why: A balance sheet report shows assets, liabilities and equity. It is a financial statement, not a statement of purpose.

q: A SWOT analysis examines which four factors?

options.t: Strengths, weaknesses, opportunities and threats
options.why: SWOT stands for strengths, weaknesses, opportunities and threats. Strengths and weaknesses are internal, while opportunities and threats are external factors.

options.t: Sales, wages, output and taxes of a business
options.why: Sales, wages, output and taxes are financial and production measures. They are not the four factors that make up a SWOT analysis.

options.t: Suppliers, workers, owners and tools of a firm
options.why: Suppliers, workers, owners and tools are groups and resources. They are not the four parts of SWOT, which are strengths, weaknesses, opportunities and threats.

options.t: Standards, wants, objectives and targets of a firm
options.why: Standards, wants, objectives and targets are planning ideas, but they do not spell SWOT. The four words in SWOT are strengths, weaknesses, opportunities and threats.

q: In a SWOT analysis, which item would be listed as a threat?

options.t: A skilled, loyal team of staff
options.why: A skilled, loyal team is a strength. It is an internal advantage, not an outside force that could hurt the business.

options.t: A new competitor opening nearby
options.why: A new competitor opening nearby is an external factor that could take customers. External negatives like this are listed as threats.

options.t: An outdated checkout system
options.why: An outdated checkout system is a weakness. It is an internal problem the business can fix, not an outside threat.

options.t: Growing demand for the item
options.why: Growing demand for an item is an opportunity. It is an external positive that the business can take advantage of.

q: Which growth strategy involves selling existing products in new markets?

options.t: Market penetration
options.why: Market penetration sells more of existing products in existing markets. It does not enter new markets, so it differs from the strategy described.

options.t: Product development
options.why: Product development creates new products for existing markets. The question describes selling existing products, so this does not match.

options.t: Diversification
options.why: Diversification means new products in new markets. It changes both product and market, whereas here the product stays the same.

options.t: Market development
options.why: Market development sells existing products in new markets, such as new regions or customer groups. The product is unchanged, but the market is new.

q: Which of the following is a measurable business goal?

options.t: Become the best company in the whole town and region
options.why: Becoming the best company in town is a vague aim. It has no number or deadline, so progress cannot be measured.

options.t: Increase online sales by 10 percent within six months
options.why: Increasing online sales by 10 percent within six months is specific, has a number and a deadline. That makes it measurable, so the business can tell whether it succeeded.

options.t: Make our customers happier with every single visit
options.why: Making customers happier is a worthwhile aim, but it has no measure or date. Without a number it is hard to know when it has been met.

options.t: Grow as much as possible, with no set target date
options.why: Growing as much as possible with no date has no target to check against. A goal with no limit or deadline cannot be measured.

q: Which type of business ownership gives its owner unlimited personal liability for the business's debts?

options.t: Sole proprietorship
options.why: A sole proprietorship has one owner who is personally responsible for all the business's debts. There is no legal separation between owner and business.

options.t: Corporation business
options.why: A corporation is a separate legal entity, so owners generally are not personally liable for its debts. That makes it the opposite of unlimited liability.

options.t: Limited liability
options.why: Limited liability limits the owner's responsibility to what they invested. It is the opposite of unlimited personal liability.

options.t: Nonprofit corporation
options.why: A nonprofit corporation is a separate legal entity. Its officers and members are generally not personally liable for its debts.

q: Ravi signs a written agreement to sell his bike to Kim for $200, and Kim pays. Which element makes this agreement a legally enforceable contract?

options.t: The buyer and seller live in the same small town
options.why: Living in the same town does not affect whether a contract is enforceable. Contracts need an offer, acceptance and consideration, not a shared location.

options.t: The agreement was signed on a weekday afternoon
options.why: The day and time a contract is signed do not matter to its validity. What counts is that the elements of a contract are present.

options.t: Each party gives something of value in the exchange
options.why: Each party giving something of value is called consideration. Ravi gives the bike and Kim gives $200, and that exchange makes the agreement enforceable.

options.t: The bike is a used item worth less than a new one
options.why: A used item can be sold under a valid contract at any price. The bike's age does not affect whether the agreement is enforceable.

q: A shop posts a sign saying 'All sales final.' Elena buys a lamp, then finds it was broken before she bought it. What law may still protect her?

options.t: A rule that buyers waive all rights when they pay cash
options.why: Paying cash does not waive a buyer's legal rights. Consumer protection laws still apply, and a broken product can be returned despite a sign.

options.t: A rule that stores must refund any purchase after 30 days
options.why: No rule requires stores to refund any purchase after 30 days. Refund rules vary and do not apply to a defect found at once.

options.t: A rule that store signs are not legally binding on shops
options.why: Store signs cannot override the law, but the rule is not that signs are never binding. Elena's protection comes from implied warranty, which exists even with a sign.

options.t: Implied warranty that the goods are fit for ordinary use
options.why: An implied warranty means goods are expected to work for their normal use. A lamp that was broken before purchase breaks that promise, whatever the sign says.

q: Which law is designed to stop businesses from fixing prices or forming monopolies?

options.t: Antitrust law
options.why: Antitrust law stops businesses from fixing prices, forming monopolies or other practices that reduce competition. It keeps markets fair for consumers and smaller firms.

options.t: Labor laws
options.why: Labor laws govern wages, hours and working conditions. They protect workers, not competition between businesses.

options.t: Copyright law
options.why: Copyright law protects original creative works. It does not deal with price fixing or monopolies.

options.t: Tax law rules
options.why: Tax rules set what individuals and businesses owe the government. They do not regulate how companies compete.

q: A bakery names its signature cookie 'Moonbite' and registers the name. Which form of intellectual property protects this name?

options.t: Copyright
options.why: Copyright protects original creative works, such as writing or art. A product name like Moonbite is protected by trademark, not copyright.

options.t: Trade secret
options.why: A trade secret is confidential information that gives a business an edge. A registered name is public, so it is not a trade secret.

options.t: Patents
options.why: Patents protect inventions. A cookie name is not an invention, so it would not be protected by a patent.

options.t: Trademark
options.why: A trademark protects names, logos and slogans that identify a business's goods. Registering Moonbite stops others from using a confusingly similar name.

q: A company's employee posts a photo that copies a freelancer's artwork without permission, and the company shares it. Which law is most likely violated?

options.t: Minimum wage law, since the freelancer was not paid hourly
options.why: Minimum wage law sets the lowest pay for workers. It is about wages and is not the law broken when art is copied without permission.

options.t: Antitrust law, because the company grew too large for its field
options.why: Antitrust law deals with monopolies and price fixing. Copying a freelancer's artwork is not about market size or competition.

options.t: Copyright law, because the artwork was used without permission
options.why: Copyright law protects an artist's original work. Using and sharing the artwork without permission is infringement, which makes the company liable.

options.t: Zoning law, because the artwork was displayed on a website
options.why: Zoning law controls how land may be used. Posting artwork on a website has nothing to do with land use.

q: What does a business license do?

options.t: Exempts the business from paying any taxes at all for good
options.why: A license does not exempt a business from taxes. Businesses still pay taxes, and a license is only permission to operate.

options.t: Gives the business government permission to operate in a location
options.why: A business license gives government permission to operate in a location. It confirms the business meets local rules and can be required to open legally.

options.t: Guarantees that the business will make a profit every year
options.why: A license does not guarantee profit. It only allows the business to operate; success depends on customers, costs and management.

options.t: Protects the business name from being used by other firms
options.why: Protecting a business name is the job of a trademark or name registration. A license is permission to operate, not name protection.

q: A supplier fails to deliver goods that a retailer ordered under a signed contract, so the retailer loses sales. What is the supplier's likely legal position?

options.t: Protected, because suppliers cannot be sued by customers
options.why: Suppliers can be sued for breaking a signed contract. A customer has legal rights when promised goods are not delivered.

options.t: Free of duty, because the delay was only a few days
options.why: A short delay does not remove the duty when delivery time was part of the contract. The retailer lost sales because of the failure to deliver.

options.t: Required only to refund the retailer's shipping costs
options.why: Refunding only shipping costs would not cover the retailer's lost sales. Damages for a breach can include the losses it caused.

options.t: In breach of contract and possibly liable for damages
options.why: Failing to deliver goods under a signed contract is a breach of contract. The supplier may have to pay damages for the retailer's lost sales.

q: What is the purpose of the Americans with Disabilities Act in the workplace?

options.t: To require reasonable accommodations and prohibit discrimination
options.why: The Americans with Disabilities Act requires reasonable accommodations and bans discrimination against people with disabilities. It helps qualified workers take part in the workplace.

options.t: To ban businesses from hiring workers under the age of 18 years
options.why: The ADA does not ban hiring workers under 18. Rules on young workers come from child labor laws, not this act.

options.t: To set minimum wages for all part-time workers in the nation
options.why: Minimum wage for part-time workers is set under other laws, such as the Fair Labor Standards Act. The ADA focuses on disability rights.

options.t: To require every firm to provide free medical care to workers
options.why: The ADA does not require employers to give free medical care. It requires reasonable accommodations, not health coverage.

q: An employer fires a worker only because she reported unsafe conditions to a safety agency. What is this called?

options.t: Downsizing, which is legal in every situation
options.why: Downsizing is cutting jobs for business reasons and can be legal. Firing someone for reporting unsafe conditions is a different, unlawful act.

options.t: Retaliation, which is illegal in many situations
options.why: Retaliation is punishing a worker for reporting a violation or using legal rights. Firing someone for contacting a safety agency is retaliation, and it is illegal in many cases.

options.t: Mediation, which employers must offer first of all
options.why: Mediation is a process where a neutral person helps settle a dispute. It is not the name for firing someone for a complaint.

options.t: Outsourcing, which is required of all employers
options.why: Outsourcing is hiring outside firms to do work. It is a business choice, not the name for punishing a worker who reported a hazard.

q: What is the main purpose of the Uniform Commercial Code?

options.t: To replace the need for written sales contracts everywhere
options.why: The UCC does not remove the need for written contracts. Some sales contracts must still be in writing under it.

options.t: To set a single national tax rate on all sales of goods anywhere
options.why: The UCC does not set tax rates. It sets rules for commercial dealings, such as the sale of goods.

options.t: To make laws for sales of goods more consistent across states
options.why: The Uniform Commercial Code makes the rules for sales of goods more consistent across states. That helps businesses trade across state lines with predictable rules.

options.t: To create the rules for hiring and firing of workers in states
options.why: Hiring and firing rules come from employment laws. The UCC covers commercial transactions, such as sales and leases of goods.

q: Under agency law, when a sales rep signs a deal within the authority the company gave, who is bound by the contract?

options.t: Only the rep, because the rep signed
options.why: The rep signed as an agent for the company, so the rep is not personally bound. Agency law makes the principal responsible for what an agent does within authority.

options.t: The customer alone, who agreed to it
options.why: The customer agreed, but the contract binds both sides. It does not bind only the customer, who also receives the company's promise.

options.t: The company, which is the principal
options.why: When an agent acts within authority, the principal, the company, is bound by the contract. The company must honor the deal the rep signed on its behalf.

options.t: Neither party, since agents cannot sign
options.why: Agents can sign for a business within their authority, and the contract is valid. It is not void just because an agent signed.

q: A customer slips on a wet floor with no warning sign and sues the store. Which legal concept is the customer relying on?

options.t: Bankruptcy, a court process for debts unpaid
options.why: Bankruptcy is a court process for people or firms who cannot pay debts. It is not a claim for injury on a wet floor.

options.t: Embezzlement, theft of funds from the firm
options.why: Embezzlement is theft of funds by someone trusted with them. It has nothing to do with a customer's injury in a store.

options.t: Arbitration, a private way to settle disputes
options.why: Arbitration is a private way to settle a dispute outside court. It is a process for resolving claims, not the basis for the claim itself.

options.t: Negligence, a failure to use reasonable care
options.why: Negligence is failing to use reasonable care, which causes harm. The store's failure to warn about a wet floor is the basis of the customer's claim.

q: Which is an example of nonverbal communication?

options.t: Making eye contact and nodding while someone talks
options.why: Eye contact and nodding send messages without words. They show attention and interest, so they are nonverbal communication.

options.t: Writing a list of tasks on a whiteboard for the team
options.why: Writing a task list is written communication. It uses words, so it is not nonverbal communication.

options.t: Sending a detailed email to a customer that day
options.why: An email uses written words, so it is written communication. Nonverbal communication relies on body language, tone and expressions.

options.t: Reading a report aloud to a team at the office
options.why: Reading a report aloud uses spoken words, so it is verbal communication. Nonverbal communication does not rely on words.

q: A manager wants to share a policy change with 200 employees at once and keep a written record. Which channel is best?

options.t: A rumor from staff
options.why: A rumor is informal, can be inaccurate and leaves no record. It is not a reliable way to share a policy change with 200 people.

options.t: A company-wide email
options.why: A company-wide email reaches all 200 employees at once and leaves a written record. It is quick, consistent and easy to refer back to.

options.t: A call to one boss
options.why: A call to one boss reaches a single person. It cannot inform 200 employees at once or leave a record for them.

options.t: A private chat with each
options.why: A private chat with each employee would take far too long for 200 people. It is not efficient, and messages might vary.

q: What is the purpose of feedback in the communication process?

options.t: To confirm the receiver understood the message
options.why: Feedback is the receiver's response that tells the sender whether the message was understood. It lets the sender clarify if something was missed, completing the loop.

options.t: To make the message longer and more detailed
options.why: Feedback is not meant to lengthen the message. It is the reply that shows how the message was received.

options.t: To ensure the message is kept secret by the sender
options.why: Feedback does not keep a message secret. It is an open response that helps both sides check understanding.

options.t: To remove the need for the sender to speak
options.why: Feedback does not remove the need for the sender to speak. It is the receiver's response to what the sender has said.

q: Which situation is an example of a communication barrier?

options.t: Asking the listener a clarifying question at the end
options.why: Asking a clarifying question helps understanding. It removes confusion, so it helps communication rather than blocking it.

options.t: Using technical jargon the listener does not understand
options.why: Technical jargon the listener does not know blocks understanding. Words the receiver cannot decode make the message unclear, so jargon is a communication barrier.

options.t: Choosing a quiet room for an important talk at work
options.why: A quiet room helps people focus. It lowers noise, so it helps communication instead of getting in the way.

options.t: Repeating the main point in a different set of words
options.why: Repeating the main point in different words can clarify the message. It supports understanding, so it is not a barrier.

q: A employee must give bad news to a customer. Which approach is most effective?

options.t: Hide the news in a long message full of side details
options.why: Hiding bad news in a long message is evasive. It can confuse or mislead the customer and damages trust.

options.t: Send the message late at night with no explanation
options.why: Sending bad news late at night with no explanation is thoughtless. The customer would be left confused and upset.

options.t: Be honest, clear and respectful, and offer next steps
options.why: Being honest, clear and respectful, and offering next steps, treats the customer fairly. It keeps trust even with bad news and gives them a way forward.

options.t: Wait until the customer asks about it directly later
options.why: Waiting until the customer asks delays the news and can make the firm look dishonest. Giving bad news promptly is more respectful.

q: During a team meeting, Dana restates a coworker's point in her own words before answering. Which listening skill is she using?

options.t: Interrupting to take over the whole talk
options.why: Interrupting to take over the talk shows no interest in the coworker's idea. Restating a point is the opposite of cutting someone off.

options.t: Avoiding the topic to keep it short
options.why: Avoiding the topic does not involve restating the coworker's point. Dana engages with it directly.

options.t: Ignoring the speaker's ideas and points
options.why: Ignoring the speaker's ideas would mean not responding to them. Dana repeats the point to show she understood it.

options.t: Paraphrasing to check her understanding
options.why: Paraphrasing means restating someone's point in your own words. It checks understanding and shows the speaker that you were listening.

q: Which type of business message is usually best for a formal job application?

options.t: A professional, well-edited cover letter and resume
options.why: A professional, well-edited cover letter and resume are expected in a formal job application. They show care, clear writing and attention to detail.

options.t: A short text message full of abbreviations and emojis
options.why: A short text full of abbreviations and emojis is too informal. It would look careless for a formal job application.

options.t: A casual social media comment on a post made online
options.why: A casual social media comment is not a proper way to apply for a job. Employers expect a formal, written application.

options.t: A voice memo with no written follow-up of any kind
options.why: A voice memo with no written follow-up leaves no document for the employer. Formal applications are normally written.

q: What is the best reason to proofread a document before sending it?

options.t: To make the document longer than it was before
options.why: Proofreading does not aim to lengthen the document. It checks for errors in spelling, grammar and facts.

options.t: To avoid answering any questions about it
options.why: Proofreading is not meant to dodge questions. It improves quality, and a document with fewer errors invites fewer questions.

options.t: To catch errors that could hurt credibility
options.why: Proofreading catches errors, such as typos or wrong figures, that could hurt your credibility. A clean document shows professionalism and care.

options.t: To make sure no one else can read the file
options.why: Proofreading does not control who can read a file. Security settings do that, while proofreading improves accuracy.

q: A presenter sees the audience looking at phones and shifting in seats. What should she do?

options.t: Stop the talk and leave the room without any notice
options.why: Leaving the room without notice is unprofessional and ends the talk. A better response is to adjust the presentation and keep the audience involved.

options.t: Ask a question or add an example to re-engage listeners
options.why: Asking a question or adding an example re-engages listeners. A change of approach pulls attention back to the talk.

options.t: Lower her voice so that fewer people can hear her
options.why: Lowering her voice makes it harder to hear, so it would lose even more of the audience. A speaker should aim to draw people in.

options.t: Speak faster and finish without changing the talk
options.why: Speaking faster and finishing without change ignores the audience's reaction. Distracted people need a change in approach, not speed.

q: What is customer service?

options.t: The price a customer pays for a product at the register in a shop
options.why: The price paid is a cost to the customer, not service. Customer service is the help a business offers around the purchase.

options.t: The advertising a business uses to attract new buyers to the shop
options.why: Advertising attracts new buyers. Customer service is help given to customers, mostly before, during and after buying.

options.t: The process of making a product in a large factory plant each year
options.why: Making a product is production. Customer service concerns how customers are helped, not how goods are made.

options.t: Assistance a business gives customers before, during and after a sale
options.why: Customer service is the help a business gives customers before, during and after a sale. It includes advice, support and fixing problems, and it builds loyalty.

q: A customer returns a toaster that stopped working after a week. Which response best builds loyalty?

options.t: Ask the customer to return after the manager gets back
options.why: Asking the customer to come back later delays the fix and is inconvenient. The customer would feel brushed off, which hurts loyalty.

options.t: Offer a coupon but refuse to replace the toaster
options.why: Offering a coupon but refusing to replace a toaster that broke within a week is unfair. It fails to solve the real problem.

options.t: Explain that the store is not responsible for goods
options.why: Saying the store is not responsible dismisses the complaint. It leaves the customer feeling ignored, so it harms loyalty.

options.t: Apologize, replace it quickly and thank the customer
options.why: Apologizing, replacing it quickly and thanking the customer fixes the problem and shows care. That turns a bad experience into a reason to return.

q: Which action most likely increases customer retention?

options.t: Raising prices after the sale so that the customers must pay more
options.why: Raising prices after a sale upsets customers and gives them reason to leave. It lowers retention.

options.t: Following up after a purchase to make sure the customer is satisfied
options.why: Following up after a purchase shows care and lets the business fix problems. Satisfied customers are more likely to buy again, which raises retention.

options.t: Reducing the number of staff on the busiest days of the week
options.why: Fewer staff on the busiest days means longer waits and worse service. That drives customers away.

options.t: Ending the returns policy for loyal customers of the shop chain
options.why: Ending the returns policy for loyal customers removes a benefit they value. It would damage trust and lower retention.

q: What is a customer loyalty program designed to do?

options.t: Replace the need for good products or service for all
options.why: A loyalty program does not replace the need for good products or service. It rewards customers, but they will not stay if quality is poor.

options.t: Reduce the number of customers who shop at the store
options.why: A loyalty program is meant to bring customers back, not reduce shoppers. It rewards them for shopping more.

options.t: Reward repeat purchases to encourage customers to return
options.why: A loyalty program rewards repeat purchases, with points, discounts or perks, to encourage customers to return. That raises retention and sales over time.
