options.t: Collect fees from customers for shopping often at stores
options.why: Loyalty programs reward customers; they do not charge fees for shopping often. Charging for loyalty would discourage repeat visits.

q: A customer is angry about a late delivery and raises their voice. What should the employee do first?

options.t: Stay calm, listen fully and acknowledge the customer's frustration
options.why: Staying calm, listening fully and acknowledging the frustration helps the customer feel heard. It reduces anger and allows the employee to solve the problem.

options.t: Explain all of the company's policies before they will listen
options.why: Reciting policies at an angry customer sounds defensive. The customer needs to be heard before they will listen to explanations.

options.t: Tell the customer to call back when they are calm and rested now
options.why: Telling the customer to call back brushes them off. It leaves the problem unsolved and the customer angrier.

options.t: Raise their own voice to match the customer's raised voice a lot
options.why: Raising your voice to match makes the conflict worse. A calm response is more likely to settle the customer.

q: Why do businesses collect customer feedback?

options.t: To find strengths and problems and improve products and service
options.why: Feedback shows what the business does well and where it falls short. Using it helps improve products and service.

options.t: To replace the need for employees in the store and shop floor
options.why: Feedback does not replace employees. It gives information that staff use to improve the business.

options.t: To prove that no changes are ever needed in the firm today
options.why: Collecting feedback shows a firm is willing to change, not that no change is needed. Feedback often points to problems to fix.

options.t: To increase the price of the product each month of the year
options.why: Feedback is not collected to raise prices. Its purpose is to learn what customers think and improve.

q: Which situation is the best example of exceeding customer expectations?

options.t: A florist refuses to correct a mistake on the order at all, ever
options.why: Refusing to fix a mistake is poor service. It falls short of expectations, so it cannot exceed them.

options.t: A florist delivers the order as promised and says nothing more
options.why: Delivering as promised meets expectations but does not go beyond them. Exceeding expectations means doing extra.

options.t: A florist fixes a wrong order and adds free flowers to apologize
options.why: Fixing a wrong order and adding free flowers does more than the customer expected. It turns a mistake into a pleasant surprise, which exceeds expectations.

options.t: A florist delivers the order late and offers no word of apology
options.why: A late delivery with no apology fails expectations. It does not exceed them, and it can lose the customer.

q: What is the value of resolving a complaint quickly?

options.t: It ensures the customer will never complain again
options.why: Quick resolution does not guarantee the customer will never complain again. It does improve the chance that they stay.

options.t: It can turn an unhappy customer into a loyal one
options.why: Resolving a complaint quickly shows care and can turn an unhappy customer into a loyal one. Customers often remember how a problem was handled.

options.t: It removes the need to track complaints from buyers
options.why: Tracking complaints stays useful even if they are solved fast. The records show patterns that the firm can fix.

options.t: It lowers the quality of future service for buyers
options.why: Fast resolution improves service quality. It does not lower it, since the customer's problem is dealt with promptly.

q: Which is an internal customer?

options.t: A supplier who delivers goods to the store each week
options.why: A supplier delivering goods to the store is an external party. An internal customer is someone inside the company.

options.t: A shopper who buys items from the store each week or month
options.why: A shopper buying items is an external customer. Internal customers are employees who depend on other staff.

options.t: A competitor who visits the store to compare prices
options.why: A competitor visiting the store is not a customer. Competitors are outside the firm and are rivals, not internal customers.

options.t: A coworker in another department who relies on your work
options.why: An internal customer is a coworker or department that relies on your work. A coworker in another department who uses your output fits this definition.

q: What is scarcity?

options.t: A tax on goods that are hard to find in shops
options.why: Scarcity is not a tax. It describes limited resources, not a charge placed on goods that are hard to find.

options.t: A surplus of goods that no buyers want to buy
options.why: A surplus is more supply than buyers want. Scarcity is the opposite situation, where resources are limited compared with wants.

options.t: Limited resources to meet unlimited wants
options.why: Scarcity is limited resources against unlimited wants. It forces people and firms to choose, which is the basis of economics.

options.t: A lack of money in a household this year
options.why: A lack of money in a household is a personal shortage. Scarcity is a broader idea about limited resources for everyone.

q: When demand for a product rises and supply stays the same, what usually happens to price?

options.t: Price falls to zero
options.why: Price would not fall to zero when demand rises. Higher demand with constant supply creates upward pressure on price.

options.t: Price stays equal
options.why: Price does not stay the same when demand rises. More buyers competing for the same supply push the price up.

options.t: The price falls
options.why: Price does not fall when demand increases. With supply unchanged, a rise in demand leads to a higher price.

options.t: The price rises
options.why: When demand rises and supply stays the same, buyers compete for the same goods. That creates a shortage at the old price, so price rises.

q: Which is an example of a fixed cost for a business?

options.t: Monthly rent for the store
options.why: Monthly rent stays the same however much the business sells. That makes it a fixed cost.

options.t: The cost of raw materials
options.why: Raw materials rise with output, so they are a variable cost. A business buys more of them when it makes more goods.

options.t: Shipping charges per order
options.why: Shipping charges per order grow with the number of orders. That makes them a variable cost.

options.t: Sales commissions earned
options.why: Sales commissions rise with sales, so they are a variable cost. They are not fixed.

q: A pizza shop raises the price of its large pizza and notices customers switching to medium pizzas. What concept does this show?

options.t: Perfect competition
options.why: Perfect competition describes a market with many sellers and identical products. It does not describe customers switching to a cheaper size.

options.t: Substitute goods
options.why: Substitute goods can replace one another. When the large pizza gets pricier, customers switch to the medium, which is a close substitute.

options.t: Diminishing return
options.why: Diminishing returns means each extra input adds less output. It is about production, not a switch between products.

options.t: Complement goods
options.why: Complement goods are used together, like pizza and a drink. Customers buying the medium instead of the large are swapping, not pairing.

q: What does gross domestic product (GDP) measure?

options.t: The total amount of money held by the government each year
options.why: The government's cash holdings are a measure of public finance. GDP counts everything a country produces, not what its government holds.

options.t: The number of people who live in the country at present
options.why: Population is a head count of residents. GDP measures output, not how many people live in the country.

options.t: The total value of goods and services produced in a country
options.why: GDP is the total value of final goods and services produced in a country in a period. It is the main measure of the size of an economy.

options.t: The average price of consumer goods in the shops of a country
options.why: The average price of goods is shown by a price index such as the CPI. GDP measures output, not price levels.

q: If a country's central bank lowers interest rates, what is the most likely effect on borrowing and spending?

options.t: Borrowing and spending tend to decrease
options.why: Lower interest rates make borrowing cheaper, so borrowing and spending tend to rise. A decrease is the opposite of what usually follows.

options.t: Borrowing and spending tend to increase
options.why: Cheaper loans encourage firms and households to borrow and spend more. This is why central banks cut rates to boost a slow economy.

options.t: Neither borrowing nor spending changes
options.why: Rates change the cost of credit, so behavior changes too. Borrowing and spending usually react to a rate cut instead of staying put.

options.t: Borrowing stops while spending doubles
options.why: Borrowing does not stop when rates fall. A cut makes loans cheaper, so borrowing normally rises, and spending does not double.

q: What is inflation?

options.t: An increase in the number of workers
options.why: More workers is about the labor force. Inflation is about prices, so a rising number of workers does not define it.

options.t: A rise in the price of one product only
options.why: A rise in the price of one product is a relative price change. Inflation is a broad rise across most goods and services.

options.t: A general decrease in prices over time
options.why: A general fall in prices is deflation, the opposite of inflation. Inflation is when the price level rises.

options.t: A general increase in prices over time
options.why: Inflation is a general rise in prices over time. Each dollar then buys less, so purchasing power falls.

q: A business operates in a market where many sellers offer nearly identical products and no seller sets the price. What market structure is this?

options.t: Perfect competition
options.why: Perfect competition has many sellers of near-identical products, and no seller can set the price. The market sets it, so each firm is a price taker.

options.t: Oligopoly market
options.why: An oligopoly has a few large sellers who influence price. The scenario has many sellers and none with price power.

options.t: Duopoly of two firms
options.why: A duopoly has just two sellers. The scenario describes many sellers, so a duopoly does not fit.

options.t: A single monopoly firm
options.why: A monopoly has one seller with price power. The scenario has many sellers and none with control, so it is the opposite.

q: What is opportunity cost?

options.t: The total price paid for an item at the store
options.why: The price paid is a money cost. Opportunity cost is the value of the next best alternative given up, whether or not money changes hands.

options.t: The cost of insurance that covers an item
options.why: Insurance cost is a money expense. Opportunity cost is about the best option forgone, not what protection costs.

options.t: The cost of an item after a sale discount
options.why: A discounted price is still the money paid. Opportunity cost measures what you give up by choosing one option over another.

options.t: The value of the next best option given up
options.why: Opportunity cost is the value of the next best option given up. Every choice has one, since time and money are limited.

q: Which describes self-awareness?

options.t: Avoiding every stressful situation that comes up at work or home
options.why: Avoiding stress is avoidance, not insight. Self-awareness means understanding your emotions rather than running from situations.

options.t: Predicting what other people will do next at work or at home
options.why: Predicting others' actions is social awareness or guesswork. Self-awareness is about knowing your own feelings and their effects.

options.t: Recognizing your own emotions and how they affect your behavior
options.why: Self-awareness is recognizing your own emotions and how they shape your behavior. It helps you respond well and choose your actions.

options.t: Hiding your feelings from all of your coworkers at the firm
options.why: Hiding feelings is suppression. Self-awareness means admitting what you feel, which is the first step to managing it.

q: A worker feels frustrated after criticism and takes a short walk before replying. Which skill is this?

options.t: Self-promotion
options.why: Self-promotion means drawing attention to your own achievements. Taking a walk to cool down has nothing to do with it.

options.t: Self-regulation
options.why: Self-regulation is controlling emotions and impulses before reacting. Walking away to calm down before replying prevents an angry response.

options.t: Competitiveness
options.why: Competitiveness is wanting to outdo others. The worker is calming down, not trying to win, so it is not the skill shown.

options.t: Procrastination
options.why: Procrastination is putting off a task without a good reason. The walk is a short, deliberate pause to manage emotion, and the worker still replies.

q: What is empathy?

options.t: Understanding and sharing another person's feelings
options.why: Empathy is understanding and sharing another person's feelings. It lets you respond with care and strengthens relationships at work.

options.t: Agreeing with every opinion that others share with you
options.why: Agreeing with every opinion is people-pleasing. You can show empathy for someone's feelings without agreeing with their views.

options.t: Giving orders to coworkers calmly each day at work
options.why: Giving orders is a leadership act. Empathy is about understanding feelings, not directing people.

options.t: Ignoring emotions to focus on tasks alone at the office
options.why: Ignoring emotions is the opposite of empathy. Empathy requires noticing and caring about how others feel.

q: Which action shows empathy toward a coworker who is overwhelmed?

options.t: Avoiding them until the busy period has ended at work
options.why: Avoiding someone who is overwhelmed leaves them alone with the problem. Empathy means showing up when a coworker needs support.

options.t: Asking how you can help and listening to their concerns
options.why: Asking how you can help and listening shows empathy. It tells the coworker you care and lets you offer help that fits their need.

options.t: Giving them more tasks to prove their strength to the boss
options.why: Piling on more tasks adds to the stress and ignores their situation. It shows no concern for how they feel.

options.t: Telling them everyone has problems and moving on quickly
options.why: Saying everyone has problems and moving on dismisses their feelings. Empathy means pausing to acknowledge and support them.

q: Two teammates disagree sharply. A third member lets each explain their view and then suggests a compromise. Which skill is the third member showing?

options.t: Conflict management using social awareness
options.why: Conflict management helps people resolve disagreement. Letting both explain and suggesting a compromise uses social awareness, noticing and respecting each person's view.

options.t: Avoidance by staying out of the conflict
options.why: Avoidance means staying out of the conflict. The third member steps in to help, so avoidance is not what is shown.

options.t: Manipulation by choosing sides in secret
options.why: Manipulation means influencing others in a sneaky way. The third member listens openly and does not take sides in secret.

options.t: Self-promotion by taking charge for credit
options.why: Self-promotion seeks credit. The third member is helping settle the dispute for the team's sake, not for personal recognition.

q: Why is emotional intelligence valuable in the workplace?

options.t: It guarantees that no conflicts happen at work at any time
options.why: EI cannot guarantee that no conflicts happen. It helps people handle them well, but disagreements still occur at work.

options.t: It replaces technical skills for any job in a firm
options.why: EI does not replace technical skills. Most jobs need both knowledge of the work and the ability to work well with people.

options.t: It removes the need for any rules at work for the staff
options.why: EI does not remove the need for rules. It helps people follow and work within them, but organizations still need guidelines.

options.t: It improves communication, teamwork and decision making
options.why: Emotional intelligence improves communication, teamwork and decision making. People who read and manage emotions well work better together.

q: Which is an example of a positive way to handle stress at work?

options.t: Blaming coworkers for every single problem
options.why: Blaming coworkers does not reduce stress. It damages trust and leaves the real problems unresolved.

options.t: Skipping meals to finish tasks faster each day
options.why: Skipping meals harms health and focus. It makes stress worse and tasks slower, not faster, in the long run.

options.t: Taking short breaks and prioritizing tasks
options.why: Short breaks restore energy, and prioritizing tasks makes the workload manageable. Both are healthy ways to cope with stress.

options.t: Ignoring all deadlines until the last day
options.why: Ignoring deadlines until the last day piles up pressure. It increases stress and the chance of mistakes or missed work.

q: What is an entrepreneur?

options.t: A person who only invests money in other firms for a profit
options.why: Someone who only invests in other firms is an investor. An entrepreneur starts and runs a business and carries its risks.

options.t: A person who starts and runs a business and takes on its risks
options.why: An entrepreneur starts and runs a business and takes on its risks in the hope of profit. They organize resources, make decisions and accept possible losses.

options.t: A person who regulates businesses for the government of a state
options.why: A person who regulates businesses is a government official. Entrepreneurs run businesses rather than oversee them.

options.t: A person who works for a fixed salary in a large firm each year
options.why: A person with a fixed salary is an employee. Entrepreneurs earn profit, which can rise or fall, and bear the risk.

q: What is the purpose of a business plan?

options.t: To describe goals and how the business will reach them
options.why: A business plan states goals and how the business will reach them. It guides decisions and helps win support from lenders and investors.

options.t: To list the daily tasks of employees only, week by week
options.why: Employee tasks are only a small piece of operations. A business plan covers markets, finances and strategy as well.

options.t: To replace the need for financial records of the firm
options.why: A business plan does not replace financial records. It includes projections, but the firm still needs actual books.

options.t: To keep the business idea secret from everyone in the town
options.why: A plan is shared with lenders, partners and staff, not hidden. Its purpose is to communicate how the business will succeed.

q: Which is a common source of start-up funding for a new small business?

options.t: Customers' credit card numbers
options.why: Customers' card numbers are private data used to pay for goods. They are not a source of money for funding a startup.

options.t: Government tax refund checks
options.why: Tax refunds go to taxpayers and are not a typical business funding source. They are small and unreliable for a startup.

options.t: Personal savings from the owner
options.why: Personal savings are a common source of start-up funding. The owner invests their own money, which avoids debt and shows commitment.

options.t: Profits from future sales of goods
options.why: Future sales do not exist yet. A new business cannot spend profits it has not earned, so it needs other funding to start.

q: Which is a risk that entrepreneurs face?

options.t: Guaranteed profit in the first month of trade for all
options.why: Profit in the first month is not guaranteed. Many new businesses lose money at first while they build a customer base.

options.t: Complete protection from competition for all firms
options.why: No business is protected from competition. Rivals can enter the market at any time, so competition is a constant risk.

options.t: Freedom from all legal duties and from paying taxes
options.why: Businesses must obey laws and pay taxes. There is no freedom from these duties for entrepreneurs.

options.t: Losing the money they invested if the business fails
options.why: Entrepreneurs can lose the money they invest if the business fails. Accepting this risk is part of starting a business.

q: Mina wants to open a cafe but is unsure customers will pay her prices. What should she do first?

options.t: Hire a large team of staff before the cafe opens its doors at all
options.why: Hiring a big team before knowing if customers will pay adds costs with no proof of demand. It puts Mina at greater financial risk.

options.t: Sign a long lease on a building before researching demand at all
options.why: Signing a long lease before researching demand locks her into high costs. If customers do not come, she is stuck paying rent.

options.t: Conduct market research and test her idea with potential customers
options.why: Market research and testing the idea with potential customers show whether people will pay her prices. It lowers risk before she spends big.

options.t: Set prices at random and simply hope for the best result of it
options.why: Setting prices at random and hoping is guesswork. Prices should rest on costs and what customers will pay.

q: What does a unique selling proposition (USP) do?

options.t: States the legal structure of the firm as a corporation
options.why: The legal structure is a separate choice, such as sole proprietorship or corporation. A USP is about what sets the business apart.

options.t: Explains how a business is different from competitors
options.why: A USP explains how a business is different from competitors and why customers should choose it. It highlights a clear advantage.

options.t: Lists all of the business's expenses for the year
options.why: Expenses are listed in financial statements. A USP concerns what makes the business stand out, not its costs.

options.t: Shows the daily schedule of employees at the shop
options.why: An employee schedule is an operations tool. A USP is a marketing idea about what makes the business special.

q: Which is an example of a franchise?

options.t: Opening a store that uses a larger company's brand and system
options.why: A franchise is a business that uses a larger company's brand and system under a license. The franchisee pays fees and follows the parent's rules.

options.t: Importing goods to sell online to buyers in other countries
options.why: Importing and selling online is a trade or retail model. It does not involve using another firm's brand and system.

options.t: Selling shares of stock to the public on an exchange market
options.why: Selling shares of stock raises money by giving up ownership. It is not a franchise arrangement.

options.t: Starting a store with a brand you own outright and run alone
options.why: A store with a brand you own outright and run alone is an independent business. A franchise relies on another company's brand and system.

q: An entrepreneur's product takes off faster than expected, and orders exceed production capacity. Which action best manages growth?

options.t: Hide the delays from buyers and promise faster shipping times
options.why: Hiding delays from buyers and promising faster shipping is dishonest. It damages trust and leads to angry customers.

options.t: Stop taking any new orders and ignore the sudden new demand
options.why: Refusing new orders ignores growth that the business has worked for. It wastes the chance to earn more.

options.t: Lower the quality of the product so that it ships out faster now
options.why: Lowering quality to ship faster hurts the brand. Customers who get a worse product may leave and not return.

options.t: Expand capacity carefully by adding staff, equipment or partners
options.why: Expanding capacity carefully, with staff, equipment or partners, lets the business meet demand without losing quality. Careful growth avoids overstretching.

q: Why is networking useful for entrepreneurs?

options.t: It replaces the need to serve customers at all in the shop
options.why: Networking does not replace serving customers. Customers are the source of income, so serving them stays essential.

options.t: It removes the need for a business plan of any kind at all
options.why: Networking does not remove the need for a business plan. A plan sets direction and is needed whatever contacts you have.

options.t: It can lead to partners, customers, advice and funding
options.why: Networking builds relationships that can lead to partners, customers, advice and funding. These contacts help a new business grow.

options.t: It guarantees that the business will succeed for years
options.why: Nothing guarantees success. Networking creates opportunities, but the business still has to deliver value.

q: Which financial statement shows a business's revenue and expenses over a period?

options.t: Income statement
options.why: An income statement shows revenue and expenses over a period, leading to profit or loss. It tells how a business performed.

options.t: Balance sheet
options.why: A balance sheet is a snapshot of assets, liabilities and equity at one date. It does not cover a period of earning and spending.

options.t: Trial balance
options.why: A trial balance lists ledger balances to check debits equal credits. It is a bookkeeping check, not a report of performance.

options.t: Cash flow report
options.why: A cash flow report tracks cash moving in and out. It is not the statement that sets out revenue, expenses and profit.

q: A shop has revenue of $80,000 and expenses of $62,000. What is its net income?

options.why: $80,000 is the revenue before expenses. Net income is what remains after subtracting expenses.
Net income equals revenue minus expenses. $80,000 minus $62,000 is $18,000.
$62,000 is the expenses. Net income subtracts them from revenue to find profit.
$142,000 adds revenue and expenses together. Net income subtracts expenses from revenue, giving $18,000.

q: What does the accounting equation state?

options.t: Assets equal revenue minus expenses for the year
options.why: Revenue minus expenses is net income. The accounting equation links assets, liabilities and equity.

options.t: Equity equals debts minus revenue each year
options.why: The accounting equation does not subtract revenue from debts. It states that assets equal liabilities plus owner's equity.

options.t: Liabilities equal assets plus equity at a date
options.why: Assets equal liabilities plus equity, not the other way round. Here liabilities have been put on the wrong side.

options.t: Assets equal liabilities plus owner's equity
options.why: The accounting equation says assets equal liabilities plus owner's equity. It shows everything the business owns is funded by debt or by the owners.

q: Which ratio compares current assets to current liabilities?

options.t: Profit margin
options.why: Profit margin compares profit with sales. It does not compare current assets with current liabilities.

options.t: Stock turnover
options.why: Stock turnover measures how quickly inventory is sold and replaced. It is about goods moving, not about short-term solvency.

options.t: Debt ratio
options.why: The debt ratio compares total debt with total assets. It looks at all debt, not just current assets and liabilities.

options.t: Current ratio
options.why: The current ratio equals current assets divided by current liabilities. It shows whether a business can pay its short-term debts.

q: A business has current assets of $90,000 and current liabilities of $60,000. What is its current ratio?

options.why: Current ratio is current assets divided by current liabilities. $90,000 divided by $60,000 is 1.5, or 1.5 to 1.
0.67 to 1 turns the formula upside down, liabilities over assets. The current ratio divides assets by liabilities, so it is 1.5.
150 to 1 is not what the numbers give. $90,000 over $60,000 equals 1.5.

options.t: 30 to 1
options.why: 30 to 1 does not follow from the figures. Dividing $90,000 by $60,000 gives 1.5 to 1.

q: What does profit margin show?

options.t: The value of inventory on hand at year end
options.why: The value of inventory is on the balance sheet. Profit margin is about profit as a share of sales.

options.t: The share of sales that becomes profit
options.why: Profit margin shows the share of sales that becomes profit. A higher margin means more profit from each dollar of sales.

options.t: How fast customers pay their bills
options.why: How fast customers pay is a measure of receivables collection. It is unrelated to profit margin.

options.t: The total amount of debt owed by it
options.why: Total debt owed appears among liabilities on the balance sheet. Profit margin is about earnings, not borrowing.

q: Net income is $12,000 on sales of $120,000. What is the profit margin?

options.why: 100% would mean all sales were profit with no costs. Net income is only a part of sales, so the margin is far lower.
90% would mean expenses were just 10% of sales. Net income of $12,000 on $120,000 is only 10%.
Profit margin equals net income divided by sales. $12,000 divided by $120,000 is 0.10, or 10%.
1% would need net income of only $1,200 on $120,000 of sales. The actual figure of $12,000 gives 10%.

q: Why do businesses prepare budgets?

options.t: To avoid paying any taxes at all in a given year
options.why: Budgets do not avoid taxes. Taxes are owed whether or not a firm budgets.

options.t: To record transactions after they have happened
options.why: Recording transactions after they happen is bookkeeping. A budget is a plan made in advance.

options.t: To prove to customers that prices are fair and low
options.why: Budgets are internal planning tools. They are not made to prove anything to customers about prices.

options.t: To plan income and spending and to control costs
options.why: A budget plans income and spending and helps control costs. Comparing results with the budget shows where to adjust.

q: A department's actual spending is $4,500 and its budget was $4,000. What is this difference called, and what does it mean?

options.t: A $0 variance because the numbers are close in value to it
options.why: Spending of $4,500 against a budget of $4,000 is not close to zero variance. A $500 gap is a real difference.

options.t: A $500 unfavorable variance because spending exceeded the budget
options.why: Spending $500 over budget is an unfavorable variance. It means the department used more than planned.

options.t: A $500 favorable variance because spending was below the plan
options.why: A favorable variance would mean spending came in below plan. Here spending was higher, so it is unfavorable.

options.t: A $4,500 profit because the budget was fully met in the end
options.why: $4,500 is the actual spending, not a profit. The budget was not met, since spending exceeded the $4,000 plan.

q: What is break-even?

options.t: The point where costs are zero for the whole year
options.why: Costs do not drop to zero at break-even. At that point revenue just covers all costs.

options.t: The point where profit is at its highest in a year
options.why: The highest profit is a different point. Break-even is where profit is exactly zero.

options.t: The point where total revenue equals total costs
options.why: Break-even is where total revenue equals total costs. Below it a business loses money, and above it a profit begins.

options.t: The point where the business has no customers
options.why: Having no customers means zero sales and a loss, not break-even. Break-even needs enough sales to cover costs.

q: What is the purpose of a job description?

options.t: To list a position's duties and requirements
options.why: A job description lists a position's duties and requirements. It helps with hiring, training and judging performance.

options.t: To show the company's yearly profit figures
options.why: Profit figures belong in financial statements. A job description is about a role, not the company's yearly results.

options.t: To record employee vacation days for the year
options.why: Vacation days are recorded in HR records. They are not the purpose of a job description.

options.t: To list the prices of the company products
options.why: Product prices go in price lists. A job description concerns what a worker does, not what the firm sells.

q: Which is an example of an employee benefit?

options.t: A fine charged for arriving late to work each day
options.why: A fine for lateness is a penalty, not a benefit. Benefits are extras that the employer gives to help workers.

options.t: The employee's regular hourly wage rate at the firm
options.why: A regular wage is the basic pay for work. Benefits are additional to wages, such as insurance or paid leave.

options.t: Paid health insurance provided by the employer
options.why: Paid health insurance is an employee benefit, provided in addition to wages. It helps workers with medical costs.

options.t: A job application fee paid by candidates to apply
options.why: Candidates do not pay to apply. A fee would be a cost, not a benefit given by the employer.

q: What is the main goal of employee training?

options.t: To replace job descriptions of workers
options.why: Training does not replace job descriptions. It teaches workers skills, while a description lists duties.

options.t: To lower the quality of work done
options.why: Training aims to raise the quality of work, not lower it. Well-trained staff do better work.

options.t: To increase the number of quitters
options.why: Training aims to keep staff, not to make them quit. Good training raises skills and morale.

options.t: To improve skills and job performance
options.why: The main goal of training is to improve skills and job performance. Trained workers are more productive and make fewer errors.

q: An employee is late three times in one month. What is the best first step for a supervisor?

options.t: Meet privately, discuss expectations and document the conversation
options.why: Meeting privately, discussing expectations and documenting is fair and professional. It gives the employee a chance to explain and creates a record.

options.t: Fire the employee at once without any warning given to him
options.why: Firing without warning is too harsh for a first step. Most firms start with a conversation and a warning.

options.t: Ignore it and hope the employee can work it out alone at home
options.why: Ignoring the issue lets it continue. Lateness three times in a month needs a response from the supervisor.

options.t: Announce the lateness to the entire staff at a team meeting
options.why: Announcing it to the whole staff embarrasses the employee. Performance matters should be handled in private.

q: A company wants to reduce turnover. Which action is most likely to help?

options.t: Raising workloads without more support
options.why: Heavier workloads without support cause burnout. That makes employees more likely to leave, not less.

options.t: Offering growth opportunities and fair pay
options.why: Growth opportunities and fair pay make employees want to stay. Turnover falls when people feel valued and see a future.

options.t: Avoiding feedback to keep things simple
options.why: Avoiding feedback leaves workers unsure how they are doing. Unclear expectations often push people to quit.

options.t: Cutting training budgets to save money now
options.why: Cutting training budgets limits growth and skills. It tends to raise turnover as people look elsewhere for development.

q: What does diversity in the workplace refer to?

options.t: Having all employees work only on the night shift
options.why: Working only the night shift is a schedule, not diversity. Diversity is about differences among people.

options.t: Having all employees do the very same task each day
options.why: Having everyone do the same task is uniformity. Diversity refers to differences among staff, not identical jobs.

options.t: Differences among staff in background and perspective
options.why: Diversity means differences among staff in background and perspective, such as culture, age, gender and experience. A mix of views can improve ideas and decisions.

options.t: Having employees who are all in one age group only
options.why: A staff all in one age group has no diversity of age. Diversity means including a range of people.

q: What is the purpose of a performance appraisal?

options.t: To decide which employees to hire for the firm
options.why: Hiring decisions are made through recruitment and selection. An appraisal looks at the work of people already employed.

options.t: To evaluate work and give feedback for improvement
options.why: A performance appraisal evaluates an employee's work and gives feedback for improvement. It helps set goals and can guide pay or promotion.

options.t: To announce each employee's pay to the whole company
options.why: Pay is not announced to everyone. An appraisal is a private review between an employee and their manager.

options.t: To list the company's products and their prices
options.why: Product lists belong in catalogs. An appraisal is about how an employee is doing.

q: What is a database?

options.t: An organized collection of data that can be searched and updated
options.why: A database is an organized collection of data that can be searched and updated. Businesses use it to store records such as customers and orders.

options.t: A type of business loan from a bank for firms and small shops
options.why: A business loan is money borrowed from a bank. It has nothing to do with storing data.

options.t: A machine used only for printing documents on paper sheets
options.why: A printing machine is a printer. A database stores and organizes data, not paper documents.

options.t: A group of employees who work with computers all day long
options.why: A group of employees who work with computers is an IT team. A database is a store of information, not a group of people.

q: Why should businesses back up important data?

options.t: To avoid ever updating the data on the computer
options.why: Backups do not stop updating. They are copies of data so that it can be recovered.

options.t: To increase the size of the original files stored
options.why: Backups do not aim to enlarge the original files. They make a separate copy for safekeeping.

options.t: To make the data harder for employees to use
options.why: Backups do not make data harder to use. They run in the background to protect it.

options.t: To restore it if the original is lost or damaged
options.why: Businesses back up data so they can restore it if the original is lost or damaged. This guards against failure, mistakes and attacks.

q: Which is a good practice for protecting customer data?

options.t: Emailing customer data to personal accounts
options.why: Emailing customer data to personal accounts moves it outside the company's control. That raises the risk of a leak.

options.t: Storing records in an unlocked public folder
options.why: An unlocked public folder lets anyone view the records. Customer data should be kept private and protected.

options.t: Sharing passwords with the whole team at work
options.why: Sharing passwords makes it impossible to tell who accessed data. It also raises the risk of misuse.

options.t: Limiting access to authorized employees only
options.why: Limiting access to authorized employees keeps customer data safe. People see only the data they need for their jobs.

q: What is data privacy?

options.t: Selling customer data to others without telling the customers
options.why: Selling customer data without telling them breaks privacy. Data privacy means protecting that information.

options.t: Posting customer data openly on a public website for all to see
options.why: Posting data on a public website exposes it to anyone. It is a breach of privacy, not protection.

options.t: Protecting personal information from misuse or unauthorized access
options.why: Data privacy is protecting personal information from misuse or unauthorized access. It respects people's rights and builds customer trust.

options.t: Keeping no records of any kind about its customers at all, ever
options.why: Privacy does not require having no records. Businesses can keep records if they protect them properly.

q: An employee receives an email from 'IT' asking for their password via a link. What should they do?

options.t: Not click and report it to the real IT department
options.why: An email from 'IT' asking for a password via a link is typically phishing. The right response is not to click and to report it to the real IT team.

options.t: Reply with the password in the email to the sender
options.why: Replying with a password gives it to an attacker. Real IT departments do not ask for passwords by email.

options.t: Click the link and enter the password quickly
options.why: Clicking the link and entering the password sends credentials to a fake site. The account can then be taken over.

options.t: Forward it to all coworkers in the office at once
options.why: Forwarding the email spreads the threat to others. It should be reported, not shared around the office.

q: What is the main purpose of a spreadsheet?

options.t: To scan business documents for computer viruses
options.why: Scanning for viruses is the job of antivirus software. A spreadsheet is for working with numbers.

options.t: To organize, calculate and analyze numerical data
options.why: A spreadsheet organizes, calculates and analyzes numerical data. It uses rows, columns and formulas to sum, sort and chart figures.

options.t: To design logos for the products of the business
options.why: Logos are made with design software. A spreadsheet is a tool for numbers.

options.t: To send marketing messages to customers by email
options.why: Marketing emails are sent with email or marketing tools. A spreadsheet is not made for sending messages.

q: Which source of data is considered primary research?

options.t: A competitor's published brochure from the show
options.why: A competitor's brochure is secondary data, gathered by someone else. Primary research is collected directly by the business.

options.t: A government report from last year on trade in goods
options.why: A government report is existing information published by others. It is secondary, not primary research.

options.t: A survey a business conducts with its own customers
options.why: A survey run with its own customers is primary research. The business collects new data directly for its own purpose.

options.t: A magazine article about the industry from last year
options.why: A magazine article is a published source made by others. That makes it secondary data.

q: What is the purpose of a management information system (MIS)?

options.t: To print employee paychecks and nothing else at all
options.why: An MIS does much more than print paychecks. It gathers and organizes information for management.

options.t: To organize information that helps managers decide
options.why: An MIS organizes information to help managers make decisions. It turns data into reports and summaries for planning and control.

options.t: To store only the addresses of customers in a file
options.why: An MIS holds many kinds of information, not only customer addresses. Its purpose is to support decision making.

options.t: To replace all of the managers in the company soon
options.why: An MIS supports managers and does not replace them. People still make the decisions.

q: What are the four Ps of the marketing mix?

options.t: People, profit, planning and output
options.why: People, profit, planning and output are not the marketing mix. The four Ps are product, price, place and promotion.

options.t: Planning, policy and performance
options.why: Planning, policy and performance are not the marketing mix. They are management words, not the four Ps.

options.t: Purchase, payment, packaging and price
options.why: Purchase, payment, packaging and price are not the four Ps. Only price is part of the marketing mix.

options.t: Product, price, place and promotion
options.why: The four Ps are product, price, place and promotion. Together they are the choices a business makes to reach customers.

q: What is market segmentation?

options.t: Dividing a market
options.why: Market segmentation is dividing a market into groups of customers with similar needs. It helps a firm target the right people.

options.t: One price for all
options.why: One price for all is a pricing approach. Segmentation instead splits customers into groups.

options.t: Selling the same way
options.why: Selling the same way to everyone is mass marketing. Segmentation tailors efforts to groups.

options.t: Merging all rivals
options.why: Merging rivals is a business combination. It is not about dividing customers into groups.

q: A sneaker company aims its new running shoe at serious athletes. What is this?

options.t: Mass production
options.why: Mass production makes large quantities of goods. Aiming a shoe at athletes is about choosing a market.

options.t: Target marketing
options.why: Target marketing means choosing a specific group of customers to aim at. Serious athletes are the group chosen for this shoe.

options.t: Price fixing
options.why: Price fixing is an illegal agreement between rivals to set prices. It has nothing to do with choosing who to sell to.

options.t: Market research
options.why: Market research gathers information about customers. The company is already acting on what it knows by aiming at athletes.

q: Which is an example of promotion?

options.t: A social media ad for a new product
options.why: A social media ad promotes a product by informing and persuading buyers. Promotion is how a business communicates with customers.

options.t: Choosing where the product will be sold
options.why: Choosing where to sell a product is place. Promotion is about communicating, not distribution.

options.t: Setting the price of the product
options.why: Setting the price is the price element. It is not a form of promotion.

options.t: Designing the product's features
options.why: Designing features is product development. Promotion tells people about the product after it is made.

q: A bakery lowers prices on day-old bread to sell it before it spoils. Which marketing mix element is being adjusted?

options.t: Place
options.why: Place is where products are sold. Lowering the price of day-old bread does not change where it is sold.

options.t: Product
options.why: Product covers the item's features and quality. The bread itself is unchanged; only its price changed.

options.t: Promotion
options.why: Promotion is advertising and publicity. The bakery changed what it charges, not how it advertises.

options.t: Price
options.why: Lowering prices to sell day-old bread adjusts the price element of the marketing mix. It clears stock before it spoils.

q: What is a brand?

options.t: The total cost of making one product in the factory plant
options.why: The cost of making a product is a production cost. A brand is how a business and its products are identified.

options.t: The list of ingredients that a product contains inside it
options.why: A list of ingredients is product information. A brand is a name, symbol or design.

options.t: A name, symbol or design that identifies a business's products
options.why: A brand is a name, symbol or design that identifies a business's products. It sets them apart from others and builds recognition.

options.t: The location where a product is sold to buyers each day of the year
options.why: Where a product is sold is its place. A brand is about identity, not location.

q: Why do companies conduct market research?

options.t: To stop customers from giving opinions about goods
options.why: Research collects customers' opinions, not stops them. It aims to learn what buyers want.

options.t: To avoid ever changing their products in the market
options.why: Companies research so they can improve and change products. Avoiding change is the opposite.

options.t: To keep prices the same forever for all of the goods
options.why: Research helps firms set suitable prices, not keep them fixed forever. Markets change.

options.t: To understand customer needs and market conditions
options.why: Market research helps a company understand customer needs and market conditions. It reduces the risk of poor decisions.

q: A company sees that most of its customers are aged 18 to 24 and use social media daily. Which promotion plan fits best?

options.t: Short video ads on social media platforms
options.why: Customers aged 18 to 24 use social media daily, so short video ads reach them where they are. The plan matches the audience.

options.t: Printed flyers mailed to older households
options.why: Flyers to older households miss the target group. They would be sent to the wrong people.

options.t: Newspaper ads in the retirement section
options.why: Retirement-section ads reach older readers, not young adults. They do not fit the audience.

options.t: Radio ads late at night in another region
options.why: Late-night radio in another region misses both the age group and the location. It would not reach the customers.

q: What is inventory?

options.t: Profit earned by the business during the year of trading
options.why: Profit is what remains after costs. Inventory is the stock of goods a business holds.

options.t: Employees who are assigned to a special project at work now
options.why: Employees on a project are staff, not inventory. Inventory is goods and materials.

options.t: Goods a business holds for sale or for use in making products
options.why: Inventory is the goods a business holds for sale or for use in making products. Managing it well avoids shortages and waste.

options.t: Money owed to a business by its credit customers at year end
options.why: Money owed by credit customers is accounts receivable. It is a different asset from inventory.

q: What is the goal of quality control?

options.t: To lower the number of products that are sold each year
options.why: Quality control does not aim to reduce sales. It aims to keep products at a good standard.

options.t: To ensure products meet standards before reaching customers
options.why: The goal of quality control is to ensure products meet standards before they reach customers. It reduces defects and complaints.

options.t: To increase the price charged for defective items to buyers
options.why: Defective items should not be sold at higher prices. Quality control tries to find and fix defects.

options.t: To avoid checking the products at all before they ship
options.why: Quality control involves checking products. Skipping checks would let faults reach customers.

q: A store orders too much inventory and much of it goes unsold. What is the main cost?

options.t: Faster delivery times to the customers of the store
options.why: Excess inventory does not speed up delivery. The problem is goods that sit unsold.

options.t: Higher customer satisfaction from more choices
options.why: Satisfaction rises when needed goods are available, but having far too many goods is a cost. Unsold stock does not please customers.

options.t: Money tied up in storage and possible markdowns
options.why: Overstocking ties up money in storage and may force markdowns. The cash cannot be used elsewhere while goods sit.

options.t: Lower storage fees due to bulk buying of the goods
options.why: Storing a lot of unsold goods raises storage costs. Buying in bulk does not lower fees when items do not sell.

q: What is a supply chain?

options.t: A list of all the employees who work for a company
options.why: A list of employees is a staff list. A supply chain is the path a product takes.

options.t: The network that moves a product to the customer
options.why: A supply chain is the network of suppliers, makers and distributors that moves a product to the customer. Each link adds value and affects cost and speed.

options.t: A set of financial statements that a company issues
options.why: Financial statements report a company's results. They are separate from the flow of goods.

options.t: A chain of retail stores that is owned by one firm
options.why: A chain of stores is a retail group. A supply chain is about moving goods from source to customer.

q: A supplier's factory shuts down, delaying a key part. What is the best way for a manufacturer to reduce this risk in the future?

options.t: Use more than one supplier for important parts
options.why: Using more than one supplier gives backup if one factory stops. It spreads risk, so one problem will not halt production.

options.t: Ignore supplier problems until they happen again
options.why: Ignoring supplier problems leaves the firm unprepared. It would suffer the same delay again.

options.t: Rely on a single supplier to save on costs
options.why: A single supplier saves effort but raises risk. If it fails, the whole production line can stop.

options.t: Stop making products that need the part now
options.why: Stopping production of items that need the part loses sales. It does not manage the risk.

q: What does just-in-time (JIT) inventory aim to do?

options.t: Order extra goods far in advance to build a stockpile each month
options.why: JIT does not stockpile in advance. Stockpiling is what it tries to avoid.

options.t: Ship the goods to customers only once each year, in bulk loads
options.why: Shipping once a year in bulk is the opposite of JIT. JIT delivers small amounts when needed.

options.t: Hold very large safety stocks at all times of the year, always
options.why: Holding large safety stocks is the opposite of JIT. JIT aims to keep inventory low.

options.t: Receive goods only as they are needed to reduce storage costs
options.why: JIT receives goods only as they are needed. It cuts storage costs and waste, but depends on reliable suppliers.

q: What is the main purpose of a safety program in a workplace?

options.t: To increase the speed of all tasks at work
options.why: Safety programs do not speed up work. Their goal is to prevent harm, even if that means careful procedures.

options.t: To prevent accidents and protect employees
options.why: A safety program aims to prevent accidents and protect employees. Fewer injuries mean fewer costs and a better workplace.

options.t: To reduce training time for new staff members
options.why: Safety programs usually add training. They do not aim to cut training time for new staff.

options.t: To replace the need for supervisors at work
options.why: Supervisors still guide safe practice. A safety program supports them and does not replace them.

q: What is a resume?

options.t: A form that people use to file their yearly taxes each spring
options.why: A tax form is filed with the tax authority. A resume is a job-seeking document.

options.t: A record of expenses that a business has paid to suppliers
options.why: A record of paid expenses is an accounting record. A resume describes a person's background.

options.t: A summary of a person's education, skills and work experience
options.why: A resume summarizes a person's education, skills and work experience. Employers use it to judge whether to interview someone.

options.t: A list of the products that the company sells in shops each year
options.why: A product list is a catalog. A resume is about a person, not a firm's products.

q: Which action shows professionalism in the workplace?

options.t: Using personal phone calls during meetings
options.why: Using personal phone calls during meetings shows a lack of focus and respect. It is unprofessional.

options.t: Gossiping about coworkers in the break room
options.why: Gossiping about coworkers harms trust. It is unprofessional.

options.t: Blaming others for your mistakes at work
options.why: Blaming others for your mistakes avoids responsibility. Professionals accept accountability.

options.t: Arriving on time and meeting commitments
options.why: Arriving on time and meeting commitments shows reliability and respect. These habits build a good reputation.

q: What is a mentor?

options.t: An experienced person who guides someone with less experience
options.why: A mentor is an experienced person who guides someone with less experience. Mentors share advice and help others grow in their careers.

options.t: A person who supervises payroll and benefit records for the staff
options.why: Someone who handles payroll and benefit records is a payroll or HR clerk. That is not a mentor.

options.t: A person who repairs the equipment in the factory plant each day
options.why: A person who repairs equipment is a technician. That is a job, not a mentoring role.

options.t: A person who orders supplies for the business each month
options.why: A person who orders supplies is a purchasing clerk. That is a job role, not a mentor.

q: What is the best way to prepare for a job interview?

options.t: Wait to see which questions come up on the day of the talk
options.why: Waiting to see the questions leaves you unprepared. Preparation improves confidence and answers.

options.t: Skip learning about the job requirements and the company
options.why: Skipping research on the job and company shows low interest. Employers expect candidates to know the basics.

options.t: Memorize one single answer for every question that is asked
options.why: One memorized answer cannot fit every question. Interviews need answers suited to each question.

options.t: Research the company and practice answers to common questions
options.why: Researching the company and practicing common questions prepares you well. You can give clear, relevant answers with confidence.

q: After an interview, which action is most appropriate?

options.t: Send a short thank-you note to the interviewer
options.why: A short thank-you note shows appreciation and interest. It leaves a good final impression.

options.t: Post details of the interview online for friends
options.why: Posting interview details online can break confidentiality. It looks unprofessional to the employer.

options.t: Say nothing and wait for the employer to call
options.why: Saying nothing misses a chance to follow up. A note keeps you in mind with the employer.

options.t: Call the interviewer each day for a week or so
options.why: Calling daily is pushy and annoying. It can hurt your chances.

q: What is a career goal?

options.t: A list of the tasks that are done each day at the firm
options.why: Daily tasks are part of a job. A career goal is a target for your future.

options.t: A specific target for one's future position or accomplishment
options.why: A career goal is a specific target for a future position or accomplishment. It gives direction and helps you plan steps to get there.

options.t: A record of your past jobs and nothing more than that, kept
options.why: Past jobs are listed on a resume. A career goal looks ahead, not back.

options.t: A salary amount that the employer sets for the new hire
options.why: A salary is pay set by an employer. A career goal is something you choose for yourself.

q: Why is lifelong learning important for career success?

options.t: Learning stops being useful once a person turns 30
options.why: Learning continues to matter at any age. Skills can help people advance or switch careers at any point.

options.t: Skills never change at all after graduation
options.why: Skills do change after graduation as technology and methods change. Staying current is needed.

options.t: Skills and industries change, so keep learning
options.why: Skills and industries change, so continuing to learn keeps you employable. It helps you adapt and grow in your career.

options.t: Employers do not place any value on new skills
options.why: Employers do value new skills. Workers who keep learning are more useful.

q: What is a mission statement?

options.t: A forecast of the company's sales for the next year or two
options.why: A forecast predicts sales. A mission statement says why an organization exists.

options.t: A list of the duties that employees perform at work each day
options.why: Duties belong in job descriptions. A mission statement covers the whole organization.

options.t: A statement of an organization's purpose and what it does
options.why: A mission statement states an organization's purpose and what it does. It guides decisions and shows customers and staff what it stands for.

options.t: A record of the profits earned in the past years of trade
options.why: Profits earned appear in financial reports. A mission statement is about purpose.

q: What does SWOT analysis examine?

options.t: Sales, wages, orders and taxes of the firm each year
options.why: Sales, wages, orders and taxes are business figures. SWOT stands for something different.

options.t: Strengths, weaknesses, opportunities and threats
options.why: SWOT stands for strengths, weaknesses, opportunities and threats. The analysis helps a business plan by looking inside and outside.

options.t: Stocks, wealth, output and trade of the nation
options.why: Stocks, wealth, output and trade of the nation are economic terms. They are not what SWOT examines.

options.t: Suppliers, workers, owners and traders of firms
options.why: Suppliers, workers, owners and traders are groups. SWOT does not examine groups of people.

q: Which is an external factor in a SWOT analysis?

options.t: A new competitor entering the market
options.why: A new competitor entering the market comes from outside the business. External factors like this are threats or opportunities.

options.t: A skilled and loyal staff of workers
options.why: A skilled and loyal staff is a strength inside the business. It is an internal factor.

options.t: Outdated equipment in the factory plant
options.why: Outdated equipment is a weakness inside the business. It is internal, not external.

options.t: A strong brand reputation in the market
options.why: A strong brand reputation is a strength the business owns. It is internal.

q: What is a competitive advantage?

options.t: A decrease in the company's prices only for a short while
options.why: A short-term price cut can be copied by rivals. It is not a lasting advantage.

options.t: A law that stops other firms from operating in the market
options.why: A law that blocks rival firms is a legal barrier. A competitive advantage comes from a firm's own strengths.

options.t: A rule requiring customers to buy from the firm each year
options.why: A rule requiring customers to buy from one firm would be unfair and illegal. A competitive advantage is earned.

options.t: A strength that lets a business outperform its rivals
options.why: A competitive advantage is a strength that lets a business outperform its rivals. It could be quality, cost, service or brand.

q: A small coffee shop cannot match a chain's low prices but offers locally roasted beans and friendly service. What strategy is it using?

options.t: Differentiation based on quality and service
options.why: Differentiation means standing out through qualities such as quality and service. Locally roasted beans and friendly service set the shop apart from the chain.

options.t: Leaving the market for good and closing
options.why: Leaving the market is giving up. The shop is competing by offering something different.

options.t: Cost leadership based on the lowest prices
options.why: Cost leadership means having the lowest prices. The shop admits it cannot match the chain on price, so it is not using this strategy.

options.t: Imitation of the chain's methods and menu
options.why: Imitation copies a rival's methods. The shop is offering something different instead.

q: Why do businesses set measurable goals?

options.t: To prevent employees from knowing what the targets are
options.why: Goals are shared so employees know what to aim for. Hiding targets would hurt performance.

options.t: To keep goals vague and flexible at all times of the year
options.why: Vague goals are hard to judge. Measurable goals give clear targets.

options.t: To avoid reporting results to the owners of the firm
options.why: Reporting results is part of accountability. Measurable goals make it possible.

options.t: To track progress and know when targets are achieved
options.why: Measurable goals let a business track progress and know when targets are achieved. They keep the team focused and show what needs adjusting.

q: A company's sales fall for three quarters while a competitor's rise. What is the best strategic response?

options.t: Cut all of the advertising budget immediately and at once now
options.why: Cutting all advertising would likely cut sales further. It does not address the cause.

options.t: Analyze causes and adjust products, prices or marketing accordingly
options.why: Analyzing the causes and adjusting products, prices or marketing responds to the problem with facts. It aims to win back sales.

options.t: Ignore the trend and simply wait for sales to recover on their own
options.why: Ignoring a falling trend risks more losses. Sales rarely recover without action.

options.t: Copy the competitor's logo and name exactly as they are shown
options.why: Copying a competitor's logo and name is illegal and unethical. It would not fix the real problem.

q: A landlord agrees by handshake to rent a shop to a baker for two years. Why might the baker want the agreement in writing?

options.t: A written lease removes the baker's duty to pay the rent due
options.why: A written lease does not remove the duty to pay rent. It sets out what each party must do.

options.t: Oral leases are always illegal in every state of the country
options.why: Oral leases are not always illegal. Many are valid, but some must be in writing and they are hard to prove.

options.t: A written lease is easier to prove and enforce if a dispute arises
options.why: A written lease is easier to prove and enforce if a dispute arises. It records the terms, such as rent and length.

options.t: A written lease lowers the monthly rent automatically each year
options.why: A written lease does not automatically lower rent. It records the rent that was agreed.

q: What is a warranty?

options.t: A tax that a seller collects on each sale that it makes in a year
options.why: A tax collected on sales is a sales tax. A warranty is a promise about a product.

options.t: A fee that is paid to the court to start a case in the county
options.why: A fee paid to start a case is a court filing fee. It is not a warranty.

options.t: A promise by a seller about the quality or performance of a product
options.why: A warranty is a promise by a seller about a product's quality or performance. If the product fails, the buyer may be entitled to a repair or refund.

options.t: A list of rules about the names of firms in a state, set each year
options.why: Rules about business names are naming laws. A warranty is a seller's promise.

q: Two owners of a landscaping business disagree and one wants to leave. Which document should have set rules for this situation?

options.t: A partnership agreement
options.why: A partnership agreement sets out how owners share profits, make decisions and handle a departure. It helps settle disputes when someone wants to leave.

options.t: A resume of the owners
options.why: A resume describes a person's work history. It does not set rules between owners.

options.t: A warranty for the firm
options.why: A warranty is a promise about a product. It does not cover how owners handle a split.

options.t: A sales receipt kept
options.why: A sales receipt is a record of one purchase. It does not set rules for the owners.

q: What is the legal term for a person who borrows money and must repay it?

options.t: Heir
options.why: An heir is a person who inherits property. It does not describe someone who borrows money.

options.t: Debtor
options.why: A debtor is a person who borrows money and must repay it. The lender is the creditor.

options.t: Plaintiff
options.why: A plaintiff is a person who brings a lawsuit. It is not the term for a borrower.

options.t: Creditor
options.why: A creditor is the one who lends money and is owed repayment. That is the opposite of a borrower.

q: A new hire signs a nondisclosure agreement. What does this protect?

options.t: The employee's right to a raise in pay each year
options.why: A raise is a pay matter. A nondisclosure agreement concerns secrecy.

options.t: The customer's right to a refund of the price paid
options.why: A customer's refund right comes from consumer law. An NDA does not cover it.

options.t: The company's right to avoid taxes on its sales
options.why: An NDA does not help avoid taxes. It deals with confidentiality, not tax.

options.t: Confidential business information from being shared
options.why: A nondisclosure agreement protects confidential business information from being shared. The employee agrees not to reveal secrets such as plans or customer lists.

q: Which is the best reason to use clear and simple language in business writing?

options.t: It reduces the need for any reply at all
options.why: Clear language does not cut replies. It helps readers understand and respond.

options.t: It makes the document look longer on the page
options.why: Length is not a goal. Clear, simple writing is easier and quicker to read.

options.t: It hides the real purpose of the note sent
options.why: A clear message makes the purpose obvious. It does not hide it.

options.t: Readers understand the message and can act
options.why: Clear and simple language helps readers understand the message and act on it. Confusing writing causes mistakes and delays.

q: A salesperson asks a customer open-ended questions during a pitch. What is the main benefit?

options.t: The pitch becomes much shorter with fewer questions to ask
options.why: Open-ended questions do not shorten a pitch. They invite longer answers.

options.t: The customer shares more detail about needs and preferences
options.why: Open-ended questions invite the customer to explain in their own words. The salesperson learns about needs and preferences and can tailor the pitch.

options.t: The customer can only answer yes or no to each question
options.why: Yes or no answers come from closed questions. Open-ended questions allow fuller answers.

options.t: The customer is prevented from speaking during the pitch
options.why: Open-ended questions bring the customer into the talk. They do not stop the customer from speaking.

q: An email to a client contains a pricing error that was sent to 50 people. What is the best action?

options.t: Wait to see if any of the recipients notice the error first
options.why: Waiting for someone to notice lets a mistake spread. The customer could be misled.

options.t: Delete your sent folder and say nothing to anyone at all
options.why: Deleting records and staying silent is dishonest. It hides the mistake instead of fixing it.

options.t: Send a prompt correction that clearly states the right price
options.why: Sending a prompt correction that clearly states the right price fixes the error and keeps trust. It shows honesty and care.

options.t: Blame the client for misreading the original email sent
options.why: Blaming the client is unfair and unprofessional. The error was the sender's.

q: What does 'tone' mean in written communication?

options.t: The writer's attitude as shown through word choice
options.why: Tone is the writer's attitude shown through word choice and style. It can sound friendly, formal or rude, and affects how the reader reacts.

options.t: The type of font that is used in the message each time
options.why: Font is a design choice. Tone is about attitude.

options.t: The volume of a speaker's voice in a large room
options.why: Volume belongs to spoken speech. Written tone is shown through words.

options.t: The length of the message in words on the page
options.why: Length is how long a message is. It is not what tone means.

q: Which of these best fits a formal business letter?

options.t: Slang, emojis and abbreviations throughout the letter
options.why: Slang, emojis and abbreviations are too casual for a formal letter. They would look unprofessional.

options.t: A proper greeting, clear body and a courteous closing
options.why: A formal business letter has a proper greeting, a clear body and a courteous closing. This structure shows respect and makes the message easy to follow.

options.t: A single run-on sentence without any punctuation
options.why: A run-on sentence without punctuation is hard to read. It is not suitable for a formal letter.

options.t: Only a subject line with no content at all in it
options.why: A subject line alone has no content. A letter needs a message.

q: A customer asks for a product that the store does not carry. What is the best response?

options.t: Say that the store never sells anything like it at any time
options.why: Saying the store never sells anything like it is rude and may be untrue. It ends the conversation without helping.

options.t: Ask the customer to stop asking for unusual items at the counter
options.why: Telling customers to stop asking is dismissive. Their requests show what they want.

options.t: Walk away to help someone else without giving an answer
options.why: Walking away leaves the customer without help. It shows poor service.

options.t: Offer a close alternative or offer to special-order the item
options.why: Offering a close alternative or a special order helps the customer. It keeps the sale and builds loyalty.

q: What does it mean to personalize service?

options.t: Tailoring interactions to a customer's needs and preferences
options.why: Personalizing service means tailoring interactions to a customer's needs and preferences. It makes customers feel valued.

options.t: Using the same script with every customer on each and every call
options.why: Using the same script for all customers is the opposite of personalizing. It ignores the person.

options.t: Giving every single customer identical offers each week
options.why: Identical offers for everyone are impersonal. Personalizing means matching what each customer wants.

options.t: Refusing to remember any of the returning customers at all
options.why: Refusing to remember returning customers ignores them. Personalizing uses what you know about them.

q: A hotel guest says the room is not clean. After the staff re-cleans it, what should a manager do next?

options.t: Assume the problem is solved and avoid the guest
options.why: Assuming it is solved and avoiding the guest does not confirm the issue. The guest may still be unhappy.

options.t: Argue that the room was already clean when you left
options.why: Arguing blames the guest. It damages the relationship.

options.t: Confirm the issue is fixed and thank the guest
options.why: Confirming that the issue is fixed and thanking the guest shows care. It completes the recovery and keeps goodwill.

options.t: Charge the guest an extra cleaning fee for the room
options.why: Charging an extra fee for a problem the hotel caused is unfair. It would anger the guest.

q: Why is word-of-mouth marketing valuable?

options.t: Customers trust recommendations from people they know
options.why: Word of mouth is valuable because customers trust recommendations from people they know. Friends and family are more credible than ads.

options.t: It cannot be changed by the quality of the service
options.why: Word of mouth depends on service quality. Great service gets good reviews and poor service gets bad ones.

options.t: It works only through paid ads in the news and press
options.why: Word of mouth is not paid advertising. It spreads between customers freely.

options.t: It costs more than any other kind of advertising does
options.why: Word of mouth costs little or nothing. It is often cheaper than other advertising.

q: What is customer lifetime value?

options.t: The number of years that a customer has lived in a town
options.why: The years someone has lived in a town have nothing to do with the value of a customer. It is a profit measure.

options.t: The price paid for one single purchase at a shop
options.why: One purchase price is a single sale. Lifetime value looks at all purchases over time.

options.t: The cost of acquiring one new customer at a time
options.why: Acquisition cost is what it costs to win a customer. Lifetime value is the profit expected from them.

options.t: The total profit expected from a customer over time
options.why: Customer lifetime value is the total profit expected from a customer over time. It helps firms decide how much to spend to win and keep customers.

q: What does the law of supply state?

options.t: Producers offer less of a product at higher prices
options.why: The law of supply says producers offer more at higher prices, not less. Higher prices make selling more profitable.

options.t: Prices never change when supply changes in a market
options.why: Prices do change when supply changes. The law links price and quantity supplied.

options.t: Producers offer more of a product at higher prices
options.why: The law of supply states that producers offer more of a product at higher prices. A higher price makes producing more worthwhile.

options.t: Buyers purchase more when prices rise in the market
options.why: Buyers buying more when prices rise is not the law of demand. Demand usually falls as prices rise.

q: Which factor would shift a product's demand curve to the right?

options.t: A fall in the price of the product itself in the market
options.why: A fall in the product's own price moves along the demand curve. It does not shift the curve.

options.t: An increase in consumers' income for a normal good
options.why: An increase in consumers' income raises demand for a normal good. It shifts the demand curve to the right.

options.t: A decrease in the number of buyers in the market
options.why: Fewer buyers lowers demand. It shifts the curve to the left.

options.t: A rise in the cost of raw materials for makers
options.why: Higher costs of raw materials affect supply. They do not shift the demand curve.

q: A bad harvest reduces the supply of coffee beans. What is the most likely effect on the price and quantity of coffee beans sold?

options.t: The price rises and the quantity sold rises
options.why: A bad harvest cuts supply, so the price rises. Quantity sold would fall, not rise.

options.t: The price falls and the quantity sold rises
options.why: Falling price and rising quantity would follow a rise in supply. A bad harvest causes the opposite.

options.t: The price rises and the quantity sold falls
options.why: When supply falls, the price rises and the quantity sold falls. Less coffee is available, and buyers pay more.

options.t: Neither price nor quantity changes at all
options.why: Supply shocks change the market. Price and quantity change after a bad harvest.

q: What is a monopoly?
