options.t: A market with many sellers of the same product in a city
options.why: Many sellers of the same product describe perfect competition. A monopoly has one seller.

options.t: A market with a single seller and no close substitutes
options.why: A monopoly is a market with a single seller and no close substitutes. The seller has power over price.

options.t: A market with two equal sellers of the same good only
options.why: Two equal sellers form a duopoly. A monopoly has just one.

options.t: A market where only the buyers set the price of goods
options.why: In a monopoly, the seller has the power to set price. Buyers do not set it.

q: Which statement describes a recession?

options.t: A time when all prices fall to zero in the whole market now
options.why: Prices do not fall to zero in a recession. A recession is a decline in economic activity.

options.t: A one-day fall in a stock price on an exchange market now
options.why: A one-day fall in a stock price is a market move. A recession lasts months.

options.t: A period of rapid economic growth and low unemployment now
options.why: Rapid growth and low unemployment describe an expansion. It is the opposite of a recession.

options.t: A period of declining economic activity lasting several months
options.why: A recession is a period of declining economic activity lasting several months. Output, jobs and spending fall.

q: A business sees demand for its product is elastic. If it raises its price by 10%, what will probably happen to total revenue?

options.t: Total revenue falls because quantity drops by a bigger percentage
options.why: When demand is elastic, a price rise causes a larger percentage fall in quantity. Total revenue falls because the drop in sales outweighs the higher price.

options.t: Total revenue doubles automatically in the market for it too
options.why: Revenue does not double. A price rise on elastic demand lowers quantity sold more than it raises price.

options.t: Total revenue rises because each customer pays more per unit
options.why: Revenue rises on a price rise only when demand is inelastic. With elastic demand, customers cut back sharply.

options.t: Total revenue stays exactly the same as it was before it rose
options.why: Revenue changes after a price rise. With elastic demand it falls.

q: A teammate is upset after a project setback. Which response shows social awareness?

options.t: Joking about the setback in front of the team at lunch
options.why: Joking about a setback in front of the team hurts the person. It shows no awareness of their feelings.

options.t: Telling them to stop being sensitive about the setback
options.why: Telling them to stop being sensitive dismisses their feelings. Social awareness means noticing others' emotions.

options.t: Noticing their mood and asking if they want to talk
options.why: Noticing their mood and asking if they want to talk shows social awareness. It reads their feelings and offers support.

options.t: Pretending nothing is wrong at the meeting with them
options.why: Pretending nothing is wrong ignores their feelings. Social awareness picks up on others' moods.

q: What is self-motivation?

options.t: Working only when a reward is guaranteed ahead of time, always
options.why: Working only for a guaranteed reward depends on outside incentives. Self-motivation comes from within.

options.t: Avoiding challenging tasks at work whenever it is possible to
options.why: Avoiding challenging tasks shows low drive. Self-motivated people take on challenges.

options.t: Waiting for a supervisor to give each instruction before work
options.why: Waiting for instructions shows dependence. Self-motivation means acting on your own.

options.t: The inner drive to pursue goals without constant outside pressure
options.why: Self-motivation is the inner drive to pursue goals without constant outside pressure. It keeps people working through setbacks.

q: A manager receives harsh feedback and feels defensive. Which response shows strong emotional intelligence?

options.t: Complaining about the person who gave the feedback to coworkers
options.why: Complaining about the person to coworkers spreads negativity. It does not use the feedback.

options.t: Pausing, asking clarifying questions and looking for useful points
options.why: Pausing, asking clarifying questions and looking for useful points shows emotional intelligence. It manages the defensive reaction and learns from feedback.

options.t: Immediately arguing back with the person who gave the feedback
options.why: Arguing back immediately lets emotion lead. It damages the relationship.

options.t: Ignoring the feedback and carrying on as before, with no change
options.why: Ignoring the feedback misses a chance to improve. Strong emotional intelligence uses feedback.

q: Why does active listening build trust?

options.t: It shows the speaker that their views are valued
options.why: Active listening shows the speaker that their views are valued. People trust those who pay attention and respect what they say.

options.t: It lets the listener control the whole conversation
options.why: Active listening does not control the conversation. It gives the speaker room to talk.

options.t: It prevents the speaker from sharing details
options.why: Active listening encourages the speaker to share. It does not prevent details.

options.t: It replaces the need to respond to the speaker
options.why: Active listening does not replace responding. A good listener also replies thoughtfully.

q: Which is a sign of low emotional intelligence?

options.t: Admitting your own mistakes openly to all of the others
options.why: Admitting your own mistakes openly shows self-awareness and accountability, which are signs of high emotional intelligence. It is a healthy habit, not a weakness.

options.t: Listening closely to other people's concerns at work
options.why: Listening closely to other people's concerns shows empathy and social awareness. Those are signs of high emotional intelligence, not low.

options.t: Reacting angrily without thinking when plans change
options.why: Reacting angrily without thinking shows poor self-regulation. When plans change, low emotional intelligence leads to outbursts that harm relationships and judgment.

options.t: Staying calm and steady under pressure at the firm
options.why: Staying calm and steady under pressure is a sign of strong self-regulation. It helps people think clearly and keeps teams stable, so it is high emotional intelligence.

q: What is a prototype?

options.t: An early sample of a product used for testing ideas
options.why: A prototype is an early sample of a product used for testing ideas. It lets an entrepreneur find flaws and gather feedback before paying for full production.

options.t: A permanent store location for the business to sell from
options.why: A permanent store location is a place of business. A prototype is a test model of a product, not a place where goods are sold.

options.t: A final report that is sent to investors of the firm
options.why: A final report to investors is a document. A prototype is a physical or working model, and it comes before a final product.

options.t: A legal document that proves ownership of the firm
options.why: Proof of ownership is shown by legal papers. A prototype is a test version of a product, not a legal record.

q: What is crowdfunding?

options.t: Receiving a tax refund from the government each spring, always
options.why: A tax refund is money returned by the government. It is not raised from many supporters to fund a new project.

options.t: Borrowing one large sum from a single bank on a fixed term
options.why: Borrowing one large sum from a single bank is a bank loan. Crowdfunding gathers small amounts from many people instead.

options.t: Selling the whole business to a single buyer in the town
options.why: Selling the whole business is an exit. Crowdfunding raises money while the founder keeps running the project.

options.t: Raising small amounts of money from many people, often online
options.why: Crowdfunding raises small amounts of money from many people, usually through an online platform. Backers may get rewards, products or a share in the business.

q: An entrepreneur has limited cash and wants to test a new product line with little risk. Which approach fits best?

options.t: Skip testing and rely on a hunch about what buyers want
options.why: Skipping testing and relying on a hunch invites costly mistakes. With limited cash, the entrepreneur needs evidence that customers want the product.

options.t: Launch a small pilot batch and gather customer feedback
options.why: A small pilot batch lets the entrepreneur test demand and collect feedback with little money at risk. They can adjust before spending more.

options.t: Borrow heavily to open several new stores in the region
options.why: Borrowing heavily to open several stores is very risky with limited cash. If the product fails, the debts remain.

options.t: Produce a very large inventory before testing demand at all
options.why: Making a very large inventory before testing demand ties up money in goods that may not sell. It is the opposite of a low-risk test.

q: What is a target market?

options.t: The competitors that the business faces in its market
options.why: Competitors are rival businesses. A target market is the group of customers a business tries to serve.

options.t: The specific group of customers a business aims to serve
options.why: A target market is the specific group of customers a business aims to serve. Knowing it helps choose products, prices and advertising.

options.t: The employees who work for the company in its offices
options.why: Employees are staff who work for the company. They are not the customers the business is trying to reach.

options.t: Every single person in the world who might buy from the firm
options.why: Trying to reach every person in the world is not a target market. A target market is a defined group, since no product suits everyone.

q: What does an entrepreneur's 'risk tolerance' describe?

options.t: How many employees they are able to supervise
options.why: The number of employees a person can supervise is their span of control. Risk tolerance is about how much uncertainty and loss a person will accept.

options.t: How many customers the business has served
options.why: The number of customers served is a measure of sales success. Risk tolerance describes an attitude to risk, not performance.

options.t: How much profit the business made last year
options.why: Last year's profit is a result. Risk tolerance describes how willing the entrepreneur is to face uncertainty.

options.t: How much uncertainty and loss they will accept
options.why: Risk tolerance describes how much uncertainty and possible loss an entrepreneur will accept. It shapes choices such as borrowing, investing and trying new ideas.

q: Which statement shows a company's assets, liabilities and equity at a point in time?

options.t: Cash flow report
options.why: A cash flow report tracks money moving in and out over a period. It does not show assets, liabilities and equity on one date.

options.t: Budget plan
options.why: A budget plan forecasts income and spending. It is a plan, not a report of what a company owns and owes.

options.t: Balance sheet
options.why: A balance sheet shows assets, liabilities and equity at a point in time. It is a snapshot of the firm's financial position.

options.t: Income report
options.why: An income report covers revenue and expenses over a period. It does not show what the company owns and owes at one moment.

q: A company has total assets of $150,000 and total liabilities of $90,000. What is the owner's equity?

options.why: Owner's equity equals assets minus liabilities. $150,000 minus $90,000 is $60,000, which is the owners' share of the business.
$240,000 adds assets and liabilities together. Equity subtracts liabilities from assets, so it must be smaller than assets.
$150,000 is the total assets. Equity is what remains after paying the $90,000 of liabilities.
$90,000 is the liabilities. Equity is assets minus liabilities, which is $60,000.

q: What is gross profit?

options.t: Total assets minus all the liabilities
options.why: Assets minus liabilities gives owner's equity, which is found on the balance sheet. Gross profit is a measure of sales performance.

options.t: Cash on hand at the end of each month
options.why: Cash on hand is a balance sheet figure. Gross profit is calculated from sales and the cost of goods sold.

options.t: Sales revenue minus the cost of goods sold
options.why: Gross profit is sales revenue minus the cost of goods sold. It shows how much is left from sales to pay operating costs.

options.t: Sales revenue minus all expenses and taxes
options.why: Revenue minus all expenses and taxes is net income. Gross profit subtracts only the direct cost of goods sold.

q: A shop sells goods for $50,000 that cost $30,000 to buy. Operating expenses are $12,000. What is net income before taxes?

options.why: Net income before taxes is sales minus the cost of goods and operating expenses. $50,000 less $30,000 less $12,000 is $8,000.
$20,000 is the gross profit, sales less cost of goods. Operating expenses of $12,000 must still be subtracted to reach $8,000.
$32,000 does not follow from the figures. Net income before taxes is $50,000 minus $30,000 minus $12,000, or $8,000.
$92,000 adds all the numbers together. Income is found by subtracting costs from sales, which gives $8,000.

q: What is liquidity?

options.t: How much profit a business earns after costs
options.why: Profit after costs is net income. Liquidity is about how quickly assets can become cash.

options.t: How easily an asset can be turned into cash
options.why: Liquidity is how easily an asset can be turned into cash. Cash is the most liquid asset, while property is much harder to sell fast.

options.t: How much debt a business owes to lenders
options.why: Debt owed to lenders is a liability. It does not measure how easily assets turn into cash.

options.t: How long a business has existed up to now
options.why: How long a business has existed is its age. It has no bearing on liquidity.

q: What is the main purpose of an employee handbook?

options.t: To track the daily sales of the business to the owner
options.why: Daily sales tracking is done through sales reports. An employee handbook is for staff, not owners.

options.t: To list each of the customer's recent purchases
options.why: Customer purchases belong in sales or customer records. They are unrelated to a staff guide.

options.t: To set the price of the company's stock on the exchange
options.why: The price of stock is set by the market. A handbook does not decide it.

options.t: To explain company policies, rules and expectations
options.why: An employee handbook explains company policies, rules and expectations. It tells staff about conduct, benefits and procedures in one place.

q: What is onboarding?

options.t: The process of ending an employee's contract with the firm now
options.why: Ending a contract is called termination. Onboarding is the opposite, welcoming and training a new hire.

options.t: The process of helping new employees learn the job and the company
options.why: Onboarding helps new employees learn the job and the company. Good onboarding helps them settle in faster and stay longer.

options.t: The process of paying overtime to employees each and every week
options.why: Paying overtime is part of payroll. Onboarding is about training new employees.

options.t: The process of advertising an open job position online for hire
options.why: Advertising an open position is recruitment. Onboarding comes after the person is hired.

q: A manager notices one employee consistently outperforms peers. What is an appropriate response?

options.t: Ignore the performance to avoid jealousy among the other peers
options.why: Ignoring strong performance can discourage the employee. Managers should recognize good work, not hide it.

options.t: Give the employee more work with no recognition or pay talk
options.why: Giving more work with no recognition or pay discussion feels unfair. It could cause the employee to leave.

options.t: Recognize the work and discuss development or promotion options
options.why: Recognizing the work and discussing development or promotion rewards effort. It keeps the employee motivated and builds loyalty.

options.t: Reduce the employee's pay to match that of the other peers
options.why: Cutting pay to match peers punishes good work. It would likely cause the employee to resign.

q: What is the difference between a wage and a salary?

options.t: A wage is pay per hour worked; a salary is a fixed amount per year
options.why: A wage is paid per hour worked, while a salary is a fixed amount per year. Wage earners are often paid for the exact hours they work.

options.t: A wage is a fixed amount per year; a salary is pay per hour
options.why: This reverses the two terms. A wage is hourly, and a salary is fixed per year.

options.t: Wages are tips given by customers; salaries are bonuses paid
options.why: Tips and bonuses are extra forms of pay. Wages and salaries are the base pay for work.

options.t: There is no difference between the two terms at all, in any way
options.why: The terms differ in how pay is calculated. Wages depend on hours and salaries are fixed.

q: Why do companies conduct exit interviews?

options.t: To reduce the paychecks of staff who are leaving
options.why: Exit interviews do not cut pay. They gather feedback from people who are leaving.

options.t: To convince employees to quit sooner than planned
options.why: Companies do not hold exit interviews to push staff out. The employee has already decided to go.

options.t: To hire the same employee back at once for a role
options.why: Rehiring someone is not the goal. The interview aims to learn from the experience.

options.t: To learn why employees leave and how to improve
options.why: Exit interviews help companies learn why employees leave and how to improve. The answers can reveal problems with pay, management or culture.

q: What is a password manager used for?

options.t: Storing and generating strong, unique passwords securely
options.why: A password manager stores and generates strong, unique passwords securely. It lets people use a different strong password for each account without memorizing them.

options.t: Deleting old accounts automatically each month with no notice
options.why: It does not delete accounts automatically. Its job is to hold passwords, not to remove accounts.

options.t: Replacing the need for any other kind of security at work
options.why: It does not replace other security. Firms still need protections such as firewalls and updates.

options.t: Sharing passwords with all coworkers openly at the office
options.why: Sharing passwords openly weakens security. A password manager protects them, and sharing should be limited and controlled.

q: What does 'encryption' do to data?

options.t: Makes it larger so that it is easier to find later
options.why: Encryption does not make data bigger so it is easier to find. It changes the data into a coded form.

options.t: Copies it to a public site for anyone to download
options.why: Copying data to a public site would expose it. Encryption protects it.

options.t: Deletes it permanently from the disk of the computer
options.why: Deleting data permanently is erasure. Encryption keeps the data but makes it unreadable without a key.

options.t: Scrambles it so only authorized people can read it
options.why: Encryption scrambles data so only authorized people with the key can read it. Even if it is stolen, it stays unreadable.

q: A company stores customer records on a laptop that is stolen. Which control would have best limited harm?

options.t: A faster internet link
options.why: A faster internet link would not protect stored records. The data would still be readable if the laptop was stolen.

options.t: Full-disk encryption
options.why: Full-disk encryption scrambles everything stored on the laptop. A thief cannot read the customer records without the key, so harm is limited.

options.t: A longer warranty plan
options.why: A longer warranty covers repairs. It does nothing to protect the data on a stolen laptop.

options.t: A brightly colored bag
options.why: A bag may be eye-catching, but it does not protect data. Encryption is the control that matters.

q: Which is an example of qualitative data?

options.t: The total revenue for the quarter in dollars
options.why: Revenue in dollars is numerical data, so it is quantitative. Qualitative data describes opinions or qualities.

options.t: The number of units sold last month by each rep
options.why: Units sold is a count, so it is quantitative. Qualitative data is descriptive.

options.t: Customer comments about why they like a product
options.why: Customer comments about why they like a product are descriptive and based on opinion. That makes them qualitative data.

options.t: The average price of items sold in the store
options.why: An average price is a number, so it is quantitative. Qualitative data is not measured in numbers.

q: What is the main benefit of cloud storage for a small business?

options.t: Internet access is no longer needed for any task
options.why: Cloud storage depends on the internet. Access needs a connection, so it does not remove the need for it.

options.t: All backups of the files become unnecessary
options.why: Backups are still important. Cloud services can fail, so firms still need copies.

options.t: Files can never be lost or hacked in any way
options.why: Cloud files can be lost or hacked. No service guarantees against loss or attack.

options.t: Access to files on many devices without servers
options.why: Cloud storage lets a small business reach its files from many devices without owning servers. That saves money and gives flexibility.

q: What is branding used to do?

options.t: Create a recognizable identity that sets a business apart
options.why: Branding creates a recognizable identity that sets a business apart. A strong brand helps customers remember and trust the business.

options.t: Increase the number of competitors in the market over time
options.why: Branding does not increase competitors. It helps a business stand out from them.

options.t: Lower the cost of the raw materials that it buys each year
options.why: Branding does not lower material costs. It shapes how customers see the firm.

options.t: Remove the need for any advertising at all in a year
options.why: Branding supports advertising and does not replace it. Firms still need to promote their products.

q: Which pricing strategy sets a low price to attract customers quickly in a new market?

options.t: Price skimming strategy
options.why: Price skimming starts high and lowers over time. It is the opposite of a low price used to enter a market quickly.

options.t: Penetration pricing
options.why: Penetration pricing sets a low price to attract customers fast in a new market. The low price wins market share, and the firm may raise it later.

options.t: Prestige pricing
options.why: Prestige pricing sets a high price to suggest quality. It does not aim to attract customers with low prices.

options.t: Cost-plus pricing
options.why: Cost-plus pricing adds a markup to costs. It is not designed to win a new market quickly.

q: Which pricing strategy sets a high initial price on a new product and lowers it over time?

options.t: Loss leader
options.why: A loss leader is a product sold below cost to bring in customers. It is not a high starting price that falls over time.

options.t: Bundle pricing
options.why: Bundle pricing sells items together at one price. It does not start high and drop later.

options.t: Price skimming
options.why: Price skimming sets a high price at first and lowers it over time. It earns more from early buyers before bringing in price-conscious customers.

options.t: Penetration
options.why: Penetration pricing starts low to win a market. It is the opposite of skimming.

q: A supermarket sells milk below cost to draw shoppers, hoping they buy other items. What is this pricing tactic?

options.t: Price skimming strategy
options.why: Price skimming starts high on a new product. Selling milk below cost to draw shoppers is the opposite.

options.t: Loss leader pricing
options.why: Loss leader pricing sells a product below cost to bring shoppers in. The store hopes they buy other items at normal prices.

options.t: Cost-plus pricing
options.why: Cost-plus pricing adds a markup to cost. A below-cost price does not follow that method.

options.t: Prestige pricing
options.why: Prestige pricing sets a high price to signal quality. Selling below cost is not a prestige approach.

q: What is a distribution channel?

options.t: A group of employees who work together in an office each day
options.why: A group of employees working together is a team. A distribution channel is the route products take.

options.t: A law that sets rules about product prices for the firm
options.why: A law on pricing is a regulation. A distribution channel is about moving goods.

options.t: The path a product takes from producer to final customer
options.why: A distribution channel is the path a product takes from the producer to the final customer. It may include wholesalers and retailers.

options.t: A television network that is used for advertising each week
options.why: A TV network is an advertising medium. A distribution channel moves products, not messages.

q: What is the purpose of a purchase order?

options.t: To bill a customer for goods that were received on time
options.why: Billing a customer is the role of an invoice. A purchase order is a buyer's request to a supplier.

options.t: To pay an employee for the hours worked in a week
options.why: Paying an employee is done through payroll. A purchase order is for buying goods or services.

options.t: To record the goods that have arrived at the dock
options.why: Recording goods that have arrived is the job of a receiving report. A purchase order is made before they arrive.

options.t: To formally request goods or services from a supplier
options.why: A purchase order formally requests goods or services from a supplier. It sets out quantities, prices and delivery terms.

q: A shipment arrives with 90 units but the invoice charges for 100. What should the buyer do before paying?

options.t: Resolve the difference and pay for what arrived
options.why: Resolving the difference before paying prevents overpaying. The buyer should pay for the 90 units that arrived and ask for a corrected invoice.

options.t: Pay the full invoice amount without checking it
options.why: Paying the full invoice means paying for 10 units that never arrived. It wastes money.

options.t: Refuse to ever do business with the supplier again
options.why: Refusing to deal with the supplier again is an overreaction. A one-time error can be fixed by talking to them.

options.t: Throw away the invoice and forget about it at once
options.why: Throwing away the invoice leaves the account unresolved. The supplier could chase payment later.

q: Why is preventive maintenance of equipment useful?

options.t: It guarantees equipment will never be replaced
options.why: Preventive maintenance does not stop replacement forever. All equipment wears out eventually.

options.t: It reduces breakdowns and unplanned downtime
options.why: Preventive maintenance reduces breakdowns and unplanned downtime. Regular servicing finds small faults before they become costly failures.

options.t: It removes the need for equipment operators
options.why: Operators are still needed. Maintenance keeps equipment working but does not replace people.

options.t: It increases accidents on the shop floor
options.why: Maintenance reduces accidents because equipment is in better condition. It does not increase them.

q: What is production capacity?

options.t: The maximum amount a business can produce in a period
options.why: Production capacity is the maximum amount a business can produce in a period. It sets the limit on how much it can sell without expanding.

options.t: The number of customers served in a day at the shop
options.why: Customers served per day measure demand or traffic. Capacity is about output.

options.t: The minimum price of a product on the shelf in a store
options.why: A minimum price is a pricing idea. Capacity is about the largest output.

options.t: The profit earned per unit sold by the firm in a year
options.why: Profit per unit is a measure of earnings. Capacity is about quantity produced.

q: Which is an example of a soft skill?

options.t: Forklift use
options.why: Forklift use is a hard skill, a technical ability learned through training. Soft skills are interpersonal.

options.t: Software use
options.why: Software use is a hard skill that can be taught and measured. Soft skills are personal qualities.

options.t: Writing code
options.why: Writing code is a technical, hard skill. It differs from interpersonal soft skills.

options.t: Teamwork
options.why: Teamwork is a soft skill, an interpersonal ability. It is useful in almost any job.

q: What is networking in a professional context?

options.t: Selling products to complete strangers only, for a fee
options.why: Selling to strangers only is a sales approach. Professional networking is about building relationships.

options.t: Working alone without any contact with other people
options.why: Working alone with no contact is the opposite of networking. Networking needs people to connect.

options.t: Building relationships that offer advice and chances
options.why: Professional networking means building relationships that offer advice and chances. Contacts can share job leads, mentoring and support.

options.t: Connecting the computers together in an office building
options.why: Connecting computers is a technical meaning of networking. In a professional context it means connecting with people.

q: A teen applying for a first job has no work history. What can they include on a resume to show value?

options.t: School activities, volunteering and relevant skills
options.why: School activities, volunteering and relevant skills show value to employers. They show responsibility and ability, even without work history.

options.t: Nothing at all, so the page is left blank for them
options.why: A blank page gives employers nothing. A first-time job seeker should list school and volunteer work.

options.t: A list of every game that you have ever played at home
options.why: A list of games is not relevant to a job. It does not show useful skills.

options.t: Invented job titles and made-up skills of a worker
options.why: Invented job titles are dishonest. Employers may check, and lying can cost the person the job.

q: What is the purpose of a cover letter?

options.t: To request a loan from a local lender or a bank for a firm
options.why: A loan request goes to a lender. A cover letter is part of a job application.

options.t: To introduce yourself and explain why you fit the job
options.why: A cover letter introduces you and explains why you fit the job. It shows interest and highlights skills, adding context to your resume.

options.t: To list every job that you have ever held in the past
options.why: Listing every job is what a resume does. A cover letter is a short, targeted introduction.

options.t: To report your income taxes to the government each spring
options.why: Income taxes are reported on tax forms. A cover letter is for a job application.

q: What is a vision statement?

options.t: A description of the current products and prices of a firm
options.why: A description of current products and prices is a product overview. A vision statement looks ahead.

options.t: A record of last year's sales figures for the firm to see
options.why: Last year's sales figures are results. A vision statement describes the future.

options.t: A list of employee benefits and perks given at work to staff
options.why: Employee benefits are part of compensation. A vision statement is not a list of perks.

options.t: A statement of what an organization hopes to become in the future
options.why: A vision statement describes what an organization hopes to become in the future. It inspires staff and gives long-term direction.

q: What is the difference between strategic and operational planning?

options.t: Strategic planning handles daily tasks for each shift; operational planning sets long-term goals
options.why: This reverses the two terms. Strategic planning sets long-term goals, and operational planning handles daily work.

options.t: Strategic planning ignores goals; operational planning sets goals for the firm now
options.why: Strategic planning does not ignore goals. It sets the long-term direction for the firm.

options.t: Strategic planning sets long-term direction; operational planning handles daily activities
options.why: Strategic planning sets long-term direction. Operational planning covers the daily activities that carry out those plans.

options.t: There is no real difference between the two forms of planning in a business at all
options.why: There is a real difference in time horizon and scope. Strategy is long-term, operations are short-term.

q: A firm chooses to enter a new country, adding new products and a new sales team. Which strategic decision is this?

options.t: A cost-cutting layoff of staff
options.why: A cost-cutting layoff reduces staff. Entering a new country with new products adds to the business, so it is growth.

options.t: A shutdown of operations
options.why: A shutdown stops operations. The firm is starting in a new country, which is the opposite of closing.

options.t: Expansion into a new market
options.why: Expansion into a new market means selling to new customers, here in another country. It is a growth decision.

options.t: A routine inventory count
options.why: An inventory count is a routine check of stock. Entering a new country is a major strategic move.

q: What is benchmarking?

options.t: Counting the benches that are in an office building
options.why: Counting benches is not a business practice. Benchmarking compares performance with others.

options.t: Setting the lowest goals that are possible to meet
options.why: Setting the lowest goals does not help improvement. Benchmarking looks at the best.

options.t: Ignoring what rivals' results show each year to us
options.why: Ignoring rivals is the opposite of benchmarking. It studies other firms' results.

options.t: Comparing performance with others' best practices
options.why: Benchmarking compares performance with others' best practices. It shows where a business can improve by learning from leaders.

q: What is a core competency?

options.t: A unique strength that gives a business an edge
options.why: A core competency is a unique strength that gives a business an edge. It is something the firm does especially well that is hard to copy.

options.t: A rule imposed by the government on firms
options.why: A government rule is a regulation. A core competency is the firm's own strength.

options.t: A cost shared among all the firms in a trade
options.why: A shared industry cost is not a competency. It is something the firm pays.

options.t: A weakness the business hopes to hide from rivals
options.why: A weakness is the opposite of a core competency. A core competency is a strength to show off.

q: What is a contract?

options.t: A report of a company's earnings for the year ahead of it
options.why: A report of future earnings is a forecast. A contract is an agreement.

options.t: A legally enforceable agreement between two or more parties
options.why: A contract is a legally enforceable agreement between two or more parties. If one side breaks it, the other can seek a remedy in court.

options.t: A list of rules posted on the wall of a business shop
options.why: A list of posted rules is a notice. It is not an agreement that binds parties.

options.t: A casual promise between friends with no legal weight
options.why: A casual promise between friends is usually not meant to have legal weight. Contracts are enforceable by law.

q: What is consideration in a contract?

options.t: Something of value that each party gives to the other
options.why: Consideration is something of value that each party gives in a contract. It can be money, goods, services or a promise to act.

options.t: A polite gesture shown by one side to the other side
options.why: Politeness is not consideration. Consideration is an exchange of value.

options.t: The time a party spends thinking about the deal first
options.why: Thinking time is not consideration. Consideration is what each side gives or promises.

options.t: The fee paid to a court to register the contract
options.why: A court fee is not consideration. Consideration is value exchanged between the parties.

q: Which person generally cannot be held to most contracts?

options.t: A manager
options.why: A manager is an adult employee who can be bound by contracts. Age is not an obstacle.

options.t: A minor
options.why: A minor generally lacks full contractual capacity, so can usually cancel most contracts. This protects young people from unfair deals.

options.t: A customer
options.why: A customer who is an adult can be bound by a contract. Being a customer does not give a way out.

options.t: An adult
options.why: An adult has full capacity to make contracts. Adults can generally be held to them.

q: What is a breach of contract?

options.t: Asking a lawyer to review the agreement before signing
options.why: Asking a lawyer to review an agreement is wise. It is not a breach.

options.t: Negotiating the terms with the other side before signing
options.why: Negotiating terms before signing is normal. It is part of forming a contract, not breaking one.

options.t: Carrying out every duty on the agreed date as promised
options.why: Doing every duty on time is the opposite of a breach. It is full performance of the contract.

options.t: Failing to carry out a duty required by the agreement
options.why: A breach of contract is a failure to carry out a duty required by the agreement. The other party may seek damages or other remedies.

q: A vendor agrees to deliver 500 chairs by June 1 but delivers 300 on June 15. What is this?

options.t: A tax law violation
options.why: Tax law violation concerns unpaid taxes. The vendor failed to deliver what was promised, which is a contract issue.

options.t: A valid change to terms
options.why: A valid change to terms needs both sides to agree. The vendor simply delivered less and late.

options.t: A breach of contract
options.why: Delivering 300 chairs on June 15 instead of 500 by June 1 breaks the contract terms. That is a breach of contract.

options.t: A trademark dispute
options.why: A trademark dispute concerns brand names. The problem here is about delivery, not names.

q: What is the main purpose of the Uniform Commercial Code (UCC)?

options.t: To set the tax rate on every sale of goods in the state
options.why: The UCC does not set sales tax. Tax rates are set by governments.

options.t: To control the hiring and firing of workers in all states
options.why: The UCC does not control hiring and firing. It is about commercial deals such as sales of goods.

options.t: To make laws for sales of goods more consistent among states
options.why: The UCC makes the laws for sales of goods more consistent among states. That helps businesses trade across state lines.

options.t: To replace the need for written contracts of sale at all
options.why: The UCC does not remove the need for written contracts. In some cases sales contracts must be written.

q: What is negligence?

options.t: Deliberately harming another person for personal gain
options.why: Deliberately harming someone for gain is an intentional wrong. Negligence is a failure of care, not intent.

options.t: Declining to sign a contract of sale at all, ever
options.why: Declining to sign a contract is a free choice. It is not negligence.

options.t: Following every safety rule perfectly at work each day
options.why: Following every safety rule perfectly is the opposite of negligence. It is careful behavior.

options.t: Failing to use reasonable care, causing harm to another
options.why: Negligence is failing to use reasonable care, causing harm to another. The person need not have meant to hurt anyone.

q: A store ignores a spill for an hour and a customer slips and is hurt. Which legal concept applies?

options.t: Antitrust law
options.why: Antitrust law is about competition and monopolies. A slip on a spill is not a market issue.

options.t: Negligence
options.why: Negligence means failing to take reasonable care. Ignoring a spill for an hour is a clear failure that led to injury.

options.t: Copyright law
options.why: Copyright law protects creative works. A spill and an injury have nothing to do with it.

options.t: Price fixing
options.why: Price fixing is an agreement between rivals on prices. It does not relate to a customer slipping.

q: What is a patent?

options.t: Exclusive rights to an invention for a set time
options.why: A patent gives exclusive rights to an invention for a set time. It stops others from making or selling the invention without permission.

options.t: Exclusive rights to a brand name or a logo
options.why: Rights to a brand name or logo belong to a trademark. A patent protects inventions.

options.t: Exclusive rights to a book or a song for a set time
options.why: Rights to a book or song belong to copyright. A patent covers new inventions.

options.t: Permission to run a business in the state or county
options.why: Permission to run a business is a license. A patent protects an invention.

q: What is a copyright?

options.t: Legal protection for brand names and logos
options.why: Protection for brand names and logos is a trademark. Copyright protects creative works.

options.t: Legal protection for inventions made by firms
options.why: Protection for inventions is a patent. Copyright covers creative expression.

options.t: Legal protection for company trade secrets
options.why: Trade secrets are protected by confidentiality law. Copyright covers creative works.

options.t: Legal protection for original creative works
options.why: Copyright protects original creative works such as books, music and art. It starts when the work is created and fixed.

q: A band writes an original song. Which protection applies automatically to the song?

options.t: Trademark
options.why: A trademark protects brand names and logos. It does not cover a song that has been written.

options.t: Copyright
options.why: Copyright protects original creative works automatically, as soon as they are written down or recorded. A new song is covered from the moment it is created.

options.t: Trade permit
options.why: A trade permit is not a form of protection. It is not a protection for a song.

options.t: Patent right
options.why: Patent rights protect inventions. A song is a creative work, so copyright applies.

q: What is limited liability?

options.t: Owners are not personally responsible for business debts beyond their investment
options.why: Limited liability means owners are not personally responsible for business debts beyond what they invested. Their personal assets are generally safe.

options.t: Owners are exempt from all taxes on any business income they make from it
options.why: Limited liability does not exempt owners from taxes. Income is still taxed.

options.t: Owners are fully responsible for all business debts, including those of other partners
options.why: This describes unlimited liability, as in a general partnership. Limited liability is the opposite.

options.t: Owners cannot lose any of their own money at all if the business should fail
options.why: Owners can still lose what they invested. Limited liability caps the loss at their investment.

q: Which business form gives the owner unlimited personal liability?

options.t: A corporation firm
options.why: A corporation is a separate legal entity, so owners are not personally liable. It does not give unlimited liability.

options.t: A nonprofit corporation
options.why: A nonprofit corporation is a separate entity with limited liability. It does not make the owner personally liable.

options.t: A sole proprietorship
options.why: A sole proprietorship is not separate from its owner. The owner is personally responsible for all debts.

options.t: A limited liability firm
options.why: A limited liability company protects its owners from the firm's debts. Unlimited liability is the opposite.

q: What is an at-will employment relationship?

options.t: Either side may end the job at any time for any lawful reason
options.why: At-will employment means either side may end the job at any time for any lawful reason. Both the employer and employee are free to leave.

options.t: Employers must provide a reason for every firing they make
options.why: Employers do not have to give a reason in at-will employment. They may end the job for any lawful reason.

options.t: Employees can be fired only after a written warning and a hearing
options.why: A written warning and hearing are not required in at-will employment. Those are protections found in some contracts.

options.t: Employees must give a year's notice before leaving a job
options.why: Employees do not need to give a year's notice. At-will employees can quit at any time.

q: What does the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA) require of employers?

options.t: Hiring only workers with disabilities and refusing the rest
options.why: The ADA does not require hiring only workers with disabilities. It bans discrimination and requires fair access.

options.t: Closing any offices that lack ramps to the door of the firm
options.why: The ADA does not require offices to close for lacking ramps. It requires reasonable accommodations.

options.t: Paying every worker with a disability twice the normal wage
options.why: The ADA does not require employers to pay workers with disabilities extra. It requires equal treatment.

options.t: Reasonable accommodations for qualified workers with disabilities
options.why: The ADA requires reasonable accommodations for qualified workers with disabilities. Examples include accessible workspaces or adjusted schedules.

q: What is antitrust law designed to do?

options.t: Require large firms to merge with each other
options.why: Antitrust law does not force firms to merge. It aims to keep competition alive.

options.t: Promote competition and prevent unfair monopolies
options.why: Antitrust law promotes competition and prevents unfair monopolies. It aims to protect consumers and smaller businesses.

options.t: Set prices for all goods and services sold by firms
options.why: Antitrust law does not set prices. Markets decide most prices.

options.t: Protect monopolies from competitors so firms keep share
options.why: Antitrust law does the opposite of protecting monopolies. It limits them.

q: Two rival gas stations secretly agree to charge the same high price. Which law is most likely broken?

options.t: Minimum wage law covering hourly pay
options.why: Minimum wage law covers hourly pay. Price agreements between rivals fall under antitrust law.

options.t: Truth in lending law on loan terms
options.why: Truth in lending law covers loan terms. It does not address price agreements between competitors.

options.t: Antitrust law against price fixing
options.why: Antitrust law bans price fixing, where rivals secretly agree on prices. Customers are harmed because competition is removed.

options.t: Child labor law on young workers
options.why: Child labor law limits work by young people. It has nothing to do with price agreements.

q: What is a communication barrier?

options.t: A tool that makes messages clearer to the receiver in time
options.why: A tool that makes messages clearer helps communication. A barrier blocks it.

options.t: A rule that requires all messages to be kept short
options.why: A rule to keep messages short is not a barrier. It may even help clarity.

options.t: A meeting held weekly by the staff at the main office
options.why: A weekly meeting is a way to communicate. It is not a barrier.

options.t: Something that blocks a message from being understood
options.why: A communication barrier is something that blocks a message from being understood. Examples are noise, jargon, language differences and distractions.

q: What is feedback in communication?

options.t: The first words a sender says to the receiver at the start of a talk
options.why: The first words a sender says are the opening. Feedback comes from the receiver.

options.t: The channel used to send a message, such as a letter or a phone call
options.why: The channel is the medium used to send a message. Feedback is the response.

options.t: The receiver's response that shows how the message was understood
options.why: Feedback is the receiver's response that shows how the message was understood. It lets the sender confirm or fix their message.

options.t: A written copy of the message that is kept in the files of the sender
options.why: A written copy kept by the sender is a record. Feedback comes back from the receiver.

q: What is active listening?

options.t: Interrupting to share your own view of things with the others
options.why: Interrupting to share your own view is not listening. Active listening focuses on the speaker.

options.t: Fully focusing on the speaker and responding thoughtfully
options.why: Active listening means fully focusing on the speaker and responding thoughtfully. It shows respect and helps you understand.

options.t: Waiting for your turn to talk to the other people there
options.why: Waiting for your turn to speak means you are not listening. Active listening engages with what is said.

options.t: Looking at your phone while someone talks to you in a meeting
options.why: Looking at your phone shows no attention. It is the opposite of active listening.

q: A customer explains a problem and the employee restates it to confirm understanding. Which skill is this?

options.t: Paraphrasing as part of active listening
options.why: Paraphrasing is restating what you heard to confirm understanding. It is a core part of active listening and shows the customer they were heard.

options.t: Changing the subject right away at once
options.why: Changing the subject ignores the problem. It does not show listening.

options.t: Ignoring the customer and citing policy
options.why: Ignoring the customer and citing policy dismisses their concern. It is not listening.

options.t: Interrupting to take control of the call
options.why: Interrupting takes over the call. It does not confirm understanding.

q: What is nonverbal communication?

options.t: Messages sent through email and text only to others at work
options.why: Email and text are written messages. Nonverbal communication does not use words.

options.t: Messages sent in spoken words only, with no gestures or tone
options.why: Spoken words are verbal communication. Nonverbal communication uses gestures, tone and expression.

options.t: Messages sent through body language, tone and facial expression
options.why: Nonverbal communication is a message sent through body language, tone and facial expression. It often shows feelings that words do not.

options.t: Messages sent only in writing on a page or a screen at work
options.why: Writing is written communication. Nonverbal communication works without words.

q: A speaker says she is excited but looks at the floor with crossed arms. What message does the audience likely receive?

options.t: Strong enthusiasm shown by her own words and acts to others
options.why: Her words show enthusiasm, but her body does not. The audience will notice the mismatch.

options.t: No message at all that the audience can pick up on from her
options.why: The audience will pick up on her body language. People always read nonverbal cues.

options.t: A clear, consistent message because the words and the look agree
options.why: Her words and body language do not agree. The message is not clear or consistent.

options.t: Mixed signals because body language clashes with the words
options.why: Words that say excited but a look at the floor with crossed arms send mixed signals. Audiences tend to believe body language over words.

q: Which channel is best for sharing a policy change with 200 employees at once?

options.t: A private talk with each single person
options.why: A private talk with each person would take far too long for 200 people. It is also not consistent.

options.t: A company-wide email or announcement
options.why: A company-wide email or announcement reaches everyone at once. It is fast, consistent and can be recorded.

options.t: A single phone call to one supervisor
options.why: A call to one supervisor reaches only one person. It does not inform 200 staff.

options.t: A rumor passed between coworkers
options.why: A rumor can be wrong. It is not a reliable way to share a policy change.

q: What is the purpose of an agenda?

options.t: To list the topics to be covered in a meeting
options.why: An agenda lists the topics to be covered in a meeting. It keeps the meeting focused and on time.

options.t: To announce the company's profits for the year
options.why: Company profits are in financial reports. An agenda is about the meeting.

options.t: To record what happened in a past meeting
options.why: Recording a past meeting is the job of minutes. An agenda looks ahead.

options.t: To list every attendee's job title and pay
options.why: Job titles and pay are HR information. An agenda does not list them.

q: What are meeting minutes?

options.t: A summary of customer surveys from the year just ended
options.why: Customer surveys are summarized in survey reports. Meeting minutes record a meeting.

options.t: The length of time a meeting lasts in hours or minutes
options.why: The time a meeting lasts is its duration. Minutes are a written record.

options.t: A list of topics for a future meeting of the group in a week
options.why: A list of future topics is an agenda. Minutes record what has already happened.

options.t: The official written record of what happened in a meeting
options.why: Meeting minutes are the official written record of what happened in a meeting. They note decisions and who is to act.

q: Why should business writing be concise?

options.t: It prevents readers from replying to it
options.why: Concise writing does not stop replies. It makes messages easy to answer.

options.t: Longer messages are always more polite
options.why: Longer messages are not always more polite. They can waste the reader's time.

options.t: Readers can understand the message quickly
options.why: Concise writing helps readers understand the message quickly. They can act on it without wading through extra words.

options.t: Short messages always hide the real meaning
options.why: Short messages do not hide meaning. Being brief means cutting needless words.

q: Which email subject line is best?

options.t: Meeting moved to Thursday at 2 p.m.
options.why: A good subject line says what the email is about. 'Meeting moved to Thursday at 2 p.m.' is specific and tells the reader what to expect.

options.t: Hello there, a quick note for you
options.why: A vague subject like 'Hello there' does not say what the email is about. It may be skipped.

options.t: Please read this immediately or else
options.why: A threatening subject sounds rude. It creates stress.

options.t: Important!!! Read this right now please
options.why: Many exclamation marks look unprofessional. Subject lines should be clear and calm.

q: What is the best way to deliver bad news to a customer?

options.t: Send it late at night without explanation
options.why: Sending bad news late at night with no explanation is thoughtless. It leaves the customer confused.

options.t: Be honest, respectful and offer next steps
options.why: Being honest, respectful and offering next steps shows care. It helps keep the customer's trust.

options.t: Wait until the customer asks about it first
options.why: Waiting for the customer to ask delays the news. Customers prefer prompt, direct information.

options.t: Hide it inside a long message of details
options.why: Hiding news in a long message is evasive. It can mislead.

q: What is jargon?

options.t: A formal business letter sent to a client by a firm
options.why: A formal business letter is a document type. Jargon is a type of language.

options.t: A clear explanation written in plain words for beginners
options.why: A clear explanation in plain words is the opposite of jargon. Jargon uses specialized words.

options.t: Specialized words that outsiders may not understand
options.why: Jargon is specialized words that outsiders may not understand. It can confuse customers and clients.

options.t: A greeting used at the start of a call to a firm
options.why: A greeting at the start of a call is a courtesy. It is not jargon.

q: A technician uses technical terms with a customer who looks confused. What should the technician do?

options.t: Ignore the confusion and move on
options.why: Ignoring the confusion leaves the customer lost. The technician should help them understand.

options.t: Explain again in plain language
options.why: Explaining again in plain language helps the customer understand. It fixes the barrier created by technical terms.

options.t: End the conversation immediately
options.why: Ending the conversation leaves the problem unsolved. It would hurt customer relations.

options.t: Use even more technical words
options.why: More technical words would increase the confusion. The technician should simplify.

q: What is persuasion?

options.t: Influencing others to accept an idea or take action
options.why: Persuasion is influencing others to accept an idea or take action. It uses reasons and evidence, not force.

options.t: Ignoring others' opinions on the subject at hand
options.why: Ignoring opinions is not persuasion. Persuading means engaging with others.

options.t: Forcing others to obey without any choice at all
options.why: Forcing others to obey is coercion. Persuasion lets people choose.

options.t: Repeating a statement louder than before to them
options.why: Repeating louder does not persuade. It lacks reasons.

q: What does tone mean in writing?

options.t: The font used in a document, with its color and size
options.why: Font, color and size are formatting. Tone is about attitude.

options.t: The length of a message in words and lines
options.why: Length is the size of a message. Tone is about attitude.

options.t: The loudness of a speaker in a large room
options.why: Loudness belongs to speech. In writing, tone comes through words.

options.t: The writer's attitude shown through word choice
options.why: Tone in writing is the writer's attitude shown through word choice. It can be friendly, formal or rude, and shapes how the reader reacts.

q: What is a customer service standard?

options.t: A set expectation for how customers should be treated
options.why: A customer service standard is a set expectation for how customers should be treated. It ensures consistent service.

options.t: A price that a customer pays for a good in a store
options.why: The price paid is a cost to the customer. A service standard is about treatment.

options.t: A discount offered once a year to all of the buyers
options.why: A yearly discount is a promotion. It is not a service standard.

options.t: A product that customers return to the store again
options.why: A returned product is a return. A standard is a guideline for service.

q: A hotel promises check-in within 5 minutes. A guest waits 20. What should staff do?

options.t: Ignore the complaint of the guest and do nothing
options.why: Ignoring the complaint leaves the guest unhappy. It breaks the hotel's promise a second time.

options.t: Blame the guest for arriving much too early to check in
options.why: Blaming the guest is unfair and rude. The hotel made the promise.

options.t: Apologize, fix the problem and offer a small gesture
options.why: Apologizing, fixing the problem and offering a small gesture shows care. It repairs the guest's experience.

options.t: Tell the guest the wait was normal for the day we have
options.why: Saying the wait was normal contradicts the 5-minute promise. It would anger the guest.

q: What is a customer complaint?

options.t: A compliment about good service from a buyer to a shop owner
options.why: A compliment is praise. A complaint says something fell short.

options.t: A statement that a product or service did not meet expectations
options.why: A complaint is a statement that a product or service did not meet expectations. It helps a firm find and fix problems.

options.t: An order for more products from a customer in the same town
options.why: An order for more products is a purchase. It is not a complaint.

options.t: A request for a store's hours of business each day of the week
options.why: A request for store hours is a simple question. It is not a complaint.

q: Which response best handles an upset customer?

options.t: Blame another department for the delay in service
options.why: Blaming another department shifts responsibility. It does not help the customer.

options.t: Tell the customer to calm down and walk away
options.why: Telling a customer to calm down and walking away dismisses them. It makes them angrier.

options.t: Argue to prove that the customer is wrong about it
options.why: Arguing to prove the customer wrong damages the relationship. Even when right, it loses goodwill.

options.t: Listen without interrupting and offer a solution
options.why: Listening without interrupting and offering a solution calms the customer. It shows respect and fixes the problem.

q: What is customer retention?

options.t: Losing customers on purpose each year
options.why: Losing customers on purpose is the opposite of retention. Retention keeps them.

options.t: Attracting only brand-new customers
options.why: Attracting new customers is acquisition. Retention is about keeping current ones.

options.t: Selling to customers one time only
options.why: Selling only once is a one-time sale. Retention aims for repeat business.

options.t: Keeping existing customers over time
options.why: Customer retention is keeping existing customers over time. Loyal customers keep buying and often recommend the firm.

q: Why is it often cheaper to keep a customer than to win a new one?

options.t: Existing customers never need any service at all
options.why: Existing customers do need service. Retention takes effort.

options.t: New customers cost more to attract through marketing
options.why: New customers cost more to attract through marketing and discounts. Keeping existing customers is usually cheaper.

options.t: Retention requires no effort from the firm at all
options.why: Retention requires effort, such as good service. It is not effortless.

options.t: New customers always pay higher prices than others
options.why: New customers do not always pay more. The main reason is acquisition cost.

q: What is a customer survey used for?

options.t: Setting the company's tax rate for the next year
options.why: Tax rates are set by governments. A survey asks customers questions.

options.t: Printing price tags for the store's goods
options.why: Price tags are printed by the store. A survey is a research tool.

options.t: Learning customers' opinions and satisfaction
options.why: A customer survey is used to learn customers' opinions and satisfaction. It shows what to improve.

options.t: Hiring new employees for the firm each year
options.why: Hiring is done through recruitment. Surveys study customers.

q: What is a loyalty program?

options.t: A program that rewards customers for repeat purchases
options.why: A loyalty program rewards customers for repeat purchases. It gives points, discounts or perks to encourage them to come back.

options.t: A program that removes all customer feedback for the firm
options.why: It does not remove feedback. Many programs collect feedback.

options.t: A program that limits the products customers can see
options.why: It does not limit products. It encourages buying.

options.t: A program that charges customers extra fees for buying
options.why: It rewards customers, so no extra fees are charged for buying.

q: A coffee shop gives a free drink after ten purchases. What is the main goal?

options.t: Encourage repeat visits
options.why: A free drink after ten purchases rewards repeat visits. The goal is to encourage customers to return.

options.t: Stop buying other items
options.why: A free drink does not stop customers buying other items. It brings them back.

options.t: Raise the price of coffee
options.why: A free drink does not raise the price of coffee. It is a reward.

options.t: Cut its costs per sale
options.why: Giving away drinks does not cut costs. It adds a cost to win loyalty.

q: What does empathy mean when serving customers?

options.t: Rushing the customer to leave the shop at once, with no help
options.why: Rushing a customer to leave shows no care. Empathy means taking time to understand.

options.t: Ignoring emotions to focus on rules and steps only
options.why: Ignoring emotions to focus on rules is the opposite of empathy. Empathy notices feelings.

options.t: Agreeing with every demand a customer makes there
options.why: Empathy does not mean agreeing with every demand. It means understanding the feelings.

options.t: Understanding and acknowledging how the customer feels
options.why: Empathy means understanding and acknowledging how the customer feels. It helps staff respond with care.

q: A customer's order arrives late for a birthday party. Which response shows empathy?

options.t: Delays happen all the time, so it is no big deal to us
options.why: Saying delays are no big deal dismisses the customer's feelings. It shows no empathy.

options.t: I'm sorry this affected your party, let me fix it right away
options.why: Apologizing, acknowledging the impact on the party and offering to fix it shows empathy. It treats the problem as real.

options.t: There is nothing I can do about it for you at this time
options.why: Saying there is nothing you can do gives up. It shows no care.

options.t: You should have ordered the cake much earlier on, I think
options.why: Blaming the customer is unkind. It avoids responsibility.

q: What is a surplus?

options.t: When quantity demanded is above the quantity supplied
options.why: Quantity demanded above supply is a shortage. A surplus is the opposite.

options.t: When a firm earns a profit in a year of trade for owners
options.why: Profit is earnings. A market surplus concerns supply and demand.

options.t: When quantity supplied is greater than quantity demanded
options.why: A surplus occurs when quantity supplied is greater than quantity demanded. Prices tend to fall until the market clears.

options.t: When supply and demand are equal at some price in the market
options.why: When supply and demand are equal, the market is at equilibrium. There is no surplus.

q: What is a shortage?

options.t: When a firm has too many workers on the staff at the shop
options.why: Too many workers is overstaffing. A shortage is about goods in a market.

options.t: When supply and demand are equal at some price in the market
options.why: When supply and demand are equal, the market is at equilibrium. There is no shortage.

options.t: When quantity supplied is above the quantity demanded
options.why: Supply above demand is a surplus. A shortage is the opposite.

options.t: When quantity demanded is greater than quantity supplied
options.why: A shortage occurs when quantity demanded is greater than quantity supplied. Prices tend to rise until demand and supply balance.

q: A new video game console sells out within minutes at its list price. What does this suggest?

options.t: The market is at equilibrium now
options.why: At equilibrium supply meets demand, so the console would not sell out in minutes. A sell-out shows demand is higher.

options.t: Supply exceeds demand at that price
options.why: If supply exceeded demand, the console would stay on shelves. A quick sell-out shows the opposite.

options.t: Demand exceeds supply at that price
options.why: A console that sells out within minutes at list price means demand exceeds supply at that price. A shortage exists, and prices may rise.

options.t: The price is too high for buyers
options.why: If the price were too high, buyers would not rush to buy. A sell-out suggests the price is low.

q: What is elasticity of demand?

options.t: How much a product costs the firm to make each unit
options.why: The cost to make a unit is production cost. Elasticity is about buyers' response to price.

options.t: How much quantity demanded changes when price changes
options.why: Elasticity of demand shows how much quantity demanded changes when price changes. Elastic demand responds a lot, inelastic demand responds little.

options.t: How quickly a product is delivered to the buyer of it
options.why: Delivery speed is a logistics matter. It does not describe elasticity.

options.t: How many stores sell the product in the town now
options.why: The number of stores is market coverage. It does not describe elasticity.

q: Which good tends to have inelastic demand?

options.t: Insulin for a patient with diabetes
options.why: Insulin is a necessity with no close substitute for the patient. Demand barely changes when price rises, so it is inelastic.

options.t: A specific brand of potato chips
options.why: A specific brand of chips has many substitutes. Buyers can switch, so demand is elastic.

options.t: A restaurant meal at a nice cafe
options.why: A restaurant meal is a choice that people can skip when prices rise. Demand is elastic.

options.t: A luxury vacation trip abroad each year
options.why: A luxury vacation is a want. Buyers cut back when prices rise, so demand is elastic.

q: What is gross domestic product (GDP)?

options.t: The total money held by the government in its accounts
options.why: The government's cash is public finance. GDP measures output.

options.t: The number of people employed in the nation at a time
options.why: The number employed is an employment figure. GDP measures production.

options.t: The total value of goods and services produced in a country
options.why: GDP is the total value of goods and services produced in a country. It is the main measure of economic size.

options.t: The average price of goods in the shops of a country
options.why: Average price of goods is a price index. GDP measures output.

q: Prices rise 4 percent while a worker's pay rises 2 percent. What happens to purchasing power?

options.t: It falls
options.why: When prices rise faster than pay, purchasing power falls. Prices rose 4 percent and pay only 2, so the worker can buy less.

options.t: It rises
options.why: Purchasing power rises only if pay grows faster than prices. Here prices outpaced pay.

options.t: No change
options.why: There is a change. Prices outpaced pay, so the worker's buying power fell.

options.t: It doubles
options.why: Purchasing power does not double. It fell because pay did not keep up with prices.

q: What is unemployment?

options.t: Having a job that you enjoy every day of the week
options.why: Having a job you enjoy is employment. Unemployment is being without work.

options.t: Working part-time by choice, with pay and hours
options.why: Part-time work by choice is employment. Unemployment is without a job while seeking one.

options.t: Choosing not to work at all, for any reason
options.why: Choosing not to work means not being in the labor force. Unemployed people are looking for work.

options.t: Being without a job while actively seeking work
options.why: Unemployment is being without a job while actively seeking work. It is a key measure of the labor market.

q: What is fiscal policy?

options.t: A bank's lending rules for loans to its customers
options.why: A bank's lending rules are credit policy. Fiscal policy is government action.

options.t: Government decisions about taxes and spending
options.why: Fiscal policy is government decisions about taxes and spending. Governments use it to influence the economy.

options.t: Central bank decisions about interest rates
options.why: Interest rates are set by the central bank. That is monetary policy.

options.t: A company's decisions about the pricing of goods
options.why: A company's pricing is business strategy. Fiscal policy is for governments.

q: What is monetary policy?

options.t: Central bank actions that influence interest rates and money supply
options.why: Monetary policy is central bank action that influences interest rates and money supply. It aims to control inflation and support growth.

options.t: Government decisions about taxes and spending each year at home
options.why: Taxes and spending are fiscal policy. Monetary policy is run by the central bank.

options.t: A store's decisions about the prices of its goods each year
options.why: A store's prices are business decisions. Monetary policy is for the economy.

options.t: A firm's decisions about hiring and firing staff for each year
options.why: Hiring and firing is a business matter. Monetary policy concerns money.

q: To slow rapidly rising inflation, the Federal Reserve is most likely to:

options.t: Print more money
options.why: Printing more money would add to inflation. The Fed would not do this to slow it.

options.t: Raise interest rates
options.why: Raising interest rates makes borrowing costlier and cools spending. That slows inflation.

options.t: Cut taxes for all
options.why: Cutting taxes is fiscal policy and would add spending. It would not slow inflation.

options.t: Lower interest rates
options.why: Lowering interest rates would boost spending and could raise inflation further.

q: What is a trade deficit?

options.t: When a country stops all of its trade abroad
options.why: Stopping all trade is a trade ban. A deficit is when imports exceed exports.

options.t: When a country exports more than it imports
options.why: Exporting more than importing is a trade surplus. A deficit is the reverse.

options.t: When a government spends more than it takes in
options.why: A government spending more than it takes in is a budget deficit. A trade deficit concerns imports and exports.

options.t: When a country imports more than it exports
options.why: A trade deficit is when a country imports more than it exports. It means more money flows out for goods than comes in.

q: A country exports $300 billion and imports $340 billion. What is its trade balance?

options.t: A surplus of $40 billion
options.why: A surplus would mean exports exceeded imports. Here imports are bigger.

options.t: A deficit of $240 billion
options.why: $240 billion does not follow from the figures. Subtract exports from imports to get the gap.

options.t: A deficit of $40 billion
options.why: Exports of $300 billion less imports of $340 billion leaves a deficit of $40 billion. Imports are higher than exports.

options.t: A deficit of $640 billion
options.why: $640 billion adds the two figures. The balance is their difference, $40 billion.

q: What is self-regulation?

options.t: Acting on every feeling at once, whatever the setting
options.why: Acting on every feeling at once is the opposite of self-regulation. It means no control.

options.t: Managing your emotions and impulses in healthy ways
options.why: Self-regulation means managing your emotions and impulses in healthy ways. It helps you stay calm and make good choices.

options.t: Avoiding every stressful task at work all day long
options.why: Avoiding every stressful task is avoidance. Self-regulation means managing stress.

options.t: Hiding all emotions from everyone else around you
options.why: Hiding all emotions is suppression. Self-regulation means handling emotions well.

q: A worker receives harsh criticism and pauses before replying calmly. Which skill is this?

options.t: Self-promotion
options.why: Self-promotion is seeking attention. Pausing to answer calmly is about control.

options.t: Rivalry for prizes
options.why: Rivalry is competing against others. The worker is staying calm.

options.t: Procrastination
options.why: Procrastination is delaying a task. Pausing before replying is a deliberate choice.

options.t: Self-regulation
options.why: Self-regulation is controlling emotions and impulses. Pausing before replying calmly after harsh criticism is a clear example.

q: What is social awareness?

options.t: Ignoring other people's feelings at work all day
options.why: Ignoring others' feelings is the opposite of social awareness. It means being unaware.

options.t: Having many social media followers who watch posts
options.why: Social media followers are an audience. Social awareness is about understanding feelings.

options.t: Recognizing and understanding other people's emotions
options.why: Social awareness is recognizing and understanding other people's emotions. It helps you respond with care and read a room.

options.t: Talking louder than others in the room at the office
options.why: Talking louder is not awareness. It ignores others.

q: What is relationship management?

options.t: Building and keeping positive relationships with others
options.why: Relationship management is building and keeping positive relationships with others. It includes communication, teamwork and resolving conflict.

options.t: Keeping score of other people's mistakes at work and home
options.why: Keeping score of mistakes damages relationships. It is not management.

options.t: Avoiding all contact with coworkers at work and at home
options.why: Avoiding contact does not build relationships. It cuts them off.

options.t: Winning every argument at the office with all staff
options.why: Winning every argument damages trust. Relationship management seeks cooperation.

q: Two teammates disagree. A third listens to both and suggests a compromise. Which skill is she using?

options.t: Conflict management
options.why: Conflict management means helping people settle disagreements. Listening to both sides and suggesting a compromise is the classic approach, and it keeps the team working together.

options.t: Fierce competition
options.why: Fierce competition pits people against each other to win. A third person who listens to both sides and proposes a compromise is trying to help, not to beat anyone.

options.t: Manipulation of others
options.why: Manipulation means influencing people through deceit or pressure for your own gain. Listening openly to both sides and suggesting a fair compromise is honest and transparent.

options.t: Avoidance of the issue
options.why: Avoidance means staying out of a conflict and hoping it fades. Here the third person steps in, listens and proposes a compromise, which is the opposite of avoiding.

q: What is stress management?

options.t: Blaming coworkers for deadlines that are missed
options.why: Blaming coworkers for missed deadlines does nothing to manage stress. It harms relationships and leaves the cause of the pressure unaddressed.

options.t: Ignoring problems until they disappear
