options.why: Ignoring problems rarely makes them disappear, and the stress usually grows. Stress management means facing pressure with healthy strategies.

options.t: Taking on more work just to feel busy at work
options.why: Piling on extra work just to feel busy adds to the load and burns people out. Real stress management lowers pressure, not raises it.

options.t: Using healthy strategies to handle pressure
options.why: Stress management means using healthy strategies, such as planning, exercise, breaks and talking to someone, to handle pressure. It keeps people productive and well.

q: Which action best reduces workplace stress?

options.t: Ignoring deadlines until the last day
options.why: Ignoring deadlines until the last day piles up work and raises stress. Starting early and pacing the work lowers pressure much more.

options.t: Working without any sleep at night for a week
options.why: Going a week without sleep damages health, focus and mood. It raises stress and the chance of mistakes instead of reducing them.

options.t: Prioritizing tasks and taking short breaks
options.why: Prioritizing tasks makes a heavy workload manageable, and short breaks restore energy and focus. Together they are the most effective way to ease stress.

options.t: Skipping meals to finish tasks faster each day
options.why: Skipping meals to save time lowers energy and concentration. The tiredness it causes makes work slower and stress higher.

q: What is resilience?

options.t: Avoiding all challenges that come along in life
options.why: Avoiding all challenges is the opposite of resilience. Resilient people face difficulties instead of running from them.

options.t: The ability to recover from setbacks and adapt
options.why: Resilience is the ability to recover from setbacks and adapt. Resilient people bounce back from failure, learn from it and keep going.

options.t: Giving up when things get hard for you at work
options.why: Giving up when things get hard shows a lack of resilience. Resilience means persisting and finding another way forward.

options.t: Never making any mistakes at work or at home
options.why: Nobody avoids all mistakes, so resilience cannot mean perfection. It means recovering and learning when mistakes or setbacks occur.

q: A salesperson loses a big deal and decides to learn from it and try again. Which trait is this?

options.t: Resilience
options.why: Resilience is bouncing back from a setback and trying again. The salesperson lost a big deal but chose to learn from it and continue.

options.t: Delaying tasks
options.why: Delaying tasks is procrastination. The salesperson is learning and trying again, which is the opposite of putting things off.

options.t: Indifference
options.why: Indifference means not caring about the result. Choosing to learn from the loss shows that the outcome mattered.

options.t: Aggression
options.why: Aggression means hostile behavior toward others. Learning from a loss and trying again is a constructive response.

q: What is an entrepreneur's role in the economy?

options.t: Setting taxes for all firms in the nation
options.why: Taxes are set by governments, not entrepreneurs. Entrepreneurs start and grow businesses within that system.

options.t: Printing money for the state and its people
options.why: Money is printed by the state's central authorities. An entrepreneur's contribution is creating businesses and products, not currency.

options.t: Creating new businesses, jobs and ideas
options.why: Entrepreneurs create new businesses, jobs and ideas. They bring innovation, give people work and drive economic growth.

options.t: Regulating trade between nations and firms
options.why: Regulating trade is a job for governments. Entrepreneurs take part in markets rather than regulate them.

q: What is start-up capital?

options.t: The profit earned in the first year
options.why: Profit earned in the first year comes after the business is running. Start-up capital is needed before that, to begin operating.

options.t: The money needed to start a business
options.why: Start-up capital is the money needed to start a business, covering equipment, inventory, licenses and early expenses. It may come from savings, loans or investors.

options.t: The tax paid by a new business each year
options.why: Taxes are paid out of earnings once trading. They are not the funds needed to launch a business.

options.t: The owner's salary for the first year
options.why: The owner's salary is a cost of running the business. Start-up capital is the money used to get it started.

q: What is bootstrapping?

options.t: Raising millions of dollars from many outside investors for a new firm
options.why: Raising millions from many outside investors is the opposite of bootstrapping. Bootstrapping avoids outside money.

options.t: Borrowing a large sum from a large bank for a new firm in the town
options.why: Borrowing a large sum from a bank is debt financing. Bootstrapping relies on the founder's own resources.

options.t: Selling the whole business outright to a competitor in the same market
options.why: Selling the whole business to a competitor is an exit. It is not a way of starting up.

options.t: Starting a business with little outside money, mostly personal savings
options.why: Bootstrapping means starting a business with little outside money, mostly the founder's savings and early sales. It keeps ownership and control with the founder.

q: Which is a typical source of funding for a start-up that wants to keep full ownership?

options.t: Merging with a rival company
options.why: Merging with a rival combines two companies. It is not a way to raise funds for a start-up, and ownership would be shared.

options.t: Giving away half of profits
options.why: Giving away half of profits means giving up a large share of the gains. That would not leave the founder with full ownership of the returns.

options.t: Personal savings or a bank loan
options.why: Personal savings and bank loans raise money without giving up ownership. A bank loan must be repaid, but the lender does not take a share of the firm.

options.t: Selling a large share of the firm
options.why: Selling a large share of the firm means giving up ownership. The question asks for ways to keep full ownership.

q: What is a business model?

options.t: A large building where products are made by workers there
options.why: A building where products are made is a factory. A business model describes how a business operates and earns money.

options.t: How a business creates, delivers and earns money from value
options.why: A business model describes how a business creates, delivers and earns money from value. It explains who the customers are and how revenue comes in.

options.t: A person who advertises a product to the general public
options.why: A person who advertises a product is a promoter or spokesperson. A business model is a plan for how the whole business works.

options.t: A small version of a product that is made for tests only
options.why: A small version of a product for tests is a prototype. A business model is about how the business makes money.

q: A start-up gives away a free app and earns money from ads. What is this?

options.t: A business model that earns revenue from advertising
options.why: A free app that earns from ads is an advertising-based business model. Users pay nothing, and advertisers pay to reach them.

options.t: A nonprofit model that has no revenue at all, ever
options.why: Nonprofit models still have revenue, such as donations. This start-up earns money from ads, so it does not fit.

options.t: A subscription model charging monthly fees to users
options.why: A subscription model charges users a regular fee. The app is free, so users are not paying.

options.t: A franchise model licensing the brand to others
options.why: A franchise model licenses a brand to others. The start-up is earning from ads, not from licensing.

q: What is a minimum viable product (MVP)?

options.t: A product that has no features at all and cannot be used yet
options.why: An MVP has just enough features to be useful and tested. A product with no features and no use would teach nothing.

options.t: The final perfect version of a product, with every feature built
options.why: The final perfect version is the goal, not the MVP. An MVP is released early so the team can learn.

options.t: A product sold only to investors and to banks, never the public
options.why: An MVP is meant for real users, so it is shown to the public. Restricting it to investors and banks defeats the purpose of testing.

options.t: A basic version of a product used to test an idea with real users
options.why: An MVP is a basic version of a product used to test an idea with real users. It lets a start-up learn quickly and cheaply before building more.

q: What is a pitch?

options.t: A short presentation that explains a business idea to investors or customers
options.why: A pitch is a short presentation that explains a business idea to investors or customers. Its goal is to win support, funding or sales.

options.t: A tax form that a firm files with the government every year to report its income
options.why: A tax form reports income to the government. A pitch is a presentation of an idea.

options.t: A list of all the expenses of the firm for the whole year ahead of it
options.why: A list of expenses is a budget. A pitch persuades an audience.

options.t: A legal contract signed by two parties who work together at the same firm
options.why: A contract between two parties is a legal agreement. A pitch comes before any deal and aims to persuade.

q: What should an investor pitch always include?

options.t: Only a long list of competitors' names and prices on the market
options.why: A list of competitors' names and prices covers only one small part. An investor wants the problem, solution, market and revenue plan too.

options.t: Only the founder's hobbies and interests outside of work and school
options.why: The founder's hobbies are not relevant to the business case. Investors want to see a plan for the business.

options.t: Only the color of the logo and the name of the brand, in detail
options.why: A logo color and brand name are small details. The pitch needs substance about the business.

options.t: The problem, the solution, the market and how the business makes money
options.why: A strong investor pitch covers the problem, the solution, the market and how the business makes money. These show that the idea is real and can earn a return.

q: What is scaling a business?

options.t: Reducing the number of customers
options.why: Reducing customers would shrink the business. Scaling means growing it.

options.t: Growing revenue faster than costs
options.why: Scaling means growing revenue faster than costs. As the business expands, each extra sale brings in more profit.

options.t: Weighing products on a big scale
options.why: Weighing products on a scale is a literal use of the word. In business, scaling means growth.

options.t: Keeping the business the same size
options.why: Keeping the business the same size is the opposite of scaling. Scaling means expanding.

q: Which is a risk of growing too fast?

options.t: Having a stronger brand overnight with no extra cost
options.why: A stronger brand overnight with no extra cost is a benefit, not a risk. Growing too fast usually costs more.

options.t: Having more choices of suppliers in the supply chain
options.why: More supplier choices are an advantage. It is not a risk of fast growth.

options.t: Running out of cash or being unable to meet demand
options.why: Growing too fast can use up cash because costs rise before payments come in. The firm may also be unable to meet demand, which harms customers.

options.t: Having too many satisfied customers to count
options.why: Having too many satisfied customers is a good problem. The real risk of fast growth is running short of resources.

q: Which ratio best measures a firm's ability to pay short-term debts?

options.t: The current ratio
options.why: The current ratio compares current assets with current liabilities. It shows whether a firm can pay debts due within a year.

options.t: Profit margin
options.why: Profit margin shows the share of sales kept as profit. It does not measure the ability to pay short-term debts.

options.t: Return on equity
options.why: Return on equity measures profit relative to owners' investment. It does not test short-term debt cover.

options.t: Inventory turnover
options.why: Inventory turnover shows how quickly stock sells. It does not measure short-term debt ability.

q: What is return on investment (ROI)?

options.t: The total amount invested in the venture by owners
options.why: The total amount invested is the cost of the investment. ROI compares the gain with that cost.

options.t: The tax paid on an investment during the year
options.why: Tax paid is a payment to the government. ROI measures the return on money invested.

options.t: The time needed to repay a loan from a bank
options.why: Time to repay a loan is the payback period or loan term. ROI measures the gain relative to cost.

options.t: The gain from an investment relative to its cost
options.why: Return on investment is the gain from an investment relative to its cost. It shows how efficiently money is used.

q: A business spends $20,000 on equipment and earns an extra $3,000 profit a year from it. What is the annual ROI?

options.why: 6.7% does not match the numbers. ROI is the annual profit divided by the cost, $3,000 over $20,000, which is 15%.
60% is far too high. Dividing $3,000 by $20,000 gives 0.15, or 15%.
ROI equals the extra profit divided by the cost. $3,000 divided by $20,000 is 0.15, so the annual ROI is 15%.
$3,000 is a dollar amount, not a percentage. ROI is the profit as a share of the cost, which is 15%.

q: What is working capital?

options.t: Total assets minus total liabilities
options.why: Total assets minus total liabilities is owner's equity. Working capital uses only current assets and current liabilities.

options.t: Current assets minus current liabilities
options.why: Working capital is current assets minus current liabilities. It shows the funds available to run day-to-day operations.

options.t: Cash plus fixed assets of the firm now
options.why: Cash plus fixed assets is not working capital. Fixed assets are long-term and are not used in day-to-day operations.

options.t: Revenue minus expenses of the firm for a year
options.why: Revenue minus expenses is net income. Working capital is based on the balance sheet, not the income statement.

q: What does a debt ratio measure?

options.t: The share of assets financed by debt
options.why: A debt ratio measures the share of assets financed by debt. A higher ratio means more borrowing and more risk.

options.t: How fast inventory sells each year
options.why: How fast inventory sells is inventory turnover. A debt ratio is about financing.

options.t: How much cash is on hand each month
options.why: Cash on hand is a liquidity matter. A debt ratio is about debt.

options.t: The share of sales kept as profit
options.why: The share of sales kept as profit is the profit margin. A debt ratio looks at assets and liabilities.

q: Liabilities are $60,000 and assets are $150,000. What is the debt ratio?

options.why: 250% inverts the formula, assets over liabilities. The debt ratio is liabilities divided by assets.
90% does not follow from the numbers. $60,000 divided by $150,000 is 0.40.
60% uses the dollar figure of $60,000 as a percent. The ratio is liabilities divided by assets, or 40%.
The debt ratio is total liabilities divided by total assets. $60,000 divided by $150,000 is 0.40, or 40%.

q: What is inventory turnover?

options.t: The profit from each product that a firm sells in a year
options.why: The profit from each product is unit profit. Inventory turnover measures how often stock sells.

options.t: The cost of storing inventory in a large warehouse over time
options.why: Storage cost is the carrying cost. Turnover measures how often stock is sold and replaced.

options.t: How many times inventory is sold and replaced in a period
options.why: Inventory turnover is how many times inventory is sold and replaced in a period. A high figure means goods sell quickly.

options.t: The number of products held in a warehouse at year end
options.why: The number of products held is the inventory level. Turnover is about the rate of selling.

q: Cost of goods sold is $240,000 and average inventory is $40,000. What is inventory turnover?

options.t: 200 times
options.why: 200 times is not what the numbers give. Turnover is cost of goods sold divided by average inventory, $240,000 over $40,000.

options.t: 6 times
options.why: Cost of goods sold divided by average inventory is $240,000 over $40,000, which is 6. Inventory sells and is replaced six times a year.

options.t: 280 times
options.why: 280 times adds the figures. The formula divides cost of goods sold by average inventory.

options.t: 0.17 times
options.why: 0.17 times turns the formula upside down. Turnover is cost of goods sold over average inventory, which is 6.

q: What is recruitment?

options.t: Finding and attracting qualified candidates for jobs
options.why: Recruitment is finding and attracting qualified candidates for jobs. It builds the pool from which a hire is made.

options.t: Paying employees each month for their time at work
options.why: Paying employees is payroll. Recruitment is about bringing in new staff.

options.t: Reviewing an employee's work each year to set a raise
options.why: Reviewing work to set a raise is a performance appraisal. Recruitment comes before someone is hired.

options.t: Ending an employee's job at the firm for cause
options.why: Ending an employee's job is termination. Recruitment is the opposite, finding people to join.

q: Which interview question is unlawful to ask?

options.t: Are you legally allowed to work here?
options.why: Asking if someone is legally allowed to work in the country is lawful. Employers must confirm eligibility.

options.t: Why are you interested in this job?
options.why: Asking why someone is interested in the job is lawful. It relates directly to the role.

options.t: Can you do the essential job duties
options.why: Asking whether the person can do the essential job duties is lawful. It focuses on ability to do the work.

options.t: Are you planning to have children?
options.why: Asking whether someone plans to have children is unlawful. Family plans are not related to doing the job and could lead to discrimination.

q: What is a performance appraisal?

options.t: A review of company profits this year
options.why: A review of company profits is a financial review. An appraisal looks at an individual employee.

options.t: A review of customer complaints made
options.why: A review of complaints concerns customers. An appraisal is about an employee's work.

options.t: A formal review of an employee's work
options.why: A performance appraisal is a formal review of an employee's work. It gives feedback and sets goals for improvement.

options.t: A review of the office layout plan
options.why: A review of the office layout is a facilities matter. It does not review a person's performance.

q: What is employee turnover?

options.t: The number of customers served each day at the store
options.why: The number of customers served is a sales or traffic figure. Turnover is about staff.

options.t: The rate at which employees leave and are replaced
options.why: Employee turnover is the rate at which employees leave and are replaced. A high rate is costly and may signal problems.

options.t: The rate at which sales grow from year to year
options.why: Sales growth is a financial figure. Turnover concerns people leaving.

options.t: The rate at which profits rise in a growing firm
options.why: Profit growth is a financial measure. Employee turnover counts departures.

q: A company with 150 employees sees 30 leave in a year. What is the turnover rate?

options.why: 30% takes the 30 leavers as a percent. Turnover is 30 divided by 150 employees.
50% is too high. Thirty leavers out of 150 is one in five.
Turnover rate equals leavers divided by employees. 30 divided by 150 is 0.20, or 20%.
5% is too low. Thirty out of 150 is 20 percent.

q: What is job rotation?

options.t: Keeping staff in one job forever, each expert at one task
options.why: Keeping staff in one job forever is the opposite of rotation. Rotation moves people around.

options.t: Cutting working hours for staff at the firm each week
options.why: Cutting working hours is a scheduling change. It is not job rotation.

options.t: Firing and then rehiring workers at the firm each year
options.why: Firing and rehiring is not rotation. Rotation moves current employees between roles.

options.t: Moving employees between different jobs to build skills
options.why: Job rotation moves employees between different jobs to build skills. It prepares staff for more roles and keeps work interesting.

q: What is diversity in the workplace?

options.t: Differences among employees such as background and experience
options.why: Diversity means differences among employees, such as background, age and experience. Different views can improve ideas and decisions.

options.t: Having employees work alone in their own rooms each day
options.why: Working alone in separate rooms is about layout. It does not describe differences among people.

options.t: Having every employee do exactly the same task each day at work
options.why: Everyone doing the same task is uniformity. Diversity refers to differences.

options.t: Hiring only people of one single age group for all of the jobs
options.why: Hiring only one age group reduces diversity. It is the opposite.

q: What is a grievance procedure?

options.t: A schedule of pay days for the staff of a firm each month
options.why: A schedule of pay days is a payroll calendar. A grievance procedure handles complaints.

options.t: A fair process for employees to raise and resolve complaints
options.why: A grievance procedure is a fair process for employees to raise and resolve complaints. It protects workers and helps firms fix problems.

options.t: A list of company rules for the staff of a shop or office
options.why: A list of company rules is a policy manual. A grievance procedure is a process.

options.t: A way to fire workers with no notice, whatever the cause
options.why: Firing without notice is not a grievance procedure. It would be the cause of a grievance.

q: What is a spreadsheet used for?

options.t: Designing company logos and signs for the firm's brand
options.why: Designing logos is done with graphics software. A spreadsheet is for numbers.

options.t: Sending video calls to team members across the world
options.why: Video calls use conferencing software. A spreadsheet works with data in cells.

options.t: Organizing and calculating data in rows and columns
options.why: A spreadsheet is used to organize and calculate data in rows and columns. It handles budgets, lists and charts.

options.t: Protecting computers from viruses and attacks online
options.why: Protecting against viruses is the job of security software. A spreadsheet does not do that.

q: Which spreadsheet function adds a column of numbers?

options.t: ROUND
options.why: ROUND changes a number to a set number of decimal places. It does not add a column of numbers.

options.t: COUNT
options.why: COUNT counts how many cells contain numbers. It does not add values.

options.t: MAX
options.why: MAX finds the largest value in a range. It does not add them.

options.t: SUM
options.why: SUM adds the numbers in a range of cells. It is the function used to total a column.

q: What is data backup?

options.t: Deleting old data that is no longer of any use to the firm
options.why: Deleting old data is data disposal. A backup keeps copies.

options.t: Making copies of data to restore it if the original is lost
options.why: Data backup is making copies of data to restore if the original is lost. It protects against failure, error and attack.

options.t: Encrypting passwords for the users of a system at the firm
options.why: Encrypting passwords is a security measure. It is not the same as backing up data.

options.t: Updating software on the computers of a firm each month
options.why: Updating software is maintenance. It does not copy data.

q: What is phishing?

options.t: A scam that tricks people into revealing sensitive information
options.why: Phishing is a scam that tricks people into revealing sensitive information, often through fake emails or sites. Attackers pose as trusted sources.

options.t: A hobby of catching fish on a lake in the summer months
options.why: Catching fish is a hobby. The similar spelling is a pun on fishing for information.

options.t: A method of encrypting data so that only the owner can read it
options.why: Encrypting data protects it. Phishing is an attack that tricks people.

options.t: A kind of spreadsheet used by firms in an office setting
options.why: A kind of spreadsheet is not phishing. Phishing is a form of fraud.

q: An email asks you to confirm your password on an unfamiliar link. What should you do?

options.t: Click and log in now
options.why: Clicking and logging in on an unfamiliar link may give your password to a scammer. It could cost you your account.

options.t: Forward it to coworkers
options.why: Forwarding it spreads the scam to coworkers. It could put them at risk.

options.t: Reply with your password
options.why: Replying with your password gives it directly to the attacker. Never share passwords by email.

options.t: Not click and report it
options.why: Not clicking and reporting it is the safe choice. It protects you and lets IT warn others.

q: What is cloud computing?

options.t: Storing data on paper in a filing cabinet for the firm's use
options.why: Storing data on paper in a cabinet is physical storage. Cloud computing uses remote servers.

options.t: Using only one computer in an office, holding all files and programs
options.why: Using one computer for everything is local computing. Cloud computing spreads work over remote servers.

options.t: Using remote servers on the internet to store and process data
options.why: Cloud computing uses remote servers on the internet to store and process data. Users can reach files from many devices.

options.t: Using computers without electricity or power in a small firm
options.why: Computers need electricity. Cloud computing runs on servers elsewhere.

q: A company sells running shoes mainly to serious athletes. What is this?

options.t: Target marketing
options.why: Target marketing means aiming at a specific group, here serious athletes. It focuses efforts on the customers most likely to buy.

options.t: Price fixing
options.why: Price fixing is an illegal agreement between rivals on prices. Aiming shoes at athletes is unrelated.

options.t: Inventory control
options.why: Inventory control manages stock levels. The company is choosing customers, not managing stock.

options.t: Mass production
options.why: Mass production makes large quantities. It does not describe aiming at a specific group.

q: What is branding?

options.t: Setting the price of products in the shops of a large firm
options.why: Setting prices is pricing. Branding creates an identity.

options.t: Creating a name or symbol that identifies a business's products
options.why: Branding creates a name or symbol that identifies a business's products. It sets them apart and builds recognition.

options.t: Counting products in a warehouse at year end to check the books
options.why: Counting stock is inventory control. It does not give the firm an identity.

options.t: Delivering goods to customers in vans each day of a week
options.why: Delivering goods is distribution. Branding is about identity.

q: What is market research?

options.t: Filing taxes for a firm at the end of a full year
options.why: Filing taxes is an accounting task. Market research collects information.

options.t: Gathering information about customers and competitors
options.why: Market research gathers information about customers and competitors. It helps a firm make informed decisions.

options.t: Making products in a factory for the firm to sell
options.why: Making products is production. Research gathers information.

options.t: Printing flyers for a big sale at the local shops
options.why: Printing flyers is advertising work. It is not research.

q: What is supply chain management?

options.t: Coordinating the flow of goods from suppliers to customers
options.why: Supply chain management coordinates the flow of goods from suppliers to customers. It includes sourcing, production, storage and delivery.

options.t: Advertising goods in the news and on the radio each day
options.why: Advertising goods is promotion. Supply chain management moves goods.

options.t: Setting prices for goods in stores that sell to the public
options.why: Setting prices is pricing. Supply chain management coordinates the flow of goods.

options.t: Hiring employees for the firm at its main head office
options.why: Hiring is human resources. It is not supply chain management.

q: A factory runs short of a key part because one supplier is late. What is the best long-term fix?

options.t: Rely on the same supplier
options.why: Relying on the same supplier leaves the risk in place. The factory would face the same delay again.

options.t: Ignore the delay and wait
options.why: Ignoring a delay and waiting does not solve the problem. Production would stay at risk.

options.t: Use more than one supplier
options.why: Using more than one supplier spreads risk. If one is late, another can fill the gap.

options.t: Stop making the product
options.why: Stopping production loses sales. It does not fix the supply problem.

q: What is quality control?

options.t: Hiring workers for the factory floor of the firm
options.why: Hiring workers is HR. Quality control checks products.

options.t: Setting the price of products after a study
options.why: Setting prices is pricing. Quality control checks products meet standards.

options.t: Promoting products on the radio and in print ads
options.why: Promoting products is marketing. Quality control is about checking output.

options.t: Checking products to ensure they meet standards
options.why: Quality control means checking products to ensure they meet standards. It finds defects before products reach customers.

q: What is a professional network?

options.t: A group of contacts who share advice and opportunities
options.why: A professional network is a group of contacts who share advice and opportunities. It can lead to jobs, mentors and partners.

options.t: A computer network inside an office that links printers
options.why: A computer network links devices. A professional network links people.

options.t: A group of competitors in the same market for goods
options.why: Competitors are rivals. A professional network is a group of helpful contacts.

options.t: A list of customers of the firm and their orders
options.why: Customers and their orders are sales records. They are not a professional network.

q: Which action best shows professionalism after making a mistake at work?

options.t: Hide it and hope no one notices
options.why: Hiding a mistake and hoping no one notices is dishonest. It can make the problem worse.

options.t: Ignore it and just carry on as usual
options.why: Ignoring a mistake and carrying on leaves it unfixed. A professional takes responsibility.

options.t: Admit it, fix it and learn from it
options.why: Admitting a mistake, fixing it and learning from it shows professionalism. It builds trust and prevents repeats.

options.t: Blame a coworker for the error
options.why: Blaming a coworker is unfair and dishonest. It damages relationships.

q: A small bakery cannot beat a chain on price but offers fresh, local products. What strategy is it using?

options.t: Imitating them
options.why: Imitating a chain means copying it. The bakery is offering something different.

options.t: Closing down
options.why: Closing down is giving up. The bakery is competing with fresh, local products.

options.t: Cost leadership
options.why: Cost leadership means having the lowest prices. The bakery says it cannot beat the chain on price.

options.t: Differentiation
options.why: Differentiation means standing out through qualities such as freshness and local products. It lets the bakery compete without cutting prices.

q: What is a tort?

options.t: A crime punished only by prison time in a state
options.why: A crime punished by prison is criminal. A tort is a civil wrong.

options.t: A civil wrong that causes harm to another person
options.why: A tort is a civil wrong that causes harm to another person. The injured person can sue for compensation.

options.t: A written agreement between two firms, signed
options.why: A written agreement is a contract. A tort is a wrong.

options.t: A tax paid to the state by a firm each year
options.why: A tax is a payment to the state. A tort is a civil wrong.

q: A customer sues a restaurant after food poisoning. Which area of law is this?

options.t: Antitrust
options.why: Antitrust law concerns competition and monopolies. A food poisoning claim is about harm.

options.t: Tort law
options.why: Food poisoning from a restaurant is a civil wrong, which falls under tort law. The customer may sue for damages.

options.t: Tax law
options.why: Tax law covers taxes. It does not apply to a harm claim.

options.t: Labor law
options.why: Labor law covers workers' rights. It does not cover a customer's injury.

q: What is a trade secret?

options.t: Confidential business information that gives a competitive edge
options.why: A trade secret is confidential business information that gives a competitive edge. Examples include recipes and customer lists.

options.t: A public record of a firm's yearly profits filed with the state
options.why: A public record of profits is not secret. A trade secret is confidential.

options.t: A government contract with a supplier of the firm's goods
options.why: A government contract is an agreement. It is not secret information.

options.t: A tax deduction used by a firm to cut the bill each year
options.why: A tax deduction reduces a tax bill. It is not a trade secret.

q: An employee takes a client list to a competitor in violation of a confidentiality agreement. What is this?

options.t: A normal career move that employers expect
options.why: Taking a client list in breach of a confidentiality agreement is not a normal career move. It breaks legal duties.

options.t: A sales promotion by a firm in a market
options.why: It is not a sales promotion. It is taking confidential information.

options.t: Misuse of confidential business information
options.why: Taking a client list to a competitor is misuse of confidential business information. The employee may face legal action.

options.t: A tax saving method used by a firm each year
options.why: It is not a tax saving method. It is a breach of confidentiality.

q: What is a non-compete agreement?

options.t: A rule about paid vacation days for the staff of a firm at work, each year
options.why: Paid vacation rules are a matter of benefits. A non-compete agreement limits working for rivals.

options.t: A promise never to quit a job at the firm that a worker has newly taken on
options.why: A promise never to quit is not a non-compete. It concerns what happens after leaving.

options.t: A guarantee of a yearly raise in pay for each of the workers at a firm
options.why: A guaranteed raise is a pay term. A non-compete limits future work.

options.t: A contract limiting an employee's ability to work for competitors after leaving
options.why: A non-compete agreement is a contract limiting an employee's ability to work for competitors after leaving. It protects the firm's secrets and clients.

q: What is arbitration?

options.t: A neutral person hears both sides and decides a dispute
options.why: Arbitration is when a neutral person hears both sides and decides a dispute. The decision is often binding.

options.t: One party decides the outcome alone, without any help
options.why: If one party decides alone, it is not arbitration. A neutral person must decide.

options.t: Two parties argue in front of a jury that then decides
options.why: A jury trial is a court case. Arbitration is private and done without a jury.

options.t: A government agency sets the price for all of the goods
options.why: A government agency setting prices is regulation. It is not arbitration.

q: What is mediation?

options.t: A jury decides the dispute in a court of law, after trial
options.why: A jury deciding in court is a trial. Mediation is a negotiation with help.

options.t: A judge issues a binding decision after hearing both sides
options.why: A judge issuing a binding decision is a court ruling. Mediation does not impose a result.

options.t: A neutral person imposes a ruling on both of the parties
options.why: A neutral person imposing a ruling is arbitration. In mediation the parties decide.

options.t: A neutral person helps parties reach their own agreement
options.why: Mediation is when a neutral person helps the parties reach their own agreement. The mediator guides talks but does not decide.

q: Two partners disagree and want a faster, private way to settle without a lawsuit. Which options fit?

options.t: A long jury trial in court
options.why: A long jury trial is public, slow and costly. It is not a quick, private option.

options.t: Mediation or arbitration
options.why: Mediation and arbitration are private and faster than court. They let partners settle without a lawsuit.

options.t: Ignoring the dispute
options.why: Ignoring a dispute does not settle it. It often makes things worse.

options.t: A public vote of staff
options.why: A public vote of staff is not a legal way to settle a dispute. It would not be binding.

q: What is the statute of limitations?

options.t: A cap on damages a court can award
options.why: A cap on damages limits what a court can award. The statute of limitations is a time limit.

options.t: A limit on the number of witnesses
options.why: A limit on witnesses is a court procedure. It is not a time limit on claims.

options.t: A deadline for bringing a legal claim
options.why: A statute of limitations is a deadline for bringing a legal claim. After it passes, the claim is usually barred.

options.t: A limit on a lawyer's fees in a case
options.why: Limits on lawyers' fees are a separate rule. The statute of limitations is about time.

q: What is an employment contract?

options.t: An agreement that sets terms of a job such as pay and duties
options.why: An employment contract is an agreement that sets the terms of a job, such as pay and duties. It protects both employer and employee.

options.t: A tax form for the workers of a firm to file every year
options.why: A tax form is filed with the government. An employment contract is an agreement.

options.t: A request for a large bank loan for a new firm in the town
options.why: A loan request goes to a bank. It is not an employment contract.

options.t: A list of company products with the prices and dates of sale
options.why: A list of products and prices is a catalog. It is not a job agreement.

q: What does the Fair Labor Standards Act cover?

options.t: Rules for food labels on goods in stores
options.why: Food labels are covered by food safety laws. The Fair Labor Standards Act covers work.

options.t: Rules for advertising of goods on air
options.why: Advertising rules are consumer protection laws. The FLSA covers workers.

options.t: Rules for stock trading and broker duties
options.why: Stock trading is regulated by securities law. The FLSA is about labor.

options.t: Minimum wage, overtime and child labor
options.why: The Fair Labor Standards Act sets minimum wage, overtime and child labor rules. It protects workers' pay and hours.

q: A 14-year-old is asked to operate dangerous machinery at work. What law is likely violated?

options.t: Securities law
options.why: Securities law covers stock trading. A teen on dangerous machinery is a labor issue.

options.t: Child labor laws
options.why: Child labor laws limit the work young people may do, especially hazardous jobs. Machinery is banned for a 14-year-old.

options.t: Copyright law
options.why: Copyright law protects creative works. It does not govern workplace safety.

options.t: Antitrust law
options.why: Antitrust law concerns competition. It does not apply to a teen's job.

q: What is product liability?

options.t: A tax placed on products sold by a firm to the whole public
options.why: A tax on products is a sales or excise tax. Product liability concerns harm.

options.t: A rule about shelf size for goods displayed in a retail store
options.why: Shelf size is a store rule. Product liability is about defective products.

options.t: A seller's responsibility for harm caused by defective products
options.why: Product liability is a seller's responsibility for harm caused by defective products. Injured buyers may seek compensation.

options.t: A buyer's duty to pay on time for goods bought on credit
options.why: A buyer's duty to pay is a payment duty. It is not product liability.

q: A blender's blade breaks and injures a user because of a design flaw. Who may be liable?

options.t: The manufacturer and possibly the seller
options.why: The manufacturer, and possibly the seller, may be liable for a defective product. A design flaw is the maker's responsibility.

options.t: No one, because accidents are normal
options.why: Accidents are not just normal when a flaw causes harm. Someone can be liable.

options.t: Only the government of the state itself
options.why: The government of the state is not the party responsible. The maker and seller are.

options.t: Only the injured user of the blender
options.why: The user is not at fault when a design flaw causes injury. Blame lies with the seller or maker.

q: What is a persuasive message?

options.t: A message that only lists facts and asks nothing of the audience
options.why: A message that only lists facts and asks nothing is informative. A persuasive message aims to influence.

options.t: A message designed to influence what an audience thinks or does
options.why: A persuasive message is designed to influence what an audience thinks or does. It uses reasons and appeals to win support.

options.t: A message that forces compliance from all of its readers
options.why: Forcing compliance is coercion. Persuasion lets people choose.

options.t: A message that hides its aim from the people reading it
options.why: Hiding its aim is deception. A persuasive message states its purpose.

q: Which is the strongest opening for a sales email?

options.t: A long paragraph about the company's history
options.why: A long history paragraph is dull and off topic. It does not grab the reader.

options.t: A list of every product the firm has sold to date
options.why: A list of every product is overwhelming. It does not connect to the reader's need.

options.t: A generic greeting with no clear purpose for writing
options.why: A generic greeting is forgettable. It does not give a reason to keep reading.

options.t: A short line that connects to the reader's problem
options.why: A short line that connects to the reader's problem shows relevance quickly. It encourages the reader to continue.

q: What is body language?

options.t: The written notes of a meeting, typed up and mailed out
options.why: Written notes of a meeting are minutes. Body language is nonverbal.

options.t: The words spoken aloud by the people in a staff meeting
options.why: Spoken words are verbal. Body language uses movement and expression.

options.t: Gestures, posture and expressions that communicate feelings
options.why: Body language is gestures, posture and expressions that communicate feelings. It can support or contradict spoken words.

options.t: The volume of a phone call between two or more people
options.why: Volume is part of tone of voice. Body language is physical.

q: What is a stakeholder?

options.t: Only the competitors of the business, since they matter
options.why: Competitors are not the only stakeholders. A stakeholder is anyone affected by the business.

options.t: Anyone affected by or interested in a business's decisions
options.why: A stakeholder is anyone affected by or interested in a business's decisions. This includes owners, employees, customers, suppliers and the community.

options.t: Only the owner of the business, since no one else is affected
options.why: The owner is only one stakeholder. Others are affected too.

options.t: Only the managers of the business, since only they decide
options.why: Managers are stakeholders, but not the only ones. Many groups have an interest.

q: A manager must announce layoffs. Which approach is best?

options.t: Send a vague email to everyone and then avoid all questions
options.why: A vague email and avoiding questions leaves people confused. It is not respectful.

options.t: Announce it publicly with no warning to those affected
options.why: Announcing layoffs publicly with no warning is harsh. Those affected deserve notice and care.

options.t: Be clear, honest and compassionate, and explain next steps
options.why: Being clear, honest and compassionate, and explaining next steps, respects the people affected. It helps them plan.

options.t: Blame the employees for the decision that was made at the top
options.why: Blaming employees is unfair. The decision was made by leaders.

q: Why is it important to know your audience when presenting?

options.t: You can tailor the message to their needs and level
options.why: Knowing your audience lets you tailor the message to their needs and level. It keeps them interested and helps them understand.

options.t: You can use the same talk for everyone with no prep
options.why: One talk for everyone ignores differences. Audiences vary in knowledge and interests.

options.t: You can avoid preparing at all, since it is not needed
options.why: Presenters must prepare. Knowing the audience guides the preparation.

options.t: You can speak as fast as possible so it ends sooner
options.why: Speaking fast does not help. It makes the message hard to follow.

q: Which visual is best for showing sales change over twelve months?

options.t: A staff list
options.why: A staff list is a list of names. It shows no sales change.

options.t: A pie chart
options.why: A pie chart shows parts of a whole. It does not show change over time well.

options.t: A store photo
options.why: A store photo shows a place. It does not show trends in sales.

options.t: A line chart
options.why: A line chart shows how a value changes over time. It suits sales over twelve months.

q: What is an elevator pitch?

options.t: A price list posted on the wall of an elevator in a building
options.why: A price list on an elevator wall is not a pitch. An elevator pitch is a short speech.

options.t: A long report presented to investors over several hours of talks
options.why: A long report over hours is the opposite of an elevator pitch. It is meant to be short.

options.t: A short, persuasive summary of an idea delivered in about 30 seconds
options.why: An elevator pitch is a short, persuasive summary of an idea delivered in about 30 seconds. It is named for a short ride.

options.t: A complaint about a building and how its elevator is being run
options.why: A complaint about a building is not a pitch. An elevator pitch promotes an idea.

q: A subscription customer pays $20 a month and stays 3 years. What is the revenue from the customer?

options.why: $60 is only three months of fees. The customer stays three years, which is 36 months.
Revenue is monthly fee times months. $20 times 36 months is $720.
$2,160 treats the fee as $60 a month. The fee is $20, so the total is $720.
$240 is one year of fees. The customer stays three years, so $720.

q: What is a service recovery?

options.t: Actions taken to fix a problem and regain a customer's trust
options.why: Service recovery is actions taken to fix a problem and regain a customer's trust. Done well, it can build loyalty.

options.t: Raising prices for everyone after a single complaint came in
options.why: Raising prices for everyone after one complaint is unfair. It does not fix the problem.

options.t: Blaming the customer for the problem in front of others
options.why: Blaming the customer damages the relationship. It is not recovery.

options.t: Ignoring a complaint until it fades away and is forgotten
options.why: Ignoring a complaint lets the customer stay unhappy. It does not recover trust.

q: A diner receives the wrong meal. Which response shows good service recovery?

options.t: Walk away without saying a single word to the diner at all
options.why: Walking away without a word is rude. It leaves the diner without help.

options.t: Tell the diner to eat what was served, since the kitchen is busy
options.why: Telling the diner to eat the wrong meal ignores the error. It is poor service.

options.t: Charge extra for the correct meal that was ordered first
options.why: Charging extra for the correct meal is unfair, since the error was the restaurant's. It would anger the diner.

options.t: Apologize, replace the meal quickly and offer a small gesture
options.why: Apologizing, replacing the meal quickly and adding a small gesture fixes the problem and shows care. This is good service recovery.

q: What is a Net Promoter Score (NPS)?

options.t: A measure of how likely customers are to recommend a business
options.why: Net Promoter Score measures how likely customers are to recommend a business. It is a common gauge of loyalty and satisfaction.

options.t: A measure of employee turnover rates over the past year
options.why: Employee turnover is a staff measure. NPS is about customers.

options.t: A measure of profit, found by subtracting costs from sales
options.why: Profit is revenue minus costs. NPS measures recommendation.

options.t: A measure of inventory levels held in the main warehouse
options.why: Inventory levels are an operations figure. NPS measures customer loyalty.

q: Why is first-contact resolution valuable?

options.t: It lets staff skip any follow-up with the customer
options.why: First-contact resolution does not mean skipping follow-up. It means solving the issue the first time.

options.t: It makes calls last as long as possible for the staff
options.why: Long calls are not the aim. Solving problems quickly is.

options.t: Problems are solved the first time the customer asks
options.why: First-contact resolution means problems are solved the first time the customer asks. It saves time and raises satisfaction.

options.t: It removes the need for any service staff at all
options.why: Service staff are still needed. Resolution is about doing the job well.

q: A student can work for $90 or study for an exam. What is the opportunity cost of studying?

options.t: Nothing, because studying is free
options.why: Studying is free in money terms, but time has value. The student gave up $90 of pay.

options.t: The total price of the exam itself
options.why: The price of the exam is not what she gave up by studying. Opportunity cost is the next best use of time.

options.t: The cost of the textbook itself
options.why: The textbook cost is an out-of-pocket expense. Opportunity cost is the value of the best alternative.

options.t: The $90 that could have been earned
options.why: The opportunity cost is the value of the next best alternative given up. By studying, the student gave up $90 she could have earned.

q: What is a substitute good?

options.t: A product that is made abroad only
options.why: A product made abroad is an import. A substitute is something that can replace another.

options.t: A product that can replace another
options.why: A substitute good is a product that can replace another. If one gets pricier, buyers may switch to the other.

options.t: A product used together with another
options.why: A product used together with another is a complement. A substitute replaces.

options.t: A product that no one ever wants
options.why: A product no one wants has no demand. It is not a substitute.

q: The price of coffee rises sharply. What is likely to happen to demand for tea?

options.t: It is zero
options.why: Demand for tea would not drop to zero. Many people still drink tea.

options.t: It falls
options.why: Demand for tea would not fall. Tea is a substitute for coffee.

options.t: It rises
options.why: When coffee gets more expensive, some buyers switch to tea. Demand for tea rises.

options.t: No change
options.why: Prices of substitutes affect demand. A rise in coffee's price changes tea demand.

q: What is a complementary good?

options.t: A product sold only in other countries
options.why: A product sold only abroad is not a complement. A complement is used with another good.

options.t: A product used together with another
options.why: A complementary good is used together with another. Examples are printers and ink, or cereal and milk.

options.t: A product that stands in for another
options.why: A product that stands in for another is a substitute. Complements go together.

options.t: A product that is given away for free
options.why: A free product is not a complement. A complement is defined by use with another good.

q: What is perfect competition?

options.t: A market with one dominant seller who can set the price
options.why: One dominant seller describes a monopoly. Perfect competition has many sellers.

options.t: A market with only a few large sellers who watch each other
options.why: A few large sellers describe an oligopoly. Perfect competition has many.

options.t: A market controlled by government rules and price limits
options.why: A market with government price limits is regulated. Perfect competition is free of such control.

options.t: A market with many sellers of identical products and easy entry
options.why: Perfect competition has many sellers of identical products and easy entry. No single seller can set the price.

q: What is an oligopoly?

options.t: A market dominated by a few large sellers
options.why: An oligopoly is a market dominated by a few large sellers. Firms watch each other and can influence price.

options.t: A market with no sellers and no buyers
options.why: A market with no sellers and no buyers has no trade. It is not an oligopoly.

options.t: A market with thousands of sellers of one good
options.why: Thousands of sellers describe perfect or monopolistic competition. An oligopoly has few.

options.t: A market with just one seller and no rivals
options.why: One seller with no rivals is a monopoly. An oligopoly has a few sellers.

q: What is a price ceiling?

options.t: A legal maximum price that can be charged
options.why: A price ceiling is a legal maximum price that can be charged. Governments use it to keep goods affordable.

options.t: A legal minimum price that can be charged
options.why: A legal minimum price is a price floor. A ceiling sets a maximum.

options.t: A tax added on to the prices of goods
options.why: A tax added to prices is a different policy. A ceiling is a price limit.

options.t: The highest price a seller wants to charge
options.why: The highest price a seller wants to charge is the seller's choice. A ceiling is set by law.

q: A price ceiling is set below the equilibrium price. What results?

options.t: A balance
options.why: A balance would mean supply equals demand. A ceiling below equilibrium prevents that.

options.t: A surplus
options.why: A surplus is more supplied than demanded. A ceiling below equilibrium causes the opposite.

options.t: Higher supply
options.why: Supply does not rise under a lower price. A ceiling reduces what sellers want to offer.

options.t: A shortage
options.why: A price ceiling below equilibrium holds the price too low. Demand exceeds supply, causing a shortage.

q: What is a tariff?

options.t: A total ban on all trade
options.why: A total ban on trade is an embargo. A tariff is a tax.

options.t: A tax on exported goods
options.why: A tax on exports is an export duty. A tariff is usually on imports.

options.t: A tax on imported goods
options.why: A tariff is a tax on imported goods. It raises their price and protects local producers.

options.t: A discount on imports
options.why: A discount on imports is a subsidy. A tariff raises the price.

q: Who usually benefits from a tariff on imported steel?

options.t: Consumers of steel goods
options.why: Consumers of steel goods pay higher prices because of a tariff. They are harmed.

options.t: Domestic steel producers
options.why: Domestic steel producers benefit because imports are more expensive. They can sell more at higher prices.

options.t: Foreign steel producers
options.why: Foreign producers lose sales because their steel costs more. They do not benefit.

options.t: Steel-using manufacturers
options.why: Steel-using manufacturers pay more for steel. They lose out.

q: What is comparative advantage?

options.t: A ban on imports of goods from other nations, set by law each year
options.why: A ban on imports is a trade barrier. Comparative advantage is about efficiency.

options.t: The ability to produce at a lower opportunity cost than others
options.why: Comparative advantage is the ability to produce at a lower opportunity cost than others. It explains why trade benefits both sides.

options.t: The ability to produce everything at a lower cost than all
options.why: Producing everything cheaper is absolute advantage. Comparative advantage is about opportunity cost.

options.t: The largest army in a region of the world, kept at the ready
options.why: The largest army is military strength. It has nothing to do with trade.

q: What is a recession?

options.t: A period of declining economic activity lasting several months
options.why: A recession is a period of declining economic activity lasting several months. Output, jobs and income fall.

options.t: A time when all prices fall to zero as demand dries up fast
options.why: Prices do not fall to zero in a recession. It is a fall in activity.

options.t: A period of rapid growth and low unemployment for years
options.why: Rapid growth and low unemployment describe a boom. A recession is the opposite.

options.t: A one-day stock market dip that soon recovers by itself
options.why: A one-day dip is a market fluctuation. A recession lasts months.

q: A coworker seems upset after a meeting. Which response shows emotional intelligence?

options.t: Joke about it in front of the team right away
options.why: Joking in front of the team could embarrass the coworker. It shows no empathy.

options.t: Ignore it completely and move on with the day
options.why: Ignoring the coworker misses a chance to help. Emotional intelligence notices feelings.

options.t: Privately ask if they want to talk and listen
options.why: Privately asking if they want to talk and listening shows care and respect. It reflects emotional intelligence.

options.t: Tell others about it as soon as the meeting ends
options.why: Telling others breaks trust. It would worsen the coworker's feelings.

q: What is self-awareness?

options.t: Predicting what other people will do before they act at all
options.why: Predicting what others will do is a different skill. Self-awareness is about yourself.

options.t: Avoiding stressful situations whenever it is possible to do so
options.why: Avoiding stress is not awareness. Self-awareness means understanding your own reactions.

options.t: Hiding your feelings from everyone so emotions do not affect the work
options.why: Hiding feelings is suppression. Self-awareness means recognizing them.

options.t: Recognizing your own emotions and how they affect your behavior
options.why: Self-awareness is recognizing your own emotions and how they affect your behavior. It helps you respond wisely.

q: What is constructive feedback?

options.t: Praise that has no details or any real substance at all
options.why: Praise with no detail does not help someone improve. Constructive feedback is specific.

options.t: Harsh criticism of a person's character, given before the team
options.why: Harsh criticism of character before the team humiliates. Constructive feedback is respectful.

options.t: Silence about problems in the hope that they go away
options.why: Silence about problems leaves them unsolved. Feedback should be shared.

options.t: Specific, respectful input meant to help someone improve
options.why: Constructive feedback is specific, respectful input meant to help someone improve. It focuses on actions and gives ways to do better.

q: Which is the best example of constructive feedback?

options.t: Do better next time, since this one was not good enough
options.why: 'Do better next time' is vague. It does not say what to improve.

options.t: Your report was clear, but adding cost data would strengthen it
options.why: Praising what is clear and suggesting cost data is specific, respectful and helpful. It shows how to improve.

options.t: Your report was bad and it needs to be done over again now
options.why: Saying the report is bad with no reasons is unhelpful. It discourages.

options.t: You never do anything right, and I doubt you will improve
options.why: Attacking the person is personal criticism. It does not help improve.

q: What is a unique selling proposition (USP)?

options.t: What makes a business different from its competitors
options.why: A USP is what makes a business different from its competitors. It gives customers a reason to choose it.

options.t: The legal form of the business, such as a partnership
options.why: The legal form is a structure choice. A USP is about difference.

options.t: A daily schedule of employees and who works each shift
options.why: An employee schedule is an operations tool. A USP is a marketing idea.

options.t: A list of the business's expenses, with the rent and wages
options.why: A list of expenses is a financial record. A USP is not about costs.

q: A new cafe promises ethically sourced beans and a quiet study space. What is this?

options.t: Its tax filing for last year
options.why: A tax filing is a legal document. The cafe's promise is about what makes it special.

options.t: Its lease agreement and rent
options.why: A lease and rent are property costs. They do not describe what sets the cafe apart.

options.t: Its unique selling proposition
options.why: Ethically sourced beans and a quiet study space make the cafe different. This is its unique selling proposition.

options.t: Its balance sheet for the year
options.why: A balance sheet shows assets and liabilities. It is not a selling point.

q: What is market research for an entrepreneur?

options.t: Studying customers and competitors before launching
options.why: Studying customers and competitors before launching shows if there is demand. It reduces the risk of starting.

options.t: Guessing what customers want, based on the owner's taste
options.why: Guessing from the owner's taste is risky. Research uses evidence.

options.t: Copying a competitor exactly, down to the last detail
options.why: Copying a competitor exactly gives no reason to choose you. Research helps find a gap.

options.t: Skipping planning and starting to sell at once
options.why: Skipping planning risks mistakes. Research comes first.

q: Which is a good first step before opening a food truck?

options.t: Buy a big truck without researching first
options.why: Buying a big truck without research risks wasted money. Research should come first.

options.t: Set prices at random without any research
options.why: Random prices could lose money or customers. Pricing should be based on costs and demand.

options.t: Open in any location without any plan
options.why: Opening anywhere without a plan may miss customers or break rules. Planning is needed.

options.t: Check permits and survey likely customers
options.why: Checking permits and surveying likely customers shows whether the truck can operate legally and has demand. It is a sound first step.

q: What is a franchise?

options.t: A special tax that is paid by large companies each year of operation
options.why: A special tax is a tax. A franchise is a right to operate a brand.

options.t: A business owned by the government and run to serve the public at a low price
options.why: A government-run business is a public enterprise. A franchise is privately owned.

options.t: The right to operate a business using another company's brand and system
options.why: A franchise is the right to operate a business using another company's brand and system. The franchisee pays fees and follows the franchisor's rules.

options.t: A store that sells used goods at low prices to local shoppers there
options.why: A store selling used goods is a thrift store. It is not a franchise by itself.

q: What is a venture capitalist?

options.t: A banker who lends to homeowners using the house as collateral
options.why: A banker lending against a house is a mortgage lender. A venture capitalist funds start-ups.

options.t: An investor who funds new businesses in exchange for ownership
options.why: A venture capitalist is an investor who funds new businesses in exchange for ownership. They aim for high returns when the firm grows.

options.t: A government regulator that enforces trade rules on firms
options.why: A regulator enforces rules. A venture capitalist invests.

options.t: A supplier of raw materials to many factories and workshops
options.why: A supplier provides materials. A venture capitalist provides funding.

q: What is the break-even point?

options.t: Where total revenue equals total costs
options.why: Break-even is where total revenue equals total costs. At that point there is no profit and no loss.

options.t: Where costs are zero for the firm
options.why: Costs do not go to zero at break-even. They equal revenue.

options.t: Where profit is highest for the firm
options.why: Highest profit is a different point. Break-even has zero profit.

options.t: Where sales are zero for the firm
options.why: Zero sales means a loss equal to fixed costs. It is not break-even.

q: Fixed costs are $8,000. Each item sells for $20 and costs $12 to make. How many items are needed to break even?

options.t: 667 items
options.why: 667 items does not match the formula. Break-even is fixed costs divided by profit per item, $8,000 over $8.

options.t: 8,000 items
options.why: 8,000 items uses fixed costs as a number of items. Divide by the $8 profit per item.

options.t: 400 items
options.why: 400 items is too low. $8,000 divided by $8 profit per item is 1,000.

options.t: 1,000 items
options.why: Each item earns $8 above its cost. $8,000 of fixed costs divided by $8 is 1,000 items to break even.

q: What is a budget variance?

options.t: A list of rules that staff must follow at work
options.why: A list of rules is a policy. A budget variance is a difference in numbers.

options.t: A type of insurance that a firm buys for protection
options.why: Insurance protects against loss. A variance compares budget and actual.

options.t: The difference between budgeted and actual amounts
options.why: A budget variance is the difference between budgeted and actual amounts. It shows where spending or revenue differed from plan.

options.t: A chart of sales made by the firm each quarter
options.why: A chart of sales is a sales report. A variance compares budget and actual.

q: What is net income?

options.t: Assets minus liabilities
options.why: Assets minus liabilities is owner's equity. Net income is a profit figure.

options.t: Revenue minus all expenses
options.why: Net income is revenue minus all expenses. It is the profit left after costs.

options.t: Revenue before any costs
options.why: Revenue before costs is gross revenue. Net income is what remains.

options.t: Cash minus all debts owed
options.why: Cash minus debts is a net cash position. Net income comes from the income statement.

q: Revenue is $450,000, cost of goods sold is $270,000 and expenses are $120,000. What is net income?

options.why: $330,000 subtracts only the cost of goods sold from revenue and forgets the $120,000 of expenses. Net income takes away every cost, so it must be lower.
$180,000 is the gross profit, revenue minus cost of goods sold. Net income also subtracts the $120,000 of operating expenses that remain.
$840,000 adds all three figures together. Net income is found by subtracting the costs from revenue, so it can never be larger than revenue.
Net income is revenue minus cost of goods sold minus expenses. $450,000 less $270,000 less $120,000 leaves $60,000 of profit for the period.

q: What is a cash flow problem?

options.t: Having too many customers to serve them all well each day
options.why: Having too many customers is a good problem and does not cause a cash shortage. A cash flow problem is about money timing, not demand.

options.t: Not having enough cash to pay bills on time even if profitable
options.why: A cash flow problem means cash runs short when bills fall due, even if the business is profitable on paper. Late customer payments or heavy spending can cause it.

options.t: Having too much profit, so the firm cannot spend it all
options.why: Having too much profit is not a problem, and profit is not trapped cash. A cash flow problem is a shortage of cash, not a surplus of earnings.

options.t: Having too many employees, so the firm cannot pay them all
options.why: Having many employees can raise costs, but the term cash flow problem is about whether cash on hand covers bills. Staff numbers are only one possible cause.

q: A new hire receives no training and makes many mistakes. What is the likely cause?

options.t: Poor onboarding and training
options.why: Without training, a new hire does not know the procedures and makes errors. Poor onboarding and training is the likely cause, and good orientation prevents it.

options.t: Too short a commute to work
options.why: A short commute does not cause mistakes on the job. It is a convenience for the employee and has nothing to do with skills or knowledge.

options.t: Too many benefits to manage
options.why: Too many benefits to manage is an administrative issue for HR. It does not explain why a new hire without training makes many mistakes.

options.t: Too much supervision for them
options.why: Too much supervision would help a new hire avoid errors, not cause them. The real gap is missing training, not too much guidance.

q: What is a job description?

options.t: A list of company products and their prices for sale now
options.why: A job description lists the duties and requirements of a position, not products and prices. Price lists belong in a sales catalog.

options.t: A record of past pay received by an employee in the firm
options.why: Past pay received is a payroll record kept for each employee. A job description describes a role, not what a person earned.

options.t: A document listing the duties and requirements of a position
options.why: A job description is a document listing the duties and requirements of a position. It guides recruiting, training and performance reviews.

options.t: A summary of interview questions the employer will ask
options.why: Interview questions are prepared by the hiring team as a separate guide. A job description describes the role being filled, not the interview.

q: What are employee benefits?

options.t: The hourly wage that a worker is paid for each hour of work
options.why: An hourly wage is basic pay, which is direct compensation. Benefits are extras given on top of pay.

options.t: A work assignment given to a worker by a manager each week
options.why: A work assignment is a task from a manager. It is part of the job, not a form of compensation.

options.t: A fine for lateness that is taken out of the paycheck now
options.why: A fine for lateness is a penalty taken from pay. Benefits are positive extras such as insurance or paid leave.

options.t: Non-wage compensation such as health insurance and paid leave
options.why: Employee benefits are non-wage compensation such as health insurance, paid leave and retirement plans. They add value beyond the paycheck.

q: Two job offers pay the same salary but one includes health insurance. Which has higher total value?

options.t: They are exactly equal in value
options.why: The two offers are not equal. Health insurance has real monetary value, since the employee would otherwise pay for it, so the offer that includes it is worth more.

options.t: The one without insurance
options.why: The offer without insurance is worth less. With the same salary, the employee would still need to pay for coverage separately.

options.t: The one with health insurance
options.why: With the same salary, the offer that includes health insurance has higher total value. Benefits add to compensation beyond the paycheck.

options.t: Neither, benefits have no value
options.why: Benefits do have value. Health insurance can be worth thousands of dollars a year, so it makes one offer better than the other.

q: What is progressive discipline?

options.t: Ignoring all misconduct and letting staff do as they please
options.why: Ignoring misconduct lets problems grow and is unfair to other workers. Progressive discipline responds to misconduct with steps.

options.t: A series of increasingly serious steps for repeated misconduct
options.why: Progressive discipline is a series of increasingly serious steps for repeated misconduct, such as a verbal warning, a written warning and then suspension or dismissal. It gives employees a chance to improve.

options.t: Firing at the first mistake, with no warning and no second chance
options.why: Firing at the first mistake with no warning is the opposite of progressive discipline. The approach is to escalate gradually.

options.t: Rewarding misconduct with bonuses and extra days off work
options.why: Rewarding misconduct would encourage more of it. Discipline is meant to correct behavior, not reward it.

q: Which field is best as a unique identifier in a customer table?

options.t: A customer ID number
options.why: A customer ID number is unique to each customer. A unique identifier lets the table tell apart two customers who might share names or cities.

options.t: Customer's city name
options.why: Many customers can live in the same city, so city name is not unique. It cannot identify one specific customer.

options.t: Favorite color code
options.why: A favorite color code is shared by many people. It cannot tell one customer apart from another.

options.t: Customer first name
options.why: Many customers share the same first name, such as Maria or John. A first name cannot serve as a unique identifier.

q: What is encryption?

options.t: Making data easier to read by removing all passwords
options.why: Encryption does not remove passwords to make data easier to read. It does the opposite, locking data so that only people with the key can read it.

options.t: Copying data to another drive for backup and safe storage
options.why: Copying data to another drive is a backup. Encryption scrambles data rather than copying it.

options.t: Scrambling data so only authorized people can read it
options.why: Encryption scrambles data so that only authorized people with the key can read it. Even if stolen, the data is useless without that key.

options.t: Deleting data permanently so no one can ever read it
options.why: Deleting data so no one can read it is erasure. Encryption keeps the data but makes it unreadable to unauthorized people.

q: A laptop with customer records is stolen. Which control best limits harm?

options.t: Full-disk encryption
options.why: Full-disk encryption scrambles everything on the laptop, so a thief cannot read the customer records without the key. It limits harm best.

options.t: A longer warranty
options.why: A longer warranty covers repairs, not stolen data. It would not stop a thief from reading the records.

options.t: A colorful laptop case
options.why: A colorful laptop case may make the laptop easier to spot, but it does not protect the data stored inside.

options.t: Faster internet access
options.why: Faster internet does nothing to protect records on a stolen laptop. Protection needs security controls such as encryption.

q: What are the four Ps of marketing?

options.t: People, profit, plans and paper
options.why: People, profit, plans and paper are not the marketing mix. They are not the four recognized Ps.

options.t: Product, price, place and promotion
options.why: The four Ps of marketing are product, price, place and promotion. Together they are the decisions a business makes to reach its customers.

options.t: Pay, purchase, produce and pack
options.why: Pay, purchase, produce and pack are business activities but not the marketing mix. The four Ps have specific names.

options.t: Plan, perform, prove and publish
options.why: Plan, perform, prove and publish are not the marketing mix. The four Ps are product, price, place and promotion.

q: A bakery changes where it sells its cakes by adding a delivery service. Which P changed?

options.t: Promotion
options.why: Promotion is how a business tells customers about a product, such as with ads. Adding delivery changes how customers get the cakes, not how they hear about them.

options.t: Product
options.why: Product is what is sold, including features and quality. The cakes are unchanged, so the product element did not change.

options.t: Price
options.why: Price is what customers pay. A delivery service changes how cakes reach customers, not what they cost.

options.t: Place
options.why: Place covers where and how customers can buy a product. Adding delivery changes how the cakes reach buyers, so it changes the place element.

q: What is positioning?

options.t: How a brand wants customers to see it compared with rivals
options.why: Positioning is how a brand wants customers to see it compared with rivals. It is the image the brand owns in customers' minds.

options.t: Where a product is stored in a warehouse before shipping
options.why: Where a product is stored is a logistics matter. Positioning is about perception, not location in a warehouse.

options.t: How a product is shipped to stores and to customers
options.why: How a product is shipped is distribution. Positioning is about how customers view the brand.

options.t: Where a store is located in a town or a city of the country
options.why: The location of a store is a place decision. Positioning is the image of a brand, not a spot on a map.

q: What is just-in-time inventory?

options.t: Shipping goods once a year in one large bulk order
options.why: Shipping goods once a year in bulk is the opposite of just-in-time. JIT delivers small amounts often, exactly when needed.

options.t: Ordering large amounts of goods in advance to keep a big stock
options.why: Ordering large amounts in advance builds a big stock. Just-in-time does the reverse, keeping stock low.

options.t: Holding large safety stocks always, at every single site
options.why: Holding large safety stocks at every site is costly. Just-in-time aims to cut inventory, not hold more.

options.t: Receiving goods only when needed to reduce storage costs
options.why: Just-in-time inventory means receiving goods only when they are needed. It lowers storage costs and waste, but needs dependable suppliers.
