options.t: The number of units held in stock at the end of every month
options.why: Units held in stock are inventory. A life cycle is about stages.

q: A restaurant's food waste costs $2,000 per month. Which action best reduces waste?

options.t: Order more of every item to be safe from shortages
options.why: Ordering more of every item adds waste. It makes spoilage worse.

options.t: Stop tracking inventory and just guess what to order
options.why: Stopping tracking removes information. The restaurant would waste more.

options.t: Ignore customer preferences and use what the chef likes
options.why: Ignoring customer preferences leads to unsold food. It increases waste.

options.t: Track what is wasted and adjust orders and portions
options.why: Tracking what is wasted and adjusting orders and portions targets the cause. The restaurant buys and serves only what it needs.

q: What is just-in-time (JIT) inventory?

options.t: Keeping large stocks for many years
options.why: Keeping large stocks for years is the opposite of JIT. JIT keeps inventory low.

options.t: Ordering everything at the start of the year
options.why: Ordering everything at the start of the year builds a big stock. JIT orders as needed.

options.t: Receiving goods only as they are needed
options.why: Just-in-time inventory means receiving goods only as they are needed. It cuts storage costs and waste.

options.t: Producing nothing at all for the market
options.why: Producing nothing is not JIT. JIT produces to match demand.

q: A company wants to cut costs without reducing quality. Which approach is most sensible?

options.t: Use cheaper, unsafe materials today
options.why: Cheaper, unsafe materials lower quality and risk harm. They would not be sensible.

options.t: Cut all training for the new staff
options.why: Cutting training raises errors and hurts quality. It is not a sensible way to cut costs.

options.t: Skip safety inspections to save time
options.why: Skipping safety inspections risks accidents and fines. It is a poor choice.

options.t: Streamline processes to remove waste
options.why: Streamlining processes removes waste while keeping quality. It lowers costs sensibly.

q: What is an emergency evacuation plan?

options.t: Steps for safely leaving a building during danger
options.why: An emergency evacuation plan sets out steps for safely leaving a building during danger. It protects people in a fire or other emergency.

options.t: A sales target for the next quarter of the year
options.why: A sales target is a business goal. An evacuation plan is a safety procedure.

options.t: A list of employee birthdays posted in the break room
options.why: A list of birthdays is a staff note. It is not a safety plan.

options.t: A parking schedule for staff cars and visitors
options.why: A parking schedule organizes cars. It is not an evacuation plan.

q: An employee is offered a chance to lead a short project. What is the best reason to accept?

options.t: It removes accountability from the whole team
options.why: Leading a project does not remove accountability. It adds responsibility.

options.t: It builds leadership skills and shows initiative
options.why: Leading a short project builds leadership skills and shows initiative. It helps the employee grow and be noticed.

options.t: It lets you avoid other tasks for a long while
options.why: Leading does not let you avoid other tasks. It may add work.

options.t: It guarantees a big raise by the end of next week
options.why: A raise is not guaranteed. Leadership experience can help in time.

q: Which is an example of a long-term career goal?

options.t: Finishing today's task before the shift ends
options.why: Finishing today's task is a daily goal. A long-term goal looks years ahead.

options.t: Eating lunch on time every day this week
options.why: Eating lunch on time is a daily habit. It is not a career goal.

options.t: Replying to one email from a client today
options.why: Replying to one email is a short task. It is not long term.

options.t: Becoming a department manager within ten years
options.why: Becoming a department manager within ten years is a long-term career goal. It sets a target position and a timeline.

q: Why follow the chain of command at work?

options.t: It keeps communication and decisions organized
options.why: Following the chain of command keeps communication and decisions organized. People know who to report to and who decides.

options.t: It prevents employees from speaking at work
options.why: It does not stop employees speaking. It guides who they speak to.

options.t: It removes accountability from the managers
options.why: It does not remove accountability. It clarifies it.

options.t: It lets you skip supervisors whenever you wish
options.why: Skipping supervisors breaks the structure. It causes confusion.

q: An applicant is asked 'Tell me about a time you solved a problem.' What is the best way to answer?

options.t: Give a vague answer with no real details at all
options.why: A vague answer with no details tells the interviewer nothing. It fails to show skill.

options.t: Describe the situation, your action and the result
options.why: Describing the situation, your action and the result shows how you solve problems. It gives a clear, concrete example.

options.t: Blame a former employer for how you left the job
options.why: Blaming a former employer sounds negative. It hurts your chances.

options.t: Say you have never had a problem at any job ever
options.why: Saying you have never had a problem is unlikely to be believed. It avoids the question.

q: What is a professional portfolio?

options.t: A list of friends and their phone numbers
options.why: A list of friends is personal. A portfolio shows professional work.

options.t: A schedule of vacation days for the staff
options.why: A vacation schedule is an HR record. It is not a portfolio.

options.t: A collection of work samples showing skills
options.why: A professional portfolio is a collection of work samples showing skills. Employers can see real examples of what you can do.

options.t: A collection of receipts from past purchases
options.why: A collection of receipts is financial records. It is not a portfolio.

q: A retailer sees that online sales are growing faster than store sales. Which strategic response is most logical?

options.t: Invest more in its online presence
options.why: Investing more in its online presence follows the growth trend. It puts resources where sales are rising.

options.t: Raise store prices and ignore it
options.why: Raising store prices and ignoring the trend wastes the signal. It could hurt sales.

options.t: Close the website for good soon
options.why: Closing the website would end the fastest-growing channel. It is illogical.

options.t: Ignore the data and keep things as is
options.why: Ignoring the data misses a clear trend. Strategy should respond to evidence.

q: A company is deciding between two expansion plans. What should managers do before choosing?

options.t: Flip a coin and follow whatever the result is
options.why: Flipping a coin leaves a major decision to chance. Managers should use analysis.

options.t: Wait for a competitor to decide for the firm
options.why: Waiting for a competitor to decide gives away control. The firm should decide itself.

options.t: Choose the first idea with no analysis at all
options.why: Choosing the first idea with no analysis is risky. Better options may exist.

options.t: Compare costs, benefits and risks of each plan
options.why: Comparing costs, benefits and risks of each plan allows an informed choice. It helps managers pick the better expansion.

q: What is delegation?

options.t: Firing everyone on the team at once
options.why: Firing everyone is not delegation. Delegation shares work.

options.t: Assigning tasks and authority to others
options.why: Delegation means assigning tasks and authority to others. It frees managers and develops employees.

options.t: Refusing to share information with the team
options.why: Refusing to share information blocks delegation. It prevents work.

options.t: Doing every task alone with no help
options.why: Doing every task alone is the opposite of delegation. It overloads one person.

q: Which is an example of demonstrating initiative at work?

options.t: Letting others handle everything while you do nothing at all
options.why: Letting others handle everything shows no initiative. It is passive.

options.t: Waiting to be told every step of the work before acting
options.why: Waiting to be told every step shows no initiative. It depends on others.

options.t: Noticing a problem and starting to fix it without being asked
options.why: Noticing a problem and starting to fix it without being asked shows initiative. It shows responsibility and drive.

options.t: Ignoring problems that are not yours to stay out of trouble
options.why: Ignoring problems that are not yours avoids initiative. Initiative acts.

q: A team member always interrupts others in meetings. Which action is best for a supportive coworker?

options.t: Interrupt them back every time they interrupt you in the meeting
options.why: Interrupting them back escalates the issue. It is rude.

options.t: Privately and kindly point out the pattern and suggest listening first
options.why: Privately and kindly pointing out the pattern lets the person improve without embarrassment. It is respectful and helpful.

options.t: Stop attending meetings so you never hear the interrupting at all
options.why: Avoiding meetings avoids the problem. It does not help the team.

options.t: Mock the person publicly in front of the whole team in meetings
options.why: Mocking the person publicly is cruel. It would harm trust.

q: What does it mean to be accountable?

options.t: Accepting responsibility for your actions and results
options.why: Being accountable means accepting responsibility for your actions and results. It includes admitting mistakes and fixing them.

options.t: Doing only what is easy and skipping the hard parts
options.why: Doing only what is easy avoids responsibility. It is not accountability.

options.t: Hiding mistakes from the boss so no one finds out
options.why: Hiding mistakes avoids responsibility. Accountable people own up.

options.t: Blaming others when things go wrong to stay clear
options.why: Blaming others avoids responsibility. Accountability means owning results.

q: A supervisor praises an employee for good work in front of the team. Which outcome is most likely?

options.t: Lower morale for the team as others feel left out
options.why: Public praise does not lower morale as a rule. It tends to raise it.

options.t: Reduced trust in the supervisor over time
options.why: Praise does not reduce trust. It builds it.

options.t: Higher motivation and a stronger team culture
options.why: Praise raises motivation and builds a stronger team culture. People feel valued and want to keep performing.

options.t: More conflict in every case within the team
options.why: Praise does not cause more conflict in every case. It usually encourages cooperation.

q: What is a personal bias?

options.t: A company policy on dress and conduct for all staff
options.why: A dress policy is a company rule. A personal bias is an individual tendency.

options.t: A required skill listed in every job advertisement
options.why: A required skill is a job requirement. It is not a bias.

options.t: A fact proven by research about every person in a group
options.why: A proven fact is not a bias. Bias is not based on evidence.

options.t: A tendency to favor or judge based on preconceived ideas
options.why: A personal bias is a tendency to favor or judge based on preconceived ideas. It can lead to unfair decisions.

q: Which statement best reflects a growth mindset?

options.t: Talent cannot change no matter what you do
options.why: Believing talent cannot change is a fixed mindset. A growth mindset believes people can improve.

options.t: Feedback should be avoided at all times
options.why: Avoiding feedback blocks growth. A growth mindset welcomes it.

options.t: Mistakes mean failure forever for you
options.why: Believing mistakes mean permanent failure is a fixed mindset. Growth mindset sees them as lessons.

options.t: Skills improve with effort and learning
options.why: A growth mindset believes skills improve with effort and learning. It leads to persistence and progress.

q: Two coworkers from different cultures have different views on punctuality. How can the manager best handle it?

options.t: Punish only one of the coworkers and ignore the cultural difference completely
options.why: Punishing only one coworker is unfair. It ignores the cultural difference.

options.t: Discuss expectations clearly and respect differences while meeting company standards
options.why: Discussing expectations clearly and respecting differences while meeting company standards works for both. It builds understanding and keeps the workplace fair.

options.t: Assume one culture is wrong and tell that coworker to adapt to the other one
options.why: Assuming one culture is wrong is disrespectful. It creates resentment.

options.t: Ignore the difference completely and let both coworkers sort it out alone later
options.why: Ignoring the difference and letting them sort it out leaves the conflict. A manager should guide.

q: What is the best way to handle disagreement in a team?

options.t: Avoid speaking to each other for the whole week
options.why: Avoiding each other does not solve disagreement. It leaves tension.

options.t: Insult those who disagree with you in team meetings
options.why: Insulting people harms relationships. It makes teamwork worse.

options.t: Discuss views respectfully and look for common ground
options.why: Discussing views respectfully and looking for common ground resolves disagreement. It keeps the team working together.

options.t: Always let the loudest person win to finish quickly
options.why: Letting the loudest person win ignores good ideas. It is unfair.

q: What does it mean to bootstrap a business?

options.t: Start with personal savings and small revenue instead of outside funding
options.why: Bootstrapping means starting with personal savings and small revenue instead of outside funding. The owner keeps control and avoids debt.

options.t: Sell shares to the public immediately to raise a lot of outside funds
options.why: Selling shares to the public is raising outside funds. Bootstrapping avoids that.

options.t: Borrow from many large banks first before spending any of your savings
options.why: Borrowing from many banks is debt financing. Bootstrapping uses your own money.

options.t: Receive a government grant in every case, with no need to repay it
options.why: A government grant is outside funding. Bootstrapping relies on yourself.

q: A product has strong reviews but poor sales because few people know it exists. What should the owner improve?

options.t: Awareness through targeted promotion
options.why: Correct. Good reviews with weak sales point to low awareness, so targeted promotion such as social media, ads or sampling gets the product in front of likely buyers.

options.t: The product's name and nothing else
options.why: A name matters for branding, but changing it alone does nothing to tell more potential customers the product exists, which is the actual problem described here.

options.t: The company's tax filing each year
options.why: Tax filing is a legal compliance task that has no effect on whether shoppers know about the product, so it cannot fix low sales caused by weak awareness.

options.t: The color of the office walls there
options.why: Office wall color is cosmetic and customers rarely see it, so it does nothing to raise awareness of a product that few people know about.

q: What is a partnership?

options.t: A business owned by shareholders with limited liability for debts
options.why: This describes a corporation, which is owned by shareholders who generally have limited liability for the debts of the business, unlike partners in a general partnership.

options.t: A business owned by two or more people who share profits and risk
options.why: Correct. A partnership is owned by two or more people who share profits, losses, decision making and, in a general partnership, personal liability for the business debts.

options.t: A business owned by one person who keeps all of the profits
options.why: This describes a sole proprietorship, where a single owner keeps all profits but also carries all of the risk and unlimited personal liability for debts.

options.t: A government agency that regulates trade and sets business rules
options.why: Government agencies such as the FTC or SBA regulate or assist business but do not own businesses for profit, so this is not a form of ownership.

q: A new company notices that rivals cannot match its low cost because of a clever process it invented. What is this?

options.t: A large trade deficit
options.why: A trade deficit means a nation imports more than it exports. It is a national measure and says nothing about one firm's cost advantage from its own process.

options.t: A local zoning rule
options.why: A zoning rule is a local land use regulation. It does not come from a firm's invention, and it would not explain why rivals cannot match low costs.

options.t: A deep recession cycle
options.why: A recession is a broad economic downturn in output and jobs. It affects all firms and is not an advantage created by a firm's own clever process.

options.t: A competitive advantage
options.why: Correct. A competitive advantage is something a firm does better than rivals, such as a proprietary low cost process, which lets it win customers or earn higher margins.

q: Why do entrepreneurs write a mission statement?

options.t: To list all employees' salaries and bonuses
options.why: Salaries and bonuses are compensation details kept in payroll and HR records, not part of a mission statement, which describes why the business exists and what it values.

options.t: To avoid making plans for the whole business
options.why: A mission statement guides planning rather than replacing it. Writing one helps a firm set goals and strategies, so avoiding plans is the opposite of its purpose.

options.t: To state the purpose and values of the business
options.why: Correct. A mission statement explains why the business exists, whom it serves and what values guide it, helping owners and employees make consistent decisions and stay focused.

options.t: To count the customers who visit in a month
options.why: Counting monthly customers is a sales or marketing metric tracked through records and reports, not the purpose of a mission statement, which expresses purpose and values.

q: An entrepreneur realizes her prototype has a safety defect after a few sales. What is the best response?

options.t: Stop sales, notify customers and fix the product
options.why: Correct. Stopping sales, notifying buyers and fixing the defect protects customers from harm, limits legal liability under product safety laws and preserves the firm's reputation and trust.

options.t: Raise the price to cover the risk and keep selling
options.why: Raising the price does not remove the danger to buyers. Knowingly selling an unsafe product can expose the owner to lawsuits and regulatory penalties.

options.t: Blame customers for misuse of the new product
options.why: Blaming customers is unethical when the defect is the company's own fault, and it leaves the hazard in place, which invites injuries, recalls and legal claims.

options.t: Keep selling quietly and say nothing to buyers
options.why: Hiding a known safety defect is unethical and may be illegal, because sellers must warn buyers and can be held liable for injuries caused by a defective product.

q: What is net worth?

options.t: The price of a house
options.why: A house price is the market value of one asset. Net worth subtracts all debts from everything owned, so a single price does not measure it.

options.t: Total income of the firm
options.why: Total income is money earned over a period, a flow figure. Net worth is a snapshot of owned assets less debts owed at a point in time.

options.t: Assets minus liabilities
options.why: Correct. Net worth equals assets minus liabilities, showing what is truly owned after debts are paid, and it is used by lenders and individuals to measure financial health.

options.t: Monthly living expenses
options.why: Monthly living expenses are recurring costs used for budgeting. They do not capture what a person owns or owes, which is what net worth shows.

q: A person has $20,000 in assets and $26,000 in debts. What is her net worth?

options.t: Positive $46,000
options.why: Adding assets and debts together ($20,000 + $26,000 = $46,000) is wrong, because debts must be subtracted from assets, not added to them to find net worth.

options.t: Negative $6,000
options.why: Correct. Net worth is assets minus liabilities: $20,000 - $26,000 = -$6,000. The person owes more than she owns, so her net worth is negative.

options.t: Negative $20,000
options.why: Negative $20,000 ignores the debts of $26,000 being subtracted. The correct calculation is $20,000 - $26,000, which gives negative $6,000 rather than this figure.

options.t: Positive $6,000
options.why: The sign is reversed. Because debts of $26,000 exceed assets of $20,000, the difference is negative $6,000, not a positive amount.

q: Why is it wise to compare prices before a large purchase?

options.t: To avoid learning about the product
options.why: Comparing prices involves learning about products and sellers, so it does the opposite of avoiding knowledge. Shoppers research items to make better informed buying decisions.

options.t: To increase the price you pay
options.why: Comparison shopping aims to lower, not raise, what you pay. Finding a higher price would defeat the purpose of checking several sellers before buying.

options.t: To guarantee the purchase is free
options.why: Comparing prices cannot make a purchase free. It only helps buyers find the lowest price or best deal for a product they still must pay for.

options.t: To get better value for the money
options.why: Correct. Comparing prices, quality and features across sellers helps a buyer find the best value for the money, which matters most on large purchases like cars or appliances.

q: A business pays $1,200 rent, $800 wages and $300 utilities monthly and earns $3,000 in sales with $700 in materials. What is its monthly profit?

options.why: Correct. Profit equals revenue minus expenses: $3,000 - ($1,200 + $800 + $300 + $700) = $3,000 - $3,000 = $0. The business exactly breaks even this month.
Subtracting only some costs gives $700, but all four expenses ($1,200 + $800 + $300 + $700 = $3,000) must come out of $3,000 sales, leaving zero.
This is the sales figure, which is revenue and not profit. Profit requires subtracting all expenses from the $3,000 earned, which leaves $0.
This equals the rent alone. Profit subtracts all expenses, rent, wages, utilities and materials totaling $3,000, from $3,000 of sales, which leaves $0.

q: What is a stock?

options.t: A discount coupon for the shop
options.why: A coupon is a promotional voucher that gives a price discount on goods. A stock represents ownership in a corporation, not a discount from a store.

options.t: A share of ownership in a company
options.why: Correct. A stock is a share of ownership in a company. Shareholders may earn dividends and gains if the price rises, but they also risk losing value.

options.t: A loan to a firm, repaid later
options.why: This describes a bond, where an investor lends money to a firm or government and is repaid with interest. A stock gives ownership, not a loan.

options.t: An insurance policy on a firm
options.why: An insurance policy transfers the risk of loss to an insurer for a premium. A stock does not protect against loss but represents company ownership.

q: What is a bond?

options.t: A bank account fee charged each month by a bank
options.why: A monthly account fee is a bank service charge. A bond is an investment in which a lender receives interest, not a fee charged by the bank.

options.t: A share of ownership in a company that is paid out
options.why: This describes a stock, which represents ownership and may pay dividends. A bond is a debt contract, so the bondholder is a lender and not an owner.

options.t: A savings account at a bank that pays low interest
options.why: A savings account is a bank deposit product that pays low interest, usually insured. A bond is a loan an investor makes to an issuer.

options.t: A loan to a government or company that pays interest
options.why: Correct. A bond is a loan made by an investor to a government or company, which promises to pay interest regularly and return the principal at maturity.

q: A saver earns 4% interest on $1,000 for one year with simple interest. How much interest does she earn?

options.why: This adds the interest to the principal ($1,000 + $40 = $1,040), which is the ending balance, not the interest earned, which is only the $40 portion.
This would be a 0.4% rate. Four percent of $1,000 is $1,000 x 0.04 = $40, so $4 understates the interest by a factor of ten.
Correct. Simple interest equals principal x rate x time: $1,000 x 0.04 x 1 year = $40. The saver earns $40 in interest for the year.
This would be a 40% rate. Four percent of $1,000 is $1,000 x 0.04 = $40, so $400 overstates the interest by a factor of ten.

q: What does depreciation measure?

options.t: The increase in a firm's sales over years
options.why: An increase in a firm's sales over time is growth in revenue. Depreciation is a decline in value, so it moves in the opposite direction from sales growth.

options.t: The interest paid on a loan each month
options.why: Monthly loan interest is a financing cost that is paid to lenders. Depreciation is a non-cash accounting allocation for the loss in value of an asset.

options.t: The cost of advertising a product online
options.why: Advertising cost is a marketing expense that is recorded in the period it is incurred. It is not related to the loss in value of equipment.

options.t: The decrease in an asset's value over time
options.why: Correct. Depreciation measures how much an asset such as a vehicle or machine loses value over time from use and age, and it is spread over its useful life.

q: Why do businesses use budgets?

options.t: To increase every expense so firms grow
options.why: Budgets are meant to control and plan spending, not raise every expense. Increasing all costs would hurt profits rather than help a business grow in a planned way.

options.t: To plan and control income and spending
options.why: Correct. A budget estimates income and expenses ahead of time so owners can plan spending, compare actual results against the plan, and control costs to reach goals.

options.t: To hide losses from the owners and lenders
options.why: Budgets increase transparency and help owners and lenders see the real picture. Hiding losses would be dishonest and is not a legitimate business use of budgeting.

options.t: To avoid tracking money coming in or out
options.why: Budgets require tracking money in and out, since actual results are compared with the plan. Avoiding tracking would make a budget useless for control.

q: What is the purpose of an employee handbook?

options.t: To advertise to customers and the wider public
options.why: Advertising to customers is the job of marketing materials. An employee handbook is an internal document for staff, not a public advertisement of the business.

options.t: To record profits and dividends paid out
options.why: Profits and dividends are recorded in accounting statements and financial records, not in an employee handbook, which covers workplace policies and employee conduct and benefits.

options.t: To explain policies, rules and expectations
options.why: Correct. An employee handbook explains company policies, rules, benefits and expectations so that workers know what is required and how they will be treated, reducing disputes.

options.t: To list product prices for the customers to see
options.why: Product prices belong in price lists or catalogs for customers. An employee handbook is an internal guide to workplace policies, not a sales document.

q: Applicants are asked about their marital status and number of children. Why is this a concern?

options.t: Such questions may lead to illegal discrimination
options.why: Correct. Questions about marital status or children are not job related and can lead to illegal discrimination under laws such as Title VII, so interviewers should avoid them.

options.t: They guarantee a better hire every time they are used
options.why: No question guarantees a better hire. These questions are not job related and can expose the employer to discrimination claims rather than improve hiring quality.

options.t: They are required by law for every single employer
options.why: No law requires employers to ask about marital status or children. Employers should ask only job related questions, so this is a false claim.

options.t: They save time so employers can pick people faster
options.why: Saving time does not justify asking improper questions. Using personal details to choose people is potentially illegal discrimination and exposes the firm to lawsuits.

q: What is a probationary period?

options.t: A time when all new employees are promoted
options.why: A probationary period does not promote everyone. It is a trial time in which the employer evaluates the new hire, who may or may not stay on.

options.t: A time when employees stop work for reviews
options.why: Stopping work for reviews is not what probation means. Employees usually keep working during probation while the employer observes performance and fit for the position.

options.t: A time for tax filing by the company's staff
options.why: Tax filing is an accounting obligation, not an HR concept. A probationary period is about evaluating a new employee, not about taxes or staff filings.

options.t: An initial time to evaluate a new employee's fit
options.why: Correct. A probationary period is an initial trial time, often 30 to 90 days, when the employer evaluates a new employee's performance, skills and fit before permanent status.

q: What does cross-training do for a business?

options.t: Teaches employees to perform multiple roles
options.why: Correct. Cross-training teaches employees to perform several roles, which gives the firm flexibility to cover absences and busy periods and gives workers broader skills.

options.t: It limits employees to a single task for good
options.why: Cross-training does the opposite of limiting workers to one task. Its purpose is to expand the range of jobs each employee can do.

options.t: Reduces employee skills over the years
options.why: Cross-training builds skills rather than reducing them. Employees learn additional duties, which makes them more valuable and gives the firm more flexibility over time.

options.t: Replaces all supervisors in the company
options.why: Cross-training does not replace supervisors. Supervisors still plan, direct and evaluate work, while cross-training just prepares staff to handle more than one role.

q: A company wants to measure employee satisfaction. Which method is most appropriate?

options.t: Asking only the manager
options.why: Asking only the manager gives a one-sided view and may miss how employees really feel. Staff themselves are the best source of satisfaction data.

options.t: Ignoring employees
options.why: Ignoring employees gathers no information at all, so satisfaction cannot be measured. Measuring requires collecting data directly from the workers who are being studied.

options.t: An anonymous survey
options.why: Correct. An anonymous survey lets employees answer honestly without fear of punishment, giving management reliable data on satisfaction that can then guide improvements.

options.t: Guessing based on sales
options.why: Guessing from sales is indirect and unreliable, since sales depend on many things besides morale. Satisfaction should be measured by asking employees directly.

q: What is a database record?

options.t: A single letter typed into a database field by a user
options.why: A single typed letter is only one character of data, not a record. A record groups many related fields, such as name, phone and address.

options.t: A complete set of related data about one item or person
options.why: Correct. A database record is a complete set of related fields about one item, person or transaction, such as a customer's name, address and phone number in one row.

options.t: A website's color theme chosen by the design team
options.why: A color theme is a design choice for how a website looks. It is not a unit of stored data in a database table.

options.t: A printer setting used for printing on paper pages
options.why: A printer setting controls how documents print. A database record is a unit of stored information about one entity, not a device configuration.

q: An employee finds a USB drive in the parking lot. What is the safest action?

options.t: Use it for personal files after plugging it in at work
options.why: Plugging an unknown drive into a work computer is dangerous because it may carry malware that infects the network, and personal use of it is not appropriate.

options.t: Plug it into a work computer to see what it holds inside
options.why: Curiosity is how attackers get in. Unknown drives can hold malware that runs automatically, so plugging one in to see its contents risks infecting the computer.

options.t: Share its contents with coworkers to find out whose it is
options.why: Sharing contents requires opening the files, which exposes the system to malware and could leak private information. The drive should not be opened by staff.

options.t: Give it to the security or IT team without plugging it in
options.why: Correct. Unknown USB drives may be planted by attackers, so the safe step is to hand it to security or IT unplugged so that specialists can inspect it safely.

q: What is a strong password?

options.t: The same code used on every site you visit
options.why: Reusing one password on every site is weak, because a breach at any one site exposes all accounts. Each account should have its own unique password.

options.t: A long mix of letters, numbers and symbols
options.why: Correct. A strong password is long and combines uppercase and lowercase letters, numbers and symbols, which makes it hard to guess or crack and should be unique to each account.

options.t: A birthday written as numbers and nothing else
options.why: A birthday is easy to find or guess and uses only digits, so it offers little protection. Personal dates should not be used as passwords.

options.t: A common word like 'password' or 'letmein'
options.why: Common words like 'password' or 'letmein' top the lists attackers try first, so they are cracked almost instantly and are among the weakest choices.

q: What is the purpose of two-factor authentication?

options.t: Adding a second step to verify identity
options.why: Correct. Two-factor authentication requires a second proof of identity, such as a code sent to a phone, so a stolen password alone cannot give access to the account.

options.t: Speeding up logins for all the users
options.why: Two-factor authentication adds a step, so it makes logins slightly slower rather than faster. Its purpose is stronger security, not speed.

options.t: Sharing passwords safely among a team
options.why: Sharing passwords is unsafe and is not what two-factor authentication does. It adds a verification step for each user's own account rather than allowing password sharing.

options.t: Deleting old accounts that nobody uses
options.why: Deleting inactive accounts is account management and housekeeping. Two-factor authentication instead verifies a user's identity during login by requiring a second step.

q: A report's numbers come from a survey of only ten people. How should a manager treat the results?

options.t: As useless in every case of this kind of survey
options.why: Saying the results are useless in every case goes too far. Small surveys can still give rough insights, but their limits should be recognized.

options.t: As proof for the entire market of buyers
options.why: Ten respondents cannot represent a whole market of buyers, so treating the results as proof would overstate what the data show and risk poor decisions.

options.t: With caution because the sample is very small
options.why: Correct. A sample of ten is too small to be statistically reliable or representative, so results should be used cautiously and confirmed with a larger, well chosen sample.

options.t: As more reliable than large surveys of the public
options.why: Larger samples are usually more reliable because they reduce sampling error. A ten person survey is less reliable than a large survey, not more.

q: What is a business record?

options.t: A document that tracks business transactions or activities
options.why: Correct. A business record, such as an invoice, receipt or ledger entry, documents transactions or activities, supporting accounting, tax reporting, legal compliance and decision making.

options.t: A collection of rumors that staff share with each other
options.why: Rumors are unverified talk and not documents. A business record is an organized, reliable account of transactions or activities that can be used as evidence.

options.t: An advertisement slogan that a firm uses on its signs
options.why: A slogan is a marketing phrase meant to promote a brand. It does not document transactions or activities, so it is not a business record.

options.t: A song recorded in a studio and played on the radio in stores
options.why: A recorded song is entertainment media, not a document of business transactions. Business records are written or electronic files tracking activities such as sales and expenses.

q: What is a marketing plan?

options.t: A list of suppliers and what the firm buys from them each year
options.why: A list of suppliers is part of purchasing records. A marketing plan covers how the firm will promote and sell to customers, not who supplies the business.

options.t: A list of employee shifts for the next two weeks at the main store
options.why: Employee shift schedules are an operations and HR document used for staffing. A marketing plan instead describes how the business will reach customers and meet sales goals.

options.t: A document describing how a business will reach its customers and goals
options.why: Correct. A marketing plan outlines target markets, the marketing mix, budget and goals, describing how the business will reach customers and achieve its objectives over a period.

options.t: A tax return filed by a business with the government each year
options.why: A tax return reports income to the government under tax law. It is a financial and legal filing, unrelated to marketing strategy.

q: A clothing brand wants to attract teens. Which promotional channel is likely to be most effective?

options.t: Radio spots at 3 a.m. on weeknights only
options.why: Radio spots at 3 a.m. on weeknights reach few listeners and almost no teens, so this timing would waste money on an audience that is asleep.

options.t: Social media platforms popular with teens
options.why: Correct. Teens spend much of their time on social media platforms, so ads there reach the target market directly and cost effectively, and they can feature influencers and trends.

options.t: Print ads in a business trade journal
options.why: Trade journals are read by industry professionals, not teens, so print ads there would miss the target market the clothing brand wants to attract.

options.t: Mailers to retirement homes in the region
options.why: Retirement homes house older adults, who are not the target teen market, so mailers sent there would reach the wrong audience and waste promotional funds.

q: What is the main goal of advertising?

options.t: To reduce product quality to cut costs on goods
options.why: Reducing quality to cut costs is a production decision. Advertising communicates about a product and does not change its quality or cost of manufacture.

options.t: To reduce the number of customers so each gets served
options.why: Advertising is meant to attract customers and raise sales, so it does the opposite of reducing the number of customers a business serves.

options.t: To set government rules for how firms may sell
options.why: Governments, not advertisers, set the rules on selling, and advertising itself is regulated by agencies such as the FTC rather than creating the rules.

options.t: To inform and persuade customers about a product
options.why: Correct. The main goal of advertising is to inform and persuade customers about a product, building awareness and encouraging them to buy or remember the brand.

q: What is a coupon?

options.t: A receipt for a refund given after a return
options.why: A receipt for a refund records a return transaction. A coupon is a voucher offered before purchase that lowers what the customer pays.

options.t: A contract with a supplier for raw materials
options.why: A supplier contract is a legal agreement about purchasing raw materials for production. A coupon is a promotional tool aimed at customers, not suppliers.

options.t: A permit to run a business in a city or town
options.why: A permit or license is a government authorization to operate a business. A coupon is a retail promotion, not a legal document from the city.

options.t: A voucher that gives a discount on a purchase
options.why: Correct. A coupon is a voucher that gives a discount on a purchase, used as a sales promotion to attract new buyers and encourage trial of a product.

q: A brand uses the same color, logo and slogan on every package and ad. What is the benefit?

options.t: Customers get confused by the same look
options.why: Consistent branding reduces confusion rather than causing it. The same look makes products easy to spot and links them in the buyer's mind.

options.t: Customers recognize and remember the brand
options.why: Correct. Using the same color, logo and slogan builds brand identity, so customers recognize and remember the brand quickly, which builds familiarity and loyalty over time.

options.t: Competitors stop selling in the market
options.why: Branding does not force competitors out of the market. Competitors keep selling, and a consistent brand only helps your products stand out from theirs.

options.t: Prices automatically fall for all goods
options.why: Consistent branding has no automatic effect on prices. Prices depend on costs, demand and competition, not on using the same logo or color.

q: What is public relations?

options.t: Setting product prices for all items sold in the stores
options.why: Setting product prices is a pricing decision in the marketing mix, handled separately. Public relations deals with the firm's image and its communication with the public.

options.t: Selling products door to door, with a large team of agents
options.why: Door to door selling is personal selling, a different promotional method. Public relations focuses on reputation and relationships rather than direct sales through agents.

options.t: Managing a company's image and relationships with the public
options.why: Correct. Public relations manages a company's image and its relationships with the public, media and community, using tools such as news releases and community events.

options.t: Making products in a factory for sale to the general public
options.why: Making products is a production activity done in a factory. Public relations is a communication function that shapes how the public views the company.

q: Which is an example of a sales promotion?

options.t: A buy-one-get-one-free offer
options.why: Correct. A buy-one-get-one-free offer is a sales promotion, a short term incentive such as a coupon, rebate or discount that encourages customers to buy now.

options.t: A product's warranty card
options.why: A warranty card records the manufacturer's repair promise after sale. It is a service document, not a short term incentive to encourage buying.

options.t: A company's annual report
options.why: An annual report summarizes a company's finances for investors and owners. It is not a promotional offer to customers, so it is not a sales promotion.

options.t: A supplier invoice for goods
options.why: A supplier invoice is a bill from a vendor for goods the business bought. It is an accounting record and not a customer promotion.

q: A company learns customers like its product but think the price is too high. What marketing mix element should it review?

options.t: Price
options.why: Correct. Customers who like a product but find the price too high are signaling a pricing issue, so the firm should review the price element of the marketing mix.

options.t: Logo
options.why: A logo is part of branding and does not set what customers pay. The complaint concerns price, not the company's visual identity, so the logo is not the element to review.

options.t: Place
options.why: Place covers where and how products are distributed. Customers like the product and object only to cost, so distribution is not the element at issue.

options.t: Promotion
options.why: Promotion covers advertising and communication. The customers already like the product, so the concern is cost rather than a lack of information about it.

q: What is an invoice?

options.t: A request for a refund sent by a customer to a store
options.why: A customer's refund request is a return or credit request. An invoice is a document the seller sends to bill the buyer.

options.t: A product warranty that comes with a new item bought
options.why: A warranty promises repair or replacement of a product after the sale. An invoice instead requests payment for goods or services that were already sold.

options.t: A bill that lists goods or services sold and the amount due
options.why: Correct. An invoice is a bill from a seller to a buyer listing the goods or services sold, their prices and the total amount due, with payment terms.

options.t: A schedule of workers for the coming week at a large shop
options.why: A worker schedule is a staffing document for planning shifts. An invoice is a financial document that requests payment from the customer.

q: A store's computer shows 50 shirts in stock, but a count finds 42. What is the difference called?

options.t: Markup
options.why: Markup is the amount added to cost to set the selling price. It is a pricing figure, not a shortfall in inventory counts.

options.t: Shrinkage
options.why: Correct. Shrinkage is the loss of inventory from theft, damage or error. Here 50 - 42 = 8 shirts are missing from the records, which is shrinkage.

options.t: Revenue
options.why: Revenue is money earned from sales. It does not describe the difference between recorded stock and a physical count of goods on hand.

options.t: Depreciation
options.why: Depreciation is the decline in value of a long term asset over time, not a count mismatch of inventory, so it does not describe missing shirts.

q: What is customer fulfillment?

options.t: Setting prices for the goods sold by a firm in a shop
options.why: Setting prices is a marketing and pricing decision made before sale. Fulfillment is about delivering the product after the customer has placed an order.

options.t: Hiring workers for the firm to staff its shops
options.why: Hiring is a human resources function. Customer fulfillment concerns completing orders so that customers receive what they bought, not staffing the firm.

options.t: Designing a logo for the firm to use on its signs
options.why: Logo design is a branding task. Fulfillment deals with order processing, packing and shipping rather than the visual identity of the company.

options.t: Getting the product to the customer after an order
options.why: Correct. Customer fulfillment is the process of receiving, packing, shipping and delivering the product to the customer after an order is placed, completing the sale.

q: What is a safety data sheet used for?

options.t: Tracking customer orders placed on the firm's main website
options.why: Tracking online orders uses order management or e-commerce software. A safety data sheet instead describes the hazards of a specific chemical product.

options.t: Promoting a product to customers through ads and sales events
options.why: Promotion uses ads and sales events. A safety data sheet is a workplace safety document and has no promotional purpose.

options.t: Informing workers about hazards of chemicals and safe handling
options.why: Correct. A safety data sheet (SDS) tells workers a chemical's hazards, safe handling, storage, first aid and emergency steps, as required by OSHA's hazard communication standard.

options.t: Listing employee pay rates and the hours worked each week
options.why: Pay rates and hours are payroll records. A safety data sheet covers chemical hazards, not employee compensation or time records.

q: A supervisor sees an employee operating a machine without protective gear. What should the supervisor do?

options.t: Wait until an accident happens before taking any action
options.why: Waiting for an accident is negligent and violates a supervisor's duty. Safety rules exist to prevent injuries, so the supervisor must act at once.

options.t: Stop the work and ensure proper safety gear is used
options.why: Correct. A supervisor must stop the unsafe work and make sure protective gear is used. OSHA requires employers to protect workers, and acting prevents injuries and fines.

options.t: Ignore it to keep production moving at full speed
options.why: Ignoring a safety violation puts the worker at risk and exposes the company to injury claims and OSHA penalties, so speed should never come before safety.

options.t: Praise the employee for working at high speed
options.why: Praising unsafe behavior encourages others to copy it. Speed does not excuse skipping protective gear, which exists to prevent injuries.

q: What is outsourcing?

options.t: Closing the business and selling off all its assets
options.why: Closing a business and selling assets is liquidation or dissolution. Outsourcing means keeping the business but paying another company to do certain tasks.

options.t: Selling to customers abroad by opening a foreign branch
options.why: Selling to customers abroad by opening a foreign branch is expansion into international markets, not outsourcing, which is contracting out work to another company.

options.t: Doing all tasks internally with the firm's own staff
options.why: Doing all tasks with the firm's own staff is insourcing, the opposite of outsourcing, where tasks are given to outside providers.

options.t: Hiring another company to perform tasks or services
options.why: Correct. Outsourcing means hiring another company to perform tasks or services, such as payroll, customer support or manufacturing, often to cut costs or use specialist skills.

q: Why is punctuality important at work?

options.t: It shows reliability and respect for others' time
options.why: Correct. Arriving on time shows reliability, responsibility and respect for coworkers' and customers' time, and it helps teams run smoothly and builds a good professional reputation.

options.t: It reduces the need for planning, so workers come in
options.why: Punctuality does not reduce planning. Arriving on time requires planning your schedule and commute, and being late usually disrupts the plans of others.

options.t: It has no effect on teamwork or morale at work
options.why: Lateness disrupts coworkers and can lower morale, so punctuality does affect teamwork. Claiming it has no effect ignores how reliability supports a team.

options.t: It only matters for managers and the leaders of teams
options.why: Punctuality is expected from every employee at every level. It is not limited to managers, and all workers affect schedules and team results.

q: An employee is asked to complete two urgent tasks at the same time. What is the best action?

options.t: Work on both without telling anyone
options.why: Working on both without telling anyone leaves the supervisor unaware of conflicts and risks missed deadlines. Communication is needed when priorities compete.

options.t: Ignore both tasks and do something else
options.why: Ignoring both tasks fails the employee's responsibilities and could harm the business. Urgent work must be handled, not set aside for something unrelated.

options.t: Clarify priorities with the supervisor
options.why: Correct. When two urgent tasks conflict, asking the supervisor which takes priority ensures the most important work is done first and shows good communication and judgment.

options.t: Do only the easier task, without asking
options.why: Doing only the easier task without asking leaves the other urgent task undone and shows poor judgment. The supervisor should decide the priority.

q: What does continuing education help workers do?

options.t: Reduce job options for the worker over time
options.why: Continuing education adds skills and qualifications, so it increases job options. Reducing them would be the opposite of its purpose.

options.t: Avoid new technology so old methods can be kept
options.why: Continuing education helps workers learn new technology and methods, not avoid them. Staying with old methods would leave skills outdated.

options.t: Stop earning raises and promotions over the years
options.why: Continuing education usually helps workers earn raises and promotions by increasing their skills, so stopping advancement is the opposite of its effect.

options.t: Keep skills current and prepare for advancement
options.why: Correct. Continuing education, through classes, certifications or training, keeps skills current as industries change and prepares workers for promotions and new responsibilities.

q: A worker wants a raise. Which approach is most professional?

options.t: Threaten to quit without a plan for what comes next
options.why: Threatening to quit with no plan is unprofessional and risky, since it may damage relationships and leave you without a job if the bluff fails.

options.t: Prepare examples of accomplishments and request a meeting
options.why: Correct. Preparing examples of accomplishments and requesting a meeting presents a professional case based on results, showing the employee's value and respecting the manager's time.

options.t: Complain to coworkers about the boss and the low pay
options.why: Complaining to coworkers spreads negativity and does not address the issue with the person who can decide. It can also hurt your reputation.

options.t: Demand a raise by email in anger to show how you feel
options.why: An angry demand by email is unprofessional and likely to be refused. Raises are better requested calmly in person with evidence of performance.

q: What is a code of conduct?

options.t: Rules describing expected workplace behavior
options.why: Correct. A code of conduct sets out rules describing the expected behavior, ethics and standards for employees, helping a workplace stay respectful, safe and legally compliant.

options.t: A schedule of events for the year ahead
options.why: A schedule of events is a calendar. A code of conduct is a policy that defines acceptable and unacceptable behavior at work.

options.t: A list of discounts offered to the customers
options.why: A list of discounts is a sales or promotion document for customers. A code of conduct is directed at employee behavior and ethics.

options.t: A map of the building showing all the exits
options.why: A building map showing exits is an emergency or safety plan. A code of conduct deals with behavior and ethical standards, not building layout.

q: What is a strategic plan?

options.t: A long-term plan describing how an organization will reach its goals
options.why: Correct. A strategic plan is a long-term plan, often three to five years, describing the mission, goals and actions an organization will take to reach its goals.

options.t: A list of customer complaints sorted by date and by the staff
options.why: A list of complaints sorted by date is a customer service log. A strategic plan sets future direction rather than recording past problems.

options.t: A daily to-do list of tasks for each employee on the whole team
options.why: A daily to-do list is an operational tool for day to day tasks. A strategic plan is broad and long-term, covering the whole organization.

options.t: A pay schedule showing when employees receive their wages each month
options.why: A pay schedule is a payroll document showing when wages are paid. A strategic plan describes how the organization will achieve long-term goals.

q: A manager reviews monthly results and finds sales are 15% below target. Which management function is in use?

options.t: Organizing
options.why: Organizing arranges people, resources and tasks into a structure. Checking results against targets is not organizing but comparing performance to plans.

options.t: Controlling
options.why: Correct. Controlling means comparing actual results, such as sales 15% below target, with goals and taking corrective action, which is what this manager is doing when reviewing monthly results.

options.t: Planning
options.why: Planning sets goals and decides actions ahead of time. The manager here is reviewing past results, which is a controlling activity, not a planning one.

options.t: Leading
options.why: Leading means motivating and directing people to work toward goals. Reviewing results against targets is monitoring performance, which falls under controlling.

q: What does an opportunity in a SWOT analysis refer to?

options.t: A competitor's strength that threatens the firm
options.why: A competitor's strength that threatens the firm is a threat in SWOT, which is an external factor that could harm the business, not an opportunity.

options.t: An internal weakness that the firm needs to fix soon
options.why: An internal weakness is a weakness in SWOT. Opportunities are external, so internal problems the firm needs to fix do not count.

options.t: A past mistake that the firm made in earlier years
options.why: A past mistake is a historical event and not an opportunity. Opportunities look ahead to external conditions that the business could use to its advantage.

options.t: An external factor that could benefit the business
options.why: Correct. In SWOT, an opportunity is an external factor, such as a new market, trend or weak competitor, that the business could use to grow or improve results.

q: Why do organizations set goals?

options.t: To make work harder so staff stay busy
options.why: Goals are meant to focus work, not to keep staff busy. Busy work without direction wastes effort and does not help an organization progress.

options.t: To prevent change in the organization
options.why: Goals often guide organizations through change and growth, so preventing change is not their purpose. Setting goals supports planned improvement.

options.t: To give direction and measure progress
options.why: Correct. Goals give people direction and a target to work toward, and they let managers measure progress and results to decide whether plans are working.

options.t: To avoid planning for the whole future
options.why: Setting goals is a part of planning for the future. Avoiding planning would be the opposite of what goal setting does for an organization.

q: A new law will raise a company's costs. Which factor is this under management?

options.t: A factor that has no effect on management decisions
options.why: A new law that raises costs clearly affects management decisions, such as pricing and budgeting. Saying it has no effect ignores the impact of laws on business.

options.t: An external factor that affects management decisions
options.why: Correct. A law is an external factor outside the company's control, such as regulation, the economy or competition, which managers must consider when making decisions.

options.t: An internal factor the manager controls at all times
options.why: Managers cannot control government laws, so this is not an internal factor. Internal factors, such as staff and resources, are within the firm's control.

options.t: A purely personal choice made by one manager alone
options.why: A new law applies to the whole company and arises outside it. It is not a personal choice by a single manager, so it is an external factor.

q: What is the difference between a contract and a promise?

options.t: A contract is legally enforceable because it has required elements
options.why: Correct. A contract is legally enforceable because it has required elements, offer, acceptance, consideration, capacity and legality, while a simple promise generally lacks them and cannot be enforced.

options.t: A contract is always spoken and a promise is always written
options.why: Contracts can be spoken or written, and many promises are written, too. Whether something is oral or written does not decide if it is a contract.

options.t: There is no difference between the two in any situation at all
options.why: There is a real legal difference. A contract meets legal requirements and can be enforced by a court, while a mere promise generally cannot.

options.t: A promise is enforced by the government and a contract is not
options.why: It is the reverse. Courts enforce contracts that meet legal requirements, while a plain promise without those elements usually is not enforced.

q: A company installs security cameras that record employees in a restroom. Which legal concern is most relevant?

options.t: Trademark protection
options.why: Trademark law protects brand names and logos. Recording employees in a restroom raises issues of personal privacy, not brand protection.

options.t: Import tariffs on goods
options.why: Import tariffs are taxes on foreign goods. They have nothing to do with cameras that record employees in a place where they expect privacy.

options.t: Antitrust rules on firms
options.why: Antitrust rules deal with monopolies and unfair competition among firms. Filming employees in a restroom is a privacy matter, not an issue of competition.

options.t: Employee privacy rights
options.why: Correct. Employees have a reasonable expectation of privacy in places like restrooms, so recording them there violates privacy rights and may lead to lawsuits or criminal charges.

q: Which is an example of intellectual property?

options.t: The delivery truck owned by the firm
options.why: A delivery truck is tangible property, a physical asset. Intellectual property consists of intangible creations of the mind, such as software or patents.

options.t: The cash in the register at the shop
options.why: Cash is a financial asset, not intellectual property. Intellectual property covers creations such as inventions, designs, works and brands.

options.t: A software program written by a company
options.why: Correct. Software is an intangible creation of the mind that is protected by copyright and sometimes patents, which makes it intellectual property owned by the company.

options.t: The office desks and filing cabinets
options.why: Desks and filing cabinets are tangible office furniture and equipment. Intellectual property is made of intangible ideas and creations rather than physical items.

q: What is the purpose of consumer protection laws?

options.t: To stop consumers from returning bought products
options.why: Consumer protection laws do not stop returns. Some laws, in fact, set return or refund rights, so this claim reverses their usual purpose.

options.t: To ban all advertising of goods in the country
options.why: These laws do not ban advertising. They only require that ads be truthful and not misleading, so advertising remains legal and common.

options.t: To protect buyers from unfair or unsafe practices
options.why: Correct. Consumer protection laws protect buyers from unfair, deceptive or unsafe practices, such as false advertising, hidden fees and dangerous products, and are enforced by agencies like the FTC.

options.t: To increase company profits at any cost to buyers
options.why: These laws limit practices that harm buyers. They are not meant to raise profits at the cost of consumers, who they are designed to protect.

q: A restaurant serves food that makes customers ill because it violated health codes. What is the likely consequence?

options.t: Immunity from health checks
options.why: Violating health codes does not give immunity. Health inspections continue, and violations often lead to more frequent inspections and penalties for the restaurant.

options.t: A reduction in taxes owed
options.why: A health violation has no link to lower taxes. Taxes owed depend on income and tax law, not on food safety record.

options.t: A government subsidy grant
options.why: Governments do not award subsidies to restaurants that make customers sick. Violations lead to penalties, not rewards or grants.

options.t: Fines, closure or lawsuits
options.why: Correct. Serving unsafe food in violation of health codes can lead to fines, forced closure by the health department and lawsuits from sick customers.

q: What does 'statute of limitations' mean?

options.t: A time limit for bringing a legal claim
options.why: Correct. A statute of limitations sets a deadline, often a few years, after which a person can no longer file a lawsuit or bring a legal claim over an event.

options.t: A limit on the number of employees in a firm
options.why: Limits on staff size come from regulation or business choice. A statute of limitations relates to time limits for legal claims, not employee numbers.

options.t: A limit on a company's profits each year
options.why: Limiting yearly profits is not a legal concept of this kind. Statutes of limitations restrict the time during which a claim may be filed.

options.t: A list of banned products in the state
options.why: A list of banned products relates to product bans or regulation. A statute of limitations sets how long someone has to file a legal claim.

q: A business signs a contract but later learns the other party lied about important facts. What may the business be able to do?

options.t: Make the contract longer than it was before
options.why: Making a contract longer does not remedy a lie about important facts. The business may instead have legal remedies for misrepresentation.

options.t: Seek to cancel the contract or claim damages
options.why: Correct. Misrepresentation of important facts can make a contract voidable, so the deceived party may seek to cancel it or claim damages for the harm caused.

options.t: Nothing, because contracts can never be changed
options.why: Contracts can be challenged or cancelled when there is fraud or misrepresentation. Saying nothing can be done is wrong, because the law offers remedies.

options.t: Force the other party to hire them at once
options.why: A court will not force the other party to hire the business. Remedies for misrepresentation are rescission or damages, not an unrelated job.

q: Why must businesses keep accurate employment records?

options.t: To advertise to customers in the area
options.why: Employment records are internal documents kept for compliance and management. They are not used to advertise to customers.

options.t: To comply with wage, tax and labor laws
options.why: Correct. Accurate employment records, such as hours, pay and tax withholdings, help a business comply with wage, tax and labor laws and prove compliance during audits or disputes.

options.t: To avoid paying staff as records show work
options.why: Records protect employees by documenting hours and pay. Using them to avoid paying staff would be illegal, as laws require employers to pay for work done.

options.t: To make hiring slower for the whole firm
options.why: Employment records do not slow hiring. They support legal compliance and good management, and hiring speed is a separate matter from record keeping.

q: What is an unfair labor practice?

options.t: A scheduled team meeting held every week at the office
options.why: A weekly team meeting is a normal management activity. It does not interfere with any employee's rights, so it is not an unfair labor practice.

options.t: A fair pay raise given to a worker for very good work done
options.why: A fair raise for good work is a lawful reward. An unfair labor practice involves illegal interference with workers' protected rights.

options.t: A worker taking a lunch break in the middle of a shift
options.why: Lunch breaks are normal and often required by law or policy. Taking one is not an unfair labor practice by an employer.

options.t: An employer action that interferes with workers' legal rights
options.why: Correct. An unfair labor practice is an employer or union action that interferes with workers' legal rights, such as firing someone for joining a union, under the National Labor Relations Act.

q: A company discovers its product label claims it is 'all natural' when it contains artificial ingredients. What should it do?

options.t: Hide the ingredients list from buyers
options.why: Hiding the ingredients list would add to the deception and may violate labeling laws. Buyers have a right to accurate information.

options.t: Blame customers for reading it carefully
options.why: Blaming customers is unethical, since the false claim is the company's responsibility. It also does not fix the misleading label.

options.t: Correct the label and stop false claims
options.why: Correct. The company should correct the label and stop false claims, because deceptive labeling violates consumer protection laws, and honest labeling protects the firm from fines and loss of trust.

options.t: Keep the label because it sells well
options.why: Keeping a false label because it sells well is deceptive advertising. It can bring penalties from the FTC and lawsuits from customers.

q: What is the purpose of a business memo?

options.t: To share short internal information or instructions
options.why: Correct. A memo is a short written message used inside an organization to share information, announcements or instructions with employees in a quick, formal way.

options.t: To entertain employees during their breaks at work
options.why: Entertaining employees is not the purpose of a business memo. Memos exist to share work related information clearly and briefly.

options.t: To replace all meetings forever and for every team
options.why: Memos do not replace all meetings. They share information in writing, but some topics still need discussion in meetings.

options.t: To send a formal contract to a customer for signature
options.why: A formal contract for a customer's signature is a legal document. A memo is an internal communication, not an agreement sent outside the company.

q: A speaker's slides contain full paragraphs of small text. What is the likely problem?

options.t: The slides will be far more persuasive
options.why: Dense paragraphs on slides overload the audience and pull attention from the speaker, so slides filled with text are usually less persuasive, not more.

options.t: Slides will not need a speaker at all
options.why: Slides support a speaker and do not replace one. Text heavy slides make the presentation worse, and the speaker is still needed to explain the ideas.

options.t: The audience may read instead of listening
options.why: Correct. Slides packed with small paragraphs make people read instead of listen, which weakens the message. Good slides use short phrases and visuals that support the speaker.

options.t: The audience will remember every word they read
options.why: People rarely remember every word they read from crowded slides. Overloaded text reduces retention, which is why slides should use key points rather than paragraphs.

q: Which is an example of oral communication?

options.t: A handwritten note on paper
options.why: A handwritten note is written communication, because the message is delivered in writing rather than by spoken words, even though it is personal.

options.t: A phone call with a customer
options.why: Correct. Oral communication uses spoken words, and a phone call with a customer is a spoken exchange that allows tone, immediate questions and quick answers.

options.t: A printed brochure from a fair
options.why: A printed brochure is written communication, since the message is delivered through printed text and images instead of speech.

options.t: An email sent to a client
options.why: An email is written communication. Its message is typed and read rather than spoken, so it is not oral communication.

q: How can you make a business presentation more engaging?

options.t: Read the slides word for word to the audience
options.why: Reading slides word for word bores the audience, because they can read it themselves. Engaging speakers add stories and explanation beyond the slide text.

options.t: Speak in a monotone for the whole talk
options.why: A monotone voice puts audiences to sleep. Engaging presenters vary pitch, pace and volume to keep attention and show enthusiasm for the topic.

options.t: Avoid looking at the audience at all times
options.why: Avoiding eye contact makes a speaker seem unprepared or unconfident and disconnects them from listeners, which lowers engagement instead of raising it.

options.t: Use clear visuals, examples and eye contact
options.why: Correct. Clear visuals, relevant examples and eye contact hold attention, make ideas easier to remember and build a connection between the presenter and the audience.

q: A manager sends a long email with several important requests in one paragraph. What is the best way to improve it?

options.t: Use short paragraphs, bullet points and a clear subject line
options.why: Correct. Short paragraphs, bullet points and a clear subject line make separate requests easy to find and answer, which helps the reader act on each one quickly.

options.t: Remove the subject line and send it with no title at all
options.why: Removing the subject line makes the email harder to identify and prioritize. A clear subject line helps readers understand the purpose before opening it.

options.t: Make the paragraph longer and add more filler text to it
options.why: Longer paragraphs with filler make important requests harder to find. Effective business writing is concise and focuses on the main points.

options.t: Add more unrelated information so the reader has a fuller view
options.why: Unrelated information distracts the reader and hides the key requests. Good emails stay focused on the purpose rather than adding extra material.

q: What does 'tone' refer to in writing?

options.t: The font size only, and not the words chosen
options.why: Tone is about attitude, not typography. Font size affects appearance, while tone comes from the words and style used by the writer.

options.t: The color of the paper that it is printed on
options.why: Paper color is a physical or design feature. Tone describes the writer's attitude as it comes across through word choice and style.

options.t: The number of pages in the whole document
options.why: The number of pages is a measure of length. Tone refers to the feeling or attitude conveyed by the language, not the document's size.

options.t: The attitude conveyed by word choice and style
options.why: Correct. Tone is the attitude a writer conveys through word choice and style, such as formal, friendly or urgent, and it affects how readers react to the message.

q: What is the role of a call to action in a message?

options.t: To tell the reader what to do next
options.why: Correct. A call to action tells the reader what to do next, such as call, reply or register, so the message leads to a clear response or result.

options.t: To apologize repeatedly to the reader
options.why: Repeated apologies weaken a message and are not the role of a call to action, which gives clear direction for the reader's next step.

options.t: To list the sender's job history
options.why: Listing the sender's job history is background information. A call to action instead asks the reader to take a specific next step.

options.t: To end the message without a request
options.why: A call to action does the opposite of ending without a request. It asks the reader for a specific action, so the message has a purpose.

q: An employee must respond to a customer in another country with different customs. Which approach is best?

options.t: Assume all customers want the same style of reply as home
options.why: Assuming all customers want the same style ignores cultural differences, and a reply that works at home may seem rude or confusing abroad.

options.t: Research local customs and adapt tone and style respectfully
options.why: Correct. Researching local customs and adjusting tone and style shows respect, avoids misunderstandings and builds trust with international customers who may expect different etiquette.

options.t: Use slang the customer may not know or even understand
options.why: Slang is often unfamiliar to people in other countries and may confuse or offend them, so clear and plain language is a better choice.

options.t: Avoid communicating with the customer in any way at all
options.why: Avoiding the customer ends the relationship and loses the sale. Differences in customs should be handled with research and respect, not by refusing to communicate.

q: What is a service level agreement?

options.t: A list of discounts only, offered to loyal customers each year
options.why: A discount list for loyal customers is a loyalty or promotion program. A service level agreement sets measurable service standards between a provider and customer.

options.t: A contract to buy stock in a public company on the market
options.why: A contract to buy stock is an investment or securities transaction. A service level agreement defines expected service quality, not the purchase of shares.

options.t: A document defining the level of service a customer can expect
options.why: Correct. A service level agreement (SLA) defines the level of service a customer can expect, such as response times and uptime, and the remedies if the provider falls short.

options.t: A map of delivery routes used by the drivers of the firm
options.why: A map of delivery routes is a logistics tool for drivers. An SLA is an agreement about service standards, not a route plan.

q: A customer thanks a store employee for remembering her name and past purchases. Which tool supports this kind of service?

options.t: A security alarm for the store doors
options.why: A security alarm protects the store from theft and intrusion. It does not store customer names or purchase histories to personalize service.

options.t: A cash register that adds up the prices
options.why: A cash register totals prices and records sales, but it does not keep customer profiles or purchase histories for a personalized greeting.

options.t: A customer relationship management system
options.why: Correct. A CRM system stores customer details and purchase history, allowing staff to remember names and preferences and provide personalized service that builds loyalty.

options.t: A paper map of the town and its roads
options.why: A paper map shows roads and has no customer data. It cannot help employees recall a shopper's name or past purchases.

q: Why does a business monitor online reviews?

options.t: To learn what customers think and respond to concerns
