options.why: Correct. Monitoring online reviews shows what customers think and lets the business answer concerns, fix problems and improve its reputation and service.

options.t: To avoid responding to customers who post online
options.why: Monitoring reviews is how a business responds to customers. Avoiding responses would ignore feedback and could damage the company's image.

options.t: To delete all negative comments from the website
options.why: Deleting negative comments hides valuable feedback and may mislead buyers. Businesses should respond to complaints and improve rather than remove criticism.

options.t: To reduce the number of customers who see the reviews
options.why: A business wants more people to see good reviews. Reducing the number of readers is not a goal and does not address customer concerns.

q: It costs a company five times more to win a new customer than to keep an existing one. What should the company prioritize?

options.t: Ignoring existing customers to chase new ones
options.why: Ignoring existing customers risks losing them, which is costly since replacing a customer costs five times more than keeping one.

options.t: Programs that keep current customers satisfied
options.why: Correct. Because keeping a customer costs far less than winning a new one, the company should invest in programs, such as service and loyalty rewards, that keep current customers satisfied.

options.t: Raising costs for loyal customers so they pay more
options.why: Raising costs for loyal customers could drive them away and defeats the goal of retention, which saves the company money.

options.t: Stopping all feedback from current customers
options.why: Feedback from current customers shows how to improve and keep them. Stopping it would remove the information needed for retention.

q: What is a customer persona?

options.t: A list of employees and the jobs that they hold
options.why: A list of employees and their jobs is an organization chart or roster. A customer persona describes a typical customer, not staff.

options.t: A customer's signature on a receipt after a purchase
options.why: A signature on a receipt confirms a purchase transaction. A persona is a profile that represents a group of target customers.

options.t: A company slogan used in its ads and on its signs
options.why: A slogan is a brand phrase used in advertising. A customer persona describes the needs, traits and behaviors of a typical customer.

options.t: A profile of a typical customer's needs and traits
options.why: Correct. A customer persona is a fictional profile of a typical customer, including needs, habits and goals, used to help design products and marketing that fit the target market.

q: What is the best way to end a customer interaction?

options.t: Thank the customer and ask if there is anything else
options.why: Correct. Thanking the customer and asking if anything else is needed ends on a positive note, shows appreciation and gives one last chance to meet the customer's needs.

options.t: Rush the customer out of the store as fast as you can
options.why: Rushing the customer out is rude and makes the customer feel unwelcome, which hurts satisfaction and the chance of repeat visits.

options.t: Walk away without a word as soon as the customer has paid
options.why: Walking away silently seems indifferent and hurts the relationship. A friendly closing, such as a thank you, leaves a good last impression.

options.t: Ask for a tip every time the customer pays the bill
options.why: Asking for a tip every time is inappropriate in most business settings and may seem pushy, so it is not a good way to end an interaction.

q: A company discovers that customers wait on hold 12 minutes. What improvement would best help service?

options.t: Remove the phone number so customers stop calling
options.why: Removing the phone number blocks customers from reaching the company and would worsen service and cause lost sales, instead of solving the long wait.

options.t: Add staff or offer callback and chat options
options.why: Correct. Adding staff or offering callback and chat options directly reduces wait times and gives customers other ways to get help, which improves satisfaction.

options.t: Ignore complaints about the long wait times
options.why: Ignoring complaints leaves a 12 minute wait unchanged and will upset customers, so the problem remains and more customers may leave.

options.t: Play louder music while customers wait on hold
options.why: Louder music does not shorten the wait, and it may annoy callers. Real improvement requires shortening waits or giving customers other options.

q: A factory buys machines that let each worker make twice as many items per hour. What increased?

options.t: Rising joblessness
options.why: Rising joblessness is not what the machines show here. Output per worker doubled, which measures productivity, not job losses or unemployment.

options.t: Every item's price
options.why: Doubling output per worker does not by itself raise item prices, and greater productivity tends to lower costs, which may even allow lower prices.

options.t: Taxes owed by firms
options.why: Taxes owed by firms depend on tax law and profits. They are not the direct result of workers making twice as many items per hour.

options.t: Labor productivity
options.why: Correct. Labor productivity is output per worker per hour. If each worker makes twice as many items per hour, productivity has doubled thanks to better capital equipment.

q: What does supply refer to?

options.t: The amount buyers want at each price, shown by the demand curve
options.why: This describes demand, the quantity buyers want at each price, shown on the demand curve. Supply comes from sellers, not buyers.

options.t: The profit that sellers earn on each unit that they sell off
options.why: Profit per unit is the difference between price and cost. Supply refers to quantities offered for sale, not the profit made on each unit.

options.t: The quantity of a good sellers are willing to offer at each price
options.why: Correct. Supply is the quantity of a good that sellers are willing and able to offer at each price, and the supply curve usually slopes upward.

options.t: The money in circulation in the economy at any given time
options.why: Money in circulation is the money supply, a monetary concept. In microeconomics, supply refers to how much of a good sellers will offer.

q: What is market equilibrium?

options.t: The price at which quantity supplied equals quantity demanded
options.why: Correct. Market equilibrium is the price at which the quantity supplied equals the quantity demanded, so there is no surplus or shortage and the market clears.

options.t: The point where sellers refuse to sell as the price is low
options.why: Sellers refusing to sell at a low price describes a supply response to price, not equilibrium, where both sides are satisfied with the quantity traded.

options.t: A price set by government only, with no market role at all
options.why: Equilibrium comes from the interaction of buyers and sellers. A price set only by government is a price control, not a market equilibrium.

options.t: A time when demand is zero for every good in the market
options.why: Zero demand for every good is not an equilibrium. Equilibrium is where supply and demand are equal at a price, with trading taking place.

q: A price ceiling set below the equilibrium price on apartments will most likely cause:

options.t: Lower demand for apartments
options.why: A price ceiling below equilibrium makes apartments cheaper, which raises the quantity demanded, so demand does not fall. Lower rents attract more renters.

options.t: Equal supply and demand
options.why: Supply and demand are equal only at the equilibrium price. A ceiling set below that price leaves demand greater than supply, so they are not equal.

options.t: A surplus of apartments
options.why: A surplus occurs when price is above equilibrium. A ceiling below equilibrium does the opposite, making buyers want more than landlords will supply.

options.t: A shortage of apartments
options.why: Correct. A price ceiling below equilibrium holds rent under the market level, so quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied, creating a shortage of apartments as seen in rent control.

q: What is entrepreneurship's role in an economy?

options.t: Raising unemployment in the whole economy
options.why: Entrepreneurs create businesses that hire workers, so they tend to lower unemployment rather than raise it across the economy.

options.t: Preventing all competition in the market
options.why: Entrepreneurs usually increase competition by entering markets with new products, so preventing competition is not their role.

options.t: Creating new businesses, jobs and innovation
options.why: Correct. Entrepreneurs start new businesses, create jobs and bring innovation, which raises output, offers consumers new choices and helps economic growth.

options.t: Reducing the variety of products for buyers
options.why: Entrepreneurs often add to product variety through innovation, so reducing the choices available to buyers is the opposite of their role.

q: Which is most likely to cause inflation?

options.t: Supply rising faster than demand
options.why: Supply rising faster than demand lowers or stabilizes prices because goods are more available, so it does not cause inflation.

options.t: Demand rising faster than supply
options.why: Correct. When demand rises faster than supply, buyers compete for limited goods and prices are bid up, which is demand-pull inflation, a general rise in prices.

options.t: A fall in the money supply today
options.why: A fall in the money supply tends to reduce spending and push prices down, which is deflationary and not a cause of inflation.

options.t: Falling production costs overall
options.why: Falling production costs lower the cost of goods and tend to reduce prices, so they would not cause inflation.

q: What does comparative advantage mean?

options.t: Selling at a higher price than all of the rivals always
options.why: Selling at a higher price than rivals is a pricing strategy. Comparative advantage is about opportunity cost in production and not about price levels.

options.t: Producing more of every good than others using fewer
options.why: Producing more of every good with fewer resources is absolute advantage. Comparative advantage is about lower opportunity cost, so even a less efficient producer can have it.

options.t: Avoiding trade entirely with every other nation in the world
options.why: Comparative advantage supports trade, since each nation specializes and trades for gains. Avoiding trade with others is the opposite of this idea.

options.t: The ability to produce a good at a lower opportunity cost
options.why: Correct. Comparative advantage is the ability to produce a good at a lower opportunity cost than others, so countries gain by specializing and trading.

q: What is active collaboration?

options.t: Working with others to share ideas and reach common goals
options.why: Correct. Active collaboration means working with others, sharing ideas and effort to reach common goals, which builds trust and produces better results than working alone.

options.t: Working alone to avoid conflict so no time is lost in talks
options.why: Working alone to avoid conflict is isolation, not collaboration. Collaboration involves interacting with others, and healthy discussion helps teams reach better solutions.

options.t: Competing against coworkers for rewards and praise
options.why: Competing against coworkers works against teamwork. Collaboration means cooperating to reach shared goals rather than fighting for individual rewards.

options.t: Taking over others' tasks without being asked to do so
options.why: Taking over tasks uninvited can be disrespectful and cause conflict. Collaboration involves coordinating roles and helping when asked, not seizing control.

q: A new employee makes a mistake that costs the company money. Which response from a leader builds trust and learning?

options.t: Publicly shame the employee in front of the whole team
options.why: Public shaming damages trust and morale, and it discourages employees from admitting mistakes, which prevents learning and may harm the team.

options.t: Discuss what happened, learn from it and provide support
options.why: Correct. Talking through the mistake, learning from it and supporting the employee builds trust and helps the employee improve while keeping the team honest and open.

options.t: Hide the mistake from everyone so no one ever finds out
options.why: Hiding a costly mistake is dishonest, prevents the company from fixing the cause and teaches employees to conceal errors instead of learning.

options.t: Fire the employee immediately in all cases to teach others
options.why: Firing in every case is harsh and ignores context. A new employee's honest error is better handled through coaching and support to build skill.

q: Why does self-awareness matter at work?

options.t: It prevents you from receiving feedback on your own faults
options.why: Self-aware people welcome feedback because it helps them see their own faults. Avoiding feedback is the opposite of self-awareness.

options.t: It lets you ignore others and what they say to you
options.why: Self-aware workers pay attention to how they affect others and listen to them, so ignoring other people is not a result of self-awareness.

options.t: Knowing your strengths and weaknesses helps you improve
options.why: Correct. Self-awareness means knowing your strengths and weaknesses, which helps you improve, choose suitable tasks and handle relationships and stress better at work.

options.t: It removes the need for goals at work for any person
options.why: Goals remain important for everyone. Self-awareness helps people set realistic goals based on their abilities, so it does not remove the need for them.

q: Which action demonstrates ethical behavior?

options.t: Reporting an accounting error even if it benefits you
options.why: Correct. Reporting an accounting error even when it benefits you shows honesty and integrity, and it follows ethical standards that protect the company and its stakeholders.

options.t: Waiting for someone else to find it so you need not tell
options.why: Waiting for someone else to find the error avoids responsibility. Ethical employees speak up when they notice a problem rather than hoping others discover it.

options.t: Hiding the error to keep a bonus for yourself later
options.why: Hiding an error to keep a bonus is dishonest and may be fraud. It puts personal gain ahead of honesty toward the employer.

options.t: Blaming a coworker for the error that you yourself made
options.why: Blaming a coworker for your own error is dishonest and unfair to the coworker. Ethical behavior means admitting your own mistakes.

q: Employees are resisting a new software system. What should a leader do to ease the change?

options.t: Ignore the complaints and make everyone use it anyway today
options.why: Ignoring complaints and forcing use breeds resentment and resistance, which makes the change harder. Leaders should listen to employee concerns first.

options.t: Cancel all communication with the staff about the system
options.why: Cutting communication leaves employees confused and increases resistance. Change goes better when leaders keep staff informed and answer questions.

options.t: Explain the benefits, listen to concerns and provide training
options.why: Correct. Explaining the benefits, listening to concerns and providing training helps people understand and feel ready for the change, which reduces resistance and speeds adoption.

options.t: Force use of the system with no explanation of the reasons for it
options.why: Forcing a system on staff with no explanation creates distrust and resistance. People accept change more readily when they understand why it is happening.

q: A founder asks 100 potential customers about a product idea and most say they would not buy it. What should she do?

options.t: Increase the price of the product to cover the costs
options.why: Raising the price does not respond to customers saying they will not buy, and it would likely lower interest further and not solve a demand problem.

options.t: Reconsider or change the idea based on the feedback
options.why: Correct. When most potential customers say they would not buy, the founder should reconsider or change the idea based on that market feedback before spending more money.

options.t: Ignore the answers and launch anyway as planned
options.why: Ignoring clear market feedback and launching anyway risks wasting money on a product few people want, so the research should guide her decision.

options.t: Hire more staff immediately to handle the demand
options.why: Hiring more staff to handle demand makes no sense when most people say they would not buy, since there is little demand to handle.

q: What is revenue for a new business?

options.t: Money borrowed from a bank that must be repaid
options.why: Borrowed money is a loan, which is a liability the business must repay. It is not revenue, which comes from selling products or services.

options.t: Money owed to suppliers for the goods it bought
options.why: Money owed to suppliers is accounts payable, a liability. Revenue is money coming in from customers rather than owed out to suppliers.

options.t: Money spent on supplies for the shop each month
options.why: Money spent on supplies is an expense that reduces profit. Revenue is the income from sales and not a cost the business pays.

options.t: Money earned from selling products or services
options.why: Correct. Revenue is the money a business earns from selling products or services before expenses are subtracted, and it is the top line of the income statement.

q: Why do entrepreneurs seek a mentor or advisor?

options.t: To raise prices on all goods
options.why: Mentors do not help raise prices on all goods. Their value is experience and advice, and pricing decisions rest with the business owner.

options.t: To avoid making decisions
options.why: Mentors help entrepreneurs make better decisions through advice, so seeking one to avoid decisions is the opposite of the purpose.

options.t: To gain experience and advice
options.why: Correct. A mentor or advisor shares experience and advice, which helps entrepreneurs avoid mistakes, find resources and make better decisions as they start and grow a business.

options.t: To reduce the customers served
options.why: Entrepreneurs seek mentors to grow and improve their businesses, and reducing the number of customers served is not a goal of mentoring.

q: What is a line of credit?

options.t: A tax payment plan for the firm to pay what it owes
options.why: A tax payment plan is an arrangement with tax authorities. A line of credit is borrowing capacity offered by a lender for general use.

options.t: A required savings account kept open for a loan
options.why: A required savings account is a deposit account, sometimes tied to a loan, but a line of credit is a flexible loan limit, not savings.

options.t: A one-time gift of money from a bank to a borrower
options.why: A gift from a bank would not need to be repaid. A line of credit is borrowed money that must be repaid with interest on what is used.

options.t: A set amount of money a borrower can use as needed
options.why: Correct. A line of credit is a set maximum amount a borrower can draw on as needed and repay, paying interest only on the amount actually used.

q: A company's current assets are $60,000 and current liabilities are $30,000. What is its current ratio?

options.why: Correct. Current ratio equals current assets divided by current liabilities: $60,000 / $30,000 = 2.0. The company has $2 of liquid assets for each $1 of short term debt.
$30,000 is the amount of current liabilities, not a ratio. The ratio divides $60,000 by $30,000 to get 2.0, a pure number without dollars.
$90,000 would come from adding the two amounts ($60,000 + $30,000). The current ratio divides assets by liabilities, giving 2.0 rather than a sum.
0.5 inverts the formula ($30,000 / $60,000). The current ratio is assets divided by liabilities, so $60,000 / $30,000 equals 2.0.

q: What is the purpose of insurance?

options.t: To avoid saving money for later in life
options.why: Insurance does not remove the need to save. It transfers risk for a premium, and people still need to save for retirement and other goals.

options.t: To protect against financial loss from risks
options.why: Correct. Insurance protects against financial loss from risks such as accidents, illness, fire or lawsuits, by pooling many people's premiums to pay claims.

options.t: To increase the chance of loss for the owner
options.why: Insurance is meant to reduce the burden of loss, not raise the chance of it. Policyholders pay premiums to transfer risk to the insurer.

options.t: To pay all of a person's bills every month
options.why: Insurance pays only for covered losses, such as accidents or damage, and not all of a person's regular monthly bills.

q: A person invests $500 at 6% compound interest for 2 years. About how much will she have?

options.why: Correct. With compound interest, $500 x 1.06 x 1.06 = $500 x 1.1236 = $561.80. Interest earned in year one also earns interest in year two.
$600 would be an investment that grew by $100. Compound interest at 6% for two years gives $500 x 1.1236 = $561.80, not $600.
$560 is simple interest on $500 for two years ($500 x 0.06 x 2 = $60). Compounding adds interest on interest, giving $561.80.
$530 reflects only one year of simple interest ($500 x 0.06 = $30). Two years of compounding at 6% gives $500 x 1.1236 = $561.80.

q: A department has many open jobs and low morale. Which HR action would best address both?

options.t: Ignore employee concerns and keep running the department as is
options.why: Ignoring employee concerns would worsen the low morale and does nothing about the open jobs, so both problems would likely get worse.

options.t: Improve recruiting while gathering feedback to fix workplace issues
options.why: Correct. Improving recruiting fills vacancies, while gathering feedback shows what causes low morale so HR can fix workplace issues. Together these address both problems.

options.t: Hire without interviewing anyone and fill every open job at once
options.why: Hiring without interviews risks poor matches and does not fix the morale problem, which may then lead to even more turnover.

options.t: Cut all benefits for the staff to save money for the whole firm
options.why: Cutting benefits would lower morale further and make recruiting harder, because employees and applicants value benefits as part of total compensation.

q: What is succession planning?

options.t: Planning the office party for the end of the year
options.why: Planning an office party is an event planning task. Succession planning prepares people for future leadership and key roles in the company.

options.t: Selecting company colors for the new logo and signs
options.why: Choosing company colors is a branding task. Succession planning is a human resources process for developing future leaders and filling key roles.

options.t: Preparing employees to fill key roles in the future
options.why: Correct. Succession planning prepares and develops employees to fill key roles in the future, so the company can keep running smoothly when leaders retire or leave.

options.t: Choosing next year's logo and the slogan of the company
options.why: Choosing a logo and slogan is marketing and branding work. Succession planning is an HR process for preparing staff to take over key positions.

q: What is malware?

options.t: Software for taking notes in class or at work
options.why: Note taking programs are productivity software that help people write. Malware is harmful software designed to damage or steal rather than help.

options.t: Software for editing photos and other pictures
options.why: Photo editing programs are legitimate creative software. Malware is software built to harm, such as viruses, ransomware and spyware.

options.t: Software that speeds up a computer by deleting its files
options.why: Malware does not truly speed up a computer, and deleting files harms it. Real performance tools are not malware, which is built to cause damage.

options.t: Software designed to harm or steal from a computer
options.why: Correct. Malware is malicious software, such as viruses, ransomware and spyware, designed to damage a computer or network, steal data or give attackers access.

q: A company stores customer credit card numbers in a plain text file anyone can open. What is the main risk?

options.t: Lower advertising costs
options.why: Storing card data in plain text does not lower advertising costs. The danger is that thieves can read the data, which has nothing to do with advertising.

options.t: Slower sales over time
options.why: Slower sales are not the main risk of unprotected card data. The immediate danger is that criminals could steal and misuse the numbers.

options.t: Improved customer trust
options.why: Exposed card numbers harm customer trust rather than improve it, since customers lose confidence in a company that fails to protect their information.

options.t: Data theft and misuse
options.why: Correct. Unprotected card numbers can be stolen and used for fraud, causing data theft, fines, lawsuits and lost trust. Sensitive data should be encrypted and access limited.

q: What is a spreadsheet formula used for?

options.t: Sending messages to other people now
options.why: Sending messages is done with email or messaging tools. A spreadsheet formula is an expression that calculates values from cell data.

options.t: Performing calculations automatically
options.why: Correct. A spreadsheet formula, such as =SUM(A1:A5), performs calculations automatically and updates results when the cell data change, saving time and reducing errors.

options.t: Storing passwords for the system's users
options.why: Storing passwords is not the role of a formula, and passwords should be kept in secure password managers rather than ordinary spreadsheet cells.

options.t: Printing posters for the store windows
options.why: Printing posters is a publishing or printing task. Spreadsheet formulas calculate values from data in cells.

q: What is direct marketing?

options.t: Communicating directly with targeted customers, such as by email
options.why: Correct. Direct marketing communicates directly with targeted customers through channels such as email, mail or phone, so the firm can measure responses and personalize offers.

options.t: Advertising only on billboards along the roads of the city
options.why: Billboards are outdoor mass advertising seen by everyone passing by. Direct marketing targets selected individuals rather than a general audience.

options.t: Selling only through stores and never through any other channel
options.why: Direct marketing is a promotion method, and it can be used with stores or online sales, so limiting selling to stores is not its meaning.

options.t: Stopping all promotion of the products the firm sells to buyers
options.why: Direct marketing is a form of promotion, so it does not mean stopping promotion. It reaches chosen customers directly with messages and offers.

q: A company wants to know if a new ad increased sales. What should it compare?

options.t: The color of the new ad used
options.why: The color of the ad does not show whether sales rose. To measure an ad's effect, sales figures must be compared across time periods.

options.t: The number of staff at the firm
options.why: Staff numbers describe the firm's size and do not show the effect of an ad. The result of advertising shows up in sales results.

options.t: Sales before and after the ad
options.why: Correct. Comparing sales before and after the ad shows whether sales rose after it ran, which gives evidence of the ad's effect, though other factors should be considered.

options.t: The cost of rent for the shop
options.why: Rent for the shop is a fixed operating cost unrelated to advertising results. It cannot show whether the new ad increased sales.

q: What is a slogan?

options.t: A price tag on an item in a large store window
options.why: A price tag shows the cost of one item and carries no brand message, so it is not a slogan, which is a memorable phrase tied to a brand.

options.t: A legal contract signed by a firm and its staff
options.why: A contract signed by a firm and its staff is an employment agreement that sets pay and duties, which has nothing to do with advertising or brand messaging.

options.t: A product warranty given to a buyer after a sale
options.why: A product warranty is a promise to repair or replace a faulty item after a sale; it protects the buyer and does not work as a brand's advertising phrase.

options.t: A short phrase that expresses a brand's message
options.why: A slogan is a short, catchy phrase that sums up a brand's message and is repeated in ads, packaging and promotion so customers remember it quickly and easily.

q: What is a bill of materials?

options.t: A job description listing a worker's duties and tasks
options.why: A job description lists a worker's duties and tasks, which is an HR document; a bill of materials lists the parts needed to build a product instead.

options.t: A list of parts and materials needed to make a product
options.why: A bill of materials (BOM) is a list of every part, material and quantity needed to make a product, and operations teams use it for planning purchases and production.

options.t: A tax form that a business files with the state each year
options.why: A tax form filed with the state reports income or sales to the government; it is a compliance record and says nothing about the parts needed to make a product.

options.t: A sales receipt handed to a customer after a purchase
options.why: A sales receipt proves a purchase and goes to the customer after the sale, while a bill of materials is an internal production list of the parts required.

q: A call center wants to reduce customer wait times without lowering service quality. Which approach is best?

options.t: Analyze call volume patterns and schedule staff accordingly
options.why: Analyzing call volume patterns shows when calls peak, so managers can schedule more agents at those times, cutting waits while keeping service quality and not adding needless cost.

options.t: Cut staff during the busy hours to save money on wages
options.why: Cutting staff during busy hours leaves fewer agents for more callers, which lengthens wait times and lowers service quality, the opposite of what the center wants.

options.t: Hide the phone number so that callers cannot reach the center
options.why: Hiding the phone number stops calls from reaching the center, which does not shorten waits for real customers and would harm the service and the firm's reputation.

options.t: Lengthen the greeting so callers hear more about the firm
options.why: A longer greeting adds seconds to every call, so each caller holds longer and the queue grows; it makes waiting times worse and does not improve service.

q: What is a warehouse used for?

options.t: Collecting taxes from the firm's customers
options.why: Collecting taxes from customers is done by government agencies or through sales tax at checkout, while a warehouse is a building for holding inventory.

options.t: Making signs and ads for the chain of stores
options.why: Making signs and ads is a marketing or production task, and a warehouse is a storage facility rather than a place where promotional materials are created.

options.t: Storing goods until they are sold or shipped
options.why: A warehouse stores goods, such as raw materials or finished products, until they are sold or shipped, which keeps inventory organized and ready to meet customer orders.

options.t: Training new managers for the firm's stores
options.why: Training new managers happens through HR programs, classrooms or on-the-job coaching; a warehouse is a physical space for storing inventory, not for training staff.

q: Why is it useful to set short-term goals?

options.t: They make goals impossible to reach for anyone
options.why: Short-term goals are small, reachable targets that build progress toward bigger aims, so they make long-term goals easier to reach rather than impossible for anyone.

options.t: They remove the need for long-term goals each year
options.why: Short-term goals support long-term goals; a plan still needs a long-term direction each year, so one cannot replace the other.

options.t: They break larger goals into manageable steps
options.why: Short-term goals split a large goal into manageable steps, which gives clear milestones, steady motivation and quick chances to measure progress and correct course along the way.

options.t: They prevent feedback from the whole team
options.why: Short-term goals do not block feedback; they make progress easy to measure, so teams can give and use feedback more often along the way.

q: During an interview, you are asked about a weakness. What is the best approach?

options.t: Blame your last manager for everything that went wrong
options.why: Blaming a former manager sounds negative and unprofessional, and it shows poor accountability, which tends to leave interviewers with a bad impression of the candidate.

options.t: Name a real weakness and explain how you are improving
options.why: Naming a real weakness and showing how you are improving it demonstrates honesty, self-awareness and a willingness to grow, which employers value highly when hiring for any role.

options.t: Refuse to answer the question and change the subject
options.why: Refusing to answer and changing the subject looks evasive, suggests you are hiding something, and gives the interviewer no evidence of self-awareness or honesty.

options.t: Say you have no weaknesses, so the interviewer sees you
options.why: Claiming to have no weaknesses is not believable and shows a lack of self-awareness; interviewers usually read it as dishonest or arrogant.

q: A manager wants to reduce risk when launching a new product. Which action is most effective?

options.t: Test the product in a small market first
options.why: Testing the product in a small market first limits possible losses, gathers real customer feedback, and lets the firm fix problems before spending on a wider launch.

options.t: Launch in every market at once to save time
options.why: Launching in every market at once exposes the whole firm to losses if the product fails, so it raises risk instead of lowering it.

options.t: Skip research to save time and money now
options.why: Skipping research removes the data that shows whether customers want the product, so mistakes are found late and costly, which raises risk instead of reducing it.

options.t: Ignore competitors and what they do there
options.why: Ignoring competitors leaves a manager unaware of rival prices and features, which makes failure more likely, so this raises risk rather than reducing it.

q: What is a license in business?

options.t: A tax paid on profits earned in the year by the firm
options.why: A tax on profits is an income tax paid to the government; a license is official permission to operate a business or carry out an activity.

options.t: A list of products for sale at the shop each season
options.why: A list of products for sale is a catalog or price list used in marketing and sales, and it is not a government or legal permission.

options.t: A discount given to loyal customers at the store monthly
options.why: A discount given to loyal customers is a sales promotion or rewards program, while a license is official permission, often from a government, to operate.

options.t: Official permission to operate or perform an activity
options.why: A license is official permission, usually from a government or owner, to operate a business or perform a regulated activity, such as selling food or practicing a trade.

q: A store sells counterfeit handbags with a famous brand's logo. What legal problem does this create?

options.t: A zoning breach by it
options.why: A zoning breach means using land in a way local zoning rules forbid; selling fake branded goods is an intellectual property violation instead.

options.t: A wage law violation
options.why: A wage law violation involves unpaid or underpaid workers, which is unrelated to selling fake goods that copy a famous brand's protected logo.

options.t: A tax audit of the shop
options.why: A tax audit is a review of a firm's tax returns by the IRS; counterfeit goods raise an intellectual property issue and do not trigger an audit by themselves.

options.t: Trademark infringement
options.why: Counterfeit goods that copy a brand's logo violate its registered trademark, so the store faces trademark infringement claims, damages and possible criminal penalties under federal law.

q: What is a breach of warranty?

options.t: A store offers a coupon for a future purchase online
options.why: A coupon for a future purchase is a sales promotion and does not involve a broken promise about a product's quality or performance.

options.t: A seller fails to meet the promises made about a product
options.why: A breach of warranty happens when a seller fails to meet the promises, express or implied, made about a product, which lets the buyer seek a repair, refund or damages.

options.t: A company changes its logo and its brand colors too
options.why: Changing a logo and brand colors is a branding decision that carries no legal duty to a buyer, so it cannot be a warranty breach.

options.t: A buyer returns an item on time with the sales receipt
options.why: A buyer returning an item on time with a receipt is a normal return under store policy, and nobody has broken any promise or warranty.

q: A team in different cities needs to collaborate daily. Which tool best supports this?

options.t: A single phone call per month for the whole team
options.why: A single monthly phone call is far too infrequent for a team that must collaborate daily, and it cannot share files, updates or quick questions.

options.t: A printed newsletter mailed out each year to staff
options.why: A printed newsletter mailed once a year is slow, one-way and out of date, so it cannot support daily collaboration among people in different cities.

options.t: A shared online workspace with chat and video
options.why: A shared online workspace with chat and video lets distant teammates message, meet, share files and track tasks in real time, which suits daily collaboration across cities.

options.t: A paper bulletin board in one office building
options.why: A paper bulletin board in one office can only be seen by people in that building, so team members in other cities cannot use it.

q: Which phrase best shows courtesy to a customer?

options.t: 'How may I help you today?'
options.why: 'How may I help you today?' is a polite, friendly offer of assistance that makes the customer feel welcome and valued, which is the core of courtesy.

options.t: 'I am busy, please wait.'
options.why: 'I am busy, please wait' sounds dismissive and shows no respect for the customer's time, so it fails to show courtesy even though it is not insulting.

options.t: 'What do you want now?'
options.why: 'What do you want now?' sounds impatient and rude, suggesting the customer is a bother, which drives customers away instead of building goodwill.

options.t: 'Make it quick, I'm busy.'
options.why: 'Make it quick, I'm busy' pressures the customer and signals that their needs are unimportant, which is discourteous and damages the customer relationship.

q: A hotel guest asks for a late checkout but the policy is firm. Which response best balances policy and service?

options.t: Break the policy secretly and give the guest the room late
options.why: Secretly breaking the policy is dishonest and unfair to other guests who followed the rule, and it can create liability problems and inconsistent treatment for the hotel.

options.t: Tell the guest to leave right away as the room is needed
options.why: Telling the guest to leave right away is rude and ignores the guest's needs; good service looks for alternatives instead of sending the guest off abruptly.

options.t: Explain the policy and offer luggage storage or another option
options.why: Explaining the policy politely and offering options such as luggage storage respects the rule while still helping the guest, which balances policy with good customer service.

options.t: Ignore the request and just hope that the guest goes away soon
options.why: Ignoring the request leaves the guest unheard and frustrated, which harms the hotel's reputation; good service always acknowledges the request and gives a clear answer.

q: What is a surplus in a market?

options.t: Quantity demanded is greater than quantity supplied
options.why: Quantity demanded greater than quantity supplied describes a shortage, where buyers want more than sellers offer, not a surplus.

options.t: No goods are produced by any firm in the market
options.why: If no goods are produced, supply is zero and there is nothing to be in surplus; a surplus needs goods that go unsold at the current price.

options.t: Supply equals demand at the market price today
options.why: When supply equals demand at the market price, the market is in equilibrium, so there is neither a surplus nor a shortage.

options.t: Quantity supplied is greater than quantity demanded
options.why: A surplus occurs when the quantity supplied exceeds the quantity demanded at the current price, leaving unsold goods that usually push the price down toward equilibrium.

q: If the price of pizza rises, which good is most likely to see higher demand?

options.t: Pizza itself at any price
options.why: Pizza itself is the good whose price rose, so the quantity demanded falls along the demand curve; its own price increase does not raise its demand.

options.t: A substitute such as burgers
options.why: Burgers are a substitute for pizza, so when pizza becomes more expensive, buyers switch to burgers and the demand for burgers rises at every price.

options.t: A product unrelated to food
options.why: A product unrelated to food has no link to pizza, so a change in pizza's price has little effect on how much people want it.

options.t: A complement such as pizza boxes
options.why: Pizza boxes are a complement, used together with pizza, so higher pizza prices cut pizza purchases and reduce demand for the boxes instead of raising it.

q: Which approach helps manage workplace stress?

options.t: Taking breaks and organizing tasks
options.why: Taking breaks and organizing tasks restores energy and makes the workload feel manageable, which lowers stress and helps keep work quality and focus steady over time.

options.t: Ignoring all deadlines and tasks
options.why: Ignoring deadlines and tasks lets work pile up and causes missed targets, which creates more stress later instead of helping manage it.

options.t: Working without rest for days on end
options.why: Working for days without rest leads to fatigue and burnout, which raises stress and lowers both health and job performance.

options.t: Blaming the coworkers for stress
options.why: Blaming coworkers does not remove the cause of the stress and harms relationships, which adds conflict and makes the workplace more stressful.

q: A leader changes plans several times without explaining why. What effect is likely on the team?

options.t: No effect on the team at all
options.why: Repeated unexplained changes do affect people, since they cannot plan ahead or understand the reasons, so claiming that there is no effect is wrong.

options.t: Better results and more trust
options.why: Changing plans without explanation tends to hurt results and erode trust, because people cannot see the reasoning, so better results and trust are unlikely.

options.t: Confusion and loss of trust
options.why: When a leader keeps changing plans without explaining why, team members feel confused about priorities and begin to doubt the leader's judgment, so trust declines.

options.t: Higher morale in the team
options.why: Unexplained changes create uncertainty and frustration, so morale is more likely to fall than rise.

q: What is a niche market?

options.t: A small, specialized segment of a larger market
options.why: A niche market is a small, specialized segment of a larger market with particular needs, which lets focused firms serve it well with less direct competition.

options.t: A market with no buyers or sellers at all
options.why: A market with no buyers or sellers does not exist in practice; a niche market has real customers who share specific needs or interests.

options.t: The whole population of a country or a city
options.why: The whole population of a country is a mass market, the opposite of a niche, which targets only a small, specific group.

options.t: A market owned by the government, where only it sells
options.why: A government-owned market where only the state sells is a monopoly, not a niche; a niche is defined by a narrow customer segment.

q: A tutoring business gets most revenue from one school. What is the main risk?

options.t: Having too many customers to handle well
options.why: Having too many customers is not a risk caused by relying on one school; the problem is the opposite, too few customers.

options.t: Gaining more bargaining power with the school
options.why: Relying heavily on one school gives the school more bargaining power over the tutoring firm, so the business loses power instead of gaining it.

options.t: Paying lower taxes on its yearly earnings
options.why: Revenue concentration has no connection to a lower tax bill; taxes depend on profit and tax law, not on how many customers a firm has.

options.t: Losing that client would sharply cut income
options.why: Depending on one client for most revenue is a concentration risk, since losing that school would sharply cut income and could threaten the whole business.

q: What is overdraft?

options.t: Earning interest on a deposit that the bank pays
options.why: Earning interest on a deposit is a benefit of saving money; an overdraft is the opposite, where the account balance drops below zero.

options.t: Spending more than the balance in a checking account
options.why: An overdraft occurs when you spend more than the balance in a checking account, and the bank may cover it but usually charges a fee or interest.

options.t: Closing an account at the bank for good this year
options.why: Closing an account permanently is a separate action from an overdraft, which describes a negative balance caused by withdrawals above the available funds.

options.t: Saving more than planned in a given month or year
options.why: Saving more than planned increases an account's balance, while an overdraft means taking out more than the balance holds.

q: A business offers 2/10, net 30 payment terms. What does 2/10 mean?

options.t: A late fee of 2 dollars for paying late
options.why: In 2/10, net 30 the 2 is a discount percentage, not a late fee in dollars; late charges are a separate matter from early-payment discounts.

options.t: A 10% discount if paid in 2 days
options.why: The 2 means a 2% discount, not 10%, and the 10 means days, not a two-day window; this option reverses the numbers in the terms.

options.t: Two payments of ten dollars each month
options.why: The terms do not describe two payments of ten dollars; they give a percentage discount for early payment and a total due date.

options.t: A 2% discount if paid within 10 days
options.why: In 2/10, net 30 the buyer may take a 2% discount if the invoice is paid within 10 days; otherwise the full amount is due in 30 days.

q: A manager wants new employees to feel welcome. Which step would help most?

options.t: Assign a mentor and introduce them to the team
options.why: Assigning a mentor and introducing the new hire to the team gives guidance and social connection, which helps newcomers feel welcome and learn the job faster.

options.t: Tell them to learn by guessing so they remember more
options.why: Telling new hires to learn by guessing leads to mistakes and anxiety, and it makes them feel unsupported rather than welcome.

options.t: Leave them alone for a whole week at work
options.why: Leaving new employees alone for a week makes them feel ignored and delays learning, which is the opposite of a welcoming onboarding experience.

options.t: Give no instructions to the new hires at all
options.why: Giving no instructions leaves new hires unsure of their duties and standards, so they feel lost and unwelcome and are likely to make mistakes.

q: What is a user ID and password used for?

options.t: To speed up the internet connection
options.why: Internet speed depends on the connection and equipment, not on login credentials, so a user ID and password cannot speed up the internet.

options.t: To print documents for the whole office
options.why: Printing documents is handled by printers and print settings; a user ID and password may control access to a printer but are not used for printing itself.

options.t: To verify who is accessing a system
options.why: A user ID and password authenticate users by checking identity before granting access, which protects systems and data from unauthorized people and tracks who did what.

options.t: To change screen colors and fonts
options.why: Screen colors and fonts are display settings changed in system preferences; they have no connection to the login credentials used to verify identity.

q: A company wants to know which products customers buy together. Which tool best helps?

options.t: A random drawing of customer names
options.why: A random drawing of customer names picks people by chance and shows nothing about which products they buy together.

options.t: Data analysis of sales records
options.why: Analyzing sales records reveals patterns, such as items often bought together, which supports decisions on product placement, bundles and promotions based on real purchase data.

options.t: The weather forecast for the week
options.why: The weather forecast may influence some sales, but it cannot show which specific products customers buy together in the store.

options.t: A guess based on the owner's mood
options.why: A guess based on the owner's mood is not data, so it cannot reliably show which products customers buy together.

q: What is a focus group?

options.t: A group of suppliers who sell goods to the whole firm
options.why: Suppliers sell goods to the firm, which makes them part of the supply chain; a focus group is made up of consumers who give opinions.

options.t: A list of competitors and their yearly sales figures
options.why: A list of competitors and their sales figures is competitive research, not a focus group, which gathers opinions directly from a small group of consumers.

options.t: A small group asked for opinions about a product or ad
options.why: A focus group is a small group of consumers led through a discussion to gather opinions about a product, ad or idea, which helps firms improve before launch.

options.t: A group of staff on their break to chat about lunch
options.why: Staff chatting on a break are not gathering data about a product; a focus group is a structured discussion with a purpose led by a moderator.

q: A brand sells the same soda in different flavors for different tastes. What strategy is this?

options.t: Product line extension
options.why: Selling the same soda in several flavors is a product line extension, which adds variations to an existing brand to appeal to different tastes and grow sales.

options.t: Price fixing among rivals
options.why: Price fixing is an illegal agreement among rivals to set prices; it has nothing to do with offering flavors for different tastes.

options.t: Vertical integration
options.why: Vertical integration means a firm controls stages of its supply chain, such as supply or distribution, and is unrelated to offering more flavors.

options.t: Market exit and closure
options.why: Market exit means leaving a market and closing a line, but the brand here is adding flavors to grow, not withdrawing.

q: What is lead time?

options.t: The time a store is open each day of the week
options.why: Store hours describe when a store is open for business, which has nothing to do with the delay between ordering and receiving goods.

options.t: The age of a product since it was first made
options.why: The age of a product since it was made is its product age, not lead time, which measures waiting between an order and its arrival.

options.t: The time of the first sale, counted from the launch date
options.why: The time from launch to the first sale is time to first sale, which is a different measure from supplier lead time.

options.t: The time between placing an order and receiving it
options.why: Lead time is the time between placing an order and receiving it, and planners use it to decide how early to reorder so stock does not run out.

q: A manager sets a reorder point of 20 units. What happens when stock falls to 20?

options.t: Employees stop selling
options.why: Reaching the reorder point does not stop sales; it signals that stock is low enough that more should be ordered to avoid running out.

options.t: A new order is placed
options.why: A reorder point is the stock level that triggers a new order; at 20 units the manager orders more so new stock arrives before inventory runs out.

options.t: The product is dropped
options.why: Dropping the product is a separate strategic decision, and reaching a reorder point only signals that more stock should be ordered.

options.t: The price is doubled
options.why: A reorder point has no link to pricing; doubling the price would not replenish inventory and would simply hurt sales.

q: What is a performance review for an employee?

options.t: A product test done in a lab by the firm
options.why: A product test in a lab evaluates goods, while a performance review evaluates an employee, so a lab test is not an employee review.

options.t: A meeting to discuss work results and goals
options.why: A performance review is a meeting where a manager and employee discuss work results, strengths and goals, which guides improvement, pay decisions and career development.

options.t: A tax filing made by the firm each year
options.why: A tax filing reports a firm's income to the government, which is unrelated to evaluating how an employee has performed.

options.t: A customer survey handed out at a store visit
options.why: A customer survey collects customer opinions about the store or product, not the employee's work results, which a performance review covers.

q: An employee wants to switch careers into marketing. Which step best prepares her?

options.t: Stop learning and stay in your current job for good
options.why: Staying put and not learning keeps her skills unchanged, which does not prepare her for a move into a new field like marketing.

options.t: Avoid networking with people who work in the field
options.why: Avoiding networking cuts her off from contacts, advice and job leads in the field, which makes switching careers harder instead of easier.

options.t: Apply with no preparation, as employers like to see
options.why: Applying with no preparation shows employers a lack of skills and effort; they favor candidates who have prepared and can demonstrate relevant knowledge.

options.t: Learn marketing skills and gain related experience
options.why: Learning marketing skills through courses and gaining related experience, such as an internship or project, builds the qualifications employers look for in career changers.

q: What is a contingency plan?

options.t: A plan to raise prices on all goods sold
options.why: Raising prices on all goods is a pricing decision, whereas a contingency plan is prepared in advance for handling an unexpected problem.

options.t: A plan to hire friends and family of the owner
options.why: Hiring friends and family is a staffing choice that does not address unexpected problems, which is the purpose of a contingency plan.

options.t: A backup plan used if something goes wrong
options.why: A contingency plan is a backup plan prepared in advance to be used if something goes wrong, which helps a business respond quickly and limit damage.

options.t: A plan to end the business and sell its assets
options.why: A plan to end a business and sell its assets is a liquidation plan, a different plan from a backup created to deal with possible problems.

q: A company enters a new country but faces unexpected regulations. Which management action best addresses this?

options.t: Research regulations and adjust the plan
options.why: Researching the regulations and adjusting the plan lets the company comply with local rules, avoid penalties and adapt its strategy to the new country.

options.t: Ignore the rules and handle trouble later
options.why: Ignoring the rules risks fines, legal action and being shut out of the market, so putting off the trouble makes problems worse.

options.t: Blame local employees for the problems
options.why: Blaming local employees solves nothing and damages morale; the regulations remain and the company still has to follow them.

options.t: Leave without analysis of the market
options.why: Leaving without analyzing the market throws away the investment and skips the chance to learn whether the plan can be adapted.

q: What is the purpose of a customer survey?

options.t: To measure satisfaction and gather ideas
options.why: A customer survey measures satisfaction and collects ideas for improvement, which helps a business learn what customers like and what needs to change.

options.t: To remove customers from the mailing list
options.why: Removing customers from a mailing list is handled through an opt-out request, not a survey, whose purpose is to gather opinions.

options.t: To advertise a product to new customers
options.why: Advertising a product to new customers is a promotion goal, while a survey collects feedback from existing or potential customers.

options.t: To collect taxes from customers in the store
options.why: Collecting taxes is a government job done through sales tax at checkout, and it has nothing to do with a customer survey.

q: What is a monetary policy?

options.t: A law about product labels and the information they carry
options.why: A law about product labels is consumer protection regulation, not monetary policy, which concerns the money supply and interest rates.

options.t: A company's pay plan for all of its staff and managers
options.why: A company's pay plan for staff is a compensation policy inside one firm, while monetary policy is set for the whole economy.

options.t: A store's return rule that sets how refunds are given
options.why: A store's return rule is a retail policy about refunds, unrelated to the national money supply.

options.t: Central bank actions that influence money and interest rates
options.why: Monetary policy is the set of actions by a central bank, such as the Federal Reserve, that influence the money supply and interest rates to steer inflation and growth.

q: When consumer confidence rises, what is a likely effect on retail sales?

options.t: They stay frozen
options.why: Retail sales do not stay frozen; they respond to how willing consumers are to spend, and higher confidence tends to increase spending.

options.t: They become illegal
options.why: Retail sales cannot become illegal because of consumer confidence; confidence is an attitude about the economy, not a legal matter.

options.t: They tend to rise
options.why: When consumers feel confident about jobs and income, they spend more freely, so retail sales tend to rise, and this is why economists track confidence surveys.

options.t: They tend to drop
options.why: Rising confidence encourages spending rather than saving, so retail sales would not tend to drop; falling confidence is what usually reduces sales.

q: Which is a risk entrepreneurs often face?

options.t: Immunity from taxes and from all rules
options.why: No business is immune from taxes and regulation; entrepreneurs must follow tax law and other rules like every other firm.

options.t: Losing invested money if the business fails
options.why: Entrepreneurs put their own money into a venture, and if the business fails they can lose that investment, which is a core financial risk.

options.t: Guaranteed profit every month, whatever happens
options.why: No business can guarantee a monthly profit, since sales and costs change; profit uncertainty is part of the risk entrepreneurs accept.

options.t: No competition at all from any other firm
options.why: Almost every business faces some competition, so having none at all is not a typical risk and rarely happens in real markets.

q: What is an invoice dispute?

options.t: A tax refund paid out to the firm by the state
options.why: A tax refund paid by the state is a government payment on a tax return, not a disagreement between a buyer and seller over a bill.

options.t: A disagreement over the amount or terms billed
options.why: An invoice dispute is a disagreement between buyer and seller over the amount, items or terms billed, and it must be resolved before payment is made.

options.t: A coupon expiring before it is used by a buyer
options.why: A coupon expiring before use is a promotion issue between a store and a shopper and does not involve an invoice.

options.t: A shipment arriving early, before the agreed date
options.why: A shipment arriving early is a delivery timing matter and does not involve disagreement about what is billed on an invoice.

q: What is the purpose of a business letter's closing?

options.t: To repeat the whole letter in a few words
options.why: Repeating the whole letter in a few words is a summary; a closing is a short polite ending, such as 'Sincerely,' followed by the sender's name.

options.t: To add a joke or a funny story to end it
options.why: A joke or funny story is out of place in a formal business letter and can look unprofessional, so it is not the purpose of a closing.

options.t: To end politely and show the sender's name
options.why: The closing ends a business letter politely, using a phrase such as 'Sincerely,' and shows the sender's name and signature so the reader knows who wrote it.

options.t: To hide the sender's identity from the reader
options.why: The closing identifies the sender rather than hiding who they are; hiding identity would make the letter useless for business purposes.

q: What is a dividend?

options.t: A payment from a company's profits to shareholders
options.why: A dividend is a payment of part of a company's profits to its shareholders, usually quarterly, and it rewards them for owning stock in the firm.

options.t: A discount from a supplier for paying an invoice early
options.why: A discount from a supplier for early payment is a cash or trade discount, unrelated to payments made to a company's shareholders.

options.t: A fee paid to a bank for a service it provides
options.why: A fee paid to a bank for a service is a bank charge, while a dividend is a payout that a company makes to its owners.

options.t: A tax paid by a business on its yearly profits
options.why: A tax a business pays on yearly profits is corporate income tax, which goes to the government instead of to shareholders as a dividend.

q: What is a salary?

options.t: A one-time bonus paid at year end
options.why: A one-time bonus paid at year end is a bonus, which is extra pay and not the fixed regular pay that defines a salary.

options.t: A payment for hours worked only
options.why: A payment for hours worked only is an hourly wage; a salary is a fixed amount that does not depend on the hours counted.

options.t: A payment for each item produced
options.why: A payment for each item produced is piece-rate pay, a different pay method from a salary, which stays the same each period.

options.t: A fixed regular payment for work
options.why: A salary is a fixed regular payment for work, such as a set annual amount paid in equal installments, regardless of the exact hours worked.

q: What is market share?

options.t: The cost of advertising a product to the public
options.why: The cost of advertising is a marketing expense and says nothing about how much of the total market a company holds.

options.t: The size of a company's profit as a percent of sales
options.why: Profit as a percent of sales is profit margin, which measures profitability rather than a company's share of the overall market.

options.t: The number of stores owned by the whole company
options.why: The number of stores a company owns shows its size or reach, not the percentage of total market sales that it captures.

options.t: A company's percentage of total sales in a market
options.why: Market share is a company's percentage of total sales in its market, for example $20 million of a $100 million market equals 20%, and it shows competitive strength.

q: What does it mean to be dependable at work?

options.t: Avoiding responsibility for your work
options.why: Avoiding responsibility is the opposite of being dependable, since a dependable person owns the tasks assigned and does not shift them to others.

options.t: Missing deadlines without giving notice
options.why: Missing deadlines without notice leaves others unable to plan and shows unreliability, which is the opposite of dependability.

options.t: Doing what you say you will do on time
options.why: Being dependable means doing what you promise on time, so coworkers and managers can trust you and rely on your work being done.

options.t: Making excuses often for missed tasks
options.why: Making frequent excuses for missed tasks shows a lack of accountability, and dependable people instead deliver results or warn others early.

q: What is a firewall's role on a company network?

options.t: Blocking unauthorized traffic
options.why: A firewall monitors network traffic and blocks unauthorized access according to security rules, protecting the company's systems and data from outside threats.

options.t: Printing reports for staff
options.why: Printing reports is done by printers and software; a firewall is a security tool and plays no part in producing documents.

options.t: Measuring employee typing speed
options.why: Typing speed is measured by typing tests, and a firewall does not track employee keystrokes or performance; it filters network traffic.

options.t: Storing files forever on disk
options.why: Storing files is the job of storage devices or servers; a firewall filters traffic and does not hold files for any length of time.

q: What is order fulfillment's goal?

options.t: To delay shipments to customers for several weeks
options.why: Delaying shipments for weeks would anger customers and hurt sales, so it is the opposite of what order fulfillment aims to do.

options.t: To deliver the right item to the customer on time
options.why: Order fulfillment aims to deliver the right item to the customer on time, from receiving the order through picking, packing and shipping, which builds satisfaction and repeat sales.

options.t: To cut advertising costs by shipping fewer orders
options.why: Shipping fewer orders loses sales and does not cut advertising costs, and fulfillment exists to deliver orders, not to reduce them.

options.t: To raise prices on all goods that are ordered
options.why: Raising prices is a pricing decision made by management and has nothing to do with fulfillment, which concerns delivering ordered goods.

q: Who is generally responsible for debts of a sole proprietorship?

options.t: The owner personally
options.why: A sole proprietorship is not separate from its owner, so the owner is personally liable for business debts, and personal assets may be used to pay them.

options.t: Only the customers
options.why: Customers are not responsible for a business's debts; they pay for goods, and the owner remains liable for what the business owes.

options.t: Only the government
options.why: The government does not take on a private business's debts; the owner must pay creditors or risk losing personal property.

options.t: No one, it is separate
options.why: A sole proprietorship is not a separate legal entity like a corporation, so there is no legal shield between the owner and the debts.

q: A supplier ships goods that do not match the sample the buyer approved. What legal principle may the buyer rely on?

options.t: Zoning rules on where a business may operate
options.why: Zoning rules control where a business may operate and have no bearing on a supplier delivering goods that fail to match an approved sample.

options.t: Child labor rules for all young workers
options.why: Child labor rules protect young workers and do not address a dispute over goods that differ from the approved sample.

options.t: Antitrust law on mergers and monopolies
options.why: Antitrust law deals with monopolies and mergers that reduce competition, which is unrelated to a supplier shipping goods that differ from the sample.

options.t: Breach of the sales agreement or warranty
options.why: Goods that do not match the approved sample breach the sales agreement or warranty under contract law, allowing the buyer to reject the goods or seek a remedy.

q: What is a union contract also called?

options.t: A lease agreement for a building
options.why: A lease agreement is a contract for renting a building or property, which is not what a union contract covering workers is called.

options.t: A sales invoice for the goods
options.why: A sales invoice is a bill for goods sold, so it is not a union agreement covering workers' pay and conditions.

options.t: A collective bargaining agreement
options.why: A union contract is called a collective bargaining agreement, which is negotiated between employers and a union and sets wages, hours and working conditions for covered workers.

options.t: A purchase warranty given to buyers
options.why: A purchase warranty is a seller's promise about a product to buyers and is unrelated to an agreement negotiated between a union and an employer.

q: Why does a business need permits to build or remodel?

options.t: To avoid paying taxes on the new building
options.why: Permits do not avoid taxes; they are approvals from local authorities, and a new building is still subject to property taxes.

options.t: To ensure work meets safety and zoning rules
options.why: Permits ensure that construction or remodeling meets building safety codes and zoning rules, which protects workers, customers and neighbors and helps avoid fines or demolition orders.

options.t: To advertise the business to local people
options.why: Advertising a business is done through marketing, and a building permit is a government approval and plays no role in promotion.

options.t: To increase the building's value automatically
options.why: A permit does not raise a building's value; it only confirms the work was approved and follows safety and zoning requirements.

q: An employee signs a non-compete agreement that bars work in the same field anywhere for 20 years. What might a court decide?

options.t: It must be enforced exactly as written by courts
options.why: Courts do not enforce every non-compete as written; they check whether the terms are reasonable, so enforcement exactly as written is not guaranteed.

options.t: It is the same as a patent held by the whole firm
options.why: A non-compete is a contract between employee and employer, while a patent is a government grant protecting an invention, so the two are not the same.

options.t: The restriction may be unreasonable and unenforceable
options.why: Courts often refuse unreasonable non-competes, and 20 years across an entire field is far too long and broad, so the restriction may be unenforceable.

options.t: It becomes void only if the employee quits on their own
options.why: A non-compete is not void just because the employee quits; courts judge its reasonableness in time, area and scope, and quitting does not change that.

q: Which greeting is most suitable for a formal letter to an unknown recipient?

options.t: Hi there, friend,
options.why: 'Hi there, friend,' is too casual and presumes a friendship, so it does not suit a formal letter to someone you do not know.

options.t: Yo, hiring crew,
options.why: 'Yo, hiring crew,' is slang and sounds unprofessional, which could hurt your chances in a formal business or job application.

options.t: What's up, first name
options.why: 'What's up, first name' is casual and assumes you know the person's name, which is not acceptable when writing to an unknown recipient.

options.t: Dear Hiring Manager,
options.why: 'Dear Hiring Manager,' is polite and formal and addresses the role when you do not know the person's name, so it suits letters to unknown recipients.

q: A manager gives instructions quickly, and the employee seems unsure. What should the manager do?

options.t: Ask the employee to restate the instructions and invite questions
options.why: Asking the employee to restate the instructions and inviting questions confirms understanding, clears up confusion and prevents errors, which makes the communication effective and shows respect.

options.t: Repeat the instructions faster and say nothing else to them
options.why: Repeating the instructions faster gives the employee even less time to absorb them, so confusion continues and mistakes become more likely.

options.t: End the conversation at once and let the employee work it out alone
options.why: Ending the conversation and leaving the employee alone provides no support, so the employee may make errors and feel unsupported by the manager.

options.t: Assume the employee understands everything that was said to them
options.why: Assuming the employee understands ignores the visible signs of confusion, so misunderstandings go uncorrected and the work may be done incorrectly.

q: What is an effective subject line for a business email?

options.t: A joke unrelated to the message, to make the reader smile
options.why: A joke unrelated to the message does not tell the reader what the email is about, so it wastes attention and may cause the email to be ignored.

options.t: A short phrase that tells what the message is about
options.why: A short subject line that tells what the message is about helps the reader decide how to prioritize it and find it again later.

options.t: A blank line with no words in it at all in the box
options.why: A blank subject line gives the reader no clue about the content, and the email may be overlooked or flagged as spam.

options.t: A long paragraph of text that covers the entire message
options.why: A long paragraph is too lengthy for a subject line, which should be brief; the details belong in the body of the email.

q: Why is it important to know your audience before presenting?

options.t: You can adjust content and tone to their needs
options.why: Knowing your audience lets you adjust the content, tone and examples to their needs and level of knowledge, which makes the presentation more relevant and persuasive.

options.t: So you can read faster during the talk to them
options.why: Reading faster is unrelated to knowing the audience; a presenter should pace the talk to the listeners so they can follow.

options.t: So you can skip the introduction and start talking
options.why: Skipping the introduction would leave the audience without context, and knowing them helps you shape the introduction instead of leaving it out.

options.t: So you can avoid preparing for the talk at all
options.why: Presentations still require preparation; knowing the audience guides what to prepare, so it does not remove the need to prepare.

q: A coworker sends a rude email. What is the best response?

options.t: Ignore all future messages from that same coworker
options.why: Ignoring all future messages from the coworker cuts off needed communication and can harm teamwork, and it does not solve the underlying problem.

options.t: Forward it to the whole company to embarrass them
options.why: Forwarding the rude email to the whole company is unprofessional, spreads conflict, and could damage your own reputation and workplace relationships.

options.t: Reply with an equally rude email to teach them
options.why: Replying rudely escalates the conflict and reflects badly on you, which makes the situation worse and does not teach anyone anything.

options.t: Reply calmly and professionally or discuss in person
options.why: Replying calmly and professionally, or discussing it in person, keeps the focus on the problem and can resolve the conflict while protecting working relationships.

q: Why should employees avoid arguing with customers?

options.t: Arguments reduce complaints from other customers
options.why: Arguing with customers increases complaints, as upset customers tell others about bad treatment; it does not reduce them.

options.t: Arguments make sales go faster in the store today
options.why: Arguments do not speed up sales; they drive customers away and create unhappy experiences that cost the store future business.

options.t: Arguments damage relationships and reputation
options.why: Arguing damages the relationship and the business's reputation, since customers who feel disrespected leave and often share their bad experience with others.

options.t: Arguments are required by policy to defend
options.why: No policy requires employees to argue with customers; good service policies call for staying calm, listening and solving the problem politely.

q: A customer repeatedly buys the same brand of coffee. What can the store do to show appreciation?

options.t: Stop stocking the coffee that the customer likes
options.why: Stopping the stock of a customer's favorite coffee would remove the item the customer wants, which shows no appreciation and may lose the customer.

options.t: Offer a loyalty reward or a personal thank-you
options.why: A loyalty reward or a personal thank-you shows the store values the customer's repeated business, which builds goodwill and encourages the customer to keep coming back.

options.t: Raise the price for that one customer only
options.why: Raising the price for a single customer is unfair and discriminatory, and it punishes loyalty instead of rewarding it.

options.t: Ignore the customer and give no thanks at all
options.why: Ignoring a loyal customer gives no recognition for their repeat business, which can make them feel unvalued and willing to shop elsewhere.

q: What is the first step in handling an angry customer?

options.t: Listen without interrupting
options.why: Listening without interrupting lets the customer vent and explain, shows respect, and gives you the facts needed to solve the problem, so it is the first step.

options.t: Blame a coworker for it
options.why: Blaming a coworker does not help the customer and shows poor teamwork, making the customer angrier instead of fixing the issue.

options.t: Argue your side loudly now
options.why: Arguing loudly escalates the conflict and shows disrespect, which makes the customer angrier instead of calming the situation.

options.t: Walk away from the customer
options.why: Walking away leaves the customer's problem unresolved and signals that the business does not care, which worsens the anger.

q: What do economists mean by 'demand'?

options.t: The cost of materials used to make a product in a factory
