options.t: A plan for what to do if something goes wrong
options.why: A contingency plan sets out what to do if something goes wrong, such as a fire, outage or supply failure, so the business can respond quickly and keep operating.

options.t: A plan to open a new store in the city soon
options.why: Opening a new store is an expansion strategy; a contingency plan is a backup response to emergencies and unexpected events.

q: A restaurant keeps a backup generator in case of power loss. What is this?

options.t: A hiring process plan
options.why: A hiring process plan covers recruitment steps; a backup generator prepares for power loss, which is a different concern.

options.t: A price discount plan
options.why: A price discount plan is a promotion tactic; a generator does not change prices but protects operations during an outage.

options.t: A marketing campaign
options.why: A marketing campaign promotes products to customers; a backup generator is not advertising, it keeps the kitchen running in an outage.

options.t: A contingency measure
options.why: A backup generator is a contingency measure because it lets the restaurant keep operating if power fails, protecting food, sales and customers from the disruption.

q: Why does a business keep emergency funds?

options.t: To cover unexpected costs without borrowing
options.why: Emergency funds cover unexpected costs, such as repairs or a revenue drop, without borrowing, which avoids interest and keeps the business stable.

options.t: To pay for yearly advertising costs only
options.why: Yearly advertising is a planned budget item; emergency funds are for unplanned costs, not routine marketing expenses.

options.t: To make employees spend more of their pay
options.why: Emergency funds protect the business; they are not designed to make employees spend more of their pay.

options.t: To avoid ever earning profits from sales
options.why: Businesses exist to earn profit; reserves are meant to protect the business from shocks and do not mean avoiding profits.

q: What is fraud?

options.t: A late payment made to a supplier by the firm
options.why: A late payment to a supplier is a breach of terms or poor cash management, but it is not intentional deception, so it is not fraud.

options.t: An honest mistake in a calculation that is corrected
options.why: An honest mistake that is corrected lacks intent to deceive, so it is an error, not fraud.

options.t: Intentional deception to gain something unfairly
options.why: Fraud is intentional deception to gain something unfairly, such as falsifying records or stealing funds, and it is a crime that can bring fines and prison.

options.t: A legal tax deduction taken by a business each year
options.why: A legal tax deduction is allowed under tax law and is not deceptive, so it is not fraud.

q: Which control best reduces the risk of employee theft of cash?

options.t: Keeping cash in an unlocked drawer that any staff member can open
options.why: An unlocked drawer anyone can open invites theft and makes it hard to trace missing cash, so it increases risk instead of reducing it.

options.t: Letting one person handle all of the cash with no second review
options.why: Letting one person handle all cash with no review removes checks and makes theft easy to hide, which raises the risk of loss.

options.t: Skipping end-of-day cash counts and bank deposits for the week
options.why: Skipping cash counts and deposits leaves cash unprotected and unverified, so theft or errors could go unnoticed for days.

options.t: Separating duties so no one person handles cash from start to finish
options.why: Separating duties means no one person handles cash from start to finish, so another employee checks the work and theft becomes harder to hide and easier to catch.

q: What is cybersecurity risk?

options.t: The chance of prices falling in the market for all goods
options.why: Prices falling in the market is market or economic risk; cybersecurity risk relates to computer systems and data.

options.t: The chance of loss from attacks on computer systems and data
options.why: Cybersecurity risk is the chance of loss from attacks on computer systems and data, such as hacking, malware or data breaches, which can cost money and trust.

options.t: The chance of a product being returned after being used
options.why: Product returns after use are a quality or customer service issue, not a risk tied to computer systems or data.

options.t: The chance of staff arriving late for work on any day
options.why: Staff arriving late is an HR attendance matter; cybersecurity risk deals with threats to computers, networks and information.

q: Which practice most reduces the risk of a phishing attack?

options.t: Sharing passwords by email with other staff members
options.why: Sharing passwords by email exposes accounts to attackers and makes phishing more effective, so it raises the risk instead of reducing it.

options.t: Turning off all security updates on staff computers
options.why: Turning off security updates leaves known weaknesses open to attackers, which makes phishing and malware attacks more likely to succeed.

options.t: Encouraging staff to click every link they receive
options.why: Clicking every link is exactly how phishing works, since attackers use fake links to steal passwords or install malware, so this raises risk.

options.t: Training employees to spot and report suspicious emails
options.why: Training employees to spot and report suspicious emails builds awareness, which is the best defense against phishing because attackers rely on someone being tricked into clicking.

q: What is financial risk?

options.t: The chance that a store will be remodeled by its owners soon
options.why: Remodeling a store is a property or planning decision, not a financial risk about losing money or paying debts.

options.t: The chance that a business will lose money or be unable to pay debts
options.why: Financial risk is the chance a business will lose money or be unable to pay its debts, often because of heavy borrowing, falling sales or unexpected costs.

options.t: The chance that products will be stolen from the main stockroom
options.why: Stolen products from a stockroom are a theft or security risk, though the loss has some financial effect, it is not defined as financial risk.

options.t: The chance that employees will resign from their jobs this year
options.why: Employees resigning is a staffing or human resources risk, not a financial risk about losing money or paying debts.

q: A firm borrows heavily to expand and sales fall. What risk has increased?

options.t: Safety risk
options.why: Safety risk concerns physical harm to people; borrowing and falling sales affect the firm's finances, not workplace safety.

options.t: Security risk
options.why: Security risk concerns theft or attacks on assets and data; heavy debt and lower sales are not security problems.

options.t: Financial risk
options.why: Heavy borrowing with falling sales makes it harder to pay interest and repay loans, so financial risk, the chance of losing money or defaulting, rises.

options.t: Legal risk
options.why: Legal risk comes from lawsuits or breaking laws; debt and falling sales are money matters, not a legal exposure.

q: What is a safety data sheet (SDS)?

options.t: A document that explains hazards and safe handling of a chemical
options.why: A safety data sheet explains a chemical's hazards, safe handling, storage, first aid and emergency steps, and OSHA requires employers to make SDSs available to workers.

options.t: A sheet that lists employees' pay and tax withholding each payday
options.why: A list of pay and tax withholding is a payroll record; a safety data sheet covers chemical hazards and handling.

options.t: A sheet that shows product prices for all the goods in the shop
options.why: A sheet showing product prices is a price list; an SDS gives safety information about hazardous chemicals, not prices.

options.t: A sheet that records sales made by the staff in the shop each day
options.why: A record of daily sales is a sales report; an SDS describes chemical hazards and safe use.

q: An employee must clean with a chemical they do not know. What should they do first?

options.t: Mix it with other cleaners to test how well it works
options.why: Mixing cleaners can create toxic gases or violent reactions, so testing them together is dangerous and never the first step.

options.t: Read the safety data sheet and follow the instructions
options.why: The SDS lists the chemical's hazards, protective equipment and safe handling, so reading it and following the instructions comes first before using an unfamiliar chemical.

options.t: Ask a customer in the store what to do about it next
options.why: A customer has no training or responsibility for workplace chemicals, so asking one is unreliable and could lead to injury.

options.t: Use it without looking at any instructions at all
options.why: Using an unknown chemical without instructions risks burns, fumes or fire, and it violates workplace safety rules.

q: What does OSHA do?

options.t: Collects income taxes from employers for the state
options.why: Collecting income taxes from employers is done by tax agencies like the IRS, not by OSHA, which handles workplace safety.

options.t: Licenses all new businesses in a state or province
options.why: Business licensing is handled by state or local agencies, not OSHA, whose focus is safety and health at work.

options.t: Sets and enforces workplace safety and health standards
options.why: OSHA, the Occupational Safety and Health Administration, sets and enforces workplace safety and health standards, inspects workplaces and can fine employers who fail to protect workers.

options.t: Sets prices for goods sold in stores across the country
options.why: Prices of goods are set by businesses in the market; OSHA does not regulate prices but deals with workplace safety.

q: What does compliance mean in business?

options.t: Advertising on as many online platforms as possible each year
options.why: Advertising on many platforms is a marketing choice and does not mean a business is following laws or rules.

options.t: Hiring as many employees as the budget will allow each year
options.why: Hiring many employees is a staffing decision; compliance is about meeting legal and regulatory requirements, not headcount.

options.t: Following the laws, rules and standards that apply to the business
options.why: Compliance means following the laws, rules and standards that apply to the business, such as safety, labor, tax and privacy requirements, which avoids fines, lawsuits and lost trust.

options.t: Choosing the lowest prices to attract more customers each month
options.why: Choosing low prices is a pricing strategy; compliance concerns obeying legal and regulatory requirements, not pricing choices.

q: What is a regulation?

options.t: A rule made by a government agency that businesses must follow
options.why: A regulation is a rule made by a government agency that businesses must follow, and it carries the force of law, with penalties such as fines for violations.

options.t: A discount offered to businesses that pay their taxes early
options.why: A discount for early taxpayers is a tax incentive, not a regulation, which is a binding rule rather than a reward.

options.t: A suggestion that businesses may ignore if they prefer at any time
options.why: Regulations are mandatory; a suggestion businesses may ignore would be a guideline or recommendation, not a binding rule.

options.t: A contract between two private companies for the sale of goods
options.why: A contract between two private companies is a private agreement, not a government rule, so it is not a regulation.

q: What is the purpose of a compliance officer?

options.t: To design advertisements for the company's new products
options.why: Designing advertisements is a marketing role; a compliance officer checks that the company follows laws and policies.

options.t: To make sure the company follows laws and internal policies
options.why: A compliance officer makes sure the company follows laws, regulations and internal policies by monitoring, training staff and investigating issues, which reduces legal and financial risk.

options.t: To repair equipment used in the company's main factory
options.why: Repairing equipment is a maintenance job; compliance officers focus on rules and legal requirements, not machinery.

options.t: To set the prices that customers pay for the products
options.why: Pricing is a management and marketing decision, while a compliance officer ensures legal and policy adherence.

q: What is a code of conduct?

options.t: A list of products offered by the company to its buyers
options.why: A list of products offered is a catalog; a code of conduct describes expected behavior, not what the company sells.

options.t: A secret list of passwords used by the managers to log in
options.why: Passwords are confidential security credentials; a code of conduct is a shared document of behavior standards, not a secret list.

options.t: A schedule of employee shifts for the whole month ahead
options.why: A schedule of shifts is a staffing plan; a code of conduct sets behavior expectations, not working hours.

options.t: A written set of rules for ethical and professional behavior
options.why: A code of conduct is a written set of rules for ethical and professional behavior, telling employees what is expected on honesty, conflicts of interest, respect and legal compliance.

q: An employee accepts an expensive gift from a supplier who wants a contract. What compliance issue does this raise?

options.t: A normal service practice accepted in most firms
options.why: Accepting costly gifts from someone seeking a contract is not normal practice; most firms have gift policies to prevent bias and bribery.

options.t: A requirement of tax law for all employees of a firm
options.why: Tax law does not require employees to take supplier gifts; gifts are a conduct issue and may even need to be reported.

options.t: A possible conflict of interest or bribery concern
options.why: An expensive gift from a supplier seeking a contract may influence the employee's decision, creating a conflict of interest or looking like a bribe, which breaks most company policies and some laws.

options.t: A way to lower company costs and raise yearly profits
options.why: A gift does not lower company costs, and it can lead to unfair contracts and legal trouble that hurt profits.

q: What is whistleblowing?

options.t: Reporting illegal or unethical activity inside an organization
options.why: Whistleblowing is reporting illegal or unethical activity inside an organization to those who can act, and many laws protect whistleblowers from retaliation.

options.t: Quitting a job without notice to start work somewhere else
options.why: Quitting without notice to take another job is just resigning abruptly; it is not reporting wrongdoing.

options.t: Asking a manager for a raise in pay after a very good year
options.why: Asking for a raise is a pay negotiation, unrelated to reporting illegal or unethical conduct.

options.t: Spreading false rumors about a coworker to damage their standing
options.why: Spreading false rumors is harmful gossip or defamation, while whistleblowing reports real wrongdoing to the proper people.

q: What is the Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA)?

options.t: An agency that sets interest rates for the banks of a nation
options.why: Setting interest rates is done by a central bank, such as the Federal Reserve, not OSHA, which is a workplace safety agency.

options.t: An agency that sets and enforces workplace safety standards
options.why: OSHA is the federal agency that sets and enforces workplace safety and health standards, inspecting workplaces and fining employers that put workers at risk.

options.t: An agency that collects federal income taxes each year
options.why: Collecting federal income taxes is the IRS's job, not OSHA's, which regulates safety in workplaces.

options.t: An agency that approves new drugs for sale to the public
options.why: Approving new drugs is the job of the Food and Drug Administration, not OSHA, which focuses on workplace safety.

q: A warehouse worker is injured because required safety guards were removed. Which agency may investigate?

options.t: FCC
options.why: The FCC regulates radio, television and communications, not workplace safety injuries, so it would not investigate a removed machine guard.

options.t: SEC
options.why: The SEC regulates securities markets and public company disclosures, not workplace safety, so it would not investigate this injury.

options.t: Fed
options.why: The Fed is the central bank that handles monetary policy and banking supervision, not workplace injuries.

options.t: OSHA
options.why: OSHA enforces workplace safety standards, including machine guarding, so it may investigate an injury caused by removed safety guards and can issue citations and fines.

q: What does the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission (EEOC) enforce?

options.t: Laws that set the minimum prices of goods
options.why: Setting minimum prices of goods is not an EEOC role; prices are set by markets and, in some cases, other agencies.

options.t: Laws that regulate all stock trading
options.why: Stock trading is regulated by the SEC, not the EEOC, which deals with employment discrimination.

options.t: Laws against workplace discrimination
options.why: The EEOC enforces federal laws against workplace discrimination based on race, sex, religion, age, disability and other protected traits, and it investigates complaints and can sue employers.

options.t: Laws that control imports and exports
options.why: Imports and exports are controlled by customs and trade agencies, not by the EEOC.

q: A manager refuses to hire a qualified applicant because of the applicant's religion. What is this?

options.t: Illegal discrimination
options.why: Refusing to hire a qualified applicant because of religion is illegal discrimination under Title VII of the Civil Rights Act, and the employer could face an EEOC complaint and lawsuits.

options.t: A required hiring practice
options.why: No law requires hiring decisions based on religion; employers must judge applicants on qualifications, not protected traits.

options.t: A legal hiring preference
options.why: Religion is a protected characteristic, so preferring or rejecting applicants for it is not a legal hiring preference.

options.t: A tax compliance step
options.why: Hiring decisions are not tax compliance steps; this is a discrimination issue, not something tax rules require.

q: What is the Fair Labor Standards Act (FLSA) mainly about?

options.t: Rules for food labeling on all packages
options.why: Food labeling is regulated by the FDA and related agencies, not by the FLSA, which covers pay and labor rules.

options.t: Rules for advertising claims in the news
options.why: Advertising claims are overseen by the FTC; the FLSA deals with wages, hours and child labor.

options.t: Rules for stock market trading and broker reports
options.why: Stock market trading and broker reports fall under securities law enforced by the SEC, not the Fair Labor Standards Act.

options.t: Minimum wage, overtime and child labor rules
options.why: The FLSA sets federal minimum wage, overtime pay rules and child labor limits, protecting workers by requiring pay for covered hours and limiting hazardous work by minors.

q: A non-exempt worker earns $14 an hour and works 44 hours. Overtime is 1.5 times pay after 40 hours. What is total pay?

options.why: $924 would come from paying all 44 hours at overtime rate (44 x $21); only the 4 hours beyond 40 earn overtime pay.
First 40 hours: 40 x $14 = $560. Overtime rate is $14 x 1.5 = $21, so 4 x $21 = $84. Total is $560 + $84 = $644.
$616 is 44 x $14 at straight time, which ignores the extra half-time premium owed for the 4 overtime hours.
$560 covers only the first 40 hours at $14, leaving out the 4 overtime hours that also earn pay at $21 each.

q: What is the purpose of record keeping for compliance?

options.t: To increase the number of forms employees fill out
options.why: Record keeping aims to document compliance, not to create more paperwork for employees to fill out.

options.t: To raise product prices for customers each year
options.why: Records do not set prices; their purpose is to document actions, not to raise what customers pay.

options.t: To prove that the company followed required rules
options.why: Records prove the company followed required rules, such as tax, safety and employment laws, which helps pass audits, defend against claims and show good faith to regulators.

options.t: To hide mistakes from regulators and from the public
options.why: Hiding mistakes from regulators would be unethical and illegal; proper records are meant to be accurate and available for review.

q: An audit finds missing safety training records. What is the best response?

options.t: Complete the training, fix the records and set up a tracking system
options.why: The best response is to complete the training, fix the records and set up a tracking system, which corrects the gap and prevents it from happening again.

options.t: Ignore the finding until the next audit comes around once more
options.why: Ignoring a finding leaves the violation in place, risks fines and injuries, and will likely be flagged again at the next audit.

options.t: Blame the auditor for the finding and argue about the report
options.why: Blaming the auditor does not fix missing records and wastes time; audit findings are meant to help improve compliance.

options.t: Destroy the audit report so no one sees it and carry on as before
options.why: Destroying an audit report is illegal obstruction and hides problems instead of solving them, which can lead to serious penalties.

q: What is a license?

options.t: A list of company rules that all staff members must follow
options.why: A list of company rules is a policy or code of conduct; a license is permission granted by an authority.

options.t: A discount for buying in bulk, given to customers who order lots
options.why: A bulk discount is a pricing incentive for large orders, not an official permission to operate.

options.t: A report of annual profits that a firm shares with its owners
options.why: A report of annual profits is a financial statement; a license is a government grant of permission.

options.t: Official permission to operate a business or practice a profession
options.why: A license is official permission from a government or authority to operate a business or practice a profession, such as a liquor license or a medical license, and operating without one can bring penalties.

q: A restaurant opens without a required health permit. What is the likely result?

options.t: Lower taxes for the whole year ahead
options.why: Lower taxes are not a result of skipping a permit; opening without one is a violation that leads to penalties, not savings.

options.t: Fines or closure by the authorities
options.why: Operating without a required health permit is illegal, so authorities can issue fines, order the restaurant closed and require it to obtain the permit before reopening.

options.t: Faster deliveries from suppliers
options.why: Supplier delivery speed is unrelated to permits; breaking health rules does not speed up deliveries.

options.t: A reward from the health department
options.why: The health department enforces rules and would not reward a violation; it is more likely to punish an unpermitted restaurant.

q: What is data privacy compliance?

options.t: Following laws that protect personal information
options.why: Data privacy compliance means following laws that protect personal information, such as rules on collecting, storing, sharing and deleting data, so customers' details stay safe and the firm avoids fines.

options.t: Storing data on unlocked shared public computers
options.why: Storing data on unlocked public computers leaves it exposed and violates privacy duties, so it is the opposite of compliance.

options.t: Selling personal data without telling customers
options.why: Selling personal data without telling customers violates privacy laws that require notice and often consent, so it breaks compliance.

options.t: Sharing customer data with anyone who asks
options.why: Sharing customer data with anyone who asks breaches privacy duties and risks identity theft, so it is a violation, not compliance.

q: A company collects customer emails but is not sure how long to keep them. What should it check?

options.t: Only the color of the email design and font
options.why: The color and font of an email design have no bearing on how long data must be kept; legal and policy rules decide retention.

options.t: Only the number of customers on the email list
options.why: The size of the list does not determine retention; laws and policies decide how long personal data may or must be kept.

options.t: Nothing, because emails can be kept forever by anyone
options.why: Personal data cannot be kept forever by anyone, since privacy laws often limit retention and require deletion when it is no longer needed.

options.t: Applicable privacy laws and its retention policy
options.why: The company should check applicable privacy laws and its retention policy, which say what data may be kept, for how long and when it must be deleted.

q: What is an internal control?

options.t: A schedule of employee shifts for the next month ahead
options.why: A schedule of shifts is a staffing plan, not a procedure that safeguards assets or the accuracy of records.

options.t: A rule that sets the price of a product, as ordered by managers
options.why: Setting a product's price is a pricing decision; internal controls are procedures that protect the business, not price rules.

options.t: A procedure that protects assets and ensures accurate records
options.why: An internal control is a procedure, such as approvals, reconciliations or separation of duties, that protects assets, prevents fraud and ensures accurate records.

options.t: A tool for advertising to customers on the radio and in print
options.why: Advertising on radio and in print is a promotion activity, while internal controls protect assets and records.

q: Why should the same person not both approve and pay invoices?

options.t: It is required for every business bank account
options.why: No rule requires this for every bank account; the practice is a recommended internal control, not a universal requirement.

options.t: It separates duties to reduce the risk of fraud
options.why: Separating the duties of approving and paying invoices means one person cannot create and pay a fake invoice alone, which reduces the risk of fraud and errors.

options.t: It lowers the cost of the invoices a firm pays
options.why: Separation of duties does not lower invoice costs; its goal is control and accuracy, not cost reduction.

options.t: It makes payments take longer to complete each month
options.why: The aim is protection against fraud, not slower payments; good controls can be built without much delay.

q: What is the Sarbanes-Oxley Act mainly about?

options.t: Accuracy and honesty in financial reporting by public companies
options.why: The Sarbanes-Oxley Act, passed in 2002 after scandals like Enron, requires accurate and honest financial reporting by public companies and holds executives accountable with internal controls and audits.

options.t: Rules for food safety in restaurants and in food shops in the state
options.why: Food safety rules come from agencies like the FDA and local health departments, not from the Sarbanes-Oxley Act.

options.t: Setting the minimum wage for workers in all industries and states
options.why: The minimum wage is set by the Fair Labor Standards Act and state laws, not by Sarbanes-Oxley.

options.t: Limits on imports from other countries and port duties charged
options.why: Import limits and port duties are trade and customs matters, not covered by Sarbanes-Oxley.

q: What is a conflict of interest?

options.t: A disagreement over office furniture, such as who gets the desk
options.why: A disagreement over furniture is an ordinary workplace dispute; a conflict of interest involves personal interests affecting work decisions.

options.t: A rivalry between two stores in the same town and area today
options.why: Rivalry between competing stores is normal competition, not a conflict of interest, which concerns one person's divided loyalties.

options.t: A debate about a company's slogan and its overall brand image
options.why: A debate over a slogan is a creative disagreement, not a situation where personal interests could affect job decisions.

options.t: A situation where personal interests could affect job decisions
options.why: A conflict of interest is a situation where personal interests could affect job decisions, such as hiring a relative, so it should be disclosed and handled to keep decisions fair.

q: A purchasing manager awards a contract to a company owned by their sibling without telling anyone. What should they have done?

options.t: Ask the sibling to hide the ownership of the whole firm
options.why: Asking a sibling to hide ownership adds deception to the conflict and worsens the violation instead of fixing it.

options.t: Disclose the relationship and step away from the decision
options.why: The manager should disclose the relationship and step away from the decision so others can judge the bids fairly, which protects the company and the manager.

options.t: Keep it secret to avoid questions from the other managers
options.why: Keeping the relationship secret hides the conflict of interest and could look like favoritism or fraud if discovered.

options.t: Award it anyway as the price was fair and nobody would know
options.why: A fair price does not remove the conflict; the issue is the undisclosed relationship, not the cost, and secrecy still breaks policy.

q: What is an ethics hotline?

options.t: A number that customers call to place orders each week
options.why: A number for customers to place orders is a sales line, not an ethics hotline, which handles reports of misconduct.

options.t: A number used to reset passwords for staff accounts
options.why: Password resets are an IT help desk function, not an ethics hotline, which is meant for reporting concerns.

options.t: A confidential way for employees to report concerns
options.why: An ethics hotline is a confidential way for employees to report concerns about misconduct, fraud or safety, often anonymously, so problems surface without fear of retaliation.

options.t: A number used to schedule deliveries to the shops
options.why: A line to schedule deliveries is a logistics service, not an ethics hotline for reporting wrongdoing.

q: What is a policy?

options.t: A list of the goods in storage at the main warehouse of the firm
options.why: A list of goods in storage is an inventory record; a policy is a statement of rules for people to follow.

options.t: A short-term plan for one project, ending when it is done now
options.why: A short-term plan for one project is a project plan, not a policy, which is an ongoing rule guiding behavior.

options.t: A message sent to customers and the press about a new product
options.why: A message about a new product is a press release or announcement, not a policy that sets rules for staff.

options.t: A formal statement of the rules a company expects people to follow
options.why: A policy is a formal statement of the rules a company expects people to follow, guiding decisions and behavior so that everyone acts consistently and legally.

q: Why should policies be communicated and enforced consistently?

options.t: So that employees do not ask any questions at all
options.why: Policies should invite understanding, not prevent questions; employees need to ask questions to follow rules correctly.

options.t: So that all employees understand and are treated fairly
options.why: When policies are communicated and enforced consistently, all employees understand the rules and are treated fairly, which reduces disputes, protects the company legally and builds trust.

options.t: So that only managers know the rules of the firm
options.why: Policies are meant for everyone to follow; keeping them known to managers alone would make compliance impossible.

options.t: So that rules can be ignored when it suits managers
options.why: Ignoring rules when it suits managers is unfair and creates risk of discrimination claims, which is why enforcement must be consistent.

q: What is a trademark?

options.t: A list of a company's competitors and all the goods that they sell
options.why: A list of competitors and their goods is market research, not a trademark, which identifies a brand and is legally protected.

options.t: A tax on branded goods that a large firm pays to the state every year
options.why: A trademark is not a tax; it is intellectual property protection, and owners register it rather than pay tax on it.

options.t: A word, symbol or design that identifies a brand and is legally protected
options.why: A trademark is a word, symbol or design that identifies a brand and is legally protected, so others cannot use confusingly similar marks and consumers can recognize the source.

options.t: A mark showing a product was inspected by a government agent first
options.why: A mark showing government inspection is a certification or grade stamp, not a trademark, which identifies a brand.

q: A business uses a competitor's logo on its own products without permission. What law is likely violated?

options.t: Trademark law
options.why: Using a competitor's logo without permission is likely trademark infringement, since a logo is protected brand identity and copying it can confuse customers and bring lawsuits.

options.t: Immigration law
options.why: Immigration law governs entry and work status of people, not the use of a logo.

options.t: Zoning law
options.why: Zoning law controls how land and buildings may be used, not whether a logo can be copied.

options.t: Minimum wage law
options.why: Minimum wage law sets pay rules for workers and does not cover copying a competitor's logo.

q: What is a contract?

options.t: A message sent to a customer after a sale
options.why: A message sent after a sale is a follow-up, not a binding agreement between parties.

options.t: A friendly promise with no legal weight at all
options.why: A friendly promise with no legal weight is a casual agreement; a contract is enforceable by law.

options.t: A list of a company's products and their prices
options.why: A list of products and prices is a catalog or price list, not an agreement between parties.

options.t: A legally enforceable agreement between parties
options.why: A contract is a legally enforceable agreement between parties, usually requiring an offer, acceptance and consideration, and either side can seek a remedy in court if it is broken.

q: A supplier fails to deliver goods as agreed in a signed contract. What has occurred?

options.t: A normal delay, no cost
options.why: A signed contract creates a duty to deliver; failing to do so is not a harmless delay without cost.

options.t: A breach of contract
options.why: Failing to deliver goods as agreed in a signed contract is a breach of contract, and the other party may seek damages, cancel the deal or demand performance.

options.t: A marketing success
options.why: Failing to deliver is not a marketing success; it harms the customer relationship and creates legal exposure.

options.t: A tax law violation
options.why: Late delivery under a contract is a contract problem, not a tax law violation, which relates to tax duties.

q: What is an environmental regulation?

options.t: A rule that limits pollution and protects natural resources
options.why: An environmental regulation is a rule that limits pollution and protects natural resources such as air, water and soil, and businesses that break it face fines and cleanup costs.

options.t: A rule that sets the price of energy for all homes and firms
options.why: Energy prices are set by markets and utility regulators, not by environmental regulations, which target pollution.

options.t: A rule that limits advertising on television and in print
options.why: Limits on advertising are consumer protection or media rules, not environmental regulations.

options.t: A rule that decides employee holidays and vacation days
options.why: Employee holidays and vacation are decided by employers and labor agreements, not by environmental rules.

q: A factory releases waste into a river without a permit. Which agency is most likely to act?

options.t: The Small Business Administration
options.why: The Small Business Administration supports small firms with loans and advice; it does not enforce pollution laws.

options.t: The Federal Reserve Board system
options.why: The Federal Reserve oversees monetary policy and banking, so it has no role in river pollution enforcement.

options.t: The Environmental Protection Agency
options.why: The Environmental Protection Agency enforces laws like the Clean Water Act, so it would act when a factory releases waste into a river without a permit, seeking fines and cleanup.

options.t: The Social Security Administration
options.why: The Social Security Administration runs retirement and disability benefits and does not enforce environmental rules.

q: What is a project?

options.t: A list of employees' duties and job titles for the whole company
options.why: A list of duties and job titles is an organization chart or job description, not a project, which has a set start and end.

options.t: A permanent department within a company, run by the senior managers
options.why: A permanent department is an ongoing part of the firm, while a project is temporary and ends when its result is delivered.

options.t: An ongoing task that is repeated every day by the staff of the department
options.why: An ongoing task repeated daily is routine operations, not a project, which is a one-time effort with an end.

options.t: A temporary effort with a defined beginning and end to create a result
options.why: A project is a temporary effort with a defined beginning and end that creates a unique result, such as a product launch or a new building.

q: What is project management?

options.t: Planning, organizing and controlling resources to complete a project
options.why: Project management is planning, organizing and controlling resources such as people, time and money to complete a project on time, within budget and to the required quality.

options.t: Setting the price of a product for sale in the market each year
options.why: Setting product prices is a marketing and finance function, not the management of a project.

options.t: Delivering goods to customers by truck, rail or ship each week
options.why: Delivering goods by truck, rail or ship is logistics and transportation, not project management.

options.t: Hiring workers for permanent positions only, to staff a department for good
options.why: Hiring for permanent positions is human resources work, whereas project management coordinates temporary work toward a goal.

q: What is the project scope?

options.t: The money spent on the project and the time worked
options.why: Money spent and time worked describe budget and effort used; scope defines which work is included in the project.

options.t: The list of everyone on the project team and their roles
options.why: The team list and roles describe project staffing, not scope, which lays out what work is and is not included.

options.t: The work that is included in the project and what is not
options.why: Project scope is the work that is included in the project and what is not, which sets clear boundaries, helps control cost and time, and prevents misunderstandings with the client.

options.t: The date the project will end and be closed out by the team
options.why: The end date is part of the schedule, not the scope, which describes the work to be done.

q: A client asks for extra features partway through a project. What is this called?

options.t: Quality control
options.why: Quality control checks that outputs meet standards; adding requested features partway through is a change of scope.

options.t: Scope creep
options.why: Scope creep is the gradual growth of a project's work beyond the original plan, such as a client adding features without matching changes to time or budget, which can cause delays and overruns.

options.t: Benchmarking
options.why: Benchmarking compares performance with the best in the industry; it has nothing to do with clients adding features.

options.t: Risk transfer
options.why: Risk transfer shifts the financial burden of a risk to another party, such as through insurance, and does not describe added client requests.

q: What is the best way to handle scope creep?

options.t: Cancel the project immediately and send the whole team home for good
options.why: Canceling the project immediately is an extreme reaction that wastes work already done and fails the client.

options.t: Accept every request without question so the client is always happy
options.why: Accepting every request without question causes scope creep, which pushes the project over budget and past its deadline.

options.t: Ignore the client and keep working on the original plan only now
options.why: Ignoring the client damages the relationship; legitimate changes can be handled through proper review instead of being dismissed.

options.t: Evaluate the change and approve it only through a formal change process
options.why: The best way is to evaluate each change for time, cost and risk and approve it only through a formal change process, which keeps the project controlled and the client informed.

q: What is a project manager's role?

options.t: Leading the team and making sure the project meets its goals
options.why: A project manager leads the team and makes sure the project meets its goals for scope, schedule, budget and quality, coordinating people and resources and communicating with stakeholders.

options.t: Setting the company's long-term mission and values for the future
options.why: Setting the company's long-term mission and values is the job of senior executives, not a project manager.

options.t: Doing every task in the project alone, with no help from the team
options.why: A project manager coordinates and leads the team; doing every task alone would be impossible and defeats the purpose of teamwork.

options.t: Selling the project's results to customers to pay for the work
options.why: Selling a project's results is a sales role; the project manager focuses on delivering the project.

q: What is a stakeholder in a project?

options.t: Only the competitors of the company that runs it
options.why: Competitors are outside parties that may not be affected by the project; stakeholders include many groups beyond rivals.

options.t: Anyone affected by or interested in the project
options.why: A stakeholder is anyone affected by or interested in the project, such as sponsors, team members, customers and the community, so managers must keep them informed and consider their needs.

options.t: Only the person who pays for the project and owns it
options.why: The funder is only one stakeholder; employees, customers and others affected by the project also count.

options.t: Only the project manager and the people on that team
options.why: The project manager and team are stakeholders, but so are sponsors, customers and others, so the group is much wider.

q: What is a milestone?

options.t: The total cost of the project, from the start to the end
options.why: The total cost of a project is the budget; a milestone is a significant point in the schedule.

options.t: A daily task for one team member, marked off by evening
options.why: A daily task for one team member is a small work item, not a significant project checkpoint like a milestone.

options.t: A significant point or achievement in a project schedule
options.why: A milestone is a significant point or achievement in a project schedule, such as completing a design or passing testing, and it helps managers track progress.

options.t: A risk that has happened and caused a delay in the work
options.why: A risk that has happened and caused delay is an issue, not a milestone, which marks progress.

q: What is a Gantt chart?

options.t: A diagram that shows who reports to whom
options.why: A diagram showing who reports to whom is an organization chart, not a Gantt chart, which displays tasks over time.

options.t: A bar chart that shows tasks over time
options.why: A Gantt chart is a bar chart that shows project tasks over time, with each bar marking when a task starts and ends, so managers can see the schedule and overlaps.

options.t: A pie chart that shows the budget parts
options.why: A pie chart showing budget parts is a different kind of graph, not a Gantt chart, which tracks time.

options.t: A table that lists customers' names
options.why: A table listing customer names is a customer list, not a Gantt chart, which charts tasks over a timeline.

q: Which tool best shows when each task starts and ends and how tasks overlap?

options.t: A Gantt chart
options.why: A Gantt chart shows when each task starts and ends along a timeline and how tasks overlap, which makes it the standard tool for project scheduling.

options.t: A pie chart
options.why: A pie chart shows parts of a whole, such as budget shares, but not timing or overlap of tasks.

options.t: A customer survey
options.why: A customer survey gathers opinions from buyers and does not show project schedules or task overlap.

options.t: A balance sheet
options.why: A balance sheet reports a firm's assets, liabilities and equity at a point in time, not project tasks.

q: What is the critical path?

options.t: The list of tasks that can be skipped without any harm to the project overall
options.why: Tasks that can be skipped without harm are not on the critical path; critical tasks cannot be skipped without affecting the project.

options.t: The most expensive set of tasks, which costs the firm the most money in total
options.why: The critical path is about time, not cost; the most expensive tasks may not determine the project's minimum length.

options.t: The longest sequence of dependent tasks that determines the project's minimum length
options.why: The critical path is the longest sequence of dependent tasks, which determines the project's minimum length, so any delay on it delays the whole project.

options.t: The shortest route between two offices for the staff who commute between them each day
options.why: The shortest route between offices is a travel concept; the critical path in project management is about task sequence and time.

q: A task on the critical path is delayed by three days. What happens to the project?

options.t: Nothing, because the other tasks will catch up automatically on their own
options.why: Tasks on the critical path have no slack, so other tasks cannot automatically make up the lost time.

options.t: The project budget becomes zero and the work stops for good this month
options.why: A delay does not erase the budget or stop the work; it affects the schedule and can raise costs.

options.t: The project finishes three days early, with no extra work from the team
options.why: A delay on the critical path cannot make the project finish early; it pushes the schedule later.

options.t: The project end date is delayed by three days unless time is made up
options.why: Because the critical path sets the project's length, a three-day delay pushes the end date back three days unless the team makes up time, such as by adding resources.

q: What is a project budget?

options.t: The list of tasks for the project and when they start
options.why: The list of tasks and start dates is the project schedule or work plan, not the budget, which covers money.

options.t: The estimated money needed to complete the project
options.why: A project budget is the estimated money needed to complete the project, including labor, materials and other costs, and managers track spending against it.

options.t: The date by which the project must end and be handed in
options.why: The date a project must end is the deadline in the schedule, not the budget.

options.t: The group of people who are working on the project team
options.why: The people on the project team are the staff or resources, not the budget, which is about estimated costs.

q: A project is budgeted at $50,000 and has spent $30,000 with 50 percent of the work done. What does this suggest?

options.t: It will finish under budget
options.why: Spending 60 percent of the budget ($30,000 of $50,000) for only 50 percent of the work suggests costs are running ahead of progress, so finishing under budget is unlikely.

options.t: It is already fully complete
options.why: With only 50 percent of the work done, the project is not complete, so this answer is wrong.

options.t: It has no budget problem
options.why: Spending 60 percent of the budget for 50 percent of the work is a warning sign, so saying there is no problem ignores the data.

options.t: It may finish over budget
options.why: $30,000 of $50,000 is 60 percent spent for 50 percent of the work, so costs are ahead of progress and the project may finish over budget unless it is corrected.

q: What is a risk in project management?

options.t: An uncertain event that could affect the project
options.why: A project risk is an uncertain event that could affect the project, positively or negatively, such as a supplier delay or a change in scope, and managers plan responses in advance.

options.t: The final report of the project, due at the end
options.why: A final report is a project deliverable at the end; a risk is an uncertain event that might happen.

options.t: The name of the project team chosen by its sponsor
options.why: The name of a project team is a label, not an uncertain event that could affect the project.

options.t: A task that is already finished and signed off
options.why: A finished and signed-off task is a completed item, not an uncertain event, which is what a risk is.

q: A key supplier may deliver late. What should the project manager do?

options.t: Hope the supplier is on time and make no plan
options.why: Hoping the supplier is on time with no plan leaves the project exposed if the delay happens, so it is not good risk management.

options.t: Blame the supplier before any delay happens
options.why: Blaming the supplier before any delay happens fixes nothing and harms the relationship, while the risk remains unmanaged.

options.t: Plan ahead, such as finding a backup supplier
options.why: Planning ahead, such as lining up a backup supplier, is a risk response that keeps the project on schedule if the key supplier is late.

options.t: Remove the task from the plan for the project
options.why: Removing the task from the plan does not remove the need for the supplier's work and would leave the project incomplete.

q: What is a deliverable?

options.t: A task that no one wants to do in the whole project team
options.why: A disliked task is not a deliverable. A deliverable is a defined output the project must produce, whether or not anyone enjoys the work behind it.

options.t: A cost that the project must avoid because it adds no value
options.why: Deliverables add value rather than avoid cost. They are the planned outputs, such as a report, a product or a service, that the sponsor expects.

options.t: A tangible or intangible result that a project must produce
options.why: A deliverable is any tangible or intangible result the project must produce, such as a prototype, report or training session. Deliverables are agreed in scope and accepted by the client.

options.t: A meeting held each week to review the project's progress
options.why: A weekly progress meeting is a status or review activity, not a deliverable. Deliverables are the results produced, while meetings are just a way to coordinate work.

q: What is the purpose of a kickoff meeting?

options.t: To start the project by aligning the team on goals and roles
options.why: A kickoff meeting launches the project by aligning the team and stakeholders on goals, roles, scope and schedule. A shared start reduces confusion and helps communication from day one.

options.t: To collect payment from the customer after the project ends
options.why: Collecting customer payment is a billing step that happens at or after delivery. A kickoff meeting happens at the start and focuses on aligning the project team.

options.t: To train new customers on the product they have just bought
options.why: Training customers on a purchased product is customer support or onboarding. A kickoff meeting is an internal project launch for the team and stakeholders, not a product lesson.

options.t: To end the project and review results with the client
options.why: Ending the project and reviewing results with the client describes closing and a final review. A kickoff meeting happens at the beginning, not the end.

q: What is a project charter?

options.t: A final bill sent to a customer when all the work is finished
options.why: A final bill is an invoice sent for payment. A project charter is a start-up document that authorizes the project, not a billing record sent after work ends.

options.t: A document that formally authorizes a project and states its purpose
options.why: A charter formally authorizes the project, names the project manager and states purpose, objectives and high-level scope. It gives the manager authority to use resources and is issued by the sponsor.

options.t: A summary of the project's mistakes and the staff who made them
options.why: A summary of mistakes and who made them is not a charter. Lessons learned reviews are done at closing and should focus on improving processes, not blaming individuals.

options.t: A list of tasks completed by the team, with the dates and names
options.why: A list of completed tasks with dates and names is a progress or completion record. A charter is written before work begins to approve the project.

q: Which is the correct order of project phases?

options.t: Execute, close, plan, monitor, initiate
options.why: This order starts with executing and ends with initiating, which is backwards. Work cannot be executed before it is planned, and a project cannot be closed before it is started.

options.t: Monitor, initiate, close, plan, execute
options.why: Beginning with monitoring and ending with execution is wrong. Monitoring tracks work already underway, so it cannot come first, and closing cannot come before execution.

options.t: Close, execute, plan, initiate, monitor
options.why: Closing first and monitoring last is impossible. Closing finishes the project, so it must come at the end after the work has been executed and checked.

options.t: Initiate, plan, execute, monitor, close
options.why: The standard phases run initiate, plan, execute, monitor and close. Each phase builds on the one before it, and monitoring happens alongside execution until the project closes.

q: What happens in the closing phase of a project?

options.t: The work is finished, results are delivered and lessons are recorded
options.why: In closing the work is finished, deliverables are handed over, contracts are closed and lessons learned are recorded. The client formally accepts the results and the team is released.

options.t: The team is first formed and the goals are chosen by the sponsor
options.why: Forming the team and choosing goals happens in initiation, at the start. Closing happens at the very end, after the work has been completed and delivered.

options.t: The schedule is first drafted by the project team and sponsor
options.why: Drafting the schedule is a planning task. Planning comes before execution, while closing is the last phase when the work is complete and results are handed over.

options.t: Most of the work is done but the plan is still changing a lot
options.why: Doing most of the work while the plan is still changing describes the execution and monitoring phases. Closing starts only when the work is substantially complete.

q: What is a status report?

options.t: A promotion for the team that finishes early
options.why: A promotion for a team that finishes early is a reward or incentive, not a report. A status report informs stakeholders on progress, not who gets rewarded.

options.t: An update on progress, issues and next steps
options.why: A status report summarizes progress to date, current issues and risks, and next steps. It keeps sponsors and stakeholders informed so they can decide or help early.

options.t: A list of staff birthdays for the whole year
options.why: A list of staff birthdays is an HR or social record. A status report is a project communication tool that covers work progress, not personal dates.

options.t: A contract for new work from a new client
options.why: A contract for new work is a legal agreement setting terms and price. A status report does not commit anyone to new work, it only reports on current work.

q: Why should project managers communicate regularly with stakeholders?

options.t: To avoid explaining problems to the sponsor later on
options.why: Regular communication does the opposite of avoiding problems. It surfaces issues early so they can be explained and solved before they grow into bigger issues for the sponsor.

options.t: To keep stakeholders out of decisions and work alone
options.why: Keeping stakeholders out of decisions weakens support and risks missing needs. Good project managers involve stakeholders so they stay informed, engaged and committed.

options.t: To make team meetings longer for no real reason at all
options.why: Lengthening team meetings for no reason wastes time. Effective communication is planned, purposeful and sized to what stakeholders need to know.

options.t: To keep expectations aligned and resolve problems early
options.why: Regular communication keeps expectations aligned, builds trust and lets problems be spotted and resolved early. It also helps secure approvals and support throughout the life of the project.

q: What is resource allocation?

options.t: Deleting old project files to free up disk space for staff
options.why: Deleting old project files is data management or housekeeping. Resource allocation is about assigning people, money and equipment to the tasks of a project.

options.t: Setting prices for the project's products and services
options.why: Setting prices for products and services is a pricing decision made by marketing and management. Resource allocation decides who and what is used on project tasks.

options.t: Assigning people, money and equipment to project tasks
options.why: Resource allocation means assigning people, money, equipment and materials to project tasks. Good allocation matches skills and capacity to the work and avoids overload or idle resources.

options.t: Selling the project's results to customers at a profit
options.why: Selling project results at a profit is a sales or revenue activity. Resource allocation happens within the project to supply the inputs needed to do the work.

q: One team member is overloaded while another has no tasks. What should the manager do?

options.t: Leave the workload unchanged for the team
options.why: Leaving the workload unchanged lets one person burn out while another sits idle, which lowers productivity and morale. A manager should act on an imbalance, not ignore it.

options.t: Rebalance the workload among team members
options.why: Rebalancing means moving some tasks from the overloaded member to the one with spare capacity. This protects quality and morale and uses the team's full capacity to meet deadlines.

options.t: Remove the overloaded member from the project
options.why: Removing the overloaded member loses skills and makes the problem worse, because the remaining people must absorb even more work. It also punishes the person doing the most.

options.t: Give the idle member a large cash bonus
options.why: A large cash bonus for an idle member rewards low output and does not fix the imbalance. Work should be redistributed so both people contribute fairly.

q: What is agile project management?

options.t: An approach that delivers work in short cycles with frequent feedback
options.why: Agile delivers work in short cycles, such as sprints, with frequent customer feedback. This lets teams adapt to changing needs and deliver usable results early and often.

options.t: An approach that finishes all planning first and never changes it
options.why: Finishing all planning first and never changing it describes a rigid, plan-driven method like waterfall. Agile welcomes change and adjusts the plan as feedback arrives.

options.t: An approach that ignores all customer input until the work is done
options.why: Agile relies heavily on customer input and collaboration throughout the project. Ignoring customers until the work is done is the opposite of the agile approach.

options.t: An approach that avoids teamwork and has each person work alone
options.why: Agile emphasizes teamwork, daily communication and shared ownership in self-organizing teams. Having each person work alone goes against its principles.

q: What is a sprint in agile?

options.t: A race between two project teams to finish a task first each week
options.why: A race between teams is not an agile practice. A sprint is a fixed work period for one team to complete agreed work, and teams collaborate rather than compete.

options.t: A meeting to assign blame for delays, held each month by managers
options.why: Assigning blame is not the purpose of any sprint event. Retrospectives look at how to improve the process, and a sprint is a work period, not a meeting.

options.t: A final presentation to the client at the end of the project
options.why: A final client presentation at the end of the project is a closing activity. A sprint is a short repeating cycle, and each sprint ends with a review of finished work.

options.t: A short, fixed period in which a team completes a set of work
options.why: A sprint is a short, fixed period, often one to four weeks, in which a team completes a set of work. Each sprint produces a usable increment that can be reviewed with the client.

q: A team plans two-week cycles, reviews work with the client and adjusts the plan. Which method is this?

options.t: Lean
options.why: Lean focuses on removing waste and improving flow, and does not by itself define fixed two-week cycles with client reviews. The described cycles, feedback and plan changes match agile.

options.t: Pricing
options.why: Pricing is a marketing decision about what to charge, not a project management method. It has nothing to do with planning work in cycles.

options.t: Agile
options.why: Agile uses short cycles, such as two-week sprints, regular reviews with the client and plan adjustments. This lets the team respond to feedback and changing needs.

options.t: Waterfall
options.why: Waterfall completes each phase fully before the next begins, with no repeated cycles. Reviewing with the client and adjusting the plan every two weeks is not how waterfall works.

q: What is the waterfall method?

options.t: An approach that repeats short cycles of work with frequent customer feedback
options.why: Short cycles with frequent customer feedback describe agile, not waterfall. Waterfall moves in a fixed sequence of phases with little feedback until later stages.

options.t: An approach used only for water projects such as dams, pipes and pumps
options.why: Waterfall is a project management method used in many industries such as software, construction and manufacturing. Its name comes from work flowing downward through phases, not water.

options.t: An approach that has no planning and where each person just works alone
options.why: Waterfall depends on detailed planning at the start and works as a team across clearly defined phases. It does not mean having no planning or working alone.

options.t: A step-by-step approach where each phase finishes before the next begins
options.why: Waterfall is a sequential approach where each phase, such as requirements, design, build and test, finishes before the next one starts. It works best when requirements are clear and stable.

q: Which project is best suited to the waterfall method?

options.t: Testing a market with unknown needs
options.why: Testing a market with unknown needs calls for flexible, iterative learning, which suits agile. Waterfall needs requirements to be known up front, and here they are not.

options.t: Building an app with unclear features
options.why: An app with unclear features will probably change as it is built and tested. Waterfall is a poor fit because it resists changes once a phase is complete.

options.t: Building a bridge from fixed plans
options.why: A bridge built from fixed plans has clear requirements, safety rules and a set sequence of steps. Waterfall fits because design must be complete before construction, and changes are costly.

options.t: Testing a new idea with rapid changes
options.why: Testing a new idea with rapid changes needs quick iteration and feedback. That is the strength of agile methods, while waterfall is too rigid for it.

q: What is a work breakdown structure (WBS)?

options.t: A rule that limits team size and the hours each person works
options.why: A rule limiting team size and hours is a staffing policy or constraint. A work breakdown structure divides the project's work into smaller tasks, not the people.

options.t: A way of dividing a project into smaller, manageable tasks
options.why: A WBS breaks the total project scope into smaller, manageable work packages. This makes tasks easier to assign, estimate, schedule and track toward the final deliverable.

options.t: A list of reasons a project failed, written after it closed
options.why: A list of reasons a project failed is a post-project review or lessons learned report. A WBS is a planning tool used before and during the work.

options.t: A chart of the company's profits by month and by year
options.why: A chart of profits by month is a financial report. A WBS shows how project work is divided and organized, not company earnings.

q: Why break a large project into smaller tasks?

options.t: Smaller tasks are easier to assign, track and estimate
options.why: Smaller tasks are easier to assign to people, track against the schedule and estimate for time and cost. This improves control and makes problems easier to spot early.

options.t: It hides the project from stakeholders and the sponsor
options.why: Breaking work down makes the project clearer to stakeholders, not hidden. It supports reporting by showing exactly what work must be completed.

options.t: It makes the project take longer on purpose for the team
options.why: The goal is better control, not delay. Smaller tasks help teams estimate accurately and finish on time, and they do not make the project slower on purpose.

options.t: It removes the need for a schedule and a budget plan
options.why: Task breakdown supports the schedule and budget, since each task can be given time and cost estimates. It does not remove the need for either.

q: What is a dependency in a project?

options.t: A team member who depends on the manager for monthly pay
options.why: A team member who relies on the manager for pay is an employment relationship. A project dependency links tasks, not people, and describes the order in which work must happen.

options.t: A client who depends on a single product from the firm
options.why: A client relying on one product from the firm is a customer relationship. Project dependencies concern relationships between tasks inside a project plan.

options.t: A cost that depends on exchange rates between nations
options.why: A cost that depends on exchange rates is a financial risk or assumption. A project dependency links tasks, so one cannot start or end until another does.

options.t: A task that cannot start or finish until another task does
options.why: A dependency means one task cannot start or finish until another task starts or finishes. For example, you cannot test software before it is built, so the schedule must reflect the order.

q: Painting a wall cannot begin until the wall is built. What type of relationship is this?

options.t: A task dependency
options.why: Painting needs the wall to be built first, so one task depends on another. This is a finish-to-start dependency, a common type of task dependency in project schedules.

options.t: A budget variance
options.why: A budget variance is the difference between planned and actual cost. The wall and paint example concerns the order of tasks, not money.

options.t: A quality audit
options.why: A quality audit checks whether processes and results meet standards. It does not describe the link between building and painting a wall.

options.t: A team conflict
options.why: A team conflict is a disagreement between people. Painting waiting on construction is a logical sequence between tasks, not a dispute.

q: What is financial information?

options.t: Data about a business's employee birthdays and work anniversaries
options.why: Employee birthdays and anniversaries are HR information. Financial information concerns a business's money, such as income, costs, assets and debts.

options.t: Data about a business's advertising colors and logos and packaging
options.why: Advertising colors, logos and packaging are marketing and branding information, not financial data. Financial information records and reports a business's money.

options.t: Data about a business's money, such as income, costs and assets
options.why: Financial information is data about a business's money, such as income, expenses, assets and liabilities. Owners, lenders and managers use it to make decisions and judge performance.

options.t: Data about a business's office layout and desk positions in rooms
options.why: Office layout and desk positions are facilities information. Financial information concerns money, such as revenue, costs and what the business owns and owes.

q: What is an income statement?

options.t: A report of revenue, expenses and profit over a period
options.why: An income statement reports revenue, expenses and resulting profit or loss over a period such as a month or year. It shows how profitable operations were during that time.

options.t: A report of cash movements by activity for a period
options.why: Cash movements by activity are shown on the statement of cash flows. The income statement reports revenue, expenses and profit, which are not always the same as cash.

options.t: A report of assets, liabilities and equity at one date
options.why: Assets, liabilities and equity at one date are shown on the balance sheet. The income statement covers a period of time rather than a single date.

options.t: A report of changes in owners' equity over a period
options.why: Changes in owners' equity over a period are shown on the statement of owner's equity. The income statement reports profit, which is one input to that statement.

q: What is a balance sheet?

options.t: A report listing a company's customers and what they buy
options.why: A list of customers and what they buy is a sales or customer record. A balance sheet reports what the company owns, owes and its owners' stake.

options.t: A report of assets, liabilities and equity at a point in time
options.why: A balance sheet reports assets, liabilities and equity at a point in time. It follows the accounting equation, assets equal liabilities plus equity, and shows financial position on that date.

options.t: A report of cash in and out during a given period of time
options.why: Cash in and out over a period is shown on the cash flow statement. The balance sheet is a snapshot at one date, not a record of movement.

options.t: A report of revenue and expenses over a full year of trading
options.why: Revenue and expenses over a year are shown on the income statement. The balance sheet shows financial position on a single date rather than results over time.

q: What is a cash flow statement?

options.t: A report of assets and liabilities on one date for the year
options.why: Assets and liabilities on one date are reported on the balance sheet. The cash flow statement covers cash movements over a period, not a snapshot of position.

options.t: A report of a company's future sales goals and plans
options.why: Future sales goals and plans belong in a sales forecast or budget. A cash flow statement reports actual cash received and paid in a past period.

options.t: A report of profit after taxes for the whole business year
options.why: Profit after taxes is reported on the income statement. The cash flow statement tracks cash, and profit can differ from cash because of credit sales and non-cash costs.

options.t: A report of cash coming in and going out during a period
options.why: The cash flow statement reports cash coming in and going out during a period, grouped into operating, investing and financing activities. It shows whether the business can pay its bills.

q: A company has high profit but little cash. Which statement would best show why?

options.t: A customer survey form
options.why: A customer survey form gathers opinions and has no financial data. It cannot explain why a profitable company is short of cash.

options.t: The mission statement
options.why: A mission statement describes purpose and values, and contains no figures. It cannot show where a company's cash went.

options.t: The cash flow statement
options.why: The cash flow statement shows cash received and paid. High profit with little cash can happen when sales are on credit, inventory is growing, or large loan payments and purchases use cash.

options.t: A marketing plan sheet
options.why: A marketing plan sheet outlines promotion strategy and has no cash records. It cannot explain a gap between profit and cash.

q: What is the accounting equation?

options.t: Assets equal revenue minus all the expenses
options.why: Assets minus expenses is not the accounting equation. Revenue minus expenses gives net income, and assets are balanced against liabilities and equity.

options.t: Equity equals debts minus revenue each year
options.why: Equity equals assets minus liabilities, not debts minus revenue. Revenue does not appear in the basic accounting equation at all.

options.t: Liabilities equal assets plus owner's equity
options.why: This reverses the equation. Liabilities equal assets minus owner's equity, since liabilities are what is left of assets after the owners' share is removed.

options.t: Assets equal liabilities plus owner's equity
options.why: The accounting equation is assets = liabilities + owner's equity. It must always balance, because everything a business owns is financed by debt or by the owners.

q: A company has assets of $90,000 and liabilities of $35,000. What is owner's equity?

options.why: $35,000 is the liabilities figure itself, not equity. Equity is assets minus liabilities, so the owners' share is $90,000 - $35,000.
Equity = assets - liabilities = $90,000 - $35,000 = $55,000. This is the owners' claim on the business after debts are paid.
$90,000 is total assets, not equity. Part of those assets is financed by $35,000 of liabilities, leaving less for the owners.
$125,000 results from adding assets and liabilities together. The equation is subtraction: $90,000 - $35,000 = $55,000 of equity.

q: What is double-entry bookkeeping?

options.t: Recording every transaction in at least two accounts
options.why: Double-entry bookkeeping records each transaction in at least two accounts, with total debits equal to total credits. This keeps the accounting equation balanced and helps catch errors.

options.t: Recording only cash sales and ignoring all credit sales
options.why: Double-entry does not mean ignoring credit sales. It records all transactions, including credit sales, with equal debits and credits in at least two accounts.

options.t: Recording each transaction on two different days
options.why: The word double refers to two accounts, not two days. Each transaction is recorded once in the books, with two or more equal and opposite entries.

options.t: Recording each transaction by two people at once
options.why: Double refers to the two sides of an entry, not two people. One person can record a transaction with a debit in one account and a credit in another.

q: What is a trial balance?

options.t: A statement of expected profits for the coming year in the plan
options.why: Expected profits for the coming year are in a budget or forecast. A trial balance lists existing account balances to check that the books are in balance.

options.t: A review of employees' performance and pay during the whole year
options.why: Employee performance reviews are an HR activity. A trial balance is an accounting check on ledger totals, not a review of staff.

options.t: A list of account balances used to check that debits equal credits
options.why: A trial balance lists all ledger account balances and checks that total debits equal total credits. If they differ, there is an error to find before preparing statements.

options.t: A test of a new product with customers to gauge their demand for it
options.why: Testing a new product with customers is market testing. A trial balance is an accounting list of balances and has no link to customer demand.

q: What is a budget?

options.t: A record of past transactions made by a business in a year
options.why: A record of past transactions is a ledger or journal. A budget looks forward, planning expected income and spending rather than recording what has happened.

options.t: A report of competitors' prices, compiled by the sales team
options.why: A report on competitors' prices is market research. A budget is an internal financial plan for the business's own income and expenses.

options.t: A list of owners and partners and the shares they hold
options.why: A list of owners and the shares they hold is a shareholder or ownership register. A budget plans money, not ownership.

options.t: A plan that estimates income and expenses for a period
options.why: A budget is a plan estimating income and expenses for a future period. Managers compare actual results with it to control spending and spot problems.

q: A department's budget was $20,000 and actual spending was $23,500. What is the variance?

options.t: $0 over budget
options.why: A $0 variance means actual spending matched the budget. Here spending of $23,500 exceeded the $20,000 budget, so there is a variance.

options.t: $43,500 over budget
options.why: $43,500 adds budget and actual together. Variance is the difference between them, not the sum, so it should be $23,500 - $20,000.

options.t: $3,500 over budget
options.why: Variance = actual - budget = $23,500 - $20,000 = $3,500. Spending above the budget is an unfavorable variance, so the department is $3,500 over budget.

options.t: $3,500 under budget
options.why: The amount of $3,500 is right, but spending $23,500 against a $20,000 budget is over, not under. Under budget would mean actual spending was lower than $20,000.

q: What is accounts receivable?

options.t: Money owed to a business by customers for sales on credit
