options.why: Accounts receivable is money owed to a business by customers who bought on credit. It is a current asset because the business expects to collect the cash soon.

options.t: Cash held in a bank account by the business each day
options.why: Cash held in a bank account is recorded as cash, not receivables. Receivables are amounts customers still owe and have not yet paid.

options.t: Money a business owes to suppliers for goods it bought
options.why: Money owed to suppliers for goods bought is accounts payable, which is a liability. Receivable is the opposite, money owed to the business.

options.t: Money the owner invests in the business at the start
options.why: Money the owner invests is owner's equity or capital. Accounts receivable arises when customers buy on credit and owe the business.

q: What is accounts payable?

options.t: Money customers owe a business for sales made on credit
options.why: Money customers owe a business is accounts receivable, an asset. Accounts payable is the opposite, an amount the business itself owes.

options.t: Money a business owes to suppliers for goods bought on credit
options.why: Accounts payable is money a business owes to suppliers for goods or services bought on credit. It is a current liability that must be paid by the due date.

options.t: Money earned from sales made to customers in a single year
options.why: Money earned from sales is revenue. Accounts payable relates to purchases made on credit, not income earned from customers.

options.t: Money the business holds as cash in its bank accounts now
options.why: Cash in the bank is an asset. Accounts payable is a liability showing what the business owes its suppliers.

q: Net credit sales are $240,000 and average receivables are $30,000. What is the receivables turnover?

options.t: 270 times
options.why: 270 times adds the sales and receivables together. Turnover divides net credit sales by average receivables, so the result is far smaller.

options.t: 8 times
options.why: Receivables turnover = net credit sales / average receivables = $240,000 / $30,000 = 8 times. The firm collects its average receivables about eight times a year.

options.t: 0.125 times
options.why: 0.125 inverts the formula: $30,000 / $240,000. Turnover puts credit sales on top, so the correct ratio is $240,000 / $30,000 = 8.

options.t: 210 times
options.why: 210 times comes from subtracting $30,000 from $240,000. Turnover is a division, so $240,000 / $30,000 = 8 times, not 210.

q: What is the current ratio?

options.t: Current assets divided by current liabilities
options.why: The current ratio is current assets divided by current liabilities. It measures liquidity, or the ability to pay short-term debts with assets that convert to cash within a year.

options.t: Sales divided by inventory held at year end
options.why: Sales divided by inventory is the inventory turnover ratio, which shows how fast stock sells. The current ratio compares current assets with current liabilities.

options.t: Total liabilities divided by total assets
options.why: Total liabilities divided by total assets is the debt ratio, which measures leverage. The current ratio looks only at short-term assets and short-term obligations.

options.t: Net income divided by total sales for the year
options.why: Net income divided by sales is the profit margin. The current ratio measures short-term liquidity using the balance sheet.

q: A company has current assets of $60,000 and current liabilities of $40,000. What is its current ratio?

options.why: 100 is not a division result here. Current ratio = $60,000 / $40,000 = 1.5, with no multiplication by 100 or use of a percentage.
0.67 inverts the ratio ($40,000 / $60,000). The current ratio puts current assets on top, so it is $60,000 / $40,000 = 1.5.
Current ratio = current assets / current liabilities = $60,000 / $40,000 = 1.5. The company has $1.50 of current assets for every $1 of short-term debt.
20 is the difference between the figures expressed in thousands ($60 - $40). The current ratio is a division, giving $60,000 / $40,000 = 1.5.

q: What is gross profit?

options.t: Sales plus the cost of goods sold
options.why: Adding cost of goods sold to sales gives a meaningless total. Gross profit subtracts the cost of goods sold from sales to show what is left to cover other costs.

options.t: Sales minus all expenses and taxes
options.why: Sales minus all expenses and taxes gives net income, not gross profit. Gross profit subtracts only the cost of goods sold.

options.t: Assets minus all of the liabilities
options.why: Assets minus liabilities is owner's equity. Gross profit is an income statement figure based on sales and cost of goods sold.

options.t: Sales minus the cost of goods sold
options.why: Gross profit = sales - cost of goods sold. It shows how much the business earns from selling goods before operating expenses, interest and taxes are paid.

q: Sales are $500,000, cost of goods sold is $320,000 and operating expenses are $110,000. What is operating profit?

options.why: Operating profit = sales - cost of goods sold - operating expenses = $500,000 - $320,000 - $110,000 = $70,000. This is the profit from regular operations before interest and taxes.
$390,000 is sales minus operating expenses ($500,000 - $110,000), skipping the cost of goods sold. All of the costs must be subtracted from sales.
$180,000 is the gross profit ($500,000 - $320,000). Operating expenses of $110,000 must still be subtracted to reach operating profit.
$930,000 adds all three figures together. Operating profit subtracts the costs from sales, so $500,000 - $320,000 - $110,000 = $70,000.

q: What is depreciation?

options.t: Selling an asset for cash at the end of its life
options.why: Selling an asset for cash is a disposal, and any gain or loss is recorded separately. Depreciation spreads an asset's cost over the years it is used.

options.t: Paying off a loan early to save interest on the debt
options.why: Paying off a loan early is debt repayment. Depreciation is the allocation of an asset's cost and has nothing to do with interest on loans.

options.t: Increasing the value of an asset over time as it ages
options.why: Depreciation decreases, not increases, the recorded value of an asset as it wears out or becomes obsolete. Assets that gain value over time are not depreciated.

options.t: Spreading the cost of an asset over its useful life
options.why: Depreciation spreads the cost of a long-term asset over its useful life. This matches the expense to the periods in which the asset helps earn revenue.

q: Equipment costs $12,000, has no salvage value and lasts 5 years. What is straight-line depreciation per year?

options.why: $12,000 is the full cost of the equipment, which would be expensed in one year. Straight-line depreciation divides the cost over its 5-year life.
Straight-line depreciation = (cost - salvage value) / useful life = ($12,000 - $0) / 5 years = $2,400 per year. The same expense is recorded each year.
$60,000 multiplies cost by the years ($12,000 x 5). Depreciation divides the cost by the useful life: $12,000 / 5 = $2,400.
$1,200 divides by 10 rather than 5. The equipment lasts 5 years, so the yearly expense is $12,000 / 5 = $2,400.

q: What is financial forecasting?

options.t: Recording past sales in a ledger at day end
options.why: Recording past sales in a ledger is bookkeeping, which looks backward. Forecasting looks ahead to estimate what revenues, costs and cash needs are likely to be.

options.t: Counting inventory at year end in the warehouse
options.why: Counting inventory at year end is a stocktake, which verifies what is on hand now. Forecasting estimates future financial results.

options.t: Estimating future revenues, costs and cash needs
options.why: Financial forecasting estimates future revenues, costs and cash needs using past data and expected trends. Managers use forecasts to plan budgets, financing and investments.

options.t: Printing a financial statement for the file copy
options.why: Printing a statement for the file is record keeping. Forecasting involves analyzing and predicting future results, not producing copies of past reports.

q: Why do lenders request financial statements?

options.t: To set the opening hours and staff on each shift
options.why: Opening hours and shift staffing are operational scheduling decisions. Lenders use financial statements to measure a borrower's finances, not to set work schedules.

options.t: To choose the business's logo and its colors
options.why: A logo and its colors are branding choices. A lender does not need financial statements for that, but for judging a borrower's financial strength.

options.t: To set the business's prices for the next year
options.why: Prices are set by the business, not by lenders. Lenders read statements to assess risk, not to decide what the borrower charges customers.

options.t: To judge whether a business can repay a loan
options.why: Lenders review income, assets, debts and cash flow to judge whether the business can repay a loan with interest. Strong statements improve the chance of approval and better terms.

q: What is an audit?

options.t: A forecast of profits for the coming year ahead
options.why: A forecast of coming profits is a projection. An audit examines records of what has already happened to check they are accurate and fair.

options.t: An independent examination of financial records
options.why: An audit is an independent examination of financial records and statements. Auditors check accuracy and compliance with accounting rules, which adds credibility for owners and lenders.

options.t: A daily entry of transactions in the sales book
options.why: Daily entry of transactions is bookkeeping, done by the firm's staff. An audit is a separate review by an independent person.

options.t: A sales meeting to talk about prices and terms
options.why: A sales meeting about prices is a commercial discussion. An audit is a review of financial records for accuracy, not a negotiation.

q: What is GAAP?

options.t: A schedule of employee pay dates and the amounts that each person receives
options.why: A schedule of pay dates is a payroll calendar. GAAP stands for Generally Accepted Accounting Principles, the standard rules for preparing financial statements.

options.t: A federal program for small businesses that gives grants to new firms each year
options.why: A federal grants program is not GAAP. GAAP is a body of accounting standards, and no money is given out under it.

options.t: Generally Accepted Accounting Principles, a set of standard accounting rules
options.why: GAAP means Generally Accepted Accounting Principles, a common set of rules and standards for recording and reporting financial information. In the US, FASB sets them for public companies.

options.t: A tax on corporate profit that large firms pay to the state each year
options.why: A tax on corporate profit is income tax, set by tax law. GAAP is a set of accounting rules and is not a tax.

q: Why must businesses follow consistent accounting rules?

options.t: So that financial statements can be compared and trusted
options.why: Consistent rules make statements comparable between periods and between firms, and reliable for owners, lenders and investors. Common standards build trust in reported numbers.

options.t: So that taxes are never paid by the firm in any year
options.why: Accounting rules do not remove taxes. Businesses still owe tax based on tax law, and accurate records are needed to figure out the correct amount.

options.t: So that every business reports the same profit each year
options.why: Firms with different results will still report different profits. Consistent rules only make sure that the figures are measured in the same way.

options.t: So that accounting is easier to ignore for most firms
options.why: Rules exist to make accounting reliable and comparable, so it cannot be ignored. Following them is required for audits, loans and, for public firms, SEC filings.

q: What is a financial ratio used for?

options.t: Printing receipts for customers at the front counter
options.why: Receipts are printed by a point-of-sale system. A financial ratio compares figures from the statements to evaluate how the business is doing.

options.t: Comparing figures to judge performance or health
options.why: Financial ratios compare figures, such as current assets to current liabilities, to judge performance, liquidity and financial health. They let users compare across periods and against competitors.

options.t: Choosing a company slogan for the next ad campaign
options.why: A slogan is a marketing decision. Ratios are analytical tools built from financial statement numbers, and they play no part in choosing slogans.

options.t: Scheduling employee shifts for the coming month
options.why: Scheduling shifts is a staffing task. Financial ratios are calculated from financial data to assess profitability, liquidity and debt levels.

q: Net income is $24,000 on sales of $300,000. What is the profit margin?

options.why: Profit margin = net income / sales = $24,000 / $300,000 = 0.08, or 8%. The business keeps 8 cents of profit from each dollar of sales.
80% would mean profit was almost all of sales. $24,000 / $300,000 is 0.08, so the correct margin is 8%, not 80%.
0.8% is off by a factor of ten. $24,000 / $300,000 = 0.08, which is 8% as a percentage.
12.5% is the result of dividing $300,000 by $24,000 incorrectly (1/8). Margin puts net income on top: $24,000 / $300,000 = 8%.

q: What is data integrity in financial systems?

options.t: Hiding data from auditors and from the state tax office
options.why: Hiding data from auditors and tax authorities is fraud and violates the law. Data integrity means the data stay accurate and reliable.

options.t: Storing data in many different formats so any program opens it
options.why: Storing data in many formats creates inconsistency and errors. Integrity depends on controlled, consistent data that stay correct.

options.t: Accuracy and consistency of financial data over its life
options.why: Data integrity is the accuracy, completeness and consistency of financial data over its life. Controls, validation and audit trails protect it from errors and unauthorized changes.

options.t: Deleting data at random from the system every single day
options.why: Random deletion destroys records and would break integrity. Records must be retained for the required period, and deleted only under a proper retention policy.

q: Which control best protects financial data from unauthorized changes?

options.t: Sharing one password among all staff
options.why: Sharing one password removes accountability, because no one can tell who made a change. It makes unauthorized changes easier and harder to trace.

options.t: Turning off all system activity logging
options.why: Turning off logging removes the record of who did what, which makes unauthorized changes undetectable. Logs are a key control for financial data.

options.t: Allowing anyone to edit any record
options.why: Letting anyone edit any record invites errors and fraud. Good control limits who can change data, based on duties.

options.t: Role-based access and an audit trail
options.why: Role-based access limits changes to authorized people, and an audit trail records who changed what and when. Together they prevent and detect unauthorized changes to financial data.

q: What is a knowledge audit?

options.t: A review of a firm's yearly tax payments to the government in the spring
options.why: A review of tax payments is a tax or accounting review. A knowledge audit looks at knowledge assets such as skills, documents and expertise, not taxes.

options.t: A review of customers' complaints about product prices each year
options.why: Reviewing customer complaints about prices is a customer feedback analysis. A knowledge audit examines what the organization knows internally and where it is missing.

options.t: A review of the number of computers in the main office building
options.why: Counting computers is an inventory of equipment. A knowledge audit studies knowledge held in people, processes and documents, not hardware numbers.

options.t: A review of what knowledge an organization has and where gaps exist
options.why: A knowledge audit identifies what knowledge an organization has, where it is stored and where gaps or risks exist. The findings guide training, documentation and knowledge sharing.

q: A company learns that only one employee knows how to run a key machine. What should it do?

options.t: Document the process and train a second person
options.why: Documenting the process and training a second person spreads the knowledge, so work continues if the expert is absent or leaves. This reduces the risk of relying on one employee.

options.t: Keep the process secret to protect the worker's job
options.why: Keeping the process secret creates a risk for the company and does not protect anyone. If that worker is absent or leaves, production stops with no one able to run the machine.

options.t: Wait until the worker leaves before acting
options.why: Waiting until the worker leaves is too late, because the knowledge would be lost with them. Knowledge transfer should be planned in advance.

options.t: Ban anyone else from touching the machine
options.why: Banning others from the machine guarantees the knowledge stays in one person. It increases risk and does not help the business continue if that person is gone.

q: What is institutional memory?

options.t: A single employee's personal diary of what they did each day
options.why: One employee's personal diary is individual knowledge, not the collective memory of the organization. Institutional memory is shared across many people and records.

options.t: The shared knowledge and history an organization holds over time
options.why: Institutional memory is the shared knowledge, history, practices and lessons an organization has built up over time. It helps new staff learn why things are done a certain way.

options.t: A list of past customers' addresses held on file by the firm
options.why: A list of past customers is a customer record. Institutional memory covers organizational know-how and history, not just contact data.

options.t: The computer storage in a company's server room for old files
options.why: Server storage is a hardware tool that may hold files. Institutional memory is the knowledge itself, held by people, processes and records.

q: What is a document management system?

options.t: Software that stores, organizes and controls access to documents
options.why: A document management system stores, organizes, tracks and controls access to documents, often with search and version control. It keeps files secure and easy to find.

options.t: A machine that prints documents faster than an office printer
options.why: Printing is just one use of documents, and a faster printer is hardware. A document management system is software for managing files, not a printing machine.

options.t: A tool that sets employee schedules for the next week or month
options.why: Setting employee schedules is done by scheduling software. A document management system organizes documents, not work hours.

options.t: A rule that bans paper in an office and in all the stores
options.why: A paperless policy is a rule, not a system. A document management system is software that stores and manages documents, whether scanned or created digitally.

q: Why is version control useful for shared documents?

options.t: It deletes all earlier versions so only the newest file is kept
options.why: Version control keeps earlier versions so they can be recovered. Deleting them would remove its main benefit and risk losing useful information.

options.t: It makes documents impossible to edit for any member of staff
options.why: Version control does not lock documents from editing. It allows many users to edit while tracking each change.

options.t: It hides who made changes and when they were made to the file
options.why: Version control records who changed a file and when, which makes changes visible and accountable. Hiding them would defeat its purpose.

options.t: It shows which version is current and lets teams recover earlier ones
options.why: Version control shows which version is current, records changes, and lets teams recover earlier versions. It prevents confusion and lost work when several people edit the same document.

q: What is a frequently asked questions (FAQ) page for?

options.t: Advertising unrelated products to the customers of the firm
options.why: Advertising unrelated products is not the purpose of an FAQ. An FAQ page helps customers by answering questions they commonly ask about the product or service.

options.t: Collecting customers' credit card numbers for future orders
options.why: Collecting credit card numbers is a payment function and would be risky on an FAQ page. An FAQ shares information and does not gather sensitive data.

options.t: Answering common questions so people can find help quickly
options.why: An FAQ page lists common questions with clear answers so people can quickly find help. It reduces calls to support staff and improves the customer experience.

options.t: Listing every employee's salary for all staff to see online
options.why: Publishing salaries is not an FAQ function and would breach privacy. FAQs answer common questions about products, services or policies.

q: What is training documentation?

options.t: A list of tasks that staff must avoid doing at work
options.why: A list of tasks to avoid is a prohibition list. Training documentation teaches people how to do their jobs correctly, with steps, examples and standards.

options.t: Written guides that teach employees how to do tasks
options.why: Training documentation is written guides, manuals or step-by-step instructions that teach employees how to do tasks. It helps new hires learn consistently and preserves knowledge.

options.t: A report of the firm's yearly profit and all costs
options.why: A report of yearly profit and costs is a financial statement. Training documentation is educational material for employees, not a record of results.

options.t: A schedule of company holidays for the whole year ahead
options.why: A holiday schedule is an HR calendar. Training documentation explains job procedures, not when the office is closed.

q: New hires keep asking the same setup questions. What is the best long-term fix?

options.t: Hire fewer new workers in the coming year or two
options.why: Hiring fewer workers does not solve the problem and may hurt growth. The repeated questions show a lack of written guidance that should be provided.

options.t: Tell them to stop asking questions so staff can get on
options.why: Telling people to stop asking prevents them from learning and causes errors. Staff should be given the answers in a lasting form instead.

options.t: Remove all written instructions from the shared drive
options.why: Removing written instructions makes the problem worse, because new hires have nowhere to look for answers. Good documentation reduces repeated questions.

options.t: Create a clear onboarding guide that answers them
options.why: A clear onboarding guide answers common setup questions once and is reusable for every new hire. It saves staff time, speeds up training and is a lasting fix.

q: What is a data governance policy?

options.t: A schedule of backup tapes only, kept by the IT team staff
options.why: A schedule of backup tapes is a narrow IT task. A data governance policy covers how all data are collected, stored, used, secured and shared.

options.t: A rule that sets product prices in the shops of the firm
options.why: Setting prices is a marketing or management decision. Data governance concerns the management and control of the organization's data.

options.t: Rules for how an organization collects, stores and uses data
options.why: A data governance policy sets rules for how an organization collects, stores, protects and uses data. It assigns responsibilities and supports quality, privacy and legal compliance.

options.t: A list of the firm's competitors and their prices each quarter
options.why: A competitor price list is market research. Data governance concerns the organization's own handling of data, not tracking rivals.

q: What is job shadowing as a way to share knowledge?

options.t: Following an experienced worker to learn how tasks are done
options.why: Job shadowing means following an experienced worker to see how tasks are done and why. It transfers practical knowledge, such as judgment and tips, that manuals may miss.

options.t: Replacing a worker for a week with no help at all from the team
options.why: Replacing a worker with no help is a sink-or-swim approach. Job shadowing involves observation and guidance from someone experienced, not being left alone.

options.t: Reading a manual alone with no practice or guidance from anyone
options.why: Reading a manual alone with no practice is self-study, not shadowing. Shadowing requires watching and learning from a person doing the job.

options.t: Watching a video of an unrelated industry for several hours
options.why: Watching a video from an unrelated industry has no link to the job. Shadowing is observing a real colleague doing the work you need to learn.

q: Which method best passes on skills that are hard to write down?

options.t: Emailing a long list of rules to them
options.why: Emailing a long list of rules works for explicit knowledge that is easily written down. Hard-to-document skills are tacit and need personal demonstration and practice.

options.t: Posting a single notice on a wall
options.why: A single wall notice is a one-way message that cannot transfer subtle skills. Tacit skills are learned through interaction and observation.

options.t: Restricting access to the expert
options.why: Restricting access to the expert prevents anyone from learning from them, so the skills stay locked in one person. Sharing needs closer contact, not less.

options.t: Mentoring and working side by side
options.why: Mentoring and working side by side lets learners watch, ask questions and practice with feedback. This is the best way to pass on tacit skills that cannot be fully written down.

q: What does it mean to curate information?

options.t: To select, organize and keep the most useful and accurate material
options.why: To curate information is to select, organize and maintain the most useful and accurate material. Curation keeps knowledge relevant, trustworthy and easy to find.

options.t: To hide information from all staff and the managers of the firm
options.why: Hiding information from staff is the opposite of curation. Curation makes the right information available and useful to the people who need it.

options.t: To collect every document without checking it at all, to avoid gaps
options.why: Collecting everything without checking is hoarding, not curation. Curation involves judging quality and relevance, which keeps out outdated or wrong material.

options.t: To delete information at random from the shared drive of the firm
options.why: Random deletion removes valuable information and has no quality test. Curation removes only material that is outdated, duplicated or inaccurate.

q: A shared drive has thousands of outdated, duplicate files. What is the best response?

options.t: Add more duplicate files to the shared drive for staff
options.why: Adding more duplicates makes the clutter worse and makes it harder to find the right file. The drive needs cleanup, not more files.

options.t: Delete every file at once without checking what they hold
options.why: Deleting everything at once without checking risks losing important records. Files should be reviewed first, and some may be needed for legal or business reasons.

options.t: Review, organize and remove or archive outdated files
options.why: Reviewing, organizing and removing or archiving outdated files keeps useful information easy to find and avoids losing records. It also reduces confusion and storage costs.

options.t: Tell staff to avoid the drive and use personal folders
options.why: Avoiding the shared drive moves information to private folders where others cannot find it. This fragments knowledge and creates new problems.

q: What is a quality circle?

options.t: A circle drawn on a chart of sales to mark the best months
options.why: A circle drawn on a sales chart is only a chart marking. A quality circle is a group of employees who meet to solve work-related quality problems.

options.t: A small group of employees who meet to solve work quality problems
options.why: A quality circle is a small group of employees who meet regularly to identify, analyze and solve quality problems in their work area. It uses worker knowledge and builds involvement.

options.t: A group of customers who test prices and report which they like
options.why: Testing prices with customers is market research. A quality circle is made up of employees and focuses on improving quality in processes.

options.t: A meeting held to assign blame for mistakes made by the staff
options.why: Quality circles are for problem solving, not assigning blame. Blame discourages honest reporting, which would defeat the circle's purpose.

q: Workers on a line meet weekly to find ways to cut defects. What is this?

options.t: A quality circle
options.why: A weekly meeting of workers to find ways to cut defects is the definition of a quality circle. It uses employees' own knowledge to improve the process.

options.t: A fierce price war
options.why: A price war is competition among sellers cutting prices. It has nothing to do with workers meeting to reduce defects.

options.t: A franchise deal
options.why: A franchise deal is a business arrangement to license a brand. It does not describe an employee group focused on quality.

options.t: A tariff on imports
options.why: A tariff is a tax on imported goods. It has no relation to employees working together on quality.

q: What is a control chart used for?

options.t: Listing employees' names and their pay rates for the year
options.why: A list of names and pay rates is a payroll record. A control chart plots process data over time against control limits to show whether a process is stable.

options.t: Choosing the color of a product and the shape of its package for display
options.why: Choosing color and package shape is product design. A control chart is a statistical quality tool for monitoring how a process performs.

options.t: Setting the price of a product that is sold in the main shops
options.why: Setting price is a marketing decision. A control chart tracks quality data, not prices.

options.t: Tracking a process over time to spot changes that signal problems
options.why: A control chart tracks a process over time against upper and lower limits. Points outside the limits, or unusual patterns, signal a problem that needs investigation.

q: What is a Pareto chart based on?

options.t: The idea that problems solve themselves over time if ignored
options.why: A Pareto chart assumes problems do not solve themselves, and ignoring them lets them continue. It identifies which causes should be fixed first.

options.t: The idea that price alone decides quality in every case
options.why: Price alone does not decide quality. The Pareto chart ranks causes of problems by how often they occur.

options.t: The idea that a few causes produce most of the problems
options.why: A Pareto chart rests on the 80/20 idea that a few causes produce most of the problems. It ranks causes so a team can fix the vital few first for the biggest gain.

options.t: The idea that all causes of a problem are equally important
options.why: The Pareto principle says causes are not equal. A small number of them produce most of the effects, which is why they are ranked by size.

q: A review shows two causes account for 80 percent of defects. What should the team do first?

options.t: Stop measuring defects at all
options.why: Stopping defect measurement would remove the data needed to improve. Measurement should continue to show whether fixes work.

options.t: Focus on fixing those two causes
options.why: Pareto analysis says to focus on the few causes producing most problems. Fixing those two causes, which account for 80 percent of defects, gives the largest improvement for the effort.

options.t: Ignore both and fix the rest
options.why: Ignoring the two causes leaves 80 percent of defects in place. Effort should go to the vital few causes, not the minor remaining ones.

options.t: Spread effort evenly across all
options.why: Spreading effort evenly wastes resources on minor causes. Pareto analysis directs resources to the biggest causes first.

q: What is a fishbone (cause-and-effect) diagram used for?

options.t: Mapping the path of a delivery truck through the streets
options.why: Mapping a truck route is route planning, done with maps or logistics software. A fishbone diagram organizes causes of a problem.

options.t: Listing the steps of a sale made in a shop to a new buyer
options.why: Listing the steps of a sale describes a flowchart or process map. A fishbone diagram groups possible causes of one problem.

options.t: Organizing possible causes of a problem to find the root cause
options.why: A fishbone diagram organizes possible causes of a problem into categories, such as people, methods, machines and materials. It helps a team find the root cause.

options.t: Showing a company's profit by month in the year to come
options.why: Profit by month is shown on a financial chart or line graph. A fishbone diagram is a quality tool for cause analysis, not a financial report.

q: What is a customer requirement in quality management?

options.t: A list of competitors' prices for the same kind of goods
options.why: Competitor prices are market data. A customer requirement is a need or expectation that the product or service must satisfy to be considered good quality.

options.t: A need or expectation a product or service must satisfy
options.why: A customer requirement is a need or expectation that a product or service must meet. Quality is measured by how well the product satisfies those requirements.

options.t: A rule that customers must follow when they shop in a store
options.why: A rule for shoppers in a store is a store policy. A customer requirement describes what customers need from the product or service.

options.t: A fee customers pay for service at a shop or store counter
options.why: A fee paid for service is a price or charge. A customer requirement is a need that the business must meet, and not a payment.

q: Customers say a fitness app crashes too often. Which quality step comes first?

options.t: Measure the crashes and find their cause
options.why: Measuring the crashes and finding the cause is the first step in quality improvement. Data show how often the app fails and why, so the right fix can be chosen.

options.t: Hide the complaints from the rest of the team
options.why: Hiding complaints stops the team from learning about the problem. Quality improvement depends on using customer feedback.

options.t: Raise the price of the app for all users
options.why: Raising the price does not fix crashes and may drive customers away. The cause of the crashes must be found and corrected.

options.t: Remove customer support for the app's users
options.why: Removing support leaves users with no help and does not fix the crashes. It would worsen customer satisfaction.

q: What is a service guarantee?

options.t: A discount for large orders placed by regular business customers
options.why: A discount for large orders is a volume discount, which is a pricing tool. A service guarantee is a promise about service quality.

options.t: A tax on services that firms must pay to the state every single year
options.why: A tax on services is a government charge. A service guarantee is a business's own promise to customers.

options.t: A list of services offered by the firm to its customers each year
options.why: A list of services offered is a service catalog. A guarantee goes further and promises a remedy if the service falls short.

options.t: A promise to fix or refund if a service does not meet stated standards
options.why: A service guarantee is a promise to fix the problem or refund the customer if a service does not meet stated standards. It reduces customer risk and builds trust.

q: A delivery firm promises a refund if a package is more than a day late. What is this?

options.t: A price skimming plan
options.why: Price skimming sets a high price on a new product, then lowers it over time. A refund promise for late delivery is not a pricing plan.

options.t: A service guarantee
options.why: A promise to refund if a package is more than a day late is a service guarantee. It commits the firm to a standard and a remedy if it fails to meet it.

options.t: A franchise fee
options.why: A franchise fee is paid by a franchisee to use a brand. It has nothing to do with refunds for late deliveries.

options.t: A reverse channel
options.why: A reverse channel moves products back from customers, as with returns or recycling. A refund promise for lateness is a quality commitment.

q: What is a quality management system (QMS)?

options.t: A tax system for firms that sets what each firm owes the state
options.why: A tax system is run by government. A quality management system is a company's own set of processes for meeting quality goals.

options.t: A scoreboard of sales only, shown on a screen in the office
options.why: A sales scoreboard tracks only sales. A QMS covers processes, responsibilities and procedures across the business to deliver quality.

options.t: A computer game for employees that tests skills at lunch time
options.why: A skills game for lunch is not a QMS. A QMS is a formal system, such as the ISO 9001 framework, used to manage quality.

options.t: A set of processes and rules for meeting quality goals consistently
options.why: A QMS is a set of processes, rules and responsibilities used to meet quality goals consistently. It includes documentation, measurement and continuous improvement, as in ISO 9001.

q: Why do many firms train all employees in quality methods?

options.t: Training removes the need for any standards at work
options.why: Training does not remove the need for standards. Standards define what good quality is, and training teaches employees how to meet them.

options.t: Training makes products cost more by law now
options.why: Training does not raise product costs by law. No law requires this, and training generally improves quality and cuts the cost of defects.

options.t: Quality depends on everyone, not just inspectors
options.why: Quality depends on everyone in the organization, not just inspectors. Training all employees in quality methods helps them prevent problems and improve their own work.

options.t: Only managers affect quality in the firm's work
options.why: Quality is affected by every employee, not only managers. Workers on the line often see the problems first, so they need quality skills.

q: What is supplier quality management?

options.t: Working with suppliers to ensure inputs meet quality standards
options.why: Supplier quality management means working with suppliers to ensure the materials and services they provide meet quality standards. Good inputs lead to good finished products.

options.t: Choosing suppliers at random without checking their quality
options.why: Choosing suppliers at random without checking quality is the opposite of managing it. Careful selection and review reduce defects and delays.

options.t: Raising prices on customers who buy the finished products
options.why: Raising prices on customers is a pricing decision. Supplier quality management concerns the quality of inputs coming from suppliers.

options.t: Ignoring supplier performance until a problem shows up in sales
options.why: Ignoring supplier performance until sales suffer is reactive. Managing supplier quality involves monitoring performance before problems reach customers.

q: A bakery's flour supplier ships low-quality flour and cakes fail. What is the best response?

options.t: Keep buying the same flour and hope the next bags are better
options.why: Buying the same flour and hoping for better results does not solve the problem. Without new requirements or checks, the cakes will keep failing.

options.t: Stop baking cakes and sell the oven to another local baker
options.why: Stopping baking and selling the oven is an extreme step that gives up the business. A better fix is to address the supplier problem.

options.t: Blame customers for complaints about the bread and cakes
options.why: Blaming customers does not address the cause, which is the poor flour. It also harms the bakery's reputation and sales.

options.t: Set quality requirements and review the supplier's performance
options.why: Setting quality requirements and reviewing the supplier's performance attacks the root cause. The bakery can inspect deliveries, reject poor flour or switch suppliers if quality does not improve.

q: What is a risk register?

options.t: A list of products on sale in the shops of the firm this week
options.why: A list of products on sale is a price or inventory list. A risk register records possible risks and how they will be handled.

options.t: A list of employees' vacation days kept by the HR department
options.why: Vacation days are HR records. A risk register tracks threats to the project or business, not staff leave.

options.t: A list of identified risks with their likelihood, impact and plans
options.why: A risk register lists identified risks with their likelihood, impact, owners and response plans. Teams review it regularly so risks stay under control.

options.t: A list of customers who pay late or do not pay at all each year
options.why: A list of late-paying customers is a credit control report. A risk register covers all kinds of risks and their handling, not one customer group.

q: A project team lists possible problems, rates each and assigns an owner. What is this?

options.t: Maintaining a risk register
options.why: Listing possible problems, rating them and assigning owners is maintaining a risk register. It helps the team prioritize and respond to the most serious risks.

options.t: Setting a retail price list
options.why: A retail price list sets selling prices. Rating possible problems and assigning owners is risk management, not pricing.

options.t: Choosing a supplier for it
options.why: Choosing a supplier is a purchasing decision. Listing and rating problems, then assigning owners, is risk register work.

options.t: Preparing a sales campaign
options.why: Preparing a sales campaign is a marketing activity. The described steps identify and manage risks.

q: What is risk probability?

options.t: The person who is in charge of a risk
options.why: The person in charge of a risk is the risk owner. Probability describes how likely the event is to happen.

options.t: The chance that a risk event will happen
options.why: Risk probability is the chance, or likelihood, that a risk event will happen. It is combined with impact to rank which risks need attention first.

options.t: The date a risk was first listed in the log
options.why: The date a risk was listed is just a log entry. Probability measures likelihood, not timing of the entry.

options.t: The cost of fixing a risk event later
options.why: The cost of fixing a risk event is part of its impact. Probability measures how likely the risk is, not how costly it is.

q: What is risk impact?

options.t: The size of the loss or harm if a risk event happens
options.why: Risk impact is the size of the loss or harm if a risk event happens, such as cost, delay or damage. Impact is rated along with probability to prioritize risks.

options.t: The list of insurance policies owned by the firm
options.why: The insurance policies a firm owns are risk responses, and not impact. Impact is the size of the possible loss.

options.t: The name of the person who first found the risk
options.why: The name of the finder is a record detail. Impact measures how serious the consequences would be.

options.t: The chance that the event will occur in a year
options.why: The chance of the event occurring in a year is probability. Impact measures the size of the consequences, not their likelihood.

q: A risk has low probability but very high impact, such as a factory fire. How is it usually managed?

options.t: It is ignored because it is unlikely
options.why: Ignoring a risk because it is unlikely is dangerous when the impact would be severe. A factory fire could end the business, so it needs a response.

options.t: With insurance and prevention measures
options.why: Rare but severe risks are managed by transferring the loss through insurance and reducing it through prevention, such as sprinklers and safety checks. This limits the damage if it does happen.

options.t: It is accepted with no plan at all
options.why: Accepting with no plan leaves the firm exposed to a very large loss. High-impact risks need planned responses even when unlikely.

options.t: It is avoided by closing the business
options.why: Closing the business to avoid a fire is an extreme response that destroys the firm to avoid a small chance. Insurance and prevention are more practical.

q: What is a business continuity plan?

options.t: A plan to hire more staff in the summer season each year
options.why: Hiring summer staff is a staffing plan. A business continuity plan keeps key operations running during and after a crisis.

options.t: A plan to raise prices every year on all the goods sold
options.why: Raising prices is a pricing plan. A continuity plan prepares for disruptions such as fires, storms or system failures.

options.t: A plan to change the company's logo and colors in stores
options.why: Changing the logo is a branding plan. A continuity plan deals with keeping the business working during a crisis.

options.t: A plan for keeping key operations running during a crisis
options.why: A business continuity plan explains how key operations will keep running, or be restored quickly, during a crisis. It covers people, sites, systems and suppliers to limit losses.

q: A store keeps off-site backups of records and a backup power source. What is this?

options.t: Price discrimination by a firm
options.why: Price discrimination is charging different prices to different buyers. Off-site backups and backup power protect operations, not pricing.

options.t: Market segmentation tasks
options.why: Market segmentation divides customers into groups. Backing up records and power has nothing to do with customer groups.

options.t: Business continuity planning
options.why: Keeping off-site backups and a backup power source helps the store keep operating after a disruption. This is business continuity planning.

options.t: Channel conflict between firms
options.why: Channel conflict is a dispute among distribution partners. Backups and standby power are protective measures against disruptions.

q: What is a disaster recovery plan?

options.t: Steps to lower prices when a firm has too much stock
options.why: Lowering prices to clear excess stock is a sales tactic. A disaster recovery plan restores systems and data after a major disruption.

options.t: Steps to start a new product line in the firm's stores
options.why: Starting a new product line is a growth strategy. A disaster recovery plan deals with restoring operations after something goes wrong.

options.t: Steps to hire an employee for the firm's open position
options.why: Hiring an employee is a staffing task. Disaster recovery focuses on recovering technology, data and facilities after a disaster.

options.t: Steps to restore systems and data after a major disruption
options.why: A disaster recovery plan sets steps to restore systems, data and facilities after a major disruption such as a fire, flood or cyberattack. It sets recovery priorities and time targets.

q: What is workplace safety training?

options.t: Teaching employees how to avoid accidents and respond to hazards
options.why: Workplace safety training teaches employees how to avoid accidents, handle equipment correctly and respond to hazards and emergencies. It reduces injuries and supports OSHA compliance.

options.t: Teaching employees to avoid reports of any kind at the firm
options.why: Avoiding reports would hide problems. Safety training encourages reporting of hazards and incidents so they can be fixed.

options.t: Teaching employees to raise prices on all goods in the shops
options.why: Raising prices is a pricing decision and is unrelated to workplace safety. Training aims to protect employees from harm.

options.t: Teaching employees to ignore hazards and keep on working
options.why: Ignoring hazards puts workers in danger. Safety training teaches employees to spot hazards and act to control them.

q: After several slips on a wet floor, which step best reduces the risk?

options.t: Remove all signs and warnings from the floor area
options.why: Removing warning signs would increase the chance of more slips. People need signs to know a floor is wet.

options.t: Ignore the incidents and wait to see what happens next
options.why: Ignoring repeated incidents allows injuries to continue and may lead to claims. Known hazards should be dealt with promptly.

options.t: Fix the leak, post warnings and clean spills promptly
options.why: Fixing the leak removes the cause, and warnings plus prompt cleanup protect people while problems occur. This is the best way to cut slips and liability.

options.t: Tell staff to walk faster across the floor to save time
options.why: Telling staff to walk faster increases the chance of slipping. It does not remove the wet floor hazard.

q: What is a supply chain risk?

options.t: The chance that a logo will be redesigned by the firm's design team
options.why: A logo redesign is a branding matter. Supply chain risk is about disruptions to sourcing, production and delivery.

options.t: The chance that a disruption in the supply chain will hurt the business
options.why: Supply chain risk is the chance that a disruption, such as a supplier failure, strike or shipping delay, will hurt the business. Firms manage it with backup suppliers and stock.

options.t: The chance that a customer will leave a review of the product on a website
options.why: A customer review is feedback, not a supply chain event. Supply chain risk concerns the flow of materials and goods.

options.t: The chance that a sale will be announced in the news or online
options.why: A sale announcement is a marketing event. Supply chain risk is about problems in the flow of goods from suppliers.

q: A company relies on one overseas supplier and a port strike halts shipments. Which step reduces this risk in future?

options.t: Relying even more on the same single supplier
options.why: Relying more on the same supplier increases exposure. If that supplier or its port is disrupted again, the business will be hit even harder.

options.t: Ordering later each time from that supplier
options.why: Ordering later does not protect against disruption, and it could cause stockouts. The firm needs alternatives, not delay.

options.t: Adding backup suppliers in other regions
options.why: Adding backup suppliers in other regions spreads the risk so one port strike or local event cannot stop supply. This diversification is a standard supply chain risk response.

options.t: Ignoring shipping news from overseas ports
options.why: Ignoring shipping news removes warning of problems. Monitoring helps, but ignoring it does not reduce the risk.

q: What is credit risk for a business?

options.t: The chance that a product will be returned by a buyer
options.why: Product returns are a sales or quality risk. Credit risk is the chance that a customer fails to pay a debt owed to the business.

options.t: The chance that a customer will not pay what they owe
options.why: Credit risk is the chance that a customer will not pay what they owe, which causes bad debts. Firms manage it by checking credit and setting terms and limits.

options.t: The chance that a store will run out of stock in a month
options.why: Running out of stock is an inventory risk. Credit risk concerns customers who buy on credit and fail to pay.

options.t: The chance that an employee will resign from the firm
options.why: An employee resigning is a human resources risk. Credit risk concerns nonpayment by customers or borrowers.

q: A firm checks a new customer's payment history before offering credit terms. What is this?

options.t: Managing credit risk
options.why: Checking a new customer's payment history before offering credit is managing credit risk. It helps predict whether the customer will pay on time.

options.t: Choosing a new logo
options.why: Choosing a logo is a branding decision. Checking payment history is aimed at the risk of not being paid.

options.t: Setting a product price
options.why: Setting a product price is a pricing decision. A payment history check judges whether to extend credit.

options.t: Planning a promotion
options.why: Planning a promotion is a marketing activity. A payment history check is a credit risk control.

q: What is reputational risk?

options.t: The chance that prices will fall by law in the market for it
options.why: Prices falling by law is a regulatory or market risk. Reputational risk is damage to the company's image and public trust.

options.t: The chance that a machine will break down in the factory today
options.why: A machine breaking down is an operational risk. Reputational risk concerns how the public views the company.

options.t: The chance that a delivery will arrive early by a few hours
options.why: An early delivery is not a risk event at all and may please customers. Reputational risk is harm to a company's image.

options.t: The chance that damage to a company's image will hurt its business
options.why: Reputational risk is the chance that damage to a company's image or public trust, from scandals, poor quality or bad service, will hurt sales, hiring and relationships.

q: A company hides a product safety problem and customers find out. What is the likely result?

options.t: No effect on sales at all in the next year
options.why: Customers who find a hidden safety problem will react strongly. Sales are likely to fall, so the effect would not be none.

options.t: Serious damage to reputation and trust
options.why: Hiding a safety problem and being found out damages the company's reputation and customers' trust. It can also lead to lawsuits, recalls, fines and lost sales.

options.t: Higher customer loyalty in the long run
options.why: Loyalty falls after a firm hides a safety problem. Customers trust honest companies and punish deception.

options.t: Lower insurance needs for the firm itself
options.why: The firm would likely need more insurance or pay higher premiums, since the risk is greater. Lower insurance needs would not follow from hiding a safety defect.

q: What is a general journal?

options.t: A list of account balances kept by the finance office staff
options.why: A list of account balances is a trial balance. A general journal is the book where transactions are first recorded in date order.

options.t: A report of annual profit that is sent to the owners and the bank
options.why: An annual profit report is an income statement. The general journal is a day-to-day record of individual transactions.

options.t: A record where transactions are first written in order by date
options.why: A general journal is the book of original entry where transactions are first recorded in date order. Entries are later posted to the ledger accounts.

options.t: A summary of a company's assets, made at the end of the year
options.why: A summary of assets at year end is a balance sheet. The general journal lists individual transactions as they happen.

q: A business buys supplies for cash. Which accounts are affected?

options.t: Supplies increase and Cash decreases
options.why: Buying supplies for cash increases the Supplies asset and decreases the Cash asset by the same amount. Total assets are unchanged, so the accounting equation still balances.

options.t: Revenue increases and Cash increases
options.why: Revenue is earned when goods or services are sold. Buying supplies is not a sale, so revenue does not change, and cash goes down.

options.t: Cash increases and Supplies decrease
options.why: Cash decreases when the business pays for supplies, and supplies increase. This option has the directions reversed.

options.t: Supplies increase and Payables decrease
options.why: Payables would increase if supplies were bought on credit. The purchase here was paid in cash, so cash decreases instead of payables.

q: What is a source document?

options.t: A list of the company's accounts and their balances
options.why: A list of accounts and balances is a trial balance or ledger. A source document is the original evidence that a transaction took place.

options.t: Evidence of a transaction, such as a receipt or invoice
options.why: A source document is original evidence of a transaction, such as a receipt, invoice or check stub. It supports the entry in the journal and is kept for audits.

options.t: A summary of a company's yearly results for the owners
options.why: A summary of yearly results is a financial statement. Source documents are individual records of single transactions.

options.t: A budget for next year that the manager has prepared
options.why: A budget is a plan for the future. A source document proves a past transaction took place.

q: What is a chart of accounts?

options.t: A list of customers and their balances kept in a ledger
options.why: A list of customers and their balances is an accounts receivable subsidiary ledger. A chart of accounts lists every account in the accounting system.

options.t: A graph of sales over time that is posted in the office
options.why: A graph of sales is a visual report. A chart of accounts is a list of account names and numbers.

options.t: A schedule of loan payments due to the bank each month
options.why: A schedule of loan payments is an amortization schedule. A chart of accounts is a full list of the accounts and not a payment plan.

options.t: A list of the accounts a business uses to record transactions
options.why: A chart of accounts is a list of all the accounts a business uses to record transactions, usually with numbers. It organizes assets, liabilities, equity, revenue and expenses.

q: Account numbers beginning with 1 usually stand for which type of account?

options.t: Revenue
options.why: Revenue accounts usually begin with the number 4. Numbers beginning with 1 are generally assets in a standard chart of accounts.

options.t: Expenses
options.why: Expense accounts usually start with 5 or higher. Numbers beginning with 1 are assets.

options.t: Assets
options.why: In a standard chart of accounts, 1 stands for assets, 2 for liabilities, 3 for equity, 4 for revenue and 5 for expenses. This numbering helps keep accounts organized.

options.t: Debts
options.why: Debts are liabilities, which usually start with 2 in a standard chart of accounts. Accounts beginning with 1 are assets.

q: What is a bank reconciliation?

options.t: Comparing a company's cash records with the bank statement
options.why: A bank reconciliation compares the company's cash records with the bank statement and explains differences, such as outstanding checks and deposits in transit. It finds errors and fraud.

options.t: Predicting next month's cash flow for the firm's bank
options.why: Predicting cash flow is a forecast. A bank reconciliation compares records for a past date to find differences.

options.t: Combining two bank accounts into one to hold money in one place
options.why: Combining accounts is a banking change. A reconciliation compares records but does not merge any accounts.

options.t: Applying for a loan from a bank to fund the whole business
options.why: Applying for a loan is a financing step. A bank reconciliation checks the accuracy of cash records.

q: Which item is subtracted from the bank statement balance in a bank reconciliation?

options.t: Interest earned
options.why: Interest earned is added to the book balance, since the bank has credited it and the company has not yet recorded it. It is not subtracted from the bank balance.

options.t: Bank collections
options.why: Bank collections are added to the book balance because the bank has collected on the company's behalf. They are not subtracted from the bank balance.

options.t: Deposits in transit
options.why: Deposits in transit are added to the bank statement balance, since the company recorded them but the bank has not yet. They are not subtracted.

options.t: Outstanding checks
options.why: Outstanding checks have been written and recorded by the company, but have not yet cleared the bank. They are subtracted from the bank balance to find the adjusted cash balance.

q: What is a petty cash fund?

options.t: A fund for paying owners their yearly dividends
options.why: Yearly dividends to owners are paid from profits through the normal bank account. Petty cash is only for small day-to-day expenses.

options.t: A small amount of cash kept for minor expenses
options.why: A petty cash fund is a small amount of cash kept on hand to pay minor expenses, such as postage or supplies. It is managed with an imprest system and vouchers.

options.t: A large fund for buying equipment and machines
options.why: Large equipment purchases go through the bank account with approvals. A petty cash fund is deliberately small.

options.t: A bank loan taken out by the business each year
options.why: A bank loan is borrowed money, a liability. Petty cash is the business's own cash set aside for small payments.

q: What is an invoice?

options.t: A list of company assets and their present yearly value
options.why: A list of assets and their value is an asset register. An invoice is a bill for goods or services sold.

options.t: A bill that lists goods or services sold and the amount due
options.why: An invoice is a bill from a seller that lists the goods or services sold and the amount the buyer owes. It also gives payment terms and a due date.

options.t: A request to buy goods sent by a customer to a supplier
options.why: A request to buy goods sent by a buyer is a purchase order. The invoice comes from the seller after the sale.

options.t: A receipt for a cash sale handed to the customer at the till
options.why: A receipt acknowledges payment already made. An invoice requests payment of an amount that is still owed.

q: What does the term 2/10, net 30 on an invoice mean?

options.t: A 2 percent discount if paid within 10 days, otherwise full in 30
options.why: The terms 2/10, net 30 mean the buyer can take a 2 percent discount by paying within 10 days. Otherwise the full amount is due within 30 days.

options.t: A 10 percent discount if paid within 2 days, else 30 days
options.why: The numbers are reversed. The discount is 2 percent for payment within 10 days, not 10 percent within 2 days.

options.t: Payment is due in 2 or 10 days, or otherwise in 30 more days
options.why: The terms do not mean payment is due in 2 or 10 days. The 2 is the discount percentage, 10 is the discount period, and 30 is the final due date.

options.t: A $2 fee if paid after 10 days, otherwise it is due in 30 days
options.why: The terms are not a $2 fee. The 2 is a percentage discount for early payment, not a fee for paying late.

q: What is payroll?

options.t: The process of advertising products in the news and online
options.why: Advertising is promotion, which communicates about products to buyers; payroll is an internal accounting function that deals with employee compensation instead.

options.t: The process of selling products to buyers in the shops
options.why: Selling products to buyers in shops is retailing or sales, a revenue activity, whereas payroll is an internal accounting task about paying staff.

options.t: The process of paying employees and withholding taxes
options.why: Payroll covers calculating wages, withholding income and Social Security taxes, and issuing paychecks. It is a core accounting function that employers must handle accurately and on time under law.

options.t: The process of ordering supplies from vendors for the shop
options.why: Ordering supplies from vendors is purchasing, which creates accounts payable for goods; payroll instead concerns paying the company's own employees and handling their withheld taxes.

q: An employee earns $1,500 gross with $225 withheld for taxes. What is net pay?

options.why: $1,500 is the gross pay before any taxes are withheld, so it is not the amount the employee actually takes home.
$225 is only the amount withheld for taxes, which is the deduction itself and not what remains after subtracting it from gross pay.
$1,725 comes from adding the withholding to gross pay ($1,500 + $225), but deductions are subtracted from gross pay to find net pay.
Net pay is gross pay minus deductions: $1,500 - $225 = $1,275. This take-home amount is what the paycheck actually pays the employee.

q: What is the purpose of financial software such as accounting packages?

options.t: Recording transactions and producing reports automatically
options.why: Accounting software records transactions and produces reports such as income statements and balance sheets automatically, which saves time, reduces manual errors, and gives managers timely financial information for decisions.

options.t: Printing marketing flyers to hand out to people in the street
options.why: Printing flyers is a marketing or design task handled by graphics tools, not the main purpose of accounting packages, which track money and transactions.

options.t: Managing employee vacation photos kept on the shared drive
options.why: Storing vacation photos is simple file storage on a shared drive and has nothing to do with the bookkeeping and reporting that accounting software performs.

options.t: Designing company logos and brand colors for the business
options.why: Designing logos and brand colors is graphic design work done in design software; accounting packages focus on recording financial transactions and reporting results.

q: What is a distribution channel?

options.t: The path a product takes from producer to consumer
options.why: A distribution channel is the route goods take from producer through any middlemen to the final consumer. Choosing channels affects cost, reach, and customer convenience for the business.

options.t: A television network that runs a company's ads
options.why: A television network carries a company's ads, which is a promotion medium; it is not the path that physical products travel to consumers.

options.t: A company's database of customer names and addresses
options.why: A customer database is an information resource used for marketing research and contact; it does not describe how products physically move to buyers.

options.t: A set of rules that guide how a company sets prices
options.why: Rules that guide how prices are set make up a pricing policy, which is separate from how products travel from producer to consumer.

q: A manufacturer sells directly to shoppers through its own website. This is an example of a:

options.t: Wholesale channel
options.why: A wholesale channel involves a wholesaler buying in bulk and reselling to retailers, but this manufacturer sells straight to shoppers with no middleman involved.

options.t: Broker channel
options.why: A broker channel uses an agent who brings buyers and sellers together without owning goods; here the maker itself sells to shoppers through its website.

options.t: Retail middleman
options.why: A retail middleman sits between maker and shopper, but this maker sells to shoppers itself through its own website, so no retailer is involved.

options.t: Direct channel
options.why: A direct channel sends products straight from the producer to the final customer with no intermediaries. Selling through the company's own website is a classic example of this.

q: Which intermediary buys goods in large quantities and resells them to retailers?

options.t: Consumer
options.why: Consumers are the final buyers who use the product; they purchase from retailers and do not buy in bulk to resell to retailers.

options.t: Auditor
options.why: An auditor is an accountant who examines financial records for accuracy, a service role that has nothing to do with buying goods and reselling them.

options.t: Wholesaler
options.why: A wholesaler buys goods in large quantities from producers and resells them in smaller lots to retailers, which gives manufacturers wider reach without needing many sales staff.

options.t: Franchisee
options.why: A franchisee operates a business under a franchisor's brand and system; it is not an intermediary that buys in bulk to resell to retailers.

q: A small candle maker wants its candles in shops across many cities but has no sales staff there. Which decision would help most?

options.t: Cut product quality to lower costs and sell cheaply
options.why: Cutting quality to sell cheaply does not solve the distribution problem of reaching distant cities, and it can damage the brand's reputation among buyers.

options.t: Use wholesalers or sales agents to reach retailers
options.why: Wholesalers and sales agents already have relationships with retailers in many cities, so the maker can reach distant shops without hiring its own sales staff there.

options.t: Stop all advertising and sell only by word of mouth
options.why: Stopping advertising while relying only on word of mouth would shrink awareness, and it does nothing to place the candles in shops across many cities.

options.t: Sell only from the factory door to walk-in shoppers
options.why: Selling only from the factory door limits reach to local walk-in shoppers, which is the opposite of getting candles into shops in many cities.

q: Which of these is an example of a retailer?

options.t: A bank lending money to businesses
options.why: A bank lends money, which is a financial service, and it does not sell goods to the shoppers who buy for personal use.

options.t: A farm selling crops to a processor
options.why: A farm selling crops to a processor sells to a business buyer, so it is a producer or supplier rather than a retailer.

options.t: A trucking company moving freight
options.why: A trucking company transports freight for others, which makes it a distribution and logistics service, not a seller of goods to shoppers.

options.t: A grocery store selling to shoppers
options.why: A retailer sells goods directly to final consumers, and a grocery store selling food to shoppers fits that definition. Other retailers include clothing shops and online stores.

q: A company chooses intensive distribution for a candy bar. What does that mean?

options.t: It sells the candy in as many outlets as possible
options.why: Intensive distribution places a product in as many outlets as possible, which suits low-cost convenience goods like candy that people buy on impulse wherever they happen to shop.

options.t: It sells only online to buyers who shop from home
options.why: Selling only online to home shoppers describes a direct online channel, which would limit availability; intensive distribution aims for maximum exposure across many types of outlets.

options.t: It sells through a few selected stores only
options.why: Selling through a few selected stores is selective distribution, a middle level that suits shopping goods, not an impulse product such as candy.

options.t: It sells only through one exclusive store in each city
options.why: One exclusive store per city is exclusive distribution, used for luxury or specialty goods; it is the opposite of putting candy everywhere.

q: What is market research?

options.t: Setting the selling price of a company's products each year
options.why: Setting prices is a pricing decision made after costs and demand are studied; it uses research but is not itself market research.

options.t: Training sales staff on how to approach all new customers
options.why: Training sales staff is part of selling and personnel development, not market research, which focuses on information about customers and markets.

options.t: Collecting and analyzing information about customers and markets
options.why: Market research collects and analyzes data about customers, competitors, and markets so firms can make informed decisions and reduce the risk of costly mistakes.

options.t: Designing the layout and displays inside of a store for shoppers
options.why: Designing store layouts and displays is visual merchandising, a promotion and sales task; market research is about gathering information, not arranging a store.

q: Which of these is primary data?

options.t: A magazine article about trends in the industry last year
options.why: A magazine article is secondary data because someone else wrote it earlier for another purpose, and it was not collected by the researcher.

options.t: Survey answers collected directly from customers for the study
options.why: Primary data is gathered firsthand for the current question, such as surveys of customers, so it fits the study exactly and is current, though it costs more.

options.t: A competitor's published annual report from last year, found online
options.why: A competitor's published annual report was produced by others for a different purpose, so it counts as secondary data even though you found it online.

options.t: A government census report on the population of a country
options.why: A government census report was collected by an agency for general use earlier, which makes it secondary data rather than primary data.

q: A cafe wants to know whether local students would buy a new cold brew. Which research method fits best?

options.t: A short survey of nearby students
options.why: A short survey of nearby students asks the actual target buyers directly about their interest in cold brew, which gives relevant primary data cheaply and quickly.

options.t: A review of last year's tax return
options.why: Last year's tax return shows the cafe's finances and says nothing about whether local students would want a new cold brew drink.

options.t: An interview with delivery drivers
options.why: Delivery drivers are not the target buyers, so interviewing them would reveal little about what local students would buy at the cafe.

options.t: A study of national coffee exports
options.why: National coffee exports are broad trade statistics that do not show demand among nearby students for one new cold brew product.

q: A company surveyed only 12 customers before deciding on a nationwide launch. What is the main weakness of this research?

options.t: Surveys can never support decisions in a business
options.why: Surveys are a common and valid research tool, so saying they can never support decisions is false; the real problem here is how few customers were asked.

options.t: The sample is too small to represent all customers
options.why: Twelve responses are too few to represent all customers nationwide, so results could be misleading. A larger, representative sample gives more reliable conclusions before a big launch.

options.t: Surveys are always too cheap to be trusted by firms
options.why: Surveys are often cheap, and low cost does not make them untrustworthy; the weakness here is the tiny sample, not the price of surveys.

options.t: Customers should never be asked any questions
options.why: Asking customers questions is exactly how surveys gather opinions, so avoiding questions would defeat research; the issue is the small number surveyed.

q: What is a database of customer purchases most useful for?

options.t: Scheduling delivery trucks
options.why: Scheduling delivery trucks is a logistics function that relies on route and order data, not on analysis of customer purchase history.

options.t: Paying suppliers on time
options.why: Paying suppliers on time is an accounts payable task handled with invoices and payment schedules, not with a database of customer purchases.

options.t: Spotting buying patterns
options.why: A purchase database reveals buying patterns, such as which items are bought together and when, helping firms stock products, target promotions, and plan offers.

options.t: Printing employee badges
options.why: Printing employee badges is an administrative human resources task that uses employee records, not customer purchase data.

q: Which of these is secondary data?

options.t: Results of a survey that you designed
options.why: Results of a survey you designed are primary data, since you collected them yourself for your own question.

options.t: Observations from your own store visits
options.why: Observations from your own store visits are primary data because you gathered them firsthand for this specific study.

options.t: Notes from your own interviews with buyers
options.why: Notes from your own interviews are primary data, collected directly by you from buyers for the current research purpose.

options.t: An industry report published last year
options.why: An industry report published last year was gathered by others for a general purpose, which makes it secondary data that is quick and cheap to obtain.

q: What is a target market?

options.t: The specific group of customers a business aims to serve
options.why: A target market is the specific group of customers a business aims to serve, chosen because their needs match the product and they can be reached effectively.

options.t: The location where a company's main store is found
options.why: The location of a main store is a site decision; it describes a place, while a target market describes a group of people.

options.t: A company's total sales figure for the whole year
options.why: Total yearly sales is a performance figure used to measure results, not the group of customers the business chooses to serve.

options.t: The group made up of all of a company's competitors in the area
options.why: Competitors are rival firms that compete for the same buyers; a target market is made up of customers, not rivals.

q: Which step comes first when building a marketing plan?

options.t: Evaluating the results of the plan
options.why: Evaluating results is the last step of the planning process, since it needs actions already carried out before outcomes can be measured.

options.t: Printing the plan in full color
options.why: Printing the plan in color is presentation detail that comes after the content is decided, not the first step of building a plan.

options.t: Spending the budget in full
options.why: Spending the budget fully is part of carrying out the plan later; a budget must first be set based on analysis and objectives.

options.t: Analyzing the current situation
options.why: Planning begins with a situation analysis of the market, customers, competitors, and the company's strengths and weaknesses, which gives the facts needed to set sound objectives.

q: Which tool compares a company's strengths with its competitors'?

options.t: Job description sheet
options.why: A job description sheet lists duties for an employee position, which is a human resources document and does not compare competitors' strengths.

options.t: Break-even chart
