options.why: A break-even chart shows the sales volume where revenue equals costs; it is a financial tool, not a comparison with rival companies.

options.t: Competitive analysis
options.why: Competitive analysis studies rivals' products, prices, and strengths so a firm can find advantages and weaknesses, and then position itself better in the market.

options.t: Payroll register report
options.why: A payroll register report lists employee pay and deductions for a pay period, which is an accounting record, not a market comparison tool.

q: A bike shop sets the objective to raise e-bike sales by 15 percent in 12 months. What must the plan add to be complete?

options.t: A smaller number of products on the shelves
options.why: Carrying fewer products does not provide the actions needed to raise e-bike sales by 15 percent and may reduce customer choice.

options.t: Strategies and actions to reach the objective
options.why: An objective states the goal, but a complete plan also needs strategies and action steps showing how, who, when, and with what budget it will be reached.

options.t: A new company logo and slogan for the shop
options.why: A new logo and slogan are branding changes that do not directly describe how e-bike sales will rise 15 percent in the year.

options.t: A list of employee birthdays for the new year
options.why: Employee birthdays have no connection to reaching a sales objective and add nothing to a marketing plan.

q: What does market share measure?

options.t: The number of employees at the head office now
options.why: Employee count at the head office measures company size and says nothing about the portion of market sales the company holds.

options.t: The size of the warehouse used to store goods
options.why: Warehouse size measures storage capacity, which is an operations figure and is unrelated to a company's portion of its market.

options.t: A company's percentage of total sales in a market
options.why: Market share is a company's sales as a percentage of total industry sales; for example, $2 million of a $20 million market equals 10 percent.

options.t: The company's total profit for the whole year
options.why: Total yearly profit shows earnings after expenses, which differs from market share, since share compares a firm's sales with those of the whole market.

q: A company learns that most of its buyers are aged 18 to 24. How should this shape the plan?

options.t: Stop selling online to young buyers
options.why: Stopping online sales to young buyers would ignore the group the data shows are the main buyers and would lose sales.

options.t: Aim promotion at that age group
options.why: Because most buyers are 18 to 24, promotion should aim at that group, using media and messages they respond to, which makes marketing spending more effective.

options.t: Ignore the data on its buyers
options.why: Ignoring data about buyers wastes the research; good planning uses customer information to shape decisions about promotion and products.

options.t: Raise prices for every customer
options.why: Raising prices for every customer does not use the age information and may drive away the very buyers the company depends on.

q: A store adds a 40 percent markup to the $50 cost of a jacket. What is the selling price?

options.why: Markup is $50 x 0.40 = $20, and cost plus markup gives $50 + $20 = $70, which is the selling price of the jacket.
$90 would be an 80 percent markup ($50 x 1.80), which is double the 40 percent markup actually stated in the question.
$55 would be only a 10 percent markup on $50 cost, much less than the 40 percent markup the store adds.
$20 is only the markup amount ($50 x 0.40); the selling price must also include the original $50 cost, giving $70.

q: A new company launches with a very low price to win customers quickly. Which strategy is this?

options.t: Prestige pricing
options.why: Prestige pricing sets a high price to signal quality and status, which is the opposite of a very low price used to win customers.

options.t: Cost-plus pricing plan
options.why: Cost-plus pricing adds a set markup to cost; it is not defined by launching very low to win customers fast.

options.t: Price skimming plan
options.why: Price skimming starts with a high price and lowers it over time, whereas this company starts low to build market share quickly.

options.t: Penetration pricing
options.why: Penetration pricing sets a low initial price to attract many customers and gain market share quickly, then prices may rise after the brand is established.

q: Which factor most directly sets the minimum price a business can charge without losing money?

options.t: Its brand color scheme
options.why: A brand color scheme affects image and recognition but has no effect on the cost floor under a price.

options.t: Its total cost per unit
options.why: Total cost per unit sets the price floor; charging below it means a loss on every item sold, so pricing must at least cover it.

options.t: Its advertising slogan
options.why: An advertising slogan is a promotion message and does not determine the lowest price at which a business avoids losing money.

options.t: Its store opening hours
options.why: Store opening hours are an operating choice that does not directly set a minimum price, unlike the cost of making each unit.

q: A retailer cuts an item's price from $80 to $60. By what percent was it marked down?

options.t: 75 percent
options.why: 75 percent is the new price divided by the old price ($60 / $80); it is not the reduction, which must be measured against the original price.

options.t: 20 percent
options.why: 20 percent confuses the $20 dollar drop with a percentage; the drop must be divided by the $80 original price to find the percent.

options.t: 25 percent
options.why: The drop is $80 - $60 = $20, and $20 / $80 = 0.25, so the markdown is 25 percent of the original price.

options.t: 33 percent
options.why: 33 percent comes from dividing the $20 drop by the new $60 price, but markdown percent is always based on the original price of $80.

q: What is price skimming?

options.t: Setting a high introductory price and lowering it over time
options.why: Price skimming sets a high introductory price to earn strong profits from early adopters, then lowers it over time as competition grows and demand softens.

options.t: Always charging the lowest price in the whole market
options.why: Always charging the lowest price in the market is a low-price or discount strategy, not skimming, which begins high.

options.t: Matching a competitor's price every week of the year
options.why: Matching a competitor's price each week is competitive or follow-the-leader pricing, which does not begin with a high price that falls over time.

options.t: Changing prices at random times for no reason at all
options.why: Changing prices randomly is not a recognized strategy; skimming is a planned high start followed by gradual price reductions.

q: Pricing an item at $4.99 instead of $5.00 is an example of:

options.t: Loss-leader pricing plan
options.why: Loss-leader pricing sells an item at or below cost to attract shoppers, but a one-cent change from $5.00 is not a loss.

options.t: Bundle pricing plan
options.why: Bundle pricing sells several items together for one price, whereas $4.99 is a single item price slightly lowered.

options.t: Cost-plus pricing
options.why: Cost-plus pricing adds a markup to cost; the $4.99 price ending is chosen for how it looks, not computed from costs.

options.t: Psychological pricing
options.why: Psychological pricing uses endings like $4.99 so the price seems lower than $5.00, because buyers focus on the leftmost digit and see a bargain.

q: What is a product line?

options.t: A queue of customers waiting at a checkout
options.why: A queue of customers waiting at a checkout is a store service issue and is unrelated to what a company sells.

options.t: A list of the debts that the company owes
options.why: A list of debts the company owes is its liabilities, an accounting term, and not a group of related products.

options.t: A group of related products sold by one company
options.why: A product line is a group of closely related products sold by one company, such as different sizes or flavors of a snack brand.

options.t: The route a delivery truck takes each day of work
options.why: The route a delivery truck takes is a logistics plan, which has nothing to do with a company's range of related products.

q: In which stage of the product life cycle are sales low and promotion costs high?

options.t: Maturity
options.why: In maturity sales peak and level off, and promotion is used to defend share rather than to build initial awareness.

options.t: Late decline
options.why: In decline sales and profits fall, and promotion is usually cut back, so it is not a stage with high promotion costs.

options.t: Rapid growth
options.why: In growth sales rise quickly and profits start to appear, so sales are not low even though promotion continues.

options.t: Introduction
options.why: In introduction sales are low as buyers learn about the product, while heavy promotion spending builds awareness, so profits are usually negative at this stage.

q: A company adds a new flavor to an existing snack brand. What is this called?

options.t: Price skimming plan
options.why: Price skimming is a pricing strategy of starting high, not the act of adding a new flavor to an existing brand.

options.t: Product line extension
options.why: A product line extension adds a new item, like another flavor, to an existing line under the same brand, using brand trust to reduce launch risk.

options.t: Channel conflict risk
options.why: Channel conflict is a disagreement among distribution partners and has nothing to do with adding a flavor to a snack brand.

options.t: Product obsolescence
options.why: Product obsolescence means a product becomes outdated or unwanted, whereas adding a new flavor is growth in the product line.

q: Sales of a mature product are flat while competition grows. Which action is most likely to extend its life?

options.t: Update its features or find new uses and markets
options.why: Updating features or finding new uses and markets can renew interest and extend a mature product's life cycle, a common strategy called product modification or market development.

options.t: Raise the price with no change to the product itself
options.why: Raising the price while changing nothing about the product gives buyers no new reason to buy, which could shrink flat sales further.

options.t: Cut all advertising and sell off the stock cheaply
options.why: Cutting all advertising and selling off stock cheaply speeds decline instead of extending life, and it signals the firm is giving up on the product.

options.t: Stop making it immediately and close the factory line
options.why: Stopping production at once abandons a product that still earns sales, and extending its life requires changes, not shutting down the factory line.

q: Besides protecting a product, what is another main purpose of packaging?

options.t: Promoting and identifying the product
options.why: Packaging also promotes and identifies the product through its design, brand name, and information, which helps shoppers recognize it on the shelf and decide to buy.

options.t: Setting its price and its discounts
options.why: Prices and discounts are set by management through pricing decisions, not through packaging, whose roles are protection, promotion, and identification.

options.t: Hiring its sellers and sales staff
options.why: Hiring sales staff is a human resources and selling decision, unrelated to the roles that packaging plays for a product.

options.t: Choosing its wholesale distributors
options.why: Choosing wholesale distributors is a channel decision; packaging protects and promotes the product rather than selecting distributors.

q: What is a warranty mainly intended to do?

options.t: Stop customers from returning any of the goods they buy
options.why: A warranty does not stop returns; it actually promises repair or replacement if the product fails, and it is a seller's commitment to buyers.

options.t: Limit how many units of the product can be sold per year
options.why: A warranty has no link to limiting sales quantities; it is a promise about product performance and not a sales cap.

options.t: Give buyers confidence the product will work as promised
options.why: A warranty is a seller's promise to repair or replace a defective product, which reduces buyer risk and builds confidence that it will work as promised.

options.t: Raise the cost of the product to buyers for good now
options.why: A warranty is a promise that protects buyers; its purpose is not to raise the price, though some cost may be built into pricing.

q: Which of these is an element of the promotional mix?

options.t: Payroll
options.why: Payroll is an accounting function for paying employees and is not part of the promotional mix.

options.t: Advertising
options.why: Advertising is paid, non-personal communication and is one of the four promotional mix elements, along with personal selling, sales promotion, and public relations.

options.t: Stock control
options.why: Stock control is inventory management, an operations task, and not one of the ways a business promotes its products.

options.t: Supply planning
options.why: Supply planning is an operations and purchasing activity about getting materials, not a method of communicating with customers.

q: A store gives out free samples of a new snack. This is an example of:

options.t: Personal selling
options.why: Personal selling is direct face-to-face or phone persuasion by a salesperson, whereas handing out free samples is a short-term incentive.

options.t: Direct mail
options.why: Direct mail sends printed promotions to customers by post, whereas free samples are given out in person in the store.

options.t: Public relations
options.why: Public relations builds goodwill through press and community activity; free samples are a short-term incentive to try a product.

options.t: Sales promotion
options.why: Sales promotion uses short-term incentives such as free samples, coupons, and contests to encourage trial and quick purchases of a product.

q: A new brand's ad explains what the product is and how it works. This ad is mainly:

options.t: Competitive
options.why: Competitive ads compare a brand with rivals to win buyers away; this ad simply explains what the product is and how it works.

options.t: Institutional
options.why: Institutional ads promote the company's image rather than a specific product, whereas this ad describes one product.

options.t: Informative
options.why: Informative advertising explains a new product's features and uses, which is typical at launch when buyers do not yet know what the brand offers.

options.t: Reminder ad
options.why: Reminder ads keep an established brand in customers' minds, so they are not suited to a new brand that must first be explained.

q: A company wants to reach teenagers on a limited budget. Which approach is most cost-effective?

options.t: A full-page ad in a business journal for banks
options.why: A full-page ad in a business journal for banks reaches financial professionals, not teenagers, so most of the spending would be wasted.

options.t: A billboard in a distant city far from teenagers
options.why: A billboard far from teenagers fails to reach the audience and wastes the limited budget on people who are not the target.

options.t: A national TV ad during the evening news each night
options.why: National TV ads during the evening news are costly and reach mostly adults, so they are poorly suited to a small budget targeting teens.

options.t: Social media posts and partnerships aimed at teens
options.why: Social media posts and partnerships reach teens where they spend time at low cost and can be targeted by age, making them the most cost-effective option.

q: What is public relations?

options.t: Building goodwill through communication with the public and press
options.why: Public relations builds goodwill and a favorable image through communication with the public and press, using tools like news releases, events, and community involvement.

options.t: Setting the prices that customers will pay in all the stores
options.why: Setting prices is a pricing decision, not public relations, which deals with relationships and image rather than what customers pay.

options.t: Designing the packaging that wraps a product safely in store
options.why: Designing packaging is a product decision about protection and appearance, which is separate from managing relations with the public.

options.t: Managing how much inventory a store holds at any one time
options.why: Managing inventory is an operations task about stock levels and has no connection to communication with the public.

q: A loyalty program gives a free coffee after 10 purchases. What does it mainly aim to do?

options.t: Raise production costs
options.why: A loyalty program does not aim to raise production costs; it costs the firm only the reward, in exchange for repeat sales.

options.t: Encourage repeat purchases
options.why: Giving a free coffee after 10 purchases rewards repeat customers and encourages them to keep buying, building loyalty and steady sales over time.

options.t: Replace advertising entirely
options.why: A loyalty program supports advertising but does not replace it, since new customers still need to learn about the business.

options.t: Reduce customer data use
options.why: Loyalty programs usually collect more customer data, such as purchase history, rather than reduce its use, and that data helps tailor offers.

q: What is the first step in the selling process?

options.t: Closing deals
options.why: Closing is near the end of the selling process, after needs are found and the product is presented.

options.t: Following up
options.why: Following up happens after the sale to ensure satisfaction, so it is the final step of the process, not the first.

options.t: Prospecting
options.why: Prospecting is finding and qualifying potential customers, which comes first because a salesperson cannot present or close without someone to sell to.

options.t: Objections
options.why: Handling objections occurs after the presentation, when the customer raises concerns, so it comes in the middle of the process.

q: A customer says, 'It's too expensive.' Which response best handles this objection?

options.t: Argue that the customer is wrong about the price
options.why: Arguing that the customer is wrong creates conflict and damages trust, and it rarely moves the buyer toward a purchase.

options.t: Acknowledge the concern and explain the product's value
options.why: Acknowledging the concern shows respect, and then explaining the product's value, such as quality or savings, helps the customer see why the price is justified.

options.t: End the conversation immediately and walk away from them
options.why: Walking away ends any chance of a sale and shows poor service, so it is the worst way to handle an objection.

options.t: Raise the price to make the product seem exclusive to buyers
options.why: Raising the price in reaction to a price complaint makes the objection worse and does not address the customer's concern about value.

q: Which question is an open-ended question a salesperson might ask?

options.t: What features matter most to you?
options.why: An open-ended question lets the customer answer in their own words, such as which features matter most, and gives the salesperson useful information about needs.

options.t: Do you like the color blue best?
options.why: This question can be answered with a simple yes or no, so it is closed rather than open-ended.

options.t: Is this your first visit here?
options.why: This question has a yes or no answer, which makes it closed and gives the salesperson little information about needs.

options.t: Are you ready to buy today or not?
options.why: This question pushes for a yes or no decision, so it is a closed question and may pressure the buyer.

q: After selling a phone, a salesperson suggests a case and a screen protector. This technique is called:

options.t: Cold calling sales
options.why: Cold calling means contacting people who have not shown interest, whereas suggesting add-ons to a customer who just bought is a different technique.

options.t: Price matching
options.why: Price matching means meeting a competitor's lower price, which is unrelated to recommending extra items after a sale.

options.t: Prospecting work
options.why: Prospecting is finding new potential customers, whereas this salesperson is offering extra items to a customer who already bought.

options.t: Suggestive selling
options.why: Suggestive selling recommends related add-on items, like a case and screen protector, to raise the sale total while also helping the customer.

q: Why do salespeople follow up with customers after the sale?

options.t: To make sure customers are satisfied and encourage repeat business
options.why: Following up checks that customers are satisfied, solves problems, and encourages repeat business and referrals, which builds long-term relationships worth more than a single sale.

options.t: To reduce the quality of the product over time for all buyers
options.why: Reducing product quality over time would harm customers and reputation, and follow-up is meant to improve satisfaction instead.

options.t: To raise the original price after the sale is made for the buyers
options.why: Raising the price after the sale is made would be unfair and unethical, and it is not the reason salespeople follow up.

options.t: To avoid having any further contact with the customer after payment
options.why: Avoiding contact after payment is the opposite of follow-up, which keeps in touch to maintain the relationship.

q: A salesperson who lists a product's features and then explains how each helps the customer is using:

options.t: Price slashing to win
options.why: Price slashing relies on discounts to win sales, whereas this salesperson explains features and how each benefits the customer.

options.t: Passive order taking
options.why: Passive order taking just records what a customer asks for, but this salesperson actively presents features and explains their benefits.

options.t: Feature-benefit selling
options.why: Feature-benefit selling lists a product's features and explains how each one helps the customer, which turns technical facts into reasons to buy.

options.t: Cold calling by phone
options.why: Cold calling is contacting people who have not shown interest, which describes how a lead is found and not how a product is presented.

q: What is a channel of distribution?

options.t: The set of prices a company charges in different regions
options.why: A set of regional prices is a pricing structure and does not describe the route a product follows to reach customers.

options.t: The path a product follows from producer to final customer
options.why: A channel of distribution is the path a product follows from producer through any intermediaries to the final customer, including wholesalers and retailers.

options.t: The list of media used to advertise a product to customers
options.why: The list of advertising media is a promotion plan, not the path that physical products take to reach customers.

options.t: The group of employees who deliver products to a warehouse
options.why: Employees who deliver products to a warehouse are part of operations staff, not the full path of ownership from producer to customer.

q: Which channel member buys goods in large quantities and resells them to retailers?

options.t: Manufacturer
options.why: A manufacturer makes the goods and sells them to wholesalers or retailers, so it is the source rather than the middleman.

options.t: Consumer
options.why: The consumer is the final buyer who uses the product, not a channel member who resells goods to retailers.

options.t: Broker
options.why: A broker brings buyers and sellers together for a fee without taking ownership or buying goods in bulk.

options.t: Wholesaler
options.why: A wholesaler buys goods in large quantities from manufacturers and resells them to retailers, which gives makers wider reach with fewer customer accounts to handle.

q: A maker of handmade soap sells directly to customers through its own website. What type of channel is this?

options.t: A direct channel
options.why: A direct channel sells straight from the maker to the customer with no middlemen, which is the case for soap sold through the maker's website.

options.t: An indirect channel
options.why: An indirect channel uses middlemen such as wholesalers or retailers, but here the maker sells directly through its own website.

options.t: A reverse channel
options.why: A reverse channel moves used or defective goods back toward the maker, not new soap sold to customers.

options.t: A dual channel
options.why: A dual channel uses two different types of channels at once, whereas this maker uses only its own website.

q: What is an indirect channel?

options.t: A route where the maker sells straight to the final customer
options.why: A route where the maker sells straight to the customer is a direct channel, which is the opposite of an indirect channel.

options.t: A route that uses one or more middlemen between maker and buyer
options.why: An indirect channel includes one or more middlemen, such as wholesalers, distributors, or retailers, between the maker and the final buyer, which widens reach but shares profit.

options.t: A route that is used only for products sold overseas now
options.why: Indirect channels are not limited to overseas sales; they are used for both domestic and foreign markets.

options.t: A route that is used only for services and never for goods
options.why: Indirect channels are used for both goods and services, so saying they are only for services is wrong.

q: Why might a small snack maker use a distributor instead of selling to every store itself?

options.t: A distributor guarantees every store will stock the product
options.why: No distributor can guarantee every store will stock a product, since each store decides what to buy.

options.t: A distributor removes the need to make a quality product
options.why: A distributor does not remove the need for quality, because stores and customers will still reject a poor product.

options.t: A distributor already reaches many stores and handles deliveries
options.why: A distributor already has relationships with many stores and handles deliveries, so a small maker can reach shoppers without building its own sales and trucking system.

options.t: A distributor always charges lower prices than the maker would
options.why: A distributor needs a margin to cover its costs, so it does not always charge lower prices than the maker would charge.

q: What is logistics?

options.t: Setting the selling price of goods based on competitor prices
options.why: Setting prices from competitor prices is a pricing decision, not logistics, which concerns moving and storing goods.

options.t: Choosing which customers should receive coupons this season
options.why: Choosing who gets coupons is a promotion decision and has nothing to do with the physical flow of goods.

options.t: Recording the money a business earns and spends each month
options.why: Recording money earned and spent is accounting, whereas logistics focuses on physical movement and storage rather than financial records.

options.t: Planning and managing the movement and storage of goods
options.why: Logistics plans and manages the movement and storage of goods, including transport, warehousing, and inventory, so products arrive at the right place and time.

q: What is a retailer?

options.t: A business that sells goods directly to final consumers
options.why: A retailer sells goods directly to final consumers, in stores or online, and it is the last link in many distribution channels.

options.t: A business that makes goods from raw materials in a plant
options.why: Making goods from raw materials is the work of a manufacturer, not a retailer, which sells finished goods to shoppers.

options.t: A business that moves goods but never sells them
options.why: A business that moves goods without selling them is a transporter or carrier, not a retailer, since retailers sell to consumers.

options.t: A business that sells goods only to other businesses in bulk
options.why: Selling goods only to other businesses in bulk describes a wholesaler, whereas a retailer sells to final consumers.

q: A bike brand sells through its own stores, a big-box chain and its website. What is this approach called?

options.t: Direct mail with no stores
options.why: Direct mail with no stores sells straight to customers by post and uses a single channel, unlike this mix of stores, chains, and website.

options.t: Exclusive distribution
options.why: Exclusive distribution limits sales to one or few outlets, whereas this brand uses several types of outlets.

options.t: Intensive distribution
options.why: Intensive distribution places a product in as many outlets as possible, which is not the same as combining a few distinct channel types.

options.t: Multichannel distribution
options.why: Multichannel distribution sells through several channels at once, such as own stores, big-box chains, and a website, to reach customers wherever they prefer to shop.

q: A luxury watch maker lets only a few high-end jewelers sell its watches. Which distribution strategy is this?

options.t: Direct distribution only
options.why: Direct distribution only would mean selling straight to customers, but this maker uses a few jewelers as intermediaries.

options.t: Selective distribution
options.why: Selective distribution uses several chosen outlets, more than a few, so it is a step wider than the limited approach shown here.

options.t: Exclusive distribution
options.why: Exclusive distribution lets only a few high-end retailers sell the product, which protects a luxury image and gives dealers strong control over presentation.

options.t: Intensive distribution
options.why: Intensive distribution puts a product in as many places as possible, which would damage the exclusive image of luxury watches.

q: A candy maker wants its product in nearly every grocery and convenience store. Which strategy fits?

options.t: Exclusive distribution
options.why: Exclusive distribution restricts a product to very few outlets, the opposite of being in nearly every grocery and convenience store.

options.t: Intensive distribution
options.why: Intensive distribution places a product in nearly every suitable outlet, which fits low-priced convenience goods like candy that shoppers buy on impulse.

options.t: Direct distribution only
options.why: Direct distribution only would sell straight to customers, so it could not put candy in nearly every store.

options.t: Selective distribution
options.why: Selective distribution uses a moderate number of chosen outlets, which is fewer than nearly every store.

q: What does inventory management do for a channel?

options.t: Creates the advertisements that appear on television
options.why: Creating television advertisements is a promotion activity, not what inventory management does for a channel.

options.t: Chooses the colors and design of a product package
options.why: Choosing package colors and design is a product decision and is unrelated to stocking goods in a channel.

options.t: Sets the price the final customer pays at checkout
options.why: Setting the checkout price is a pricing decision, not inventory management, which deals with stock levels rather than price.

options.t: Keeps enough goods on hand without holding too much
options.why: Inventory management balances supply and demand, keeping enough goods on hand to meet sales without tying up money in excess stock that costs to store.

q: A store runs out of a popular item every weekend. What is the most likely channel problem?

options.t: The item has no brand name that customers can recognize
options.why: A missing brand name would hurt recognition, but it would not cause a popular item to sell out every weekend.

options.t: The item has too many colors for customers to choose from
options.why: Too many colors might confuse choice, but it does not explain why a popular item runs out every weekend.

options.t: Too little inventory is being ordered for peak demand
options.why: Running out every weekend points to ordering too little for peak demand, so the store should raise order quantities or reorder points before busy days.

options.t: The item is priced too low for any customer to want it
options.why: A price that is too low to attract buyers would cause slow sales, not a sellout of a popular item.

q: What is a supply chain?

options.t: The network of businesses that move a product from raw materials to customer
options.why: A supply chain is the network of businesses and activities that move a product from raw materials through production and distribution to the final customer.

options.t: The group of customers who buy a product regularly from a shop each week
options.why: Regular shoppers who buy a product each week are customers, not the network of firms that move goods.

options.t: The set of ads that a product appears in on television and in print
options.why: A set of ads is a promotion campaign, not the network of suppliers, makers, and carriers that handles goods.

options.t: The list of every price that a product has sold at since the firm was first founded
options.why: A price history list is a record of past prices, which is not the series of firms that move a product to customers.

q: A storm closes a key port and a retailer's shelves empty. Which approach best reduces this risk in the future?

options.t: Ignoring delivery times when choosing suppliers
options.why: Ignoring delivery times when choosing suppliers makes disruptions more likely and does nothing to protect shelves from a closed port.

options.t: Using more than one supplier and shipping route
options.why: Using more than one supplier and shipping route spreads risk, so if one port closes the retailer can still get goods by another path.

options.t: Ordering only at the last possible minute each time
options.why: Ordering at the last possible minute leaves no buffer, so any delay such as a storm would empty shelves even faster.

options.t: Relying on one supplier to simplify the paperwork
options.why: Relying on one supplier makes paperwork simpler but raises risk, since a single disruption can stop the entire supply.

q: What is channel conflict?

options.t: A disagreement between members of a distribution channel
options.why: Channel conflict is a disagreement between members of a distribution channel, such as a maker and its retailers, often over prices, territories, or competing sales routes.

options.t: A disagreement between two employees on a work schedule
options.why: A schedule disagreement between two employees is an internal workplace matter, not a conflict among channel members.

options.t: A disagreement between two customers in a checkout line
options.why: A quarrel between customers in a line is not a channel conflict, because customers are not members of a distribution channel.

options.t: A disagreement between a firm and its tax advisers
options.why: A dispute with tax advisers is a professional services matter and does not involve members of a distribution channel.

q: A maker starts selling online at lower prices than its retailers charge, and the retailers complain. What is this?

options.t: Price skimming
options.why: Price skimming means starting with a high price, but here the maker undercuts its own retailers by selling lower online.

options.t: Brand extension
options.why: Brand extension applies an existing brand name to a new product, which is not the same as competing with retailers online.

options.t: Channel conflict
options.why: Channel conflict arises when a maker competes with its own retailers, such as selling online below their prices, which can damage the retail relationships it depends on.

options.t: Market segmenting
options.why: Market segmenting divides buyers into groups with similar needs, which is unrelated to a maker undercutting its retailers.

q: What does a freight carrier do?

options.t: Creates the advertising for a product launch
options.why: Creating advertising is done by an agency or marketing team, whereas a freight carrier physically moves goods.

options.t: Transports goods from one location to another
options.why: A freight carrier transports goods from one location to another by truck, rail, ship, or air, which links makers, warehouses, and stores in the channel.

options.t: Sets the final shelf price at a store location
options.why: Shelf prices are set by the retailer, and a carrier has no role in deciding what the final customer pays.

options.t: Tests the quality of products before sale
options.why: Testing product quality is a quality control job done by the maker or a lab, not by a freight carrier.

q: What is warehousing?

options.t: Selling goods to final consumers in a shop or online
options.why: Selling goods to final consumers is retailing, whereas warehousing concerns the storage of goods before they are sold or shipped.

options.t: Making goods from raw materials in a factory using machines
options.why: Making goods from raw materials is manufacturing or production, not warehousing, which only stores finished products.

options.t: Promoting goods through public events and fairs for buyers
options.why: Promoting goods through public events and fairs is a promotion activity, unrelated to storing goods in a warehouse.

options.t: Storing goods until they are needed for sale or shipment
options.why: Warehousing is storing goods until they are needed for sale or shipment, which balances supply with demand and keeps products available to fill orders promptly.

q: What is a benefit of using drop shipping for a small online store?

options.t: The store does not need to hold inventory
options.why: With drop shipping the supplier ships orders straight to the customer, so the store does not need to buy, store, or manage inventory, which lowers startup cost and risk.

options.t: The store earns the full retail price
options.why: The store does not earn the full retail price, because it pays the supplier a wholesale price and keeps only the difference.

options.t: The store fully controls shipping quality
options.why: Drop shipping gives the store little control over shipping quality, since the supplier packs and ships orders.

options.t: The store never needs to deal with returns
options.why: Returns still happen under drop shipping and the store must coordinate them with the supplier, so it cannot ignore returns.

q: What is a reverse channel?

options.t: A route that delivers new products to customers faster each season
options.why: Delivering new products faster describes a forward distribution improvement, whereas a reverse channel moves goods back from customers.

options.t: A route that is used only for foreign sales in other lands
options.why: A reverse channel is not limited to foreign sales; it is about returning products regardless of the market location.

options.t: A route that removes retailers from the whole channel
options.why: Removing retailers is called disintermediation or direct selling, not a reverse channel, which carries goods backward toward the maker.

options.t: A route that returns used or defective products to the maker
options.why: A reverse channel returns used, recalled, or defective products from customers back to the maker for repair, recycling, or refund.

q: What is order fulfillment?

options.t: The steps for hiring new staff for a store or a head office
options.why: Hiring new staff is a human resources process and has nothing to do with filling a customer's order.

options.t: The steps for filing a company's yearly taxes with the state
options.why: Filing yearly taxes is a legal accounting duty and is not part of receiving and delivering a customer's order.

options.t: The steps from receiving an order to delivering it to the customer
options.why: Order fulfillment covers the steps from receiving an order through picking, packing, and shipping to delivering it, so customers get what they ordered promptly and correctly.

options.t: The steps for designing a new product line for a large firm
options.why: Designing a product line is a product planning task, which happens before sales and has no connection to filling orders.

q: Which measure best shows whether order fulfillment is working well?

options.t: The number of followers on the company's account
options.why: Follower counts measure social media reach, not whether orders are being filled correctly and delivered on time.

options.t: The percent of orders delivered correctly and on time
options.why: The percent of orders delivered correctly and on time directly measures fulfillment quality, since late or wrong orders cause returns and unhappy customers.

options.t: The length of the company's mission statement text
options.why: Mission statement length says nothing about how well orders are picked, packed, and delivered to customers.

options.t: The number of colors in the company's logo design
options.why: The number of colors in a logo is a branding detail that has no link to fulfillment performance.

q: Why do many companies use retailers rather than only selling directly?

options.t: Retailers pay the manufacturer's tax bills each year in full
options.why: Retailers do not pay a manufacturer's taxes; each business pays its own tax bills.

options.t: Retailers give customers convenient places to see and buy products
options.why: Retailers give customers convenient places to see, compare, and buy products, so makers reach many more buyers than they could through their own selling alone.

options.t: Retailers remove all competition from the whole market for goods
options.why: Retailers do not remove competition from a market, and they often compete with each other.

options.t: Retailers design the products that the maker will sell to the public
options.why: Retailers sell products the maker designs; they do not design the products that the maker sells to the public.

q: What is marketing research?

options.t: Delivering products to customers on a set schedule each week
options.why: Delivering products on a set schedule is a distribution or logistics activity, not research about customers.

options.t: Setting prices based on a competitor's latest clearance sale
options.why: Setting prices from a competitor's clearance sale is a pricing tactic, which may use research but is not itself marketing research.

options.t: Training employees to greet customers politely at the door
options.why: Training employees to greet customers is customer service training, which is a human resources task and not research.

options.t: Gathering and studying information about customers and markets
options.why: Marketing research gathers and studies information about customers, competitors, and markets so that firms can make sound decisions about products, prices, and promotion.

q: What is primary research?

options.t: Information a business collects itself for a specific purpose
options.why: Primary research is information a business collects itself for a specific purpose, through methods like surveys, interviews, observation, and experiments, so it fits the question exactly.

options.t: Information that was collected earlier by someone else in the past
options.why: Information collected earlier by someone else is secondary research, which is cheaper but may not match the current question.

options.t: Information that comes from the government only each year
options.why: Government information is secondary research, and primary research is not limited to government sources.

options.t: Information that is purchased from a data broker only once
options.why: Purchased data from a broker was collected by others, so it counts as secondary data, not primary research.

q: What is secondary research?

options.t: Information collected only through experiments
options.why: Experiments are a way of gathering primary data directly, not a definition of secondary research.

options.t: Information that is not useful to a business
options.why: Secondary research can be very useful, since it saves time and money, so saying it is not useful is wrong.

options.t: Information that was already collected by others
options.why: Secondary research uses information that others have already collected, such as industry reports, government statistics, and articles, which is quick and cheap but may be dated.

options.t: Information a business gathers itself for one purpose
options.why: Information a business gathers itself for one purpose is primary research, the opposite of secondary research.

q: Which is an example of primary research?

options.t: Reading an industry report from last year
options.why: An industry report from last year was collected by others, so using it is secondary research, not primary.

options.t: Surveying customers about a new flavor
options.why: Surveying customers about a new flavor gathers new data firsthand for the question at hand, which makes it primary research.

options.t: Reading a magazine article about trends
options.why: A magazine article was written by someone else earlier, so reading it is secondary research.

options.t: Using census data from a government website
options.why: Census data was collected by the government for general use, so using it is secondary research.

q: What is a survey?

options.t: A plan that decides where products will be placed in stores
options.why: A plan deciding where products go in stores is a merchandising or placement plan, not a tool for gathering opinions.

options.t: A tool that predicts next year's sales without using data
options.why: A survey does not predict sales without data; it collects real responses from people, and forecasts depend on data.

options.t: A set of questions used to collect information from people
options.why: A survey is a set of questions used to collect information from a sample of people about opinions, habits, or needs, by mail, phone, or online.

options.t: A report that lists a company's past expenses and costs
options.why: A list of past expenses is an accounting report, not a method for collecting answers from people.

q: What is a focus group?

options.t: A small group that discusses a product or idea with a moderator
options.why: A focus group is a small group led by a moderator in a discussion about a product or idea, giving deep opinions and reasons that numbers alone cannot show.

options.t: A team of employees who set product prices for the whole firm
options.why: A team of employees who set prices is an internal pricing committee, not a research group of consumers.

options.t: A large survey sent to thousands of anonymous customers each month
options.why: A large survey sent to thousands is a mass survey, unlike a focus group, which is small and discussion-based.

options.t: A group of retailers that stock a product from the maker
options.why: A group of retailers stocking the product is a set of channel partners, not a discussion group of consumers led by a moderator.

q: A company wants deep reasons why customers dislike its packaging. Which method fits best?

options.t: A report of total units sold last year
options.why: A report of total units sold shows how much was sold, not why customers dislike the packaging, so it gives no deep reasons.

options.t: A price comparison with two rivals
options.why: A price comparison with rivals shows relative cost and says nothing about customers' feelings toward the packaging design.

options.t: A count of the stores that stock it
options.why: Counting stores that stock the product measures availability, which does not explain why customers dislike the packaging.

options.t: A focus group with open discussion
options.why: A focus group lets customers discuss and explain their feelings about the packaging in their own words, giving deep reasons and ideas that sales numbers cannot show.

q: What is a sample in marketing research?

options.t: A list of every customer a company has on record now
options.why: A list of every customer is the whole population, not a sample, which is only a part chosen from it.

options.t: A free product given out at a store event for people to try
options.why: A free product given out for trial is a promotional sample, a different meaning of the word than in research.

options.t: A draft of a new advertisement for a local store's sale
options.why: A draft of an advertisement is a promotional piece, not a group of people chosen for a study.

options.t: A smaller group chosen to represent a larger population
options.why: A sample is a smaller group chosen from a larger population to represent it, so researchers can learn about everyone without surveying every person.

q: Why is a random sample useful?

options.t: It guarantees that everyone chosen will like the product
options.why: A random sample cannot guarantee that everyone likes the product; it simply selects people without regard to their opinions.

options.t: It lets researchers choose only people who will agree with them
options.why: Choosing only people who will agree would create bias, which is the opposite of what random selection achieves.

options.t: Every member of the group has an equal chance of being chosen
options.why: In a random sample every member of the group has an equal chance of being chosen, which reduces bias and makes results more likely to represent the whole population.

options.t: It removes the need to ask any questions of the people studied
options.why: Researchers still must ask questions of the people selected, because random sampling only decides who is asked and not what is learned.

q: What is a database in marketing?

options.t: A group of salespeople who call customers by telephone
options.why: A group of salespeople calling customers is a telemarketing team, not an organized store of information.

options.t: An organized collection of customer and market information
options.why: A marketing database is an organized collection of customer and market information that can be searched and analyzed to guide decisions about products and promotions.

options.t: A building where products are stored before shipping to stores
options.why: A building where products are stored is a warehouse, which holds goods rather than information.

options.t: A set of television commercials made for a single brand
options.why: A set of television commercials is a promotion campaign, not a store of customer information.

q: What is customer relationship management (CRM) software used for?

options.t: Storing customer details and tracking interactions
options.why: CRM software stores customer details and tracks interactions such as purchases, calls, and emails, so firms can serve customers better and build loyalty.

options.t: Designing the layout of a large retail store floor
options.why: Designing store layouts is a merchandising task done with planning tools, not what CRM software is built to do.

options.t: Scheduling delivery trucks for a distribution center
options.why: Scheduling delivery trucks uses logistics software, not CRM, which focuses on customer information and communication.

options.t: Printing price tags for the products in a store
options.why: Printing price tags is a pricing and merchandising task, unrelated to managing customer relationships.

q: A store notices that customers who buy a tent often buy sleeping bags too. How can it use this data?

options.t: Display the two items together and promote a bundle
options.why: Because customers who buy tents often buy sleeping bags, displaying them together and promoting a bundle makes use of the pattern and raises sales.

options.t: Stop recording what customers buy at checkout
options.why: Stopping tracking of purchases would throw away the data that revealed the pattern, so the store would learn nothing more.

options.t: Raise the price of tents so that fewer people buy them
options.why: Raising tent prices would reduce tent sales and ignores the opportunity to sell sleeping bags alongside tents.

options.t: Remove sleeping bags from the whole store entirely
options.why: Removing sleeping bags would lose sales of an item customers want with tents, so it contradicts what the data shows.

q: What is a demographic?

options.t: A type of advertisement shown on television and on radio
options.why: A type of advertisement is a promotion format, not a population characteristic, which is what a demographic is.

options.t: A characteristic of a population such as age, income or gender
options.why: A demographic is a measurable characteristic of a population, such as age, income, gender, or education, that helps firms describe and group customers.

options.t: A store where a product is sold to buyers in a mall or town
options.why: A store location is a place, not a characteristic of people in a population.

options.t: A price that a company charges for a product in a market
options.why: A price charged for a product is part of the marketing mix, not a population characteristic.

q: What is psychographic information?

options.t: Data about the prices of competing products in stores
options.why: Prices of competing products are competitor data, not information about customers' lifestyles and attitudes.

options.t: Data about customers' ages and home addresses only
options.why: Ages and addresses are demographic and geographic data, which differ from psychographics, covering lifestyles and attitudes.

options.t: Data about the weather where customers live and work
options.why: Weather data describes the environment, not customers' interests, values, or opinions.

options.t: Data about customers' lifestyles, interests and attitudes
options.why: Psychographic data describes customers' lifestyles, interests, values, and attitudes, which helps marketers understand why people buy and how to appeal to them.

q: Which is an example of psychographic data?

options.t: Customers who earn over $50,000 a year
options.why: Earning over $50,000 a year is an income figure, which is demographic data rather than psychographic.

options.t: Customers who live in the same zip code
options.why: Living in the same zip code is geographic data, not a measure of lifestyle or attitudes.

options.t: Customers who value eco-friendly products
options.why: Valuing eco-friendly products reflects customers' values and attitudes, which is psychographic data and helps shape messages for that segment.

options.t: Customers who are between 25 and 34 years old
options.why: Being between 25 and 34 years old is an age range, which is demographic data, not psychographic.

q: What is market segmentation?

options.t: Dividing a market into groups with similar needs
options.why: Market segmentation divides a broad market into smaller groups of buyers with similar needs or traits so a business can serve them better with a focused marketing mix.

options.t: Combining all competitors into one big group
options.why: Combining all competitors into one group is not segmentation, which splits customers, not rivals, into groups.

options.t: Selling only to the largest customer in the market
options.why: Selling only to the largest customer concentrates risk and is not segmentation, which divides the whole market into groups.

options.t: Setting one price for every group of customers
options.why: Setting one price for every group ignores differences between segments, whereas segmentation tailors marketing to each group.

q: A sneaker company creates different ads for teens and for adults over 50. What is this?

options.t: Channel conflict in retail
options.why: Channel conflict is a dispute among distribution partners and has nothing to do with making different ads for different age groups.

options.t: Targeting market segments
options.why: Creating different ads for teens and older adults is targeting market segments, since each age group is reached with messages that suit its interests.

options.t: Price fixing by two brands
options.why: Price fixing is an illegal agreement between competitors on prices, which is not what separate ads for age groups involves.

options.t: Mass marketing to everyone
options.why: Mass marketing uses one message for everyone, but this company tailors ads to different groups.

q: What is data mining?

options.t: Digging for minerals used to make electronic parts
options.why: Digging for minerals is mining in the literal sense and has no connection to analyzing data.

options.t: Typing information into a spreadsheet by hand
options.why: Typing information into a spreadsheet is manual data entry, not data mining, which analyzes data that already exists.

options.t: Deleting old records to free up storage space
options.why: Deleting old records is data cleanup or storage management, not the search for patterns that data mining performs.

options.t: Searching large data sets for useful patterns
options.why: Data mining uses software to search large data sets for useful patterns, such as which products sell together, so firms can predict behavior and target offers.

q: Why is data accuracy important in marketing?

options.t: Accurate data guarantees success always
options.why: Accurate data does not guarantee success, because other factors like competition and execution matter too.

options.t: Accurate data makes goods cost less
options.why: Accurate data does not lower costs of goods, since production costs depend on materials, labor, and efficiency.

options.t: Wrong data can lead to poor decisions
options.why: Wrong data can lead to poor decisions, such as misjudging demand or targeting the wrong customers, which wastes money, so firms check data quality.

options.t: Accurate data removes all research
options.why: Accurate data does not remove research, since firms still need to collect and analyze information.

q: A survey was answered mostly by customers who already love the brand. What is the main problem?

options.t: A price that is too high for customers
options.why: A price that is too high would affect sales, but it is not a flaw in how the survey sample was chosen.

options.t: Sample bias that may overstate satisfaction
options.why: Sample bias occurs when respondents do not represent all customers; answers from loyal fans may overstate satisfaction and hide the complaints of others.

options.t: A store location that is much too far away
options.why: A distant store location is a place issue and is not related to who answered the survey.

options.t: Too few questions on the printed survey form
options.why: Too few questions on a form would limit the detail, but the main flaw described is who answered, not how many questions.

q: What is a competitor analysis?

options.t: Testing a firm's website speed on mobile phones
options.why: Testing website speed is a technical check of a firm's own site and does not study rivals.

options.t: Counting the employees at all of the firm's offices
options.why: Counting employees at all offices is an internal human resources figure, not a study of competitors.

options.t: Reviewing a firm's own yearly tax filing forms
options.why: Reviewing a firm's own tax filing is a financial compliance task, not an analysis of competitors.

options.t: Studying rivals' products, prices and strategies
options.why: Competitor analysis studies rivals' products, prices, and strategies to find strengths, weaknesses, and gaps that the firm can use to compete better.

q: What is a SWOT analysis used for in marketing?

options.t: Reviewing strengths, weaknesses, opportunities and threats
options.why: SWOT reviews strengths, weaknesses, opportunities, and threats, which are internal and external factors a firm uses to plan its marketing strategy.

options.t: Ranking customers by how much they spend each year in a store
options.why: Ranking customers by spending is customer analysis, such as an ABC or value ranking, not what SWOT does.

options.t: Counting the number of stores that sell a product online
options.why: Counting stores that sell online is a market count, not a structured review of strengths and threats.

options.t: Setting daily prices for products in the store's shops
options.why: Setting daily prices is a pricing task, whereas SWOT is a planning tool for evaluating a firm's position.

q: What is a trend?

options.t: A fixed price that never changes over the years
options.why: A fixed price that never changes is the opposite of a trend, which describes change over time.

options.t: A product that is no longer sold in the shops
options.why: A product no longer sold is a discontinued item, not a general direction of change.

options.t: A general direction in which something is changing
options.why: A trend is a general direction in which something is changing, such as growing demand for healthy food, and helps firms spot opportunities early.

options.t: A single sale made on one particular day last month
options.why: A single sale on one day is an isolated event and does not show a direction over time.

q: What is point-of-sale (POS) data?

options.t: Information about a product's design
options.why: Product design information comes from development and engineering, not from sales recorded at the checkout.

options.t: Information about a competitor's plans
options.why: Competitor plans come from competitor analysis, whereas POS data comes from a firm's own sales records.

options.t: Information collected when a sale is made
options.why: POS data is collected when a sale is made, such as items, prices, times, and quantities, and it shows what sells and when in near real time.

options.t: Information about a company's staff members
options.why: Staff information comes from human resources records, not from checkout and sales systems.

q: POS data shows umbrella sales rising every time it rains. How should a store use this?

options.t: Stock more umbrellas when rain is forecast
options.why: Since umbrella sales rise with rain, stocking more umbrellas before forecast rain meets expected demand and avoids lost sales.

options.t: Reduce umbrella stock before rainy weeks
options.why: Reducing stock before rainy weeks is backwards, since the data shows demand rises when it rains.

options.t: Stop tracking weather and sales together
options.why: Stopping tracking of weather and sales together would waste the pattern the data revealed.

options.t: Raise the price of raincoats only in summer
options.why: Raising raincoat prices only in summer ignores the umbrella pattern and has no link to the rainy periods shown in the data.

q: What is customer privacy in marketing research?

options.t: Using data without telling customers how it is used
options.why: Using data without telling customers how it is used is a privacy violation and poor ethics, not the definition of privacy.

options.t: Protecting personal information collected from customers
options.why: Customer privacy means protecting personal information collected from customers, such as names and contact details, by storing it securely and using it only as agreed.

options.t: Sharing customer data with every business that asks for it
options.why: Sharing customer data with every business that asks violates privacy and may break laws and customer trust.

options.t: Posting customers' names on a public notice board
options.why: Posting customers' names on a notice board would expose personal information, which is the opposite of protecting privacy.

q: A company wants to survey minors online. What should it consider first?

options.t: Whether the survey can be finished within a minute by a child
options.why: Finishing within a minute is a convenience issue, but legal rules about minors take priority over survey speed.

options.t: Whether the questions are written in bold type or not
options.why: Bold type is a formatting detail and is far less important than legal rules about collecting data from children.

options.t: Which prize will attract the most answers very quickly
options.why: Choosing a prize to attract answers is secondary and offering rewards to children raises ethical concerns, so the law comes first.

options.t: Laws that protect children's privacy and parental consent
options.why: Laws such as COPPA protect children's privacy and require parental consent for collecting data from children under 13, so a company must plan for them first.

q: What is a marketing information system (MIS)?

options.t: A system that collects, organizes and reports marketing data
options.why: An MIS collects, organizes, analyzes, and reports marketing data so managers can make decisions, bringing information from many sources together in a usable form.

options.t: A system that prints advertisements and posters for events
options.why: Printing ads and posters is a production and promotion task, not a system for managing information.

options.t: A system that delivers products to customers each day
options.why: Delivering products daily is a distribution function and not an information system.

options.t: A system that pays employees each month on the last payday
options.why: Paying employees monthly is a payroll function, not a system for marketing information.

q: What is a questionnaire?

options.t: A tool for printing store coupons
options.why: Printing store coupons is a promotion task and is unrelated to collecting survey answers.

options.t: A report of final survey results
options.why: A report of final survey results is the output after analysis, whereas a questionnaire is the tool used to collect data.

options.t: A written set of survey questions
options.why: A questionnaire is a written set of survey questions given to respondents, so well-designed questions are clear, unbiased, and easy to answer.

options.t: A list of answers a firm wants
options.why: A list of answers a firm wants would be a biased wish list, whereas a questionnaire asks questions to learn real answers.

q: Which survey question is the least biased?

options.t: Don't you agree our service is the best?
options.why: This question pushes respondents to agree with the statement, so it is a leading question that biases the answers.

options.t: Surely you loved our excellent service?
options.why: This question assumes the respondent loved the service, which is leading and loaded, so it produces biased results.

options.t: Why is our service better than all others?
options.why: This question assumes the service is better than all others, so it suggests the answer instead of asking neutrally.

options.t: How satisfied are you with our service?
options.why: This question is neutral and lets respondents rate their satisfaction without being nudged toward an answer, which gives more honest and reliable data.

q: What does a customer satisfaction score measure?

options.t: How many ads were shown on television last year
options.why: Ads shown on television measure promotion exposure, not the level of customer happiness.

options.t: How happy customers are with a product or service
options.why: A customer satisfaction score measures how happy customers are with a product or service, usually from survey ratings, and helps firms improve and keep customers.

options.t: How many customers visited a store last week or online
options.why: The number of visitors is traffic, not a measure of how satisfied customers feel.

options.t: How much a product costs to produce each year
options.why: Production cost is an accounting figure and is unrelated to how customers feel about a product.

q: What is a marketing plan?

options.t: A list of the products a business already sells to its customers today
options.why: A list of current products describes a product mix, not a plan for reaching future marketing goals.

options.t: A schedule showing when employees will take their vacations
options.why: A vacation schedule is a human resources document, not a marketing plan.

options.t: A written guide for how a business will reach its marketing goals
options.why: A marketing plan is a written guide that describes goals, target markets, strategies, budget, and actions for reaching marketing objectives over a period of time.

options.t: A record of the money a business earned in the past year alone
options.why: A record of money earned last year is an income statement, which is a financial record of the past and not a plan.

q: What is a marketing objective?

options.t: A general wish to become popular without any measure
options.why: A vague wish to be popular has no measure or deadline, so it cannot guide planning or be checked later; real objectives are specific and measurable.

options.t: A specific result a marketing plan aims to achieve
options.why: Correct. A marketing objective is a specific, measurable result, such as a sales or awareness target, that the marketing plan is designed to achieve within a set time.

options.t: A description of the product's color and shape
options.why: Color and shape describe product design features, not a marketing objective, which states a result the plan should achieve such as sales growth or market share.

options.t: A list of the competitors that a company dislikes
options.why: A list of disliked competitors is not a goal; competitor analysis informs planning, but an objective states the result the company itself wants to achieve.

q: Which is the best example of a measurable marketing objective?

options.t: Make more customers happy by doing better marketing
options.why: Making customers happy is a worthy aim, but it has no number, deadline or method of measurement, so it cannot be judged as met or missed.

options.t: Improve the brand image through better advertising
options.why: Improving brand image is too vague to measure unless tied to a number and deadline, such as a survey score rising by a set amount.

options.t: Become the most popular brand someday very soon
options.why: Becoming most popular someday is a wish with no figure or timeline, so nobody can tell whether the company has actually reached it.

options.t: Increase online orders by 15 percent in six months
options.why: Correct. It names a metric (online orders), an amount (15 percent) and a deadline (six months), which makes it specific, measurable and time-bound like a good objective.

q: What is the marketing mix?

options.t: The combination of product, price, place and promotion
options.why: Correct. The marketing mix, the four Ps, is the set of controllable tools a business blends to satisfy its target market: product, price, place and promotion.

options.t: The combination of profits, losses, taxes and fees
options.why: Profits, losses, taxes and fees are financial results and costs found on income statements, not the controllable marketing tools that make up the marketing mix.

options.t: The combination of employees, offices, tools and funds
options.why: Employees, offices, tools and funds are business resources, not the four Ps; the marketing mix covers how the offering is created, priced, distributed and promoted.

options.t: The combination of ads, coupons, samples and signs
options.why: Ads, coupons, samples and signs are only parts of promotion, one of the four Ps, so this list covers just a single element of the mix.

q: What is positioning?

options.t: How a brand wants customers to see it compared with rivals
options.why: Correct. Positioning is the image a brand wants to hold in customers' minds relative to competing brands, such as the safest, cheapest or most luxurious choice.

options.t: How a product is shipped to a customer by truck or rail
options.why: Shipping by truck or rail is transportation, part of distribution or place, and has nothing to do with the image customers hold of a brand.

options.t: Where a product is stored in a warehouse before shipment
options.why: Warehouse storage is part of distribution and inventory handling; positioning concerns the mental image of a brand rather than where goods are physically kept.

options.t: Where a store is located on a map of the whole town area
options.why: A store's map location is a place or site selection decision; positioning is about perception of a brand in customers' minds, not geography.

q: A car maker emphasizes safety in all of its ads. What is it doing?

options.t: Lowering its price below rivals
options.why: Lowering price below rivals would be a pricing or cost-leadership move, but the ads here stress safety, not low cost, so price is not the focus.

options.t: Positioning its brand around safety
options.why: Correct. Repeating a safety message in all ads builds a distinct image in customers' minds, which is positioning the brand around the benefit of safety.

options.t: Opening more dealerships in town
options.why: Opening dealerships is a distribution decision about place, while the situation describes the message in the ads, which is a positioning choice.

options.t: Making its cars lighter to save fuel
options.why: Lighter cars for fuel savings would be a product design choice about efficiency; the ads stress safety, so this does not match the described emphasis.

q: What is a marketing budget?

options.t: The money a company owes to its suppliers each month
options.why: Money owed to suppliers is accounts payable, a liability on the balance sheet, and it is not funds reserved for marketing work.

options.t: The money a company earns from selling products each month
options.why: Money earned from selling products each month is sales revenue; a budget is a plan for spending, not income already received.

options.t: The money employees receive in their paychecks each week
options.why: Employee paychecks are payroll expenses, a labor cost across the company, and are not the funds set aside specifically for marketing activities.

options.t: The money set aside to carry out marketing activities
options.why: Correct. A marketing budget is the amount of money a company plans to spend on activities such as advertising, research and promotions during a period.

q: A store has $2,000 for marketing. Which choice best uses the budget?

options.t: Spend it on gifts for the owner's friends and family only
options.why: Gifts for the owner's friends and family do not target likely buyers or build sales, so they waste limited marketing money on non-customers.

options.t: Spend none of it and wait for customers to arrive
options.why: Spending nothing and waiting leaves sales to chance; customers cannot buy from a store they do not know about, so a budget exists to be used.

options.t: Pick the channels most likely to reach the target market
options.why: Correct. Limited funds work best when directed at channels, such as social media or local ads, that reach the target market most cost-effectively.

options.t: Spend all of it on one large billboard in another state
options.why: One billboard in another state would reach people far from the store who are unlikely to shop there, wasting most of a small $2,000 budget.

q: What is a competitive advantage?

options.t: Something that lets a business perform better than its rivals
options.why: Correct. A competitive advantage is a strength, such as lower cost, better quality or unique service, that lets a business outperform rivals and attract customers.

options.t: A list of the rivals that a business wishes to beat in sales
options.why: A list of rivals to beat is part of competitor analysis, not an advantage; an advantage is a real strength the business already has.

options.t: A rule that stops other businesses from opening nearby in a town
options.why: No rule stops other businesses from opening nearby in a free market; blocking competitors by rule is not what competitive advantage means.

options.t: A law that sets the price of every product in a shop or store
options.why: A law setting every product's price would be government price control, which is not a business advantage and does not describe competitive advantage.

q: A small bakery cannot match a chain's low prices but bakes fresh daily with local ingredients. What is its advantage?

options.t: Government protection from other bakeries
options.why: Bakeries get no government protection from competitors in a free market, and the bakery here competes through freshness and local ingredients, not legal shelter.

options.t: Differentiation based on quality and freshness
options.why: Correct. Competing on fresh, local, higher-quality products rather than price is differentiation, which lets a small firm succeed against a chain's lower prices.

options.t: A monopoly on all baked goods in the town
options.why: A monopoly means a single seller controls the whole market; the bakery faces a chain competitor, and having fresh bread does not give it exclusive control.

options.t: Cost leadership based on the lowest possible price
options.why: Cost leadership means having the lowest prices, but the passage says the bakery cannot match the chain's low prices, so this strategy does not apply.

q: What is a product life cycle?

options.t: The path a product takes from the factory to a store shelf
options.why: Moving a product from factory to shelf describes the distribution or supply chain, not the stages of demand a product moves through over time.

options.t: The time that a customer owns a product after buying it
options.why: How long a customer owns a product is its useful life or durability, which differs from the market stages a product passes through.

options.t: The steps used to design a new product in the factory
options.why: Design steps describe new-product development, which happens before launch, whereas the life cycle tracks sales stages after the product reaches the market.

options.t: The stages a product goes through from launch to decline
options.why: Correct. The product life cycle describes four stages, introduction, growth, maturity and decline, that guide pricing, promotion and strategy decisions over time.

q: Sales of a new gadget are rising quickly and competitors are entering. Which life-cycle stage is it in?

options.t: Maturity
options.why: Maturity is when sales growth slows and flattens, but here sales are still rising quickly, so the product has not yet reached this stage.

options.t: Decline
options.why: Decline brings falling sales as buyers move on, which is the opposite of the quickly rising sales described for this gadget.

options.t: Growth
options.why: Correct. Rapid sales growth and new competitors entering the market are the signs of the growth stage, when profits start to rise and rivals take notice.

options.t: Launch
options.why: Launch, or introduction, has slow sales, high costs and few competitors, while this gadget already has fast growth and rivals entering.

q: A product's sales have flattened and many rivals sell similar versions. Which stage is this?

options.t: Introduction
options.why: Introduction has low, slowly building sales and few rivals, but this product has flat sales and many similar competitors, so it is further along.

options.t: Maturity
options.why: Correct. Sales leveling off while many competitors offer similar versions is typical of maturity, when companies fight for share with price and differentiation.

options.t: Decline
options.why: Decline means sales are falling steadily, but this product's sales have only flattened, which describes a stable mature market instead.

options.t: Growth
