options.t: A file that stores customer passwords in a secure vault
options.why: Storing passwords is a security function. A dashboard presents marketing metrics rather than credentials.

q: A manager checks a dashboard each morning to see web visits, sales and email results. What is this for?

options.t: Replacing market research, as dashboards show buyers
options.why: Dashboards show performance data but not buyer motives. They cannot replace market research, which explains why people buy.

options.t: Monitoring performance and spotting problems early
options.why: Checking web visits, sales and email results each morning monitors performance. This lets the manager spot problems early and react before they grow.

options.t: Hiding results from the team and the other managers
options.why: A dashboard shares results with the team rather than hiding them. Its purpose is visibility.

options.t: Setting employees' pay for the whole year ahead of time
options.why: Pay is set by compensation plans. A dashboard monitors results and does not set salaries.

q: What is a conversion funnel?

options.t: A tool for pouring liquids into bottles in a factory line
options.why: A funnel for pouring liquids is a literal tool. In marketing it is a model of customer steps.

options.t: A rule about shipping times and delivery dates for a seller
options.why: Shipping times and delivery dates are logistics terms. A conversion funnel describes customer stages.

options.t: The steps a customer takes from first awareness to purchase
options.why: A conversion funnel maps the steps a customer takes from awareness to purchase. The numbers narrow at each step, which shows where marketing loses prospects.

options.t: A list of products on sale at the front of the shop today
options.why: A list of products on sale is a display or catalog. A conversion funnel tracks customer progress toward buying.

q: What is the difference between gross pay and net pay?

options.t: Net pay is the amount before any deductions are taken out
options.why: This reverses the definitions. Gross pay is the amount before deductions, so net pay is the lower amount left after deductions are taken out.

options.t: They are always equal in value for every worker
options.why: Gross and net pay are rarely equal, since taxes and other deductions are subtracted from gross pay. Only a worker with no deductions would see equal amounts.

options.t: Gross pay is net pay minus taxes and other deductions
options.why: This reverses the relationship. Net pay is gross pay minus deductions, not the other way around, because gross pay is the larger figure.

options.t: Net pay is gross pay minus taxes and other deductions
options.why: Net pay, or take-home pay, equals gross pay minus taxes and other deductions. Gross pay is the full amount earned before anything is withheld from the paycheck.

q: Jordan earns $15 an hour and works 20 hours in a week. What is Jordan's gross pay for the week?

options.why: $35 comes from adding the hours and the rate (15 + 20) instead of multiplying them, so it ignores that pay grows with every hour worked.
$3,000 is far too high; it looks like 15 x 200 or an extra zero added, but 20 hours at $15 cannot produce that much weekly pay.
Gross pay is hourly rate times hours worked: $15 x 20 = $300. Gross pay is the total earned before taxes and other deductions are taken out.
$150 is only half the correct amount; it would be 10 hours at $15. Jordan worked 20 hours, so the pay is 15 x 20 = $300.

q: Which form does a new employee complete so the employer withholds the correct amount of income tax?

options.why: A 1099 reports income paid to independent contractors, not employees, and it is not used to set income tax withholding for a new hire.
The W-4 lets a new employee state filing status and allowances or adjustments so the employer withholds the right federal income tax from each paycheck.
The W-2 is issued by the employer after the year ends to report wages and taxes withheld, so it does not set withholding for a new hire.
The I-9 verifies identity and legal authorization to work in the United States. It has nothing to do with how much income tax is withheld.

q: Which is a payroll deduction that the law requires?

options.t: Social Security tax
options.why: Social Security tax is part of FICA, which federal law requires employers to withhold from nearly every paycheck, with the employer paying a matching share.

options.t: A charity donation
options.why: A charity donation through payroll is voluntary; the employee chooses to give, so it is not a deduction the law requires.

options.t: Union dues paid out
options.why: Union dues are set by a union agreement and paid by members, not required by law for every worker, so this is not a legal deduction.

options.t: A voluntary pension
options.why: A voluntary pension or retirement contribution is the employee's choice by definition, so it is not a deduction the law forces on every worker.

q: Marcus earns a salary of $36,000 a year and is paid every two weeks, or 26 times a year. About how much is his gross pay per paycheck?

options.why: $3,000 is the 12 month figure ($36,000 / 12 = $3,000), but Marcus is paid 26 times a year, so each paycheck is much smaller.
Gross pay per paycheck is annual salary divided by pay periods: $36,000 / 26 is about $1,385, before taxes and other deductions are subtracted.
$692 is about half of the right amount; it comes from dividing by 52 weekly periods. The question says 26 biweekly paychecks, so use 26.
$1,500 comes from dividing by 24 pay periods, as for a twice monthly schedule. Marcus is paid every two weeks, which is 26 periods, so the result is $1,385.

q: Which is a likely result of building more job skills?

options.t: Higher earning potential
options.why: Stronger job skills make workers more valuable to employers, which usually leads to better pay, promotions and more job options over a career.

options.t: Automatic loan approval
options.why: Skills do not trigger automatic loan approval; lenders look at credit history, income and debts, not whether a person learned new skills.

options.t: Lower job opportunities
options.why: More skills tend to widen the set of jobs a person qualifies for, so job opportunities rise rather than fall.

options.t: Fewer chances to be promoted
options.why: Skills usually make promotion more likely, since employers advance workers who can handle bigger responsibilities. Fewer chances would be the opposite of the real effect.

q: Which type of income is money earned from assets, such as interest on a savings account, without doing regular work for it?

options.t: Tip earnings
options.why: Tips are earned by serving customers, so they are active income tied to work performed, not money produced by an asset.

options.t: Sales commissions
options.why: Sales commissions are a percentage of sales a worker makes, so they depend on regular selling work and are active earned income.

options.t: Hourly wages
options.why: Hourly wages are paid for time worked on the job, which makes them active income rather than money earned from an asset.

options.t: Passive income
options.why: Passive income comes from assets such as interest, dividends or rental property with little ongoing work, which is why it matches the description in the question.

q: What is a share of stock?

options.t: An insurance policy for losses
options.why: An insurance policy transfers risk of loss to an insurer in exchange for premiums. A share of stock is not a policy and does not cover losses.

options.t: A loan from an investor to a firm
options.why: A loan from an investor to a firm describes a bond, where the investor is a lender. A stock holder is an owner, not a lender.

options.t: A unit of ownership in a company
options.why: A share of stock is a unit of ownership, so shareholders own part of the company and may earn dividends or gains if its value rises.

options.t: A savings account at a local bank
options.why: A savings account at a bank holds deposits and pays interest, usually insured. Stock is ownership in a company with no guaranteed value.

q: What is a bond?

options.t: A loan to a company or government that pays interest
options.why: A bond is a loan from an investor to a company or government, which repays the principal on a set date and pays interest along the way.

options.t: A share of ownership in a company that is listed
options.why: Ownership of a company is a share of stock, not a bond. Bondholders are lenders and do not own part of the issuer.

options.t: A fee a bank charges on an account below its minimum
options.why: A fee for falling below a minimum balance is a bank account charge, not an investment. A bond is a loan that pays the holder interest.

options.t: A type of tax paid on investment income each year
options.why: Taxes on investment income are paid to the government and are not an investment product. A bond is a debt security that earns interest for the lender.

q: Spreading money across many different investments mainly helps reduce:

options.t: Inflation completely for every investor
options.why: Diversification cannot remove inflation, which affects the buying power of all money and every investor; it only spreads out the risk among holdings.

options.t: Every kind of risk that investors face
options.why: Diversifying cannot eliminate every risk, such as market wide downturns that hit most investments at once. It mainly reduces the risk tied to any one holding.

options.t: The risk from any single investment
options.why: By owning many different investments, a loss in any single one has a smaller effect on the total. This reduces firm specific risk, though not market risk.

options.t: All taxes owed on investment income
options.why: Diversification does not change taxes owed; investment income is taxed according to tax law no matter how many different holdings an investor has.

q: A $1,000 investment earns 5 percent simple interest per year. How much interest does it earn over 3 years?

options.why: $1,150 would add the principal to $150, or use compound growth with extra years. The question asks only for the interest earned, not the final balance.
$50 is one year of interest (5 percent of $1,000). The investment runs 3 years, so the interest must be multiplied by 3.
$157.63 is the compound interest result (1,000 x 1.05 cubed minus 1,000). The question states simple interest, which does not earn interest on interest.
Simple interest equals principal x rate x time: $1,000 x 0.05 x 3 = $150, the same $50 added each year with no compounding.

q: Which investment is generally considered the lowest risk?

options.t: Start-up company shares
options.why: Start up shares are highly risky because many new companies fail, so investors can lose their entire investment. They are not a low risk choice.

options.t: U.S. Treasury bonds
options.why: U.S. Treasury bonds are backed by the full faith and credit of the federal government, so default risk is very low, making them among the safest investments.

options.t: Speculative tokens
options.why: Speculative tokens are volatile digital assets whose prices swing widely with little underlying value, so they sit among the highest risk choices.

options.t: Penny stock shares
options.why: Penny stocks are low priced shares of small companies that trade thinly and swing sharply, so they carry far more risk than government bonds.

q: Which best describes a mutual fund?

options.t: One company's share held by one investor alone
options.why: A single company's share held by one investor is direct stock ownership. A mutual fund instead pools money from many investors into one portfolio.

options.t: A pool of many investors' money buying securities
options.why: A mutual fund pools money from many investors and a manager buys a mix of stocks, bonds or other securities, giving small investors built in diversification.

options.t: A bank loan used to buy a house or a new car
options.why: A bank loan used to buy a house or car is a mortgage or auto loan, which is borrowing, not an investment fund that holds securities.

options.t: A government grant given to small businesses
options.why: A government grant is money given to small businesses for a purpose and is not repaid. A mutual fund is an investment pooled from investors.

q: Why is starting to invest early helpful?

options.t: Investments never lose any value
options.why: Investments can and do lose value, especially in the short run, so claiming they never lose any value is false, and early investing does not change that.

options.t: No taxes are owed on early gains
options.why: Gains are generally taxable whenever they are realized, or as dividends and interest are earned, so starting early does not erase taxes owed.

options.t: Fees are always zero at the start
options.why: Funds, brokers and accounts can charge fees from the very start, so starting early does not make fees zero. Compounding is the real advantage.

options.t: Growth has more time to compound
options.why: Returns earn further returns, so more years allow the growth to build on itself. This is compounding, which makes early investing so powerful.

q: What does a credit score summarize?

options.t: How reliably a person has repaid debts
options.why: A credit score summarizes credit history, such as paying on time, how much is owed and credit age, to show how reliably a person repays debts.

options.t: A person's yearly income from work
options.why: Income is not part of the score calculation; lenders may check income separately. Scores reflect how debts were handled, not how much a person earns.

options.t: The interest rate on all of their loans
options.why: The interest rate on loans is set by lenders, partly based on the score, but the score does not simply report the rate on all of someone's loans.

options.t: The balance in a savings account at a bank
options.why: Savings account balances are not reported to credit bureaus, so they do not appear in a score. The score reflects borrowing and repayment behavior.

q: Which action most helps build a good credit history?

options.t: Using the full limit on every card
options.why: Using the full limit on every card gives a high utilization ratio, which hurts the score. Experts suggest staying well below about 30 percent of limits.

options.t: Missing a payment now and then
options.why: Missed payments are reported to credit bureaus and lower the score, since payment history is the biggest part of credit scoring.

options.t: Paying bills on time every month
options.why: Payment history is the largest factor in a credit score, so paying every bill on time builds a record of reliability that lenders value.

options.t: Applying for many new cards at once
options.why: Many new applications create hard inquiries and lower the average age of accounts, which can lower the score. Credit should be added gradually.

q: A credit card has an APR of 24 percent. What does APR tell you?

options.t: The yearly cost of borrowing as a percentage
options.why: APR, or annual percentage rate, shows the yearly cost of borrowing as a percentage, including interest and some fees. At 24 percent, $100 owed costs about $24 a year.

options.t: The card's credit limit set by the bank
options.why: The credit limit is the maximum balance the issuer allows, which is a separate term from APR, which only measures the cost of borrowing.

options.t: The yearly fee for owning the card with the bank
options.why: An annual fee is a separate charge, while APR measures the cost of borrowing as a yearly percentage. A card can have a high APR and no annual fee.

options.t: The minimum monthly payment you must make
options.why: The minimum payment is the smallest amount due each month, set by the issuer, and is separate from APR, which is the yearly borrowing cost.

q: Sam owes $500 on a card with 2 percent monthly interest and makes no payment. About how much interest is added in one month?

options.why: $100 would be 20 percent of $500, ten times the real rate. At 2 percent monthly the charge is much smaller, since 0.02 x 500 is $10.
Monthly interest is balance times monthly rate: $500 x 0.02 = $10. With no payment made, that interest is added to the balance owed.
$1 is only 0.2 percent of $500, so it is a tenth of the correct amount. At 2 percent, 500 x 0.02 equals $10.
$50 would be a 10 percent monthly rate, five times the stated 2 percent. The correct figure is 500 x 0.02 = $10.

q: Which habit helps a cardholder avoid paying interest?

options.t: Paying only the minimum amount due each month
options.why: Paying only the minimum leaves most of the balance, so interest keeps accumulating on it. This is the slowest and most expensive way to repay.

options.t: Skipping a payment every now and then to save
options.why: Skipping payments brings late fees, penalty rates and credit score damage, and interest keeps accruing, so it never saves money.

options.t: Taking cash advances to cover other bills
options.why: Cash advances usually start charging interest right away with no grace period and carry extra fees, so they add interest instead of avoiding it.

options.t: Paying the full statement balance each month
options.why: Paying the full statement balance by the due date usually keeps the grace period, so purchases are never charged interest on the card.

q: Which type of lender typically charges the highest interest rates?

options.t: A credit union
options.why: Credit unions are member owned nonprofits that typically offer lower interest rates than most other lenders, so they are not the costliest option.

options.t: Student loan agency
options.why: Student loans from agencies often have capped or federally set rates, which are usually lower than short term consumer loans like payday loans.

options.t: A payday lender
options.why: Payday lenders make short term, small loans with fees that equal annual rates of 300 percent or more, among the costliest forms of credit.

options.t: A mortgage bank
options.why: A mortgage is secured by the home and usually has a lower rate than unsecured loans, so mortgage banks are not the highest priced lenders.

q: Which best describes a secured loan?

options.t: A loan guaranteed only by the borrower's verbal promise to repay it later
options.why: A loan backed only by a verbal promise has no collateral and is unsecured by nature. A secured loan requires pledging an asset.

options.t: A loan backed by collateral the lender can claim if the borrower does not repay
options.why: A secured loan is backed by collateral, such as a car or house, that the lender can take (repossess) if the borrower defaults, lowering the lender's risk.

options.t: A loan with no interest that must be repaid in full within a single day
options.why: A one day loan with no interest is not a standard loan product, and a secured loan is defined by collateral, not by interest or repayment time.

options.t: A loan that charges no interest and requires no promise of repayment at all
options.why: A loan with no interest and no repayment promise would effectively be a gift. A secured loan is a real debt with collateral behind it.

q: What is insurance?

options.t: A savings plan that guarantees a return on every dollar saved
options.why: Insurance does not guarantee a return on savings; it pays out only when a covered loss happens. A savings plan is a different financial product.

options.t: A type of loan that must be repaid with interest over a long time
options.why: A loan gives money now to be repaid with interest. Insurance instead pays claims for covered losses and is paid for with premiums.

options.t: A way to transfer financial risk to a company in return for premiums
options.why: Insurance transfers the chance of a large loss to an insurer, which pools many customers' premiums and pays covered claims, such as accidents or medical bills.

options.t: A tax refund paid by the government each spring to every taxpayer
options.why: A tax refund is money the government returns after a tax filing and not every taxpayer gets one. It has no link to insurance coverage.

q: What is an insurance deductible?

options.t: The amount you pay before the insurance begins to pay
options.why: A deductible is the amount the policyholder pays out of pocket on a covered claim before the insurer starts paying its share of costs.

options.t: The maximum amount the insurer will ever pay out
options.why: The maximum an insurer will pay is the policy limit, a different term. A deductible is what you pay first, not the cap on payout.

options.t: A refund of premiums for coverage that went unused
options.why: Premiums are not refunded just because a policy went unused, and a deductible is an out of pocket cost on a claim, not a refund.

options.t: The monthly payment that is made to the insurer
options.why: The monthly payment to the insurer is the premium. The deductible is paid only when a claim is made, before coverage begins.

q: Which kind of insurance covers a person's medical expenses?

options.t: Auto insurance
options.why: Auto insurance covers vehicle damage and liability from car accidents. It may include limited medical payments but is not meant for general medical expenses.

options.t: Life insurance
options.why: Life insurance pays a death benefit to beneficiaries when the insured person dies. It does not cover the insured person's medical bills.

options.t: Renter's insurance
options.why: Renter's insurance covers a tenant's belongings and liability for the rented home, not medical expenses for illness or injury.

options.t: Health insurance
options.why: Health insurance pays all or part of medical costs such as doctor visits, hospital stays and prescriptions, in exchange for premiums plus deductibles and copays.

q: Casey chooses a higher deductible on a car insurance policy. What is the most likely effect?

options.t: A higher premium and a lower cost in a claim later on
options.why: A higher deductible usually lowers the premium, since the insured takes on more risk. A higher premium paired with lower claim costs describes a low deductible instead.

options.t: Coverage for all damage with no limits of any kind
options.why: A deductible does not extend coverage to everything; policies still have limits and exclusions, and a higher deductible only shifts more cost to the driver.

options.t: A lower premium but more out-of-pocket cost in a claim
options.why: With a higher deductible Casey pays more on a claim but the insurer's risk drops, so the premium is lower. It suits people with savings to cover the gap.

options.t: No change in the premium or the cost of a claim later
options.why: Changing the deductible changes both sides: the premium goes down and the cost paid on a claim goes up. They do not stay the same.

q: Which action reduces the risk of identity theft?

options.t: Using strong, unique passwords
options.why: Strong, unique passwords make accounts hard to guess or crack, and one breach will not expose other accounts. This lowers the risk of identity theft.

options.t: Reusing one password everywhere
options.why: Reusing one password lets a thief who gets it from one breach log in to every other account, which raises the risk of identity theft.

options.t: Posting your birth date publicly
options.why: A public birth date gives thieves a key detail to answer security questions or open accounts in your name, increasing identity theft risk.

options.t: Sharing your PIN with friends
options.why: A PIN should be kept private; sharing it lets others access accounts and cards, which makes fraud and identity theft more likely.

q: What does renter's insurance mainly protect?

options.t: The tenant's credit score history
options.why: Credit history is tracked by credit bureaus, and renter's insurance does not protect or change a tenant's score. It covers physical belongings and liability.

options.t: A renter's belongings and liability
options.why: Renter's insurance covers the tenant's personal property from losses like theft or fire and gives liability coverage if someone is hurt in the unit.

options.t: The building's structure and walls
options.why: The building structure is the landlord's responsibility and is covered by the landlord's own property policy, not by a tenant's renter's insurance.

options.t: The landlord's income from rent
options.why: Renter's insurance does not replace rent income for a landlord. A landlord would need a separate landlord policy to cover lost rental income.

q: Why should people keep an emergency fund?

options.t: To invest in risky stocks for higher returns
options.why: Risky stocks can lose value quickly, so they are a poor place for money needed in an emergency. An emergency fund should be safe and available.

options.t: To pay for vacations that have been planned
options.why: Vacations are planned wants, not unexpected expenses. Planned spending should come from a separate savings goal, not the emergency fund.

options.t: To avoid ever needing to buy any insurance
options.why: An emergency fund does not replace insurance; many large losses, such as a major accident or illness, can exceed any savings, so coverage is still needed.

options.t: To cover unexpected expenses without borrowing
options.why: An emergency fund covers surprises like car repairs or job loss, so you avoid borrowing on credit cards or loans and paying interest.

q: What is the main purpose of a savings account?

options.t: To buy stocks and bonds each week
options.why: Buying stocks and bonds is investing, which is done through brokerage accounts. A savings account is mainly for safe storage, not weekly trading.

options.t: To borrow money from a bank at once
options.why: Borrowing from a bank is a loan, which creates debt. A savings account holds your own money and pays you interest.

options.t: To keep money safe and earn interest
options.why: A savings account keeps money safe, usually insured, and pays interest, so the balance grows while staying accessible for future needs.

options.t: To pay bills automatically each month
options.why: Automatic bill payments are typically handled from a checking account. The main purpose of savings is to store money and earn interest.

q: Which describes compound interest?

options.t: Interest earned only on the original deposit
options.why: Interest only on the original deposit is simple interest. Compound interest also earns interest on interest already added, so it grows faster.

options.t: A fee for opening an account at a local bank
options.why: An account opening fee is a bank charge, not a type of interest. Compound interest is earnings that are added to the balance.

options.t: Interest charged only once at the start
options.why: Interest charged once at the start is not compounding. Compounding repeats on a schedule, with each period's interest earning more interest.

options.t: Interest on the deposit and earlier interest
options.why: Compound interest is calculated on the deposit plus the interest already earned, so the balance grows faster the longer it stays in the account.

q: A saver deposits $200 at 3 percent simple interest for one year. How much interest is earned?

options.why: $206 is the final balance (200 + 6), not the interest. The question asks only how much interest is earned, which is $6.
Simple interest equals principal x rate x time: $200 x 0.03 x 1 = $6. After one year the total would be $206.
$60 is ten times too large; it comes from misplacing a decimal. Three percent of $200 is 200 x 0.03 = $6.
$0.60 is ten times too small. Converting 3 percent to 0.03 and multiplying by $200 gives $6, not 60 cents.

q: Which is the best first step to build an emergency fund?

options.t: Set a target and transfer a fixed amount automatically each payday
options.why: Setting a target and automating a fixed transfer each payday builds the fund steadily and removes the temptation to skip. It is a proven way to start saving.

options.t: Wait until money is left at month end before saving anything
options.why: Waiting for leftover money usually means nothing is saved, since spending expands to fill income. Saving should come first, not last.

options.t: Put all of your savings money into one single risky stock today
options.why: Putting all savings in one risky stock could wipe out the fund. An emergency fund needs safety and easy access, not risk.

options.t: Spend first and then save whatever is left over at the end
options.why: Spending first and saving what is left is the opposite of paying yourself first. There often is little left, so the fund never grows.

q: Which of these is protected by FDIC insurance, within limits?

options.t: A cryptocurrency wallet on a phone
options.why: A crypto wallet is not a bank deposit, so FDIC insurance does not cover it. Crypto prices swing widely and losses are not insured.

options.t: A savings account at an insured bank
options.why: FDIC insurance protects deposits such as savings and checking accounts at insured banks, up to $250,000 per depositor, per bank, per ownership category.

options.t: A personal loan made to a friend
options.why: A personal loan to a friend is an informal debt with no insurance. If the friend does not repay, no agency covers the loss.

options.t: Shares held in a stock brokerage account
options.why: Brokerage accounts may have SIPC protection against broker failure, but not FDIC insurance, and it does not cover investment losses from market declines.

q: What does the Rule of 72 estimate?

options.t: How much income tax a person owes in a single year of work
options.why: Income tax owed depends on tax brackets, deductions and credits, not on the Rule of 72, which only estimates how fast money doubles.

options.t: The best age at which a person should retire from work
options.why: The Rule of 72 has no connection to retirement age. It is a quick math shortcut for growth of money at a given interest rate.

options.t: How long it takes money to double at a given interest rate
options.why: Dividing 72 by the annual interest rate estimates the years needed to double money. At 6 percent, money doubles in about 12 years.

options.t: The monthly payment that is due on a loan or a bill
options.why: Loan payments come from payment formulas involving the amount, rate and term. The Rule of 72 estimates doubling time, not a monthly payment.

q: Which is a specific and measurable savings goal?

options.t: Save more money at some point in the future or so
options.why: Saving more at some point in the future is vague, with no amount or date, so progress cannot be measured. A good goal needs both.

options.t: Spend a lot less on the things that you buy each month
options.why: Spending a lot less is not measurable because it gives no number or timeframe to check, so a person cannot tell whether the goal was met.

options.t: Become wealthy by the time that you are older, with no plan
options.why: Becoming wealthy later has no amount, no deadline and no plan, which makes it a wish rather than a specific, measurable goal.

options.t: Save $600 in six months by setting aside $100 a month
options.why: Saving $600 in six months by setting aside $100 a month has an amount, a deadline and a plan ($100 x 6 = $600), so it is specific and measurable.

q: What is a budget?

options.t: A plan for how to use income
options.why: A budget is a plan for how to use income by assigning money to expenses, savings and goals, so spending can be tracked against the plan.

options.t: A bank account for savings
options.why: A savings account is a place to hold money at a bank. A budget is a plan for spending and saving, not an account.

options.t: A type of tax on your income
options.why: Income tax is a government charge on earnings. A budget is a personal plan and is not a tax at all.

options.t: A list of past debts only
options.why: Looking only at past debts would ignore income and future spending. A budget is a forward looking plan covering income, expenses and savings.

q: Which of these is a fixed expense?

options.t: Movie tickets
options.why: Movie tickets are a discretionary, variable expense that changes depending on how often you go, so they are not a fixed expense.

options.t: Gift money
options.why: Gift money varies by occasion and is optional, so it changes from month to month and is not a fixed expense.

options.t: Monthly rent
options.why: Monthly rent is the same amount each month under a lease, which makes it a fixed expense that is predictable when budgeting.

options.t: Restaurant meals
options.why: Restaurant meals change with how often you eat out and what you order, which makes them a variable, discretionary expense.

q: Ana earns $2,000 a month and follows the 50/30/20 rule. How much is set aside for needs?

options.why: $600 is 30 percent of $2,000, the share the 50/30/20 rule gives to wants, not to needs.
The 50/30/20 rule sets 50 percent of income for needs: $2,000 x 0.50 = $1,000. The rest is 30 percent for wants and 20 percent for savings.
$400 is 20 percent of $2,000, the savings and debt portion of the rule. Needs get the larger 50 percent share, or $1,000.
$1,400 is 70 percent, which would combine needs and wants. The rule gives needs only 50 percent, so $2,000 x 0.50 = $1,000.

q: Which is the best way to compare the price of two cereal boxes of different sizes?

options.t: Compare the unit price per ounce
options.why: Unit price per ounce puts different sized boxes on equal footing, so you can see which gives more cereal for the money.

options.t: Choose the one with a popular mascot
options.why: A popular mascot is marketing, not value. It tells you nothing about the cost per ounce and can push buyers toward worse deals.

options.t: Compare the sizes of the boxes
options.why: A bigger box is not always cheaper per ounce, so comparing sizes alone does not show which one gives the better value.

options.t: Compare the brand names only
options.why: Brand names alone do not show cost. Two brands can differ widely in price per ounce, so name comparison ignores the real price.

q: What is comparison shopping?

options.t: Buying the first item that you happen to see
options.why: Buying the first item you see skips any comparison, so you may overpay or miss better options. That is the opposite of comparison shopping.

options.t: Buying an item on impulse with no planning
options.why: Impulse buying means purchasing without a plan, which is the opposite of comparing options to find the best price or quality.

options.t: Paying only in cash instead of using a card
options.why: How you pay, cash or card, is a payment method and has nothing to do with comparing sellers on price and features.

options.t: Checking prices and features at several sellers
options.why: Comparison shopping means checking prices, features and quality across several sellers so you can pick the best value for your money.

q: Which habit best helps control impulse buying?

options.t: Using store credit freely whenever you are shopping
options.why: Store credit encourages spur of the moment purchases without paying right away, so it increases impulse buying rather than controlling it.

options.t: Waiting 24 hours before a non-essential purchase
options.why: A 24 hour wait gives time for the urge to fade and lets you decide whether the item is really needed, which cuts down impulse purchases.

options.t: Browsing online sale sites every single day
options.why: Browsing sale sites daily exposes you to constant temptation and promotions, which increases impulse buying instead of controlling it.

options.t: Shopping for non-essentials while you are hungry
options.why: Shopping while hungry or emotional weakens self control, and studies show people buy more. It encourages impulse buying, not limits it.

q: Leo has $50 left until payday. He needs lunch money and wants new headphones. How should he prioritize?

options.t: Cover needs like lunch first, then use anything left on wants
options.why: Needs come before wants in a budget. Lunch is a need, so Leo covers it first and spends only what is left on the headphones.

options.t: Buy the headphones first and worry about lunch later on
options.why: Buying wants first while skipping needs puts a basic need at risk. A want should never come before food.

options.t: Split the money evenly between lunch and the headphones
options.why: Splitting evenly treats a need and a want as equal, but needs have priority, and half of $50 on headphones may leave lunch underfunded.

options.t: Put everything on a credit card until the next payday comes
options.why: Putting everything on credit adds debt and interest for a want, with no plan to repay. Needs come first and debt should be avoided.

q: What is gross income?

options.t: The amount saved each month for emergencies only
options.why: Money saved for emergencies is savings, not income. Gross income is the total earned before anything is subtracted.

options.t: The amount left after paying taxes and deductions
options.why: The amount left after taxes and deductions is net income, or take home pay. Gross income is the total before those are removed.

options.t: The amount spent on needs each month by a family
options.why: Spending on needs is an expense category and says nothing about total income earned. Gross income is the full amount before deductions.

options.t: The total amount earned before taxes and deductions
options.why: Gross income is the total earned from wages and other sources before taxes and deductions, so it is always larger than net income.

q: What is net income (take-home pay)?

options.t: The amount an employer pays in payroll taxes each year
options.why: Payroll taxes paid by the employer are a business cost and are not what the employee takes home. Net income is the employee's pay after deductions.

options.t: The total amount earned before any deductions are taken out
options.why: The total before deductions is gross income. Net income is lower because taxes and deductions have already been subtracted.

options.t: The amount left after taxes and deductions are taken out
options.why: Net income, or take home pay, equals gross pay minus taxes and deductions such as insurance and retirement. It is what lands in your bank account.

options.t: The amount of a yearly bonus paid out to the staff
options.why: A yearly bonus is extra pay on top of wages. It is a type of earnings, not a measure of pay after deductions.

q: Maya earns $20 an hour and works 30 hours in a week. What is her gross pay for the week?

options.why: $150 is wrong; it comes from adding 20 + 30 times 3 or a similar error. Pay is rate times hours: $20 x 30 = $600.
$6,000 is ten times too large and likely a misplaced zero. Maya earns $20 x 30 hours = $600.
Gross pay equals hourly rate times hours worked: $20 x 30 = $600. This is before taxes and deductions are taken out.
$50 is the sum of the rate and the hours (20 + 30). Pay must be multiplied: $20 x 30 = $600.

q: A worker earns $16 an hour. Overtime is paid at 1.5 times the hourly rate for hours over 40. What is the overtime rate?

options.t: $24 per hour
options.why: Overtime at 1.5 times the regular rate means $16 x 1.5 = $24 per hour. It applies to hours over 40 in a week under U.S. wage law.

options.t: $16 per hour
options.why: $16 is the regular rate, which has no overtime premium added. Overtime is time and a half, which is 1.5 x $16 = $24.

options.t: $17.50 per hour
options.why: $17.50 does not match the 1.5 multiplier. It appears to add a flat amount, while 1.5 x $16 is exactly $24.

options.t: $32 per hour
options.why: $32 is double time (2 x $16), not time and a half. The problem says 1.5 times, so the rate is $24 per hour.

q: What is a W-4 form used for?

options.t: Reporting total yearly wages to the IRS for the employer
options.why: Reporting yearly wages to the IRS is done by the W-2 the employer files and gives the worker. The W-4 is completed by the employee.

options.t: Requesting a tax refund from the IRS in the spring
options.why: A refund is requested by filing a tax return (Form 1040). The W-4 only affects how much is withheld from each paycheck.

options.t: Applying for a credit card at a bank or a store
options.why: A W-4 is an employment tax form, not a credit application. Credit cards use their own applications that check credit history.

options.t: Telling an employer how much income tax to withhold
options.why: The W-4 tells an employer the employee's filing status and adjustments so the correct amount of federal income tax is withheld from pay.

q: What is a W-2 form?

options.t: A form that reports income for independent contractors
options.why: Income for independent contractors is reported on a 1099, not a W-2. The W-2 is for employees.

options.t: A form showing yearly wages and taxes withheld by an employer
options.why: The W-2 is sent by employers each January and reports total wages for the year plus taxes withheld, which workers use to file their tax returns.

options.t: A form for applying for a job at a firm or a store in town
options.why: Applying for a job uses a job application, not a W-2. The W-2 is a tax document issued after a person has worked for the employer.

options.t: A form that sets the federal tax withheld from each paycheck
options.why: Withholding is set by the employee's W-4. The W-2 is the year end report that shows the wages and taxes that were actually withheld.

q: Which deduction is withheld from most paychecks to fund Social Security and Medicare?

options.t: Property tax
options.why: Property tax is paid by owners of real estate to local governments and is not taken from paychecks to fund Social Security or Medicare.

options.t: Sales tax
options.why: Sales tax is added at the register when buying goods. It is not withheld from wages and does not fund Social Security.

options.t: Excise tax
options.why: Excise taxes apply to specific goods like gasoline or tobacco. They are not withheld from paychecks for Social Security and Medicare.

options.t: FICA tax
options.why: FICA stands for the Federal Insurance Contributions Act. It is withheld from paychecks at 7.65 percent (6.2 Social Security plus 1.45 Medicare), matched by the employer.

q: In earning income, what is a tip?

options.t: A fixed monthly salary paid by an employer to staff
options.why: A fixed monthly pay is a salary, not a tip. A tip is extra money from a customer, not a set payment from an employer.

options.t: A short-term loan from the employer to the worker
options.why: A short term loan from an employer is an advance. A tip is a gift of money from a customer and is never repaid.

options.t: Money a customer gives for service on top of the price
options.why: A tip is money a customer gives for good service on top of the bill. It is common in restaurants and counts as taxable income.

options.t: A payment made by the government to service workers
options.why: Government payments to workers are wages or benefits. A tip comes from customers, not from the government, and is taxable income.

q: What is the main difference between an employee and an independent contractor?

options.t: Employees pay no income taxes on their wages
options.why: Employees do pay income taxes on wages, usually through withholding. Saying they pay none is false, so it cannot be the difference.

options.t: Employers withhold tax; contractors pay their own
options.why: Employers withhold income tax and payroll taxes for employees. Independent contractors get a 1099 and handle their own taxes, including self employment tax.

options.t: Contractors always earn more than employees do
options.why: Contractors do not always earn more than employees; earnings vary by job, and contractors also pay their own taxes and often get no benefits.

options.t: Employees always get to choose their own working hours
options.why: Employees often have schedules set by employers, while contractors usually control their own hours. So employees do not always choose their hours.

q: Which is an example of passive income?

options.t: Rent received from a property you own
options.why: Rent from property you own is passive income, because it arrives from an asset with little ongoing work compared with a job.

options.t: Wages earned from a full-time job
options.why: Wages from a full time job are earned income because you trade your time and labor for pay. They are not passive.

options.t: Tips earned from serving tables daily
options.why: Tips come from serving customers, which is active work. This makes them earned income, not passive income.

options.t: Pay earned for babysitting on weekends
options.why: Babysitting pay is earned by working, so it is active income. Passive income comes from assets like rentals or investments.

q: Which is an example of earned income?

options.t: Interest on a savings account
options.why: Interest on savings comes from money in an account, not from work, so it is investment income, not earned income.

options.t: Wages from a part-time job
options.why: Earned income is money received for work, such as wages, salaries, tips and self employment pay. A part time job pays wages.

options.t: Rent from a rental property
options.why: Rent from a rental property is passive income from an asset. Earned income is paid for work done.

options.t: Dividends from stock shares
options.why: Dividends are payments from owning stock shares, which makes them investment income rather than earned income from work.

q: What is a bonus?

options.t: A loan advanced by the employer against future pay, repaid soon
options.why: A loan advanced against future pay is a pay advance, which must be repaid. A bonus is extra pay that does not need repayment.

options.t: A tax that is taken out of every paycheck by the state or city
options.why: A tax taken from every paycheck is a payroll or income tax deduction. A bonus adds to pay and is not a tax.

options.t: A fixed amount deducted from pay for health insurance cover
options.why: A fixed deduction for health insurance is a premium withheld from pay. A bonus increases a paycheck rather than reducing it.

options.t: Extra pay on top of regular wages for good performance or results
options.why: A bonus is extra pay above regular wages, given for strong performance, meeting goals or company results. It is still taxable income.

q: What is a commission?

options.t: Pay based on a percentage of sales a worker makes
options.why: A commission is pay based on a percentage of the sales a worker makes, which rewards selling more and is common in sales jobs.

options.t: Pay based on the number of hours worked each week
options.why: Pay based on the number of hours worked is an hourly wage. A commission depends on sales results, not time.

options.t: Pay that is given as a gift from the boss at holidays
options.why: A holiday gift from the boss is a gift or bonus, not a commission, which is earned from sales.

options.t: Pay based on a fixed amount for the whole year
options.why: A fixed yearly amount is a salary. A commission varies with sales, so it can be higher or lower from month to month.

q: A salesperson earns a 4% commission on $25,000 of sales. What is the commission?

options.why: $4,000 is 16 percent of $25,000. The rate here is 4 percent, so the commission is much less than that.
$10,000 is 40 percent of the sales. The commission rate is 4 percent, which gives $1,000.
Commission is rate times sales: 0.04 x $25,000 = $1,000. This pay is earned in addition to or instead of a base salary.
$100 is only 0.4 percent of $25,000, a tenth of the right amount. Four percent of $25,000 is $1,000.

q: Which employee benefit usually has the greatest financial value?

options.t: A free parking sign nearby
options.why: A parking sign gives no real financial value; it only marks a spot and does not pay for anything the worker would otherwise buy.

options.t: A company logo mug as a gift
options.why: A logo mug is a small gift worth only a few dollars, far below the value of benefits that replace thousands in costs.

options.t: A holiday card from the boss
options.why: A holiday card is a kind gesture with almost no financial worth, so it is not a major benefit.

options.t: Employer-paid health insurance
options.why: Employer paid health insurance can be worth thousands of dollars per year in premiums, so it is among the most valuable benefits a job can offer.

q: What does an employer 401(k) match mean?

options.t: The employer adds money based on the employee's own contributions
options.why: A 401(k) match means the employer adds money, often a percentage of what the employee contributes. It is free retirement savings and worth taking in full.

options.t: The employer charges a fee for joining the plan each year
options.why: A match is a benefit, not a fee. Charges for joining a plan are plan fees, which are separate from an employer's contribution.

options.t: The employer takes money from the employee's account each pay period
options.why: Employee contributions come out of pay by the employee's choice. A match adds employer money; it never takes money away from the account.

options.t: The employer lends the employee money for retirement plans
options.why: A match is a contribution, not a loan, and the employer does not lend retirement money. The employee does not have to repay it.

q: What is a minimum wage?

options.t: The highest hourly pay an employer may give any worker in the nation
options.why: The minimum wage is the lowest pay allowed, not the highest. Employers may pay above the minimum wage, so it is not a cap.

options.t: The pay that applies to workers who receive tips only in a state
options.why: Tipped workers are covered by minimum wage rules too, with tip credit rules, so a minimum wage is not limited to tipped workers.

options.t: The lowest hourly pay an employer may legally pay a covered worker
options.why: A minimum wage is the lowest hourly pay an employer may legally pay most covered workers. The federal rate is $7.25 and states can set higher rates.

options.t: The pay that applies to managers and executives only in a firm
options.why: Minimum wage laws protect hourly workers at the low end of pay. They are not limited to managers or executives, who usually earn salaries.

q: Why does education generally increase earning potential?

options.t: Education guarantees a job without any further effort
options.why: Education does not guarantee a job. Workers still need to find employment and perform well, so a promise of a guaranteed job is false.

options.t: Educated workers have skills employers pay more for
options.why: Education builds knowledge and skills that employers value, so educated workers tend to qualify for higher paying roles and earn more over time.

options.t: Education reduces the need to work for a living
options.why: Education does not remove the need to work. People still need income, and education only improves how much they can earn.

options.t: Education lowers the amount of taxes a person owes
options.why: Education does not reduce taxes. Higher earners may in fact pay more tax, so this is not why education raises earning potential.

q: What is a side hustle?

options.t: Extra work for income beyond a main job
options.why: A side hustle is extra work done outside a main job to earn additional income, such as freelancing, tutoring or reselling goods.

options.t: A tax form that is used only for extra jobs
options.why: A tax form is a document like a 1099 or W-4. A side hustle is the work itself, not a form, though its income may need reporting.

options.t: A promotion at work to a higher position
options.why: A promotion is a move to a higher position within the same job. A side hustle is separate work done for extra income.

options.t: A loan from a friend to cover expenses
options.why: A loan from a friend is borrowed money that must be repaid, not earned income. A side hustle brings in new income by working.

q: A teen earns $400 from mowing lawns on their own. Who is responsible for reporting that income?

options.t: No one, because lawn mowing is exempt under tax rules
options.why: Lawn mowing income is not exempt. Self employment earnings are generally taxable, and income of $400 or more triggers self employment tax filing.

options.t: The city government where the teen lives and works
options.why: A city government does not report a person's private earnings. The person who earned the money is responsible for reporting it.

options.t: The teen, who may need to report self-employment income
options.why: The teen earned the money as self employed, so the teen is responsible for tracking and reporting it. Net earnings of $400 or more usually require filing.

options.t: The customers who paid for the mowing and the lawn work
options.why: Customers who pay for services generally do not report on behalf of a worker for small jobs. The worker must report their own income.

q: What is a pay stub?

options.t: A bill that is sent to the employee each month by the firm
options.why: A bill is a request for payment. A pay stub is given to an employee to show how a paycheck was calculated.

options.t: A record of gross pay, deductions and net pay for a pay period
options.why: A pay stub shows gross pay, each deduction (taxes, insurance, retirement) and net pay for a pay period, helping workers check their paycheck is correct.

options.t: A tax return filed at the end of the year by each worker
options.why: A tax return is filed once a year with the government. A pay stub comes with each paycheck and shows pay details only.

options.t: A job application filled out by a candidate before hiring
options.why: A job application is filled out before being hired. A pay stub is given after work is done and pay is issued.

q: A pay stub shows gross pay of $800, taxes of $120 and insurance of $30. What is net pay?

options.why: $770 only subtracts the $30 insurance and ignores the $120 in taxes. Both deductions must come out of the $800 gross.
$950 adds the deductions to gross pay instead of subtracting them. Deductions reduce pay, so net must be less than $800.
$680 subtracts only the taxes ($800 - $120) and misses the $30 insurance deduction. Both amounts must be taken from gross pay.
Net pay equals gross pay minus deductions: $800 - $120 - $30 = $650. This take home amount is what the employee actually receives.

q: What is the difference between a need and a want?

options.t: A want is something that is required by law for all people
options.why: Laws do not require wants for everyone. A want is something nice to have, while a need is essential, like food or shelter.

options.t: A need is something that you must save up for first
options.why: A need is not something to save up for first; needs like food and housing must be met right away, before wants.

options.t: A need always costs less money than a want does in a year
options.why: Cost does not define a need. A need can be expensive, such as rent, and a want can be cheap, so cost does not separate them.

options.t: A need is essential; a want is something you would like
options.why: A need is essential for living, such as food, shelter and basic clothing, while a want is something you would like but can live without.

q: Which is the best first step before making a large purchase?

options.t: Borrow the money before researching the product
options.why: Borrowing before researching commits you to debt and interest without knowing if the product is right or fairly priced.

options.t: Ask a friend to buy it for you at their store
options.why: Asking a friend to buy it for you at their store is not a research step and does not help you find the best price or quality.

options.t: Compare prices and features from several sellers
options.why: Comparing prices and features from several sellers helps you find the best value and avoid overpaying for a large purchase.

options.t: Buy from the first store that you happen to visit
options.why: Buying from the first store you visit skips any comparison, so you may pay more than necessary for the same item.

q: What is unit pricing?

options.t: The cost per unit of measure, such as per ounce
options.why: Unit pricing is the cost per unit of measure, such as per ounce or per pound, which makes items of different sizes easy to compare.

options.t: The shipping cost charged for each online order
options.why: Shipping costs are an added fee for delivery. Unit pricing divides the price by the quantity to find the cost per unit.

options.t: The total cost of one whole shopping trip each week
options.why: The total cost of a shopping trip is the sum of everything bought. Unit pricing is per item or measure, not an overall total.

options.t: The tax that is added at the store checkout counter
options.why: Sales tax is added at checkout based on a percentage of the price. Unit price is the price divided by the amount, not a tax.

q: A 16 oz bottle costs $3.20 and a 24 oz bottle costs $4.20. Which is the better unit price?

options.t: It cannot be determined by anyone
options.why: The answer can be determined with simple division: price divided by ounces gives each bottle's cost per ounce.

options.t: The 24 oz bottle at $0.175 per ounce
options.why: The 24 oz bottle costs $4.20 / 24 = $0.175 per ounce, versus $3.20 / 16 = $0.20 for the small bottle. So the larger one is the better value.

options.t: They are exactly equal per ounce
options.why: They are not equal: $3.20 / 16 = $0.20 per ounce and $4.20 / 24 = $0.175 per ounce, so the larger bottle costs less per ounce.

options.t: The 16 oz bottle at $0.20 per ounce now
options.why: The 16 oz bottle does cost $0.20 per ounce ($3.20 / 16), but that is higher than the $0.175 per ounce of the 24 oz bottle, so it is not the better deal.

q: What is impulse buying?

options.t: Waiting a week before buying anything at all
options.why: Waiting a week before buying is the opposite of impulse buying. It is a strategy to avoid acting on a sudden urge.

options.t: Buying only what is on a planned list at the store
options.why: Buying only items on a planned list is disciplined shopping, the opposite of impulse buying.

options.t: Making an unplanned purchase on a sudden urge
options.why: Impulse buying is making an unplanned purchase on a sudden urge, often driven by emotion, displays or sales, rather than a real need.

options.t: Comparing prices before buying anything at all
options.why: Comparing prices before buying is planned shopping and the opposite of impulse buying, which happens without thought or comparison.

q: Which habit best prevents impulse buying?

options.t: Waiting a day before buying non-essential items
options.why: Waiting a day gives time for the urge to pass and lets you judge if the item is truly needed, which prevents impulse buys.

options.t: Saving credit card numbers in every app and website
options.why: Saving card numbers in every app makes purchases quick and easy, which encourages impulse buying instead of preventing it.

options.t: Shopping when you are bored or in a bad mood
options.why: Shopping when bored or upset leads to emotional spending, which increases impulse purchases rather than preventing them.

options.t: Ignoring your budget when you shop in the store
options.why: Ignoring your budget makes overspending easy. A budget helps prevent impulse buying by setting limits, so ignoring it does the opposite.

q: Which expense is variable?

options.t: A car loan payment due every month
options.why: A car loan payment is the same amount each month under the loan agreement, which makes it a fixed expense rather than a variable one.

options.t: Monthly rent for an apartment or house
options.why: Rent is set by a lease and stays the same each month, so it is a fixed expense, not a variable one.

options.t: A monthly insurance premium on a policy
options.why: Insurance premiums are set amounts due on a regular schedule, making them fixed expenses and not variable.

options.t: Money spent on entertainment each month
options.why: Entertainment spending changes from month to month depending on choices, so it is a variable expense that can be adjusted when budgeting.

q: Which expense is fixed?

options.t: Clothing bills
options.why: Clothing spending changes with needs and choices from month to month, which makes it variable rather than fixed.

options.t: Monthly rent
options.why: Monthly rent is a set amount due each month under a lease, so it is a fixed expense that is easy to plan for.

options.t: Grocery spending
options.why: Grocery spending changes with prices, household size and shopping habits, so it is a variable expense, not a fixed one.

options.t: Gas for a car
options.why: Gas costs depend on how much you drive and on fuel prices, so they vary each month and are not a fixed expense.

q: After tracking spending, a student finds $120 a month goes to snacks and only $40 to savings. What is the best adjustment?

options.t: Increase snack spending, since other costs cannot be cut
options.why: Increasing snack spending would worsen the imbalance. Snacks are a flexible want, so claiming other costs cannot be cut does not justify spending more.

options.t: Borrow money to cover snacks and other small daily treats
options.why: Borrowing for snacks creates debt and interest for a want. It makes the problem worse rather than solving it.

options.t: Reduce snack spending and move the difference toward savings
options.why: Cutting snack spending frees money, and putting the difference toward savings improves the balance between wants and savings, which tracking is meant to reveal.

options.t: Stop tracking spending to avoid stress and extra work
options.why: Tracking is what shows where money goes. Stopping it hides the problem and prevents the student from making better choices.

q: What is an opportunity cost of spending $50 on a game?

options.t: What else that $50 could have been used for
options.why: Opportunity cost is the value of the next best alternative given up, so it is what else the $50 could have bought or funded.

options.t: The shipping cost for the order of the game
options.why: Shipping is a direct cost, a price paid, not the value of the best alternative given up. Opportunity cost is about the forgone option.

options.t: The $50 price tag of the video game itself
options.why: The $50 price tag is the money cost. Opportunity cost is the other use of that $50 that you gave up to buy the game.

options.t: The sales tax paid on the game at checkout
options.why: Sales tax is part of the actual price paid. Opportunity cost is the best alternative given up, not an added charge.

q: What is a warranty?

options.t: A coupon that gives a discount on the item next time
options.why: A coupon is a discount offer for a future purchase. A warranty is a promise about product quality and repair.

options.t: A store rule that stops all returns after a day
options.why: A store rule limiting returns is a return policy, which is different from a warranty, which covers defects after purchase.

options.t: A tax that is charged on the products you buy
options.why: Sales tax is a government charge added at checkout. A warranty is a seller's or maker's promise about the product.

options.t: A seller's promise to repair or replace defects
options.why: A warranty is a seller's or manufacturer's promise to repair or replace a product with defects for a stated time, protecting the buyer.

q: What should you check before agreeing to a free trial that asks for a card?

options.t: Whether the logo is attractive and eye-catching
options.why: A logo says nothing about cost or terms. Looks do not tell you whether you will be charged after the trial ends.

options.t: Whether it renews into a paid plan and how to cancel
options.why: Many free trials renew into paid plans automatically if not canceled. Check the renewal terms, price and how to cancel before giving your card.

options.t: Whether friends have used it before you did so
options.why: Other people's use does not show whether you will be billed. The trial terms are what matter, not popularity.

options.t: Nothing, because free trials are always free of any charge
options.why: Free trials are not always free; many convert to paid subscriptions and charge the card on file unless you cancel in time.

q: What is a return policy?

options.t: A law that forces stores to refund all purchases ever made
options.why: No law forces stores to refund all purchases. Return policies are mostly set by each store, with some state rules.

options.t: A tax on returned items that a store collects each year
options.why: A return policy is not a tax. Stores do not collect a yearly tax on returned items, so this option is made up.

options.t: A store's rules for returning or exchanging purchases
options.why: A return policy states when and how a store accepts returns or exchanges, including time limits, receipts and refund type.

options.t: A rule about advertising that a store has to follow
options.why: Advertising rules are set by laws and agencies. A return policy deals with returns and exchanges, not advertising.

q: Which action best protects you from online shopping scams?

options.t: Clicking links in unsolicited emails from strangers
options.why: Clicking links in unsolicited emails is risky because they often lead to phishing sites that steal your information.

options.t: Sending money by gift cards to a seller you just met
options.why: Scammers ask for gift cards because they are untraceable and hard to recover, so paying a stranger that way is a classic sign of fraud.

options.t: Sharing your password with the seller to speed up checkout
options.why: Sharing your password lets someone take over your account and steal your information, so never share it with a seller.

options.t: Buying from secure, reputable sites and checking reviews
options.why: Buying from secure, reputable sites (look for https) and checking reviews lowers the risk of fraud and gives you better recourse if something goes wrong.

q: What is a sales tax?

options.t: A tax charged on gifts people give
options.why: Gifts may be subject to a gift tax in some cases, but that is separate from a sales tax, which applies when buying goods.

options.t: A tax added to prices at purchase
options.why: A sales tax is a percentage added to the price of goods and services at the time of purchase, collected by the seller for the state or local government.

options.t: A tax charged on income earned
options.why: A tax on income earned is an income tax, collected on wages and other earnings, not a sales tax added at purchase.

options.t: A tax charged on property owned
options.why: A tax on owned property is a property tax, usually paid yearly by owners of homes or land, not a sales tax.

q: A jacket costs $60 and the sales tax rate is 8%. What is the total price?

options.why: Sales tax is price times rate: $60 x 0.08 = $4.80. Total price is $60 + $4.80 = $64.80, which is what the customer pays at checkout.
$60.80 adds only 80 cents, which would be a 1.33 percent tax. Eight percent of $60 is $4.80, so the total is $64.80.
$68.00 adds $8, which is a tax of about 13.3 percent. The rate is 8 percent, so $4.80 is added, giving $64.80.
$48.00 subtracts 20 percent from the price instead of adding 8 percent tax. Tax raises the price, so the total is above $60.

q: Why is saving money important?

options.t: It guarantees you will never need a job again
options.why: Saving does not guarantee you never need a job. Savings can run out, and most people need ongoing income.

options.t: It makes you spend more money on things you want
options.why: Saving means spending less now, not more. Putting money aside lets it be used for later needs and goals.

options.t: It prepares you for emergencies and future goals
options.why: Saving prepares you for emergencies and future goals, like a car, school or retirement, and reduces the need to borrow.

options.t: It removes the need for a budget in your life
options.why: Saving does not remove the need for a budget; a budget is the tool that helps you decide how much to save.

q: What is an emergency fund?

options.t: Money set aside for unexpected costs like repairs
options.why: An emergency fund is money set aside for unexpected costs such as car repairs, medical bills or job loss, so you can avoid borrowing.

options.t: Money that is borrowed to pay for emergencies
options.why: Borrowed money is debt that must be repaid with interest. An emergency fund is your own saved money.

options.t: Money invested in stocks in order to grow quickly
options.why: Investments in stocks can lose value quickly, so they are not suited for an emergency fund, which needs to be safe and available.

options.t: Money that is set aside for a vacation next summer
options.why: Money for a vacation is a planned savings goal. An emergency fund covers unexpected costs, not planned trips.

q: Where should an emergency fund generally be kept?

options.t: In a long-term account that charges penalties on withdrawals
options.why: A long term account with withdrawal penalties makes the money hard to reach in an emergency, so it is a poor place for the fund.

options.t: In a safe, easily accessible account such as a savings account
options.why: A savings account is safe, usually FDIC insured, and lets you withdraw quickly, which fits an emergency fund that must be available.

options.t: Under a mattress at home where thieves may well look for it
options.why: Cash at home earns no interest and can be lost, stolen or destroyed. It is not as safe as an insured bank account.

options.t: In a risky stock that could lose its value quite quickly
options.why: A risky stock can lose value just when you need the money, so it is the wrong place for an emergency fund.

q: What is interest on a savings account?

options.t: A fee that you pay each time you withdraw from an ATM
options.why: A fee for ATM withdrawals is a bank charge, not interest. Interest is money the bank pays you.

options.t: The amount of money that you deposit in the bank
options.why: The money deposited is called the principal. Interest is what the bank pays on top of that for using your money.

options.t: A tax that is charged on your savings each year
options.why: Interest on savings is earned by you, not charged. A tax on savings would be a different concept, and interest itself may be taxable income.

options.t: Money the bank pays you for keeping your money there
options.why: Interest is the money a bank pays you for keeping your money there, because the bank lends out deposits and shares part of its earnings.

q: What is compound interest?

options.t: Interest that is paid only when a person retires from work
options.why: Interest paid only at retirement is not compound interest. Compounding adds interest to the balance on a regular schedule.

options.t: Interest that decreases a little each year until it is gone
options.why: Compound interest does not shrink each year; because it builds on a growing balance, the interest amount tends to rise over time.

options.t: Interest that is earned only on the original deposit amount
options.why: Interest only on the original deposit is simple interest. Compound interest also earns interest on previous interest.

options.t: Interest earned on both the original deposit and previous interest
options.why: Compound interest is earned on the original deposit plus interest already earned, so growth speeds up over time. This is why early saving matters.

q: Which account will grow the most over 10 years, if all have the same rate?

options.t: The one with no interest paid
options.why: An account with no interest would not grow at all, so it would grow the least of the group, not the most.

options.t: The one that pays simple interest
options.why: Simple interest only earns on the original deposit, so it grows more slowly than an account that compounds interest on interest.

options.t: The one that compounds most often
options.why: With the same rate, the account that compounds most often adds interest to the balance more frequently, so it grows the most over 10 years.

options.t: The one with the highest fees only
options.why: High fees reduce the balance, so an account with the highest fees would grow the least, not the most.

q: What is the main advantage of starting to save early?

options.t: Banks always pay younger savers higher rates each year
options.why: Banks do not always pay younger savers higher rates; rates depend on the account and market, not the saver's age.

options.t: Compound interest has more time to grow your money
options.why: Starting early gives compound interest more time to build, so each dollar saved early grows much more by retirement.

options.t: You can spend all of your income right away today
options.why: Spending all income right away is the opposite of saving. Starting to save early is about setting money aside.

options.t: You will never need to save any money again later
options.why: You will always need to save over a lifetime, since expenses continue. Starting early only makes the saving easier.

q: What is a certificate of deposit (CD)?

options.t: A savings product that holds money for a set term at a fixed rate
options.why: A CD holds money for a set term at a fixed rate, and early withdrawal usually brings a penalty. It is generally FDIC insured.

options.t: A stock that pays dividends every quarter to its owners each year
options.why: A stock that pays dividends is an ownership share, not a CD. A CD is a deposit with a bank, not a stock.

options.t: A loan from a bank that must be repaid in monthly parts over years
options.why: A loan repaid in monthly parts is an installment loan. A CD is a deposit that earns interest for you.

options.t: A checking account that allows unlimited withdrawals at any bank branch
options.why: A checking account allows frequent withdrawals. A CD locks money for a set term, which is why it pays a higher rate.

q: What does FDIC insurance protect?

options.t: Cash that is kept in a drawer at home for safety
options.why: Cash kept at home is not in a bank, so FDIC insurance does not cover it if it is lost or stolen.

options.t: Bank deposits up to the legal limit if a bank fails
options.why: FDIC insurance protects bank deposits up to $250,000 per depositor, per bank, per ownership category if the bank fails.

options.t: Stocks that you own through a broker or an app
options.why: Stocks held through a broker are not covered by FDIC insurance and can lose value. Brokerage accounts may have SIPC coverage for broker failure only.

options.t: Your credit score at the credit bureaus on your report
options.why: Credit scores are tracked by credit bureaus, and FDIC insurance has nothing to do with them. It covers bank deposits.

q: A person has $300,000 in one account at a single FDIC-insured bank. How much is insured, in the standard individual case?

options.why: $300,000 is the whole balance, but FDIC insurance has a limit per depositor, per bank, per ownership category, so the entire amount is not insured.
$50,000 is an old, lower figure that does not match today's limit. The standard limit is $250,000.
The standard FDIC limit is $250,000 per depositor, per bank, per ownership category, so $250,000 of the $300,000 is insured and $50,000 is not.
$100,000 was the limit before 2008 and no longer applies. Today's standard limit is $250,000.

q: What is a savings goal?

options.t: A specific amount you plan to save by a date
options.why: A savings goal is a specific amount you plan to save by a certain date, such as $600 in six months, which gives you something to aim for.

options.t: A required bill that comes in every month
options.why: A required monthly bill is a fixed expense. A savings goal is something you choose to work toward.

options.t: A plan for repaying a loan over time in parts
options.why: A plan for repaying a loan is a repayment schedule. A savings goal is about building money, not paying off debt.

options.t: A fee that is charged by a bank for an account
options.why: A bank fee is a charge for services. A savings goal is a target amount you set for yourself.

q: Leo wants $600 in 6 months. How much must he save each month?

options.why: $3,600 is $600 times 6, which multiplies instead of dividing. The monthly amount must be $600 split over 6 months.
$36 is far too small; it would only reach $216 after 6 months. Dividing $600 by 6 gives the right monthly amount.
$60 a month for 6 months totals only $360, which falls short of $600. The goal requires $600 / 6 = $100 a month.
Monthly savings equal the goal divided by months: $600 / 6 = $100. Saving that amount each month for 6 months reaches the $600 goal.

q: What does 'pay yourself first' mean?

options.t: Skipping saving so you can spend a lot more money now
options.why: Skipping saving to spend more is the opposite of paying yourself first, which puts saving ahead of spending.

options.t: Spending on wants before you pay the bills so you enjoy it
options.why: Spending on wants before bills is risky and not what pay yourself first means; it is about saving, not wants.

options.t: Borrowing money to give yourself a reward each month
options.why: Borrowing for a reward adds debt. Paying yourself first uses your own income, moved to savings before other spending.

options.t: Moving money to savings before spending on other things
options.why: Pay yourself first means moving money into savings as soon as you are paid, before spending on other things, so saving becomes a habit.

q: What is automatic saving?

options.t: Regular automatic transfers into savings
options.why: Automatic saving sets up regular transfers into savings, often each payday, so saving happens without relying on willpower.

options.t: Withdrawing money from savings every week
options.why: Withdrawing money from savings every week would drain the account. Automatic saving adds money, it does not take it out.

options.t: Closing the savings account once a year
options.why: Closing the account once a year does not build savings. Automatic saving keeps the account open and growing.

options.t: Spending money automatically on small items
options.why: Automatic spending on small items is the opposite of saving. Automatic saving moves money into savings, not out for purchases.

q: What is the Rule of 72 used for?

options.t: Setting the age at which a person must retire
options.why: The Rule of 72 does not set a retirement age. It estimates how long it takes for money to double.

options.t: Estimating how long money takes to double
options.why: Dividing 72 by the annual interest rate estimates the years it takes money to double. At 8 percent, money doubles in about 9 years.

options.t: Finding the monthly payment on a loan
options.why: Loan payments are found with payment formulas or calculators. The Rule of 72 only estimates doubling time for growth.

options.t: Calculating the taxes owed on income
options.why: Taxes owed are found using tax tables and rates. The Rule of 72 estimates how long money takes to double.

q: Using the Rule of 72, about how many years will it take money earning 4% to double?

options.t: 72 years
options.why: 72 years is the number 72 itself, not divided by the rate. The Rule of 72 divides 72 by the interest rate.

options.t: 30 years
options.why: 30 years does not match the rule. Dividing 72 by 4 gives 18, so money doubles in about 18 years at 4 percent.

options.t: 18 years
options.why: Years to double is about 72 divided by the rate: 72 / 4 = 18 years. A higher rate would shorten that time.

options.t: 4 years
options.why: 4 years is just the rate itself. The rule divides 72 by 4, which gives 18 years, not 4.
