options.why: Keeping savings apart makes them less visible and harder to spend on impulse, which helps you reach goals such as an emergency fund.

q: What is an emergency fund goal for most households?

options.t: No set amount is needed for any household
options.why: Experts recommend a cushion for emergencies such as job loss or medical bills, so claiming no amount is needed is poor advice for any household.

options.t: Ten years of expenses held in a savings pot
options.why: Ten years of expenses is far larger than the usual guideline and would tie up money that could be invested; most advice is three to six months.

options.t: Three to six months of essential expenses
options.why: Financial advisors suggest three to six months of essential costs, enough to cover rent, food and bills if income stops, with more for unstable income.

options.t: One day of expenses kept in a savings account
options.why: One day of expenses would not cover a real emergency such as job loss, which can last weeks or months; the guideline is far larger.

q: Essential expenses are $1,800 a month. What is a three-month emergency fund?

options.why: A three-month fund covers three months of essential costs, so $1,800 x 3 = $5,400 kept in an easily accessible savings account.
$21,600 is a full year of expenses ($1,800 x 12), which is much more than the three-month goal asked about.
$600 is one third of a single month's expenses ($1,800 / 3), which is not what a three-month fund requires.
$1,800 is only one month of essential expenses; a three-month fund requires multiplying that monthly amount by three, giving $5,400.

q: What is interest rate risk for savers?

options.t: The risk that a bank fails and closes its doors
options.why: Bank failure is a separate risk, called institutional risk, and FDIC insurance covers deposits up to $250,000 per depositor, so it is not interest rate risk.

options.t: The risk that you forget your PIN when you go to the ATM
options.why: Forgetting a PIN is an access inconvenience, not a financial risk related to rates; interest rate risk concerns the return you earn.

options.t: The risk that rates fall and new deposits earn less
options.why: When rates fall, savings accounts and maturing CDs reinvest at lower rates, so savers earn less income than before on new deposits.

options.t: The risk that prices rise and your money buys less
options.why: That describes inflation risk, where rising prices erode purchasing power; interest rate risk is about changes in the rate your savings earn.

q: Which choice best protects savings from both loss and inflation over many years?

options.t: All money in one risky stock that the investor believes will grow
options.why: A single stock concentrates risk; if the company fails, you can lose much of your savings, so it does not protect against loss.

options.t: All cash under a mattress at home for the long term ahead
options.why: Cash under a mattress earns no interest and loses buying power to inflation, and it can be lost or stolen, so it is unsafe.

options.t: Spending it all now on whatever you feel like buying
options.why: Spending everything now leaves no savings, so there is nothing to protect; it does not guard against loss or inflation in the future.

options.t: A mix of safe savings and diversified long-term investments
options.why: Safe savings give stability and liquidity while diversified investments, like index funds, historically outpace inflation over decades, so a mix balances loss risk and inflation risk.

q: What is a credit report error you should dispute?

options.t: Your correct name and address on the report
options.why: Your correct name and address are accurate information, so there is nothing to dispute; disputes are for inaccurate or fraudulent items.

options.t: An account you never opened listed in your name
options.why: An account you never opened may signal identity theft or a reporting mistake, and disputing it with the bureau protects your score and credit.

options.t: A late payment that you really made last year
options.why: A late payment you actually made late is accurate, so a dispute would not succeed; only inaccurate information can be removed.

options.t: An account you opened and repaid in full years ago
options.why: A properly closed, paid-off account is accurate and can even help your history; there is no error to dispute in it.

q: After disputing a credit report error, what must the credit bureau generally do?

options.t: Investigate and correct or remove inaccurate items
options.why: Under the Fair Credit Reporting Act, the bureau must investigate a dispute, usually within 30 days, and correct or delete items it cannot verify.

options.t: Ignore the dispute and leave the report just as it is
options.why: The law requires bureaus to look into disputes, not ignore them; leaving the report unchanged without investigating would break the rules.

options.t: Charge you a fee to look into the dispute each time
options.why: Disputing errors is free; credit bureaus may not charge you to investigate a dispute about inaccurate information on your report.

options.t: Raise your credit score by a set number of points
options.why: Bureaus fix errors but do not give bonus points; your score changes only if removing the error changes what the scoring model sees.

q: What is a credit limit increase?

options.t: A higher borrowing limit on a card
options.why: A credit limit increase raises the maximum you may borrow on a card, and it can lower your utilization ratio if your balance stays the same.

options.t: A new loan for the card's holder
options.why: A new loan is separate borrowed money with its own terms; a limit increase only changes how much you can charge on the existing card.

options.t: A higher interest rate on the card
options.why: A higher interest rate raises the cost of carrying a balance; a limit increase raises the borrowing cap, which is not the same thing.

options.t: A decrease in your balance owed there
options.why: A decrease in balance owed comes from making payments; a limit increase changes your borrowing ceiling and leaves the balance as it was.

q: Your balance is $600 on a $2,000 limit. The limit rises to $3,000. What happens to utilization if the balance stays the same?

options.t: It stays at 30% for good
options.why: Utilization is balance divided by limit, so when the limit changes and the balance stays the same, the ratio changes; it does not stay at 30%.

options.t: It becomes zero at once
options.why: With a $600 balance on a $3,000 limit, utilization is 20%, not zero; it would be zero only if the balance were paid off.

options.t: It rises from 30% to 40%
options.why: Utilization falls instead of rising: $600 / $3,000 = 20%, so a bigger limit lowers the ratio, which is not 40%.

options.t: It falls from 30% to 20%
options.why: Before, $600 / $2,000 = 30%; after the increase, $600 / $3,000 = 20%, and lower utilization generally helps credit scores.

q: What is a minimum payment trap?

options.t: Never using the card, so that no interest is ever charged on it
options.why: Never using the card avoids interest and is not a trap; the minimum payment trap occurs when you carry a balance and pay little each month.

options.t: Paying only the minimum so the debt lasts long and costs more interest
options.why: Paying only the minimum keeps most of the balance accruing interest, so repayment drags on for years and the total interest paid can exceed the original purchase.

options.t: Paying the full balance so that no interest is charged at all each time
options.why: Paying the full balance avoids interest through the grace period, which is the smart approach rather than a trap.

options.t: Paying more than the minimum each month, so that the balance is cleared fast
options.why: Paying more than the minimum clears debt faster and cuts interest, which is the way out of the trap, not the trap itself.

q: Which choice reduces interest costs on a card balance the fastest?

options.t: Skipping payments for a few months now
options.why: Skipping payments brings late fees, penalty rates and credit damage, and interest keeps adding to the balance, so it increases costs.

options.t: Making new purchases on the card itself
options.why: New purchases add to the balance and interest charges, so this makes your debt larger instead of reducing interest costs.

options.t: Paying more than the minimum each month
options.why: Payments above the minimum go mostly toward principal, so the balance and the interest charged on it shrink faster, saving money.

options.t: Paying only the minimum due every month
options.why: Minimum payments mostly cover interest, so the balance falls slowly and interest costs stay high compared with paying more.

q: What is a personal loan?

options.t: A loan only for businesses that is repaid in equal monthly installments
options.why: Personal loans are available to individuals, not only businesses, and the equal installment feature does not make it a business-only loan.

options.t: A tax refund paid by the state to a person who files a return
options.why: A tax refund is money returned by the government, whereas a personal loan is borrowed money that must be repaid with interest.

options.t: A gift from a bank to a customer that is never repaid in any form
options.why: A bank never gives free money; a personal loan must be repaid with interest, typically in fixed monthly installments over a set term.

options.t: Money borrowed for a personal purpose that is repaid in installments
options.why: A personal loan lends a lump sum for needs like debt consolidation or medical bills, usually unsecured, repaid in fixed installments with interest.

q: A $3,000 loan at 8% simple interest for 1 year costs how much interest?

options.why: $2,400 is eight times the real interest figure; simple interest is principal x rate x time = $3,000 x 0.08 x 1 = $240.
Simple interest = $3,000 x 8% x 1 year = $240, which is the cost of borrowing before adding it to the principal.
$3,240 is the total repaid, principal plus interest ($3,000 + $240), not the interest cost alone that the question asks for.
$24 results from misplacing a decimal; 8% of $3,000 is $240, so $24 is ten times too small.

q: What is a home equity loan?

options.t: A grant given by the government to needy home owners
options.why: A government grant is free money that need not be repaid; a home equity loan is borrowed money secured by your home and must be repaid.

options.t: A loan for a car only, with the car as collateral
options.why: An auto loan uses the car as collateral; a home equity loan uses the owner's equity in their home as collateral.

options.t: A loan secured by the value you own in your home
options.why: A home equity loan lets you borrow against the part of your home you own, but if you cannot repay, the lender can foreclose on the house.

options.t: A loan with no collateral and no interest to pay
options.why: Home equity loans have interest and collateral; they are not free, and the house secures the loan, which makes missing payments risky.

q: What is a deductible's role in lowering premiums?

options.t: Taking on more of the first costs yourself lowers the insurer's risk
options.why: A higher deductible means you pay more of the first costs, so the insurer pays out less often and charges a lower premium.

options.t: It removes the insurer from your claims, so you pay all costs
options.why: A deductible does not remove the insurer from claims; the insurer still pays covered costs above the deductible amount.

options.t: It has no effect on premiums, since the insurer sets them all
options.why: Deductibles do affect premiums; insurers offer lower premiums for higher deductibles because the policyholder shares more of the risk.

options.t: It increases the insurer's risk, so premiums go up for you as well in time
options.why: A higher deductible lowers the insurer's risk, so premiums go down; saying risk increases and premiums rise reverses the true relationship.

q: Which situation shows a good reason to choose a higher deductible?

options.t: You have no savings at all to cover the costs
options.why: With no savings, a high deductible could be impossible to pay after a loss, so a lower deductible is safer.

options.t: You expect to make many claims during the next year
options.why: If you expect many claims, a high deductible would make you pay out of pocket repeatedly, so a low deductible suits that situation better.

options.t: You have an emergency fund to cover the first costs
options.why: Having an emergency fund means you can cover the deductible if a loss happens, so you can safely take the lower premium that goes with it.

options.t: You want the highest possible premium every single month
options.why: Higher deductibles come with lower premiums, not the highest; wanting the highest premium would be a reason for a low deductible.

q: What is insurance fraud?

options.t: Filing an honest claim for a real loss that happened
options.why: Filing an honest claim for a real loss is the proper use of insurance and is not fraud, because there is no deception.

options.t: Paying a premium late and getting a fee for it
options.why: Paying a premium late may bring a fee or a lapse in coverage, but it is a billing issue and not fraud.

options.t: Comparing quotes from several firms to find a deal
options.why: Comparing quotes is smart shopping and fully legal; it involves no lying or false claims, so it is not fraud.

options.t: Lying or exaggerating to get an insurer to pay
options.why: Insurance fraud is knowingly lying or exaggerating to collect money, such as faking a theft or inflating a claim, and it is a crime with fines and jail.

q: A person reports a car stolen when it was sold. What is this?

options.t: Risk reduction
options.why: Risk reduction means lowering the chance or size of a loss, such as installing alarms; reporting a sold car stolen is deception.

options.t: Insurance fraud
options.why: Claiming a sold car was stolen to collect money is a false claim, which is insurance fraud and can lead to criminal charges and a denied claim.

options.t: A legal claim
options.why: A legal claim is an honest request for payment on a real loss; this case involves a lie, so it is not a legal claim.

options.t: Avoiding risk now
options.why: Avoiding risk means not doing an activity that could cause a loss; reporting a false theft is not risk avoidance but fraud.

q: What is a replacement cost policy?

options.t: A policy that pays to replace items at current prices
options.why: Replacement cost coverage pays what it costs to buy a new equivalent item today, without subtracting depreciation, though premiums are usually higher.

options.t: A policy that pays only the item's depreciated value
options.why: That describes actual cash value, which subtracts depreciation for age and wear; replacement cost pays the full current price instead.

options.t: A policy that pays nothing at all for lost items or goods
options.why: A policy that pays nothing would be of no use; replacement cost policies pay out for covered losses at the current cost of replacing items.

options.t: A policy that pays double the value of any lost items
options.why: Policies pay up to the cost of replacing the item and never double it; paying double would let owners profit from a loss.

q: A 5-year-old laptop worth $200 is stolen. A new one costs $900. Which policy type pays more?

options.t: Actual cash value
options.why: Actual cash value pays the depreciated worth, about $200 for the old laptop, which is far less than the $900 for a new one.

options.t: They pay the same
options.why: The two policy types pay differently here: ACV gives about $200 for the aged laptop, while replacement cost gives up to $900.

options.t: Neither pays
options.why: Both policy types pay for a covered theft, so saying neither pays ignores that the laptop is stolen and covered in this case.

options.t: Replacement cost
options.why: Replacement cost pays up to the $900 needed to buy a new laptop, while actual cash value would pay only the $200 depreciated value.

q: What is a home inventory for insurance?

options.t: A tax record of what you owe each year to the state
options.why: A tax record of what you owe is a tax statement; a home inventory lists your belongings and values to support an insurance claim.

options.t: A list of home repair tools kept in the garage shed
options.why: A list of tools kept in a shed covers just a few items; an insurance inventory covers all belongings, with values, photos and receipts.

options.t: A list or photos of belongings with their values
options.why: A home inventory records items and their values, often with photos or receipts, so you can prove what you owned if you must make a claim.

options.t: A bill from the insurer for your next premium
options.why: A premium bill is a request for payment from the insurer; a home inventory is a record you create of your own belongings.

q: After a fire, why is a home inventory helpful?

options.t: It speeds up and supports your insurance claim
options.why: After a fire, an inventory proves what you owned and what it was worth, which speeds up the claim and helps you get a fair payout.

options.t: It lowers the deductible on your policy right away
options.why: An inventory does not change your deductible, which is set in the policy; it only helps document the loss for your claim.

options.t: It cancels your premium for the next year or two
options.why: The inventory does not cancel premiums; you still owe premiums, and it only helps you document belongings for a claim.

options.t: It prevents any future fire, as insurers see it
options.why: An inventory cannot prevent fires; it is a record made for documenting losses after the fact, and does not change fire risk.

q: What is a retirement account's tax advantage?

options.t: The account pays for your groceries, as money is sent to the store
options.why: Retirement accounts do not pay for groceries; their tax advantage is about how contributions or earnings are taxed, not about spending money.

options.t: Taxes may be deferred or reduced on contributions or earnings
options.why: Accounts such as 401(k)s and IRAs may let contributions reduce taxable income now or let earnings grow tax-deferred or tax-free, increasing long-term growth.

options.t: No taxes ever apply to any account that you open at a bank
options.why: Taxes do apply to many bank accounts, as interest is taxable; retirement accounts are special because they offer tax breaks that others do not.

options.t: Taxes are doubled on every dollar that you put into it
options.why: Retirement accounts reduce taxes, not double them; the account gives a tax advantage, though early withdrawals can bring taxes and penalties.

q: Why is it important to take full advantage of an employer 401(k) match?

options.t: It lowers your income tax to zero every year
options.why: A match does not cut your tax to zero; pre-tax contributions may lower taxable income, but you still owe tax on the rest.

options.t: It lets you withdraw anytime with no penalty ever
options.why: Early withdrawals from a 401(k) generally bring a 10% penalty plus income tax, so a match does not allow penalty-free withdrawals anytime.

options.t: It guarantees investment gains every single year
options.why: Investment returns are never guaranteed, and the match is a contribution from your employer, not a promise that investments will gain.

options.t: It adds free money to your retirement savings
options.why: An employer match, such as 50 cents per dollar up to a limit, is an immediate return on your contribution, so skipping it means giving up part of your pay.

q: What is portfolio diversification across asset classes?

options.t: Holding different types such as stocks, bonds and cash
options.why: Correct. Diversification spreads money across stocks, bonds, cash and other asset classes, so a drop in one holding is cushioned by others, which lowers overall portfolio risk.

options.t: Holding only cash forever and never buying anything else
options.why: Holding only cash is not diversification. Cash is one asset class, and over many years inflation steadily erodes its buying power, so growth is limited.

options.t: Holding only one type of asset for the whole long term
options.why: Holding a single type of asset is the opposite of diversification. All the money rises and falls together, leaving the investor fully exposed to one kind of risk.

options.t: Holding only your employer's stock for job and savings
options.why: Owning only your employer's stock concentrates risk in one company. If the firm struggles, both your paycheck and your investments are hurt at the same time.

q: An investor holds only stock in the company that employs them. What extra risk do they take?

options.t: Less risk than a diversified fund, as they know it
options.why: Holding one company's stock is riskier than a diversified fund, not safer. Familiarity with the employer does not remove the chance that its share price falls sharply.

options.t: Both their job and savings depend on one company
options.why: Correct. Owning only your employer's stock puts your paycheck and your savings at the mercy of one company, so a layoff or a stock collapse can hit both together.

options.t: No extra risk at all for the investor or the job
options.why: There is extra risk. Concentrating in one firm creates company-specific risk that diversification would reduce, and it ties your income and investments to the same outcome.

options.t: Guaranteed high returns for the investor over time
options.why: Stocks never carry guaranteed returns, and a single company's shares can swing widely. High returns are possible but never promised, and losses can be large.

q: What is the purpose of a résumé when looking for work?

options.t: To apply for a bank account in your own name today
options.why: A bank account application uses identification and forms, not a résumé. A résumé is a career document aimed at employers, not at financial institutions.

options.t: To list the prices of items you want to buy for a new home
options.why: A résumé does not list prices of items to buy. That would resemble a shopping or wish list, while a résumé summarizes a person's work qualifications.

options.t: To show an employer your skills, education and experience
options.why: Correct. A résumé summarizes your skills, education and work experience on one or two pages so an employer can quickly judge whether you fit the job.

options.t: To record your monthly spending and your bank bills
options.why: Recording monthly spending and bank bills is the job of a budget or ledger. A résumé is a marketing document about your qualifications, not a spending record.

q: Which factor most affects how much a worker can earn over a career?

options.t: The worker's favorite food at lunch time each day
options.why: A favorite lunch food has no link to earning power. Employers pay for the value of what a worker can produce, not personal food preferences.

options.t: Skills, experience and education that employers value
options.why: Correct. Skills, experience and education raise a worker's productivity and scarcity, which lets them command higher pay and promotions across a career.

options.t: The color of the worker's car and its model year
options.why: Car color and model year are personal choices with no bearing on pay. Employers do not set wages based on what a worker drives.

options.t: The number of social media posts a worker writes weekly
options.why: Social media post count does not determine earnings. Employers pay for job skills and results, and heavy posting is not a qualification for higher wages.

q: What is an apprenticeship?

options.t: A vacation for new hires in their first year
options.why: An apprenticeship is work and training, not a vacation. New hires in apprenticeships earn wages while learning a trade under experienced workers.

options.t: A loan for starting a business, repaid
options.why: A loan for starting a business describes small business financing, not an apprenticeship. Apprentices are paid employees, not borrowers repaying a startup loan.

options.t: A tax on skilled workers that they pay yearly
options.why: An apprenticeship is not a tax. Apprentices earn pay while training, and no yearly levy on skilled workers is called an apprenticeship.

options.t: Paid on-the-job training in a skilled trade
options.why: Correct. An apprenticeship combines paid on-the-job training with classroom instruction in a skilled trade such as electrician or plumber, and ends in a recognized credential.

q: What is self-employment?

options.t: Working for yourself rather than for an employer
options.why: Correct. A self-employed person earns income from their own business or services instead of wages from an employer, and is responsible for their own taxes and benefits.

options.t: Working without pay in a job that helps other people
options.why: Unpaid work that helps others is volunteering. Self-employment is done to earn income for yourself, not to work without pay.

options.t: Working only at night in a big city factory or shop
options.why: The time or place of work does not define self-employment. A self-employed person may work any hours, and many do not work in factories at all.

options.t: Working for a large corporation that pays you a salary
options.why: Working for a corporation on salary is regular employment. A self-employed person has no employer and earns income from their own business.

q: Which is a benefit of self-employment compared with a regular job?

options.t: Employer-paid benefits such as health insurance
options.why: Self-employed people usually pay for their own health insurance. Employer-paid benefits are a feature of regular jobs, not self-employment.

options.t: No need to pay taxes on the income that you earn
options.why: Self-employed workers still owe income tax and also pay both halves of Social Security and Medicare through self-employment tax, so taxes are not avoided.

options.t: More control over your schedule and decisions
options.why: Correct. Being your own boss gives more control over hours, clients and business decisions, though it also brings less stable income and more responsibility.

options.t: Guaranteed steady income, as pay is the same
options.why: Self-employed income often rises and falls with customers and seasons. A guaranteed, unchanging paycheck is more typical of a salaried job.

q: What is unemployment insurance?

options.t: A bonus for finding a job that the government pays to a worker in their first month
options.why: Unemployment insurance is not a bonus for finding work. It pays eligible workers a temporary benefit while they are out of a job and searching.

options.t: A refund of payroll taxes paid back to a worker by the state when they retire
options.why: It is not a refund of payroll taxes at retirement. Retirement income comes from Social Security, while unemployment insurance pays weekly benefits after a job loss.

options.t: A loan for job seekers from the state that must be repaid with interest once hired
options.why: It is not a loan and nothing is repaid with interest. Benefits are funded by employer payroll taxes and given to eligible workers who were laid off.

options.t: Temporary income for eligible workers who lose a job through no fault of their own
options.why: Correct. Unemployment insurance, funded by employer payroll taxes, gives temporary income to eligible workers laid off or let go through no fault of their own while they look for work.

q: What is a pay raise based on merit?

options.t: An increase given for strong performance
options.why: Correct. A merit raise rewards an employee's strong performance or achievements with higher pay, unlike an across-the-board raise given to everyone or a cost-of-living adjustment.

options.t: An increase given automatically to everyone
options.why: An increase given automatically to everyone is a general or across-the-board raise, not a merit raise, which depends on individual performance.

options.t: A fee paid to the employer for the raise
options.why: A raise is paid by the employer to the worker. The employee does not pay the employer a fee for receiving a merit raise.

options.t: A cut in pay given for poor results overall
options.why: A cut in pay for poor results is a pay reduction or penalty. A merit raise is an increase tied to good performance.

q: Prices rise 3% and your employer gives a 3% cost-of-living raise. What happens to your buying power?

options.t: It falls sharply by a lot
options.why: With a 3% raise against 3% inflation, purchasing power does not fall sharply. The extra pay offsets the higher prices almost exactly.

options.t: It stays about the same
options.why: Correct. A 3% raise matches 3% price growth, so your income keeps pace with costs and your real buying power stays about the same.

options.t: It rises sharply every year
options.why: A raise equal to inflation does not boost buying power. Prices rose by the same 3%, so extra income buys no more than before.

options.t: It disappears from your pay
options.why: Buying power does not vanish. Your pay still buys about the same goods as before because the raise matches the 3% price increase.

q: What is an unplanned expense?

options.t: A cost that is zero in every single month of the year
options.why: A cost that is zero every month would not be an expense at all. An unplanned expense is a real cost, just one you did not budget for.

options.t: A cost you pay every month on the first day of the month
options.why: A cost paid on the first of each month is a recurring fixed expense such as rent, which is planned in advance, not unplanned.

options.t: A cost that you did not expect, such as a car repair
options.why: Correct. An unplanned expense is an unexpected cost, such as a car repair or medical bill, which an emergency fund is designed to cover.

options.t: A cost in your budget, such as the rent paid each month
options.why: Rent paid each month is a planned fixed expense already in your budget. Unplanned expenses are the ones you did not see coming.

q: A phone screen breaks and costs $120 to fix. What helps you pay without debt?

options.t: Ignoring the repair
options.why: Ignoring a broken screen does not solve the problem and may leave you without a working phone. It is not a way to pay for the repair.

options.t: A payday loan
options.why: A payday loan carries very high fees and interest, so borrowing $120 this way creates more debt. It is the opposite of paying without debt.

options.t: A new credit card
options.why: A new credit card means borrowing, so the $120 becomes debt with interest if not repaid in full. It does not avoid debt.

options.t: An emergency fund
options.why: Correct. An emergency fund is cash saved for surprises like a $120 repair, letting you pay immediately without borrowing or paying interest.

q: What is a store loyalty program's drawback?

options.t: It may encourage spending more than you planned
options.why: Correct. Loyalty programs reward purchases with points or discounts, which can tempt shoppers to buy more than planned just to earn rewards.

options.t: It always raises prices in the shop for everyone
options.why: Loyalty programs do not raise prices for everyone. They offer members discounts or points, and the drawback is overspending, not higher shelf prices.

options.t: It bans returns of any kind for all the members
options.why: Joining a loyalty program does not ban returns. Return policies are set separately by the store and are not removed by membership.

options.t: It removes all discounts, so members pay full price
options.why: Loyalty programs usually add member discounts, not remove them. Members do not have to pay full price, so this is not their drawback.

q: What does it mean to shop around?

options.t: Buy the most expensive item that you can find
options.why: Buying the most expensive item is the opposite of shopping around. Shopping around aims to find the best value, often at a lower price.

options.t: Walk around the shop without buying anything
options.why: Walking through a shop without buying is browsing. Shopping around means actively comparing prices and quality among sellers before deciding.

options.t: Compare prices and quality at several sellers
options.why: Correct. Shopping around means comparing prices, quality and terms at several sellers so you can pick the best value for your money.

options.t: Buy from the first seller you meet to save time
options.why: Buying from the first seller skips comparison entirely. Saving time may cost more money because you never learn whether better prices exist.

q: Two stores sell the same headphones: one at $80 with free returns, the other at $72 with no returns. Which is better if you may need to return them?

options.t: They are identical in every way
options.why: The two offers are not identical. The $80 headphones include free returns while the $72 pair allow none, so the protection differs even if the product matches.

options.t: The $80 store with free returns
options.why: Correct. If a return is possible, free returns protect you. A failed $72 purchase is a total loss, while the $80 pair can be refunded.

options.t: Neither store is the better deal
options.why: One store is better when you may need to return the item. Free returns have real value, so the two are not equal for this buyer.

options.t: The $72 store, as its price is low
options.why: The lower price saves $8 but gives up return protection. If the headphones are defective or unwanted, the $72 would be wasted.

q: What is a service charge on a bank account?

options.t: A tax on interest earned in the account
options.why: A tax on interest is an income tax matter, not a service charge. A service charge is a fee the bank itself charges for account services.

options.t: A fee a bank charges for account services
options.why: Correct. A service charge is a fee a bank charges, such as a monthly maintenance fee, for running and servicing the account.

options.t: A reward for opening an account, like a gift
options.why: A reward for opening an account is a sign-up bonus. A service charge costs the customer money rather than giving a gift.

options.t: A loan payment made each month to the bank
options.why: A monthly loan payment goes toward borrowed money. A service charge is a fee for account services, not a loan repayment.

q: What is a debit card purchase limit for?

options.t: Limiting how much can be spent in a period for security
options.why: Correct. A purchase limit caps how much a debit card can spend in a period, which reduces losses if the card is lost or stolen.

options.t: Raising your credit score by showing how much you can spend
options.why: Debit cards do not build credit scores because they use your own money rather than borrowed credit. A spending cap has nothing to do with scores.

options.t: Earning interest on the money in your card account
options.why: Purchase limits do not earn interest. Interest on an account comes from the bank paying you on balances, not from a spending cap.

options.t: Paying taxes on the money you spend with the card
options.why: A purchase limit does not pay taxes. Sales tax is added at checkout, and the limit only restricts how much you can spend.

q: What is a goal-based savings plan?

options.t: Saving random amounts with no aim in mind at all
options.why: Saving random amounts with no aim lacks goals. A goal-based plan names specific targets, amounts and deadlines.

options.t: Spending all income first, then saving whatever is left
options.why: Spending first and saving leftovers is the opposite of a planned approach. Goal-based saving sets money aside first for each goal.

options.t: Saving specific amounts for specific goals by set dates
options.why: Correct. A goal-based plan sets target amounts and dates, such as $2,400 in 8 months, so you know how much to save each period.

options.t: Never saving any money for any goal at all in life
options.why: Never saving for any goal is not a plan at all. It leaves nothing for emergencies or purchases, the opposite of goal-based saving.

q: You need $2,400 for a laptop in 8 months. How much per month?

options.why: $19,200 comes from multiplying $2,400 by 8 instead of dividing. The monthly amount must be far smaller than the total goal.
$3,000 does not match the goal. Saving $3,000 a month for 8 months would total $24,000, ten times the $2,400 needed.
$30 a month for 8 months saves only $240, one tenth of the $2,400 target. The decimal is misplaced.
Correct. Divide the goal by the months: $2,400 / 8 = $300 per month, so saving $300 monthly reaches the laptop in 8 months.

q: What is a Series I savings bond designed to protect against?

options.t: Inflation
options.why: Correct. Series I savings bonds pay a rate that combines a fixed rate with an inflation rate adjusted twice a year, protecting buying power against rising prices.

options.t: Bank failure
options.why: Bank failure is covered by FDIC insurance, not by I bonds. I bonds are backed by the US government but are designed for inflation protection.

options.t: High taxes
options.why: I bonds do not shield you from taxes in general. Interest is exempt from state and local tax, but their design purpose is inflation protection.

options.t: Stock losses
options.why: I bonds are not tied to stock markets, so they do not guard against stock losses. Their rate adjusts with inflation instead.

q: What is a credit union savings account?

options.t: An account that is not insured by anyone at all, ever
options.why: Credit union accounts are federally insured, up to $250,000 per depositor, by the NCUA. They are not uninsured.

options.t: A savings account held at a for-profit stock exchange firm
options.why: A for-profit stock exchange firm is not a credit union. Credit unions are not-for-profit and owned by their members, not by outside shareholders.

options.t: A loan from a union that helps its workers buy a home
options.why: A savings account is a deposit product, not a loan. A credit union is a financial cooperative, not an arm of a labor union.

options.t: A savings account at a member-owned financial cooperative
options.why: Correct. A credit union is a not-for-profit cooperative owned by its members, and its savings accounts typically offer competitive rates and low fees.

q: Which agency insures deposits at federally insured credit unions?

options.t: The Internal Revenue Service (IRS) office
options.why: The IRS collects federal taxes and does not insure bank or credit union deposits. Deposit insurance is handled by other agencies.

options.t: The Social Security Administration (SSA)
options.why: The SSA runs Social Security retirement and disability benefits. It does not insure deposits at credit unions.

options.t: The National Credit Union Administration
options.why: Correct. The NCUA, through the National Credit Union Share Insurance Fund, insures member deposits at federal credit unions up to $250,000 per depositor.

options.t: The Federal Trade Commission (FTC) office
options.why: The FTC protects consumers from unfair business practices and enforces competition law. It does not insure deposits at credit unions.

q: What does it mean for money to be liquid?

options.t: It is stored as water in a tank
options.why: Liquid does not mean stored as water. In finance, liquidity describes how easily an asset converts into cash, not its physical form.

options.t: It can be turned into cash quickly
options.why: Correct. Liquid assets, such as cash or a savings account, can be converted to cash quickly with little or no loss of value.

options.t: It never changes in value over time
options.why: Liquidity does not mean a stable value. A liquid asset may still change in price; the term only concerns how quickly it becomes cash.

options.t: It cannot be spent at all by anyone
options.why: Liquid money can be spent easily. An asset that cannot be spent is illiquid, the opposite of liquid.

q: Which is the most liquid place to keep money?

options.t: A plot of city land
options.why: Land takes time to sell and its price can vary, so it is illiquid. It cannot be turned into cash quickly.

options.t: A savings account
options.why: Correct. Savings accounts allow you to withdraw cash almost any time with little or no penalty, making them highly liquid.

options.t: A five-year CD
options.why: A five-year CD locks money until maturity, and early withdrawal usually triggers a penalty, so it is less liquid than a savings account.

options.t: A house in a city
options.why: A house can take months to sell and has transaction costs, so it is one of the least liquid assets people own.

q: What is credit utilization's effect on your score?

options.t: High utilization can lower your score
options.why: Correct. Credit utilization is the share of available credit you use. High utilization suggests heavy borrowing and tends to lower your credit score.

options.t: It deletes old debt from the lender
options.why: Utilization does not delete debt. It measures how much of your credit limit you are using and never erases balances owed.

options.t: High utilization raises your score
options.why: High utilization hurts rather than helps. Lenders see heavy use of available credit as a sign of risk, so scores generally drop.

options.t: It has no effect on your credit score
options.why: Credit utilization has a strong effect on credit scores. It is one of the main factors, typically about thirty percent of a FICO score.

q: Which action best improves your credit score over time?

options.t: Maxing out your credit cards each month
options.why: Maxing out cards drives credit utilization high, which lowers your score. Lenders see it as risky borrowing.

options.t: Missing payments on your bills now and then
options.why: Missed payments are reported to credit bureaus and damage scores. Payment history is the largest factor in most scoring models.

options.t: Paying on time and keeping balances low
options.why: Correct. Payment history and utilization are the biggest score factors, so on-time payments and low balances steadily build a stronger credit score.

options.t: Closing all old accounts to cut your history
options.why: Closing all old accounts shortens credit history and cuts available credit, which usually raises utilization and lowers your score.

q: What is a deferred payment plan?

options.t: A gift of free goods that the seller hands out to every customer who comes in
options.why: A gift of free goods is a giveaway. A deferred payment plan is a credit arrangement where you buy now and pay later.

options.t: A tax refund paid by the state to a person who files a return on time each and every year
options.why: A tax refund is money returned by the government. A deferred payment plan is a seller's offer, not a government payment.

options.t: An interest-free loan that you never have to repay to the seller in any case
options.why: A deferred payment plan is not a gift loan. You must pay the seller what you owe, and many plans charge interest if unpaid on time.

options.t: An offer to pay later, sometimes with interest charged if not paid in full on time
options.why: Correct. A deferred payment plan lets you buy now and pay later, often with interest charged if the balance is not paid in full by the due date.

q: A 'no interest for 12 months' offer charges back interest if not paid in full by month 12. What is the risk?

options.t: The offer improves your credit score automatically
options.why: Such an offer does not automatically improve your credit score. Credit history depends on how you manage the account, not on the promotion.

options.t: The seller pays your interest for the whole year
options.why: The seller does not pay your interest. With deferred interest, the interest builds in the background and is charged to you if you miss the deadline.

options.t: A large interest charge if you miss the deadline
options.why: Correct. With deferred interest, if any balance remains after month 12, interest is charged back to the purchase date, which can mean a large sudden cost.

options.t: No risk at all if you miss the final payment date
options.why: Missing the final date carries real risk. The retroactive interest can be added to your balance, so the offer is risky if unpaid in time.

q: Two loans of $10,000 have the same rate. One has a 3-year term and the other 5 years. Which has the lower total interest?

options.t: They cost the same
options.why: The two loans do not cost the same. With the same rate, the longer term accrues interest for more months and costs more overall.

options.t: The 3-year loan
options.why: Correct. At the same rate, a shorter 3-year term means the balance falls faster and interest accrues for fewer months, so total interest is lower.

options.t: The 5-year loan
options.why: The 5-year loan has smaller payments but higher total interest, because the principal is outstanding longer. Its total cost is greater, not lower.

options.t: Neither loan costs
options.why: Both loans charge interest at a stated rate, so each costs something. The 3-year loan simply costs less overall than the 5-year loan.

q: What is a copayment?

options.t: A fixed amount you pay for a covered service at the time of care
options.why: Correct. A copayment is a fixed fee, such as $25, that you pay at the time of a covered service while the insurer pays the rest.

options.t: A fine for missing an appointment with a doctor or clinic
options.why: A fine for a missed appointment is a no-show or cancellation fee, which is separate from the copay charged for covered services.

options.t: The yearly total you pay for insurance, billed in equal monthly parts
options.why: The yearly total you pay for insurance, billed in monthly parts, is the premium. A copayment is paid per service when care is received.

options.t: The insurer's profit on each policy that it sells in a year
options.why: The insurer's profit on policies is not the copayment. A copay is the customer's fixed share of the cost of a covered service.

q: A plan has a $25 copay per doctor visit. You have 4 visits. What do you pay in copays?

options.why: $29 adds 4 to $25, which is not how copays work. Each visit costs $25, so you multiply the copay by the number of visits.
$25 is the copay for only one visit. With 4 visits you owe this amount four times.
$6.25 comes from dividing $25 by 4. The copay applies to each visit, so you multiply rather than divide.
Correct. Each visit costs a $25 copay, so 4 visits cost 4 x $25 = $100.

q: After the deductible, a $2,000 bill has 20% coinsurance. How much do you pay?

options.why: $1,600 is the insurer's share, which is 80% of $2,000. Coinsurance means you pay the 20% that remains.
$40 would be 2% of $2,000, a decimal slip. Twenty percent of $2,000 is much larger.
Correct. With 20% coinsurance you pay 20% of the bill: 0.20 x $2,000 = $400, and the insurer covers the other $1,600.
Paying the full $2,000 ignores insurance. After the deductible, coinsurance means the insurer covers its percentage, so you owe only your share.

q: What is long-term care insurance?

options.t: Coverage for home theft and burglary losses
options.why: Theft and burglary losses are covered by homeowners or renters insurance. Long-term care insurance covers personal care needs, not property.

options.t: Coverage for a short hospital stay only, no home
options.why: Short hospital stays fall under health insurance. Long-term care insurance covers extended help with daily living, often over months or years.

options.t: Coverage for car repairs after a bad accident
options.why: Car repairs after an accident belong to auto insurance. Long-term care insurance has nothing to do with vehicles.

options.t: Coverage for extended care such as nursing homes
options.why: Correct. Long-term care insurance pays for extended services such as nursing homes, assisted living or home health aides, which regular health insurance often does not cover.

q: Why might someone buy long-term care insurance?

options.t: To avoid ever needing care of any kind in later life
options.why: Insurance cannot prevent the need for care. It only helps pay for care if the need arises in later life.

options.t: To protect savings from the high cost of extended care
options.why: Correct. Extended care can cost tens of thousands per year, and long-term care insurance helps protect retirement savings from being drained by those bills.

options.t: To pay for groceries and other everyday goods each week
options.why: Everyday groceries are regular living costs not paid by insurance. Long-term care policies cover extended care services only.

options.t: To lower their taxes to zero, since premiums are deductible
options.why: Premiums are not a way to cut taxes to zero. Some may be partly deductible, but no deduction brings a tax bill to zero.

q: What is a no-fault insurance state?

options.t: A state where your own insurer pays for your injuries regardless of fault
options.why: Correct. In a no-fault state, each driver's own insurer pays for their injuries up to a set limit regardless of who caused the crash, which speeds up claims.

options.t: A state where only the at-fault driver is paid for injuries by the insurers
options.why: That describes a traditional at-fault system, where the responsible driver's insurer pays. In no-fault states each insurer pays its own policyholder.

options.t: A state where no one needs insurance for their cars on the roads
options.why: Almost every state requires some auto insurance, including no-fault states, so no state lets all drivers go without coverage.

options.t: A state where insurers never pay any claims to any injured driver
options.why: No-fault insurers do pay claims. The term means fault does not decide whose insurer pays for injuries, not that claims are denied.

q: What is gap insurance?

options.t: Coverage for gaps in your teeth that need dental care and braces for children
options.why: Gap insurance has nothing to do with teeth or dental care. It is an auto coverage that handles a loan shortfall after a total loss.

options.t: Coverage for routine repairs and servicing of your car every single year
options.why: Routine repairs and servicing are maintenance costs, sometimes covered by a service contract, not by gap insurance.

options.t: Coverage for gaps in your schedule when you cannot drive to work or to school
options.why: Gap insurance is not about schedule gaps. It covers the money difference between what the car is worth and the loan balance.

options.t: Coverage for the difference between a car's value and what you owe on a loan
options.why: Correct. If a car is totaled or stolen, regular insurance pays only its market value, and gap insurance covers the remaining loan balance.

q: A car loan balance is $18,000 but the car is totaled and worth $14,000. What does gap insurance help cover?

options.t: Nothing at all is owed
options.why: Something is owed. The lender still expects the $18,000 balance, and the insurer pays only the car's $14,000 value.

options.t: The $4,000 difference
options.why: Correct. The insurer pays the $14,000 value, leaving $18,000 - $14,000 = $4,000 owed on the loan, which gap insurance covers.

options.t: The full $18,000 loan
options.why: Gap insurance does not pay the full loan. The regular policy covers the car's value of $14,000, and gap covers only the shortfall.

options.t: A new set of car tires
options.why: New tires are a maintenance item and not covered by gap insurance, which concerns only the loan balance beyond the car's value.

q: What is a stock's volatility?

options.t: How much and how quickly its price moves up and down
options.why: Correct. Volatility describes how widely and quickly a price swings, and high volatility means larger gains or losses over short periods.

options.t: How long the company has existed since it was founded
options.why: How long a company has existed is its age or track record, not the volatility of its stock price.

options.t: How much dividend it pays out each year to owners
options.why: Dividends paid to owners describe income, not volatility. A stock can pay large dividends and still have a stable price.

options.t: How many shares exist in the whole company today
options.why: The number of shares is its shares outstanding. Volatility measures price movement, not share count.

q: Which investment is usually the most volatile?

options.t: A short-term Treasury bill
options.why: A Treasury bill is backed by the US government and has a short term, so its price barely moves. It is among the least volatile.

options.t: A federally insured account
options.why: Federally insured accounts keep their value because of deposit insurance. Their balances do not swing, so they are not volatile.

options.t: A single small-company stock
options.why: Correct. A single small-company stock depends on one business, with less stability and thinner trading, so its price can swing widely.

options.t: A broad bond index fund today
options.why: A broad bond index fund holds many bonds and tends to move gently, so it is far less volatile than one small stock.

q: What does it mean to buy and hold?

options.t: Buying only on margin with money borrowed from a broker
options.why: Buying on margin means borrowing from a broker, which adds risk. Buy and hold is about keeping investments, not borrowing to buy them.

options.t: Buying and selling every day to gain from small moves
options.why: Buying and selling daily is day trading. Buy and hold is the opposite approach of staying invested for years.

options.t: Buying investments and keeping them for the long term
options.why: Correct. Buy and hold means purchasing investments and keeping them through market ups and downs, aiming for long-term growth with lower trading costs.

options.t: Selling after one week of holding your investment
options.why: Selling after one week is short-term trading. Buy and hold needs a long horizon, often years or decades.

q: What is a stock dividend reinvestment plan (DRIP)?

options.t: A plan that sells shares automatically each month or year
options.why: A DRIP does not sell shares on a schedule. It does the opposite by using dividends to purchase more shares.

options.t: A plan that uses dividends to buy more shares automatically
options.why: Correct. A dividend reinvestment plan automatically uses cash dividends to buy more shares, often with no commission, which lets holdings compound over time.

options.t: A plan that sends all dividends from the company to a charity
options.why: A DRIP keeps the dividends invested in the same company rather than sending them to charity. Giving to charity is a separate choice.

options.t: A plan that cancels dividends paid to all shareholders
options.why: A DRIP does not cancel dividends. The company still pays them, and the plan simply turns them into additional shares.

q: A stock pays $1 a share in dividends and you own 50 shares. How much do you receive?

options.why: $0.02 is a tiny number from a decimal mistake. The dividend is $1 per share across 50 shares, so the total is much higher.
$5,000 comes from multiplying by 5,000 instead of 50. The correct total is far smaller than this.
$1 is the dividend for only one share. You own 50 shares, so you receive that amount fifty times.
Correct. Dividends are paid per share, so 50 shares x $1 per share = $50 received.

q: What is a bond's yield?

options.t: The return an investor earns, often shown as a percent of price
options.why: Correct. Yield is the return an investor earns on a bond, often shown as a percent of its price, such as current yield or yield to maturity.

options.t: The date the bond ends and the principal is due back to you in full
options.why: The date the principal is due back is the maturity date, not the yield. Yield is a rate of return.

options.t: The fee paid to a broker when the bond is first sold to you
options.why: The fee paid to a broker is a commission or markup. It is a cost of trading rather than the bond's return.

options.t: The amount borrowed by the issuer when the bond is sold
options.why: The amount borrowed by the issuer is the bond's principal or face value, not the yield an investor earns.

q: What is a savings bond versus a stock?

options.t: Both are ownership in a company, and both pay dividends to all their holders
options.why: Savings bonds are loans to the government, not ownership in a company, and they pay interest rather than dividends.

options.t: Both are loans to the government, and both pay a fixed rate of interest each year to holders
options.why: Stocks are not loans to the government, and they pay no fixed interest. Only the bond part of this statement is right.

options.t: They are the same thing, as both are shares in a firm that pay a yearly dividend
options.why: They are different. A stock is an ownership share in a company, while a savings bond is a debt the government owes you.

options.t: A savings bond is a loan to the government; a stock is partial ownership of a company
options.why: Correct. A savings bond is a loan to the government that pays interest, while a stock is partial ownership of a company and may pay dividends.

q: Which is generally safer for money you need in two years?

options.t: Cryptocurrency and coins
options.why: Cryptocurrency prices can swing sharply in days, so it is a poor choice for money needed in two years.

options.t: A stock pick on margin funds
options.why: Buying a stock on margin uses borrowed money and magnifies losses, which is unsuitable for a short two-year goal.

options.t: A short-term CD or Treasury
options.why: Correct. A short-term CD or Treasury security returns principal and a known interest rate within a short period, so there is little risk of loss by the date needed.

options.t: A single risky stock pick
options.why: One risky stock can fall sharply with no time to recover. With a two-year horizon it is too uncertain to be considered safe.

q: What is a spread in bond or stock trading?

options.t: The difference between the bid and ask prices
options.why: Correct. The spread is the gap between the highest price a buyer will pay (bid) and the lowest a seller will accept (ask), and it is a hidden trading cost.

options.t: The tax on trades of stocks, bonds and funds
options.why: A tax on trades is a transaction or capital gains tax, not a spread, which is a price difference inside the market.

options.t: The size of a company in the stock market today
options.why: A company's size in the market is its market capitalization. The spread concerns the bid and ask quotes of a security.

options.t: The number of shares traded on the exchange daily
options.why: The number of shares traded is trading volume. The spread is measured in price, not in shares.

q: What is a good rule before making a large purchase on credit?

options.t: Choose the card with the largest limit you can get
options.why: The largest limit does not make a purchase affordable. A high limit can tempt you to borrow more than you can repay.

options.t: Confirm you can afford the payments within your budget
options.why: Correct. Before a large credit purchase, make sure the payments fit your budget, including interest, so the debt does not strain your finances.

options.t: Ignore the interest rate and the fees you will pay
options.why: Ignoring interest and fees hides the true cost of credit. Interest can add a lot to the price, so it must be weighed.

options.t: Buy it first and plan the payments later, once bills arrive
options.why: Buying first and planning payments later risks missed payments and debt. Budgeting should come before taking on credit.

q: Why is it wise to review your savings plan once or twice a year?

options.t: Income, costs and goals change over time
options.why: Correct. Income, expenses and goals change over time, so reviewing your savings plan once or twice a year keeps it realistic and on track.

options.t: Plans never need any changes at all, ever
options.why: Plans do need changes. A raise, a new expense or a different goal can all make an older plan out of date.

options.t: Banks require a new plan from every customer
options.why: Banks do not require customers to make new savings plans. Reviewing your plan is a personal habit, not a bank rule.

options.t: Reviews remove the need to save any money
options.why: Reviewing a plan does not replace saving. It checks that your saving amounts still match your goals so you keep saving.

q: A worker earns $18 per hour and works 35 hours in a week. What is her gross pay for the week?

options.why: $18 is her pay for one hour only. She worked 35 hours, so you must multiply the hourly rate by hours worked.
$6,300 comes from a decimal error multiplying by 350. Gross pay is $18 x 35, far less than this.
$53 adds the rate and hours: 18 + 35. Pay is found by multiplying, not adding.
Correct. Gross pay is hourly rate times hours worked: $18 x 35 = $630 before taxes and deductions.

q: What is the main difference between a wage and a salary?

options.t: A wage is paid yearly and a salary is paid hourly, to workers of all kinds
options.why: This reverses the definitions. A wage is paid hourly and a salary is paid as a fixed yearly amount.

options.t: A wage is paid by the hour and a salary is a fixed amount per pay period
options.why: Correct. Wages are paid by the hour, so pay varies with hours worked, while a salary is a fixed amount for each pay period regardless of hours.

options.t: A salary is only for part-time work, while a wage is only for full-time jobs
options.why: Salary and wage are not tied to part-time or full-time work. Either type of pay can apply to both kinds of jobs.

options.t: A wage is always higher than a salary, for the same hours of work done
options.why: Neither is always higher. Which pays more depends on the job, the hours worked and the rate agreed with the employer.

q: A worker's gross pay is $1,200 and deductions total $240. What is her net pay?

options.why: $240 is only the deductions. Net pay is what remains after subtracting those deductions from gross pay.
$1,200 is the gross pay before deductions. Net pay is lower after the $240 is taken out.
Correct. Net pay equals gross pay minus deductions: $1,200 - $240 = $960, the amount she takes home.
$1,440 adds the deductions to gross pay: $1,200 + $240. Deductions are subtracted, not added.

q: Which item on a pay stub shows money withheld for Social Security and Medicare?

options.t: Net pay
options.why: Net pay is the amount left after withholdings, so it is not the line showing money withheld for Social Security and Medicare.

options.t: Gross
options.why: Gross is total pay before anything is withheld, so it cannot show Social Security and Medicare contributions.

options.t: Hours
options.why: Hours shows time worked, not money withheld. It does not itemize any tax deductions on the pay stub.

options.t: FICA
options.why: Correct. FICA stands for Federal Insurance Contributions Act and covers the Social Security and Medicare taxes withheld from your paycheck.

q: What is overtime pay?

options.t: Extra pay for hours worked beyond a standard limit
options.why: Correct. Overtime is extra pay, usually 1.5 times the regular rate, for hours worked beyond a standard limit such as 40 hours a week.

options.t: A bonus for arriving early at work each single day
options.why: A bonus for arriving early is a punctuality incentive. Overtime relates to extra hours worked, not to arrival time.

options.t: Pay for vacation days that you have taken off
options.why: Pay for vacation days taken off is paid time off. Overtime is for additional hours actually worked.

options.t: A tax refund paid at the end of each year to workers
options.why: A year-end tax refund is money returned by the government. Overtime is earned pay from extra hours.

q: A worker earns $20 an hour and receives time and a half for hours over 40. What does she earn for a 44-hour week?

options.why: $880 pays all 44 hours at the regular $20 rate. Overtime hours should earn time and a half, so pay is higher.
Correct. 40 hours x $20 = $800, plus 4 overtime hours x $30 ($20 x 1.5) = $120, so the total is $920.
$960 pays all 48 hours worked at regular pay or miscounts the overtime. Only 4 hours earn the $30 rate.
$800 counts only the first 40 hours and leaves out the 4 overtime hours, which add 4 x $30 = $120.

q: Which is an example of a benefit offered by many employers?

options.t: A parking ticket
options.why: A parking ticket is a fine, a cost to the driver, not a benefit offered by an employer.

options.t: A delivery charge
options.why: A delivery charge is a fee for shipping goods and is not a benefit employers offer.

options.t: Health insurance
options.why: Correct. Health insurance is a common employer benefit, with the employer often paying part of the cost on top of the worker's wages.

options.t: A late fee charge
options.why: A late fee is a penalty for paying after the due date and is a cost, not a benefit.

q: A worker gets a $2 per hour raise on a $16 hourly wage. By what percent did the wage rise?

options.why: Correct. The percent change is the raise divided by the old wage: $2 / $16 = 0.125, or 12.5%.
16.0% comes from mixing up the numbers. Divide the $2 raise by the original $16 wage, which gives 12.5%.
2% takes the dollar amount as a percent. The raise is $2, which is a larger share of a $16 wage.
50% is far too large. A $2 raise on a $16 wage is only one eighth of the old wage.

q: Why does education often affect lifetime earnings?

options.t: Education prevents job changes, since degree holders stay put
options.why: Education does not prevent job changes. It usually opens more job options, so degree holders often have more choices.

options.t: Education lowers all pay, since schooling costs so much time and money
options.why: Education does not lower pay. Though schooling costs time and money, higher education generally leads to higher lifetime earnings.

options.t: Employers ignore skills and look only at the hair color or height
options.why: Employers value skills and qualifications. Hair color and height are not legitimate pay factors and may not be used to discriminate.

options.t: More education and skills can qualify a person for higher-paying jobs
options.why: Correct. More education and skills make workers more productive and qualified for higher-paying jobs, which raises lifetime earnings on average.

q: What is self-employment income?

options.t: A lottery prize won by chance on a ticket at a shop
options.why: A lottery prize comes from chance, not from working. Self-employment income is earned by operating a business.

options.t: Money a person earns by running their own business
options.why: Correct. Self-employment income is the profit a person earns from their own business or freelance work, rather than wages from an employer.

options.t: A tax refund paid by the state to a worker each spring
options.why: A tax refund is money returned by the government, not income earned from running a business.

options.t: Money from a parent's allowance paid to a teen weekly
options.why: An allowance from a parent is a gift of money. Self-employment income is earned from your own work.

q: A freelancer earns $4,000 in a month and sets aside nothing for taxes. What is the likely problem?

options.t: A refund of tax, as freelancers get breaks
options.why: Freelancers do not get tax refunds for skipping payments. They owe self-employment and income taxes, so setting nothing aside is risky.

options.t: No tax obligation at all this year or next
options.why: Freelancers have a tax obligation. Self-employment income is taxed, and estimated payments are usually due quarterly.

options.t: A large tax bill at the end of the year
options.why: Correct. No tax is withheld from freelance pay, so without setting money aside the freelancer may face a large bill, plus possible penalties, at filing time.

options.t: Lower income next year than in this year
options.why: Not saving for taxes does not by itself change next year's income. The issue is an unexpected tax bill, not lower earnings.

q: What is a gig job?

options.t: A government benefit paid out to people who are out of work
options.why: A government benefit for people out of work is unemployment insurance. A gig job is work you perform for pay.

options.t: Short-term or task-based work, often arranged through an app
options.why: Correct. Gig work is short-term or task-based work, such as ride-share driving or delivery, often found through an app, with workers paid per task.

options.t: A volunteer role with no pay at a charity or a local hospital
options.why: A volunteer role has no pay, whereas a gig job pays for each task completed.

options.t: A permanent salaried role with a fixed wage and full benefits
options.why: A permanent salaried role with benefits is a standard full-time job, the opposite of a temporary gig.

q: What is a résumé gap and how should a worker address it?

options.t: A mistake to hide from every employer that you meet
options.why: A résumé gap should not be hidden. Employers notice gaps, and being honest about them builds trust.

options.t: A reason never to apply, as employers hire no one with a gap
options.why: Employers do hire people with résumé gaps. Gaps from school, family or illness are common, and a clear explanation helps.

options.t: A period without work; be honest and explain what you did
options.why: Correct. A résumé gap is a period without paid work. Be honest and briefly explain what you did, such as study, caregiving or volunteering.

options.t: A required legal form that every worker must file with the state
options.why: A résumé gap is not a legal form. It is simply a time period without listed employment.

q: Two jobs offer $40,000. Job A has no benefits; Job B offers health insurance worth $5,000 a year. Which has the higher total compensation?

options.t: Job B, because benefits add value
options.why: Correct. Both pay $40,000, but Job B adds $5,000 of insurance, so total compensation is $45,000 versus $40,000.

options.t: They are always exactly identical
options.why: The two are not identical. Job B includes $5,000 in benefits that Job A lacks, so total compensation differs.

options.t: Job A, because it has fewer parts
options.why: Fewer parts do not make compensation higher. Job A offers salary only, so its total of $40,000 is lower than Job B's $45,000.

options.t: Neither one has any compensation
options.why: Both jobs pay a salary, so each has compensation. Job B simply has more once benefits are included.

q: What is a probation period at a new job?

options.t: A permanent guarantee of keeping the job
options.why: A probation period gives no guarantee of keeping the job. The employer is evaluating whether the worker fits the position.

options.t: A tax break for new workers in the first year
options.why: Probation is not a tax break. It is an employment term and has no connection to taxes.

options.t: A long paid vacation for new workers each year
options.why: Probation is not a vacation. New workers are usually working and often get limited or no time off in that period.

options.t: An initial time when performance is reviewed
options.why: Correct. A probation period is an initial time, often 30 to 90 days, when the employer reviews performance before confirming the job permanently.

q: What does 'take-home pay' mean?

options.t: Pay received after taxes and deductions
options.why: Correct. Take-home pay, also called net pay, is what remains after taxes and deductions are subtracted from gross pay.

options.t: Pay before taxes and any deductions
options.why: Pay before taxes and deductions is gross pay. Take-home pay is lower than that amount.

options.t: The hours worked in each pay period
options.why: Hours worked in a pay period measure time, not money. Take-home pay is a dollar amount.

options.t: A company's profit for the whole year ahead
options.why: A company's yearly profit is a business measure. Take-home pay refers to an individual worker's paycheck.

q: A teen wants a summer job but has no experience. Which step would most improve her chances?

options.t: Skip applications and just wait for a job offer
options.why: Skipping applications and waiting means employers never see her. Jobs go to people who actively apply.

options.t: Refuse every interview that you are ever offered
options.why: Refusing every interview removes her chance to get hired. Interviews are how employers choose new workers.

options.t: Volunteer, build skills and prepare a clear résumé
options.why: Correct. Volunteering and other activities build skills and references, and a clear résumé presents them, which raises hiring chances even without paid experience.

options.t: Apply with no contact details at all on your résumé
options.why: A résumé without contact details prevents employers from reaching her, so it greatly reduces her chances.

q: A consumer sees a $60 sweater on sale for 25% off. What is the sale price?

options.why: $15 is the amount of the discount (25% of $60), not the price. The sale price is the original price minus the discount.
$35 subtracts 25 dollars instead of 25 percent. The discount is a percentage of $60.
$75 adds the discount to the price. A sale lowers the price, so it must go down from $60.
Correct. 25% of $60 is $15, so the sale price is $60 - $15 = $45.

q: Which is an example of an impulse purchase?

options.t: Paying rent on the first day of every month
options.why: Rent is a planned monthly obligation. Impulse purchases are unplanned buys made on the spur of the moment.

options.t: Buying a candy bar at checkout without planning
options.why: Correct. An impulse purchase is an unplanned, spur-of-the-moment buy, such as grabbing candy at the checkout, usually triggered by display or emotion.

options.t: Buying groceries from a planned weekly list
options.why: Groceries bought from a planned weekly list are deliberate, planned purchases, not impulse buys.

options.t: Saving for a bike over months from each paycheck
options.why: Saving over months for a bike is planned, goal-based spending, the opposite of an impulse purchase.

q: A phone costs $480 up front or $25 per month for 24 months. What is the total cost of the monthly plan?

options.why: $480 is the up-front price only. The monthly plan costs more in total because 24 payments of $25 add up to more.
$120 is the difference between the plan and the cash price, not the plan's total cost.
Correct. The monthly plan costs 24 x $25 = $600, which is $120 more than paying $480 up front.
$49 adds 24 and 25. Total cost comes from multiplying the monthly payment by the number of months.

q: What is a unit price?

options.t: The cost per single unit, such as per ounce
options.why: Correct. Unit price is the cost per single unit, such as per ounce or per item, which lets you compare different package sizes fairly.

options.t: The tax on a purchase at the store till
options.why: Tax on a purchase is sales tax. Unit price is about the cost per unit of measure.

options.t: The price after a coupon is applied at checkout
options.why: The price after a coupon is the final or discounted price, not the unit price.

options.t: The total cost of everything in a shopping cart
options.why: The total cost of a shopping cart is the cart total. Unit price is a per-unit value.

q: Why is it useful to keep receipts?

options.t: They raise the item's price, as stores charge a receipt fee
options.why: Stores do not charge for receipts. Receipts record what you paid and do not raise an item's price.

options.t: They prove a purchase for returns, warranties and budgeting
options.why: Correct. Receipts are proof of purchase for returns, warranty claims and tracking spending in your budget.

options.t: They replace warranties and stores' return policies entirely
options.why: Receipts do not replace warranties or return policies. They support them by proving when and where you bought the item.

options.t: They are never needed for returns or for warranty claims
options.why: Receipts are often required for returns and warranty claims, since they prove the purchase.

q: A store sells a 12-pack of juice for $6.00 and a 20-pack for $9.00. Which has the lower unit price?

options.t: The 12-pack at $0.50 each
options.why: The 12-pack costs $6.00 / 12 = $0.50 each, which is higher than the 20-pack's unit price.

options.t: The 12-pack at $0.40 each
options.why: $0.40 is a miscalculation. $6.00 divided by 12 is $0.50 per juice.

options.t: They cost the same per juice
options.why: The two sizes do not cost the same per juice. $0.50 versus $0.45 shows the 20-pack is cheaper.

options.t: The 20-pack at $0.45 each
options.why: Correct. $9.00 / 20 = $0.45 per juice, which is lower than $6.00 / 12 = $0.50, so the 20-pack is the better value.

q: What is a budget category?

options.t: A bank fee charged for using a machine at another bank
options.why: A fee for using another bank's machine is an ATM fee, not a budget category.

options.t: A type of loan from a bank that is repaid in installments
options.why: A loan repaid in installments is an installment loan. A budget category is a planning group.

options.t: A group of related expenses, such as food or transportation
options.why: Correct. A budget category groups related expenses, such as food, housing or transportation, so you can plan and track spending in each area.

options.t: A tax return line that lists the income you earned in the year
options.why: An income line on a tax return is not a budget category, which is used for planning spending.

q: A shopper uses a coupon for $5 off a $40 item with 8% sales tax applied after the coupon. What is the total?

options.why: $43.20 applies the 8% tax to the full $40 price without the coupon. Tax here is applied after the coupon.
Correct. $40 - $5 = $35 after the coupon, and tax is 8% x $35 = $2.80, so the total is $35 + $2.80 = $37.80.
$45.00 adds the coupon amount to the price instead of subtracting it, which is not how a coupon works.
$35.00 is the price after the coupon but before tax. The 8% sales tax must still be added.

q: What is a good first step before making a large purchase?

options.t: Research prices, reviews and your budget
options.why: Correct. Researching prices, reading reviews and checking your budget helps you decide whether the purchase is wise and affordable.

options.t: Ignore your budget and all of the prices
options.why: Ignoring prices and your budget leads to overspending. A good first step involves gathering information.

options.t: Ask a stranger to pay so the cost is shared
options.why: Asking a stranger to pay is unrealistic and not a financial plan. You are responsible for your own purchases.

options.t: Buy immediately without a plan or a budget
options.why: Buying immediately without a plan is an impulse purchase, which can cause regret and debt.

q: A person spends $15 a day on lunch for 20 workdays. How much does she spend in the month on lunch?

options.why: $35 adds 15 and 20. Her spending is the daily cost times the number of days, so multiply.
$150 is only 10 days of lunches. She buys lunch on 20 workdays, so the total must be larger.
$600 uses 40 days or a doubling error. $15 x 20 workdays is lower.
Correct. Daily cost times days gives $15 x 20 = $300 spent on lunch in the month.

q: What is an advantage of paying with cash?

options.t: It is safe from loss or theft anywhere
