options.t: Equity must always change
options.why: Equity does not change in every transaction. For example, borrowing cash changes assets and liabilities, but equity stays the same.

q: A business has assets of $60,000 and liabilities of $22,000. What is owner's equity?

options.why: $60,000 is the total assets, not equity. Equity is what remains after subtracting the $22,000 of liabilities.
$82,000 adds assets and liabilities, which is the wrong operation. Equity is found by subtraction, not addition.
$22,000 is the liabilities, which is what the business owes. Equity is the owner's share after debts.
Owner's equity = assets - liabilities = $60,000 - $22,000 = $38,000. This is the owner's claim after all debts.

q: The owner withdraws $800 from the business for personal use. What happens?

options.t: Cash decreases and owner's equity decreases
options.why: A withdrawal takes cash out of the business and reduces owner's equity through the drawing account. Assets and equity fall by the same $800.

options.t: Liabilities increase and cash decreases
options.why: Liabilities do not increase, because no debt is created. Money simply leaves the business for the owner.

options.t: Cash decreases and expenses also increase
options.why: A withdrawal is not an expense. It reduces equity directly through the drawing account and does not affect net income.

options.t: Cash increases and equity also increases
options.why: Cash decreases when the owner withdraws money, so cash cannot increase. Equity also falls rather than rises.

q: Which principle says a business should record revenue when it is earned, not necessarily when cash is received?

options.t: Materiality
options.why: Materiality concerns whether an item is large enough to affect decisions. It does not determine when revenue is recorded.

options.t: Going concern
options.why: Going concern assumes the business will continue operating. It does not decide the timing of revenue recognition.

options.t: Revenue timing
options.why: This is the revenue recognition principle, also called the realization principle, which records revenue when earned, regardless of when payment is received.

options.t: Cost principle
options.why: The cost principle records assets at what was paid. It does not address when revenue should be recorded.

q: What does the matching principle require?

options.t: Assets match liabilities exactly on every date
options.why: Assets equaling liabilities and equity is the accounting equation, not the matching principle. Matching deals with timing of expenses and revenues.

options.t: All revenue is recorded when cash arrives in full overall
options.why: Recording revenue when cash arrives is cash-basis accounting. The matching principle belongs to accrual accounting and pairs expenses with revenue.

options.t: Each debit matches a credit in the same period
options.why: Equal debits and credits is double-entry. The matching principle concerns pairing expenses with the revenue they help earn in the period.

options.t: Expenses are matched to the revenue they helped earn
options.why: The matching principle requires recording expenses in the same period as the revenues they helped produce, so net income reflects true performance.

q: Under the cost principle, how is land bought for $90,000 that is now worth $130,000 recorded?

options.t: At $40,000, the gain only, not cost
options.why: The $40,000 is only the increase in market value. Under the cost principle, the asset is recorded at what was paid, not at a gain.

options.t: At $90,000, the original purchase price
options.why: The cost principle records land at its original purchase price of $90,000, and it is not adjusted for later market value changes.

options.t: At $110,000, the average of the two
options.why: An average of cost and market value is not used. The cost principle uses actual cost, which is objective and verifiable.

options.t: At $130,000, the current market value
options.why: Recording at market value of $130,000 would violate the cost principle. Historical cost is used because it is documented and objective.

q: Why must a business keep personal and business finances separate?

options.t: Personal expenses are always tax deductible
options.why: Personal expenses are not always deductible. Mixing finances makes it harder to know which costs are truly business expenses.

options.t: The law forbids owners from using any bank
options.why: The law does not forbid owners from using banks. Separate accounts are a good practice, not a legal ban on banking.

options.t: Banks charge less for separate accounts
options.why: Banks do not necessarily charge less. The reason for separation is how accounting treats the business, not bank fees.

options.t: The business is treated as its own unit
options.why: The business entity concept treats the business as separate from its owner, so records show only business activity and give accurate financial statements.

q: Which concept assumes a business will keep operating into the foreseeable future?

options.t: Going concern
options.why: Going concern assumes the business will continue operating into the foreseeable future, so assets are recorded at cost rather than liquidation value.

options.t: Consistency
options.why: Consistency means using the same accounting methods from period to period. It does not assume the business continues.

options.t: Conservatism
options.why: Conservatism says to choose the option that is less likely to overstate assets or income. It is unrelated to the business continuing.

options.t: Full disclosure
options.why: Full disclosure requires reporting all information that affects users' decisions. It does not assume the business will continue operating.

q: A bookkeeper uses straight-line depreciation in year one and a different method in year two for the same asset. Which concept is violated?

options.t: Business entity
options.why: Business entity separates owner and business finances. Changing a depreciation method has nothing to do with that concept.

options.t: Time period
options.why: Time period divides the life of the business into reporting periods. Switching methods is not a violation of that concept.

options.t: Consistency
options.why: Consistency requires using the same methods from period to period so statements can be compared. Changing depreciation methods without reason breaks that rule.

options.t: Cost principle
options.why: The cost principle deals with recording assets at original cost. It does not govern changing a depreciation method.

q: What is the purpose of a chart of accounts?

options.t: To show the profit for each year
options.why: Profit per year is reported on the income statement. The chart of accounts is only a list of accounts, not a result.

options.t: To list the accounts a business uses
options.why: A chart of accounts is an organized list of all accounts a business uses, each with a name and number, making recording and finding entries easier.

options.t: To list the owner's personal investments
options.why: Personal investments of the owner are separate from the business accounts, so the chart of accounts does not list them.

options.t: To record customers' payment history
options.why: Customers' payment history is kept in receivable records. The chart of accounts lists account names and numbers only.

q: Account numbers beginning with 1 in a typical chart of accounts usually represent which type?

options.t: Assets
options.why: In a typical numbering scheme, accounts starting with 1 are assets, followed by liabilities as 2, equity as 3, revenue as 4, and expenses as 5.

options.t: Debts owed
options.why: Debts owed are liabilities, which usually begin with 2 in the chart of accounts, not 1.

options.t: Revenue
options.why: Revenue accounts normally begin with 4 in a typical chart of accounts, not with 1.

options.t: Expenses
options.why: Expense accounts normally begin with 5 or higher, so they are not the accounts numbered with 1.

q: What does a trial balance prove?

options.t: Entries were posted correctly
options.why: A trial balance cannot prove entries were posted correctly. Errors like posting to the wrong account can still leave debits equal to credits.

options.t: Every transaction was recorded
options.why: A trial balance cannot prove every transaction was recorded, since a missed transaction would leave both sides still equal.

options.t: Total debits equal total credits
options.why: A trial balance proves that the total of all debit balances equals the total of all credit balances, which supports the accuracy of the math.

options.t: The business earned a profit
options.why: A trial balance does not show profit. Net income is shown on the income statement, not on the trial balance.

q: A trial balance shows debits of $18,400 and credits of $17,900. Which error would most likely explain the difference?

options.t: A $500 debit went to the wrong debit account
options.why: A debit posted to the wrong debit account would not change the total debits or credits, so the totals would still be equal.

options.t: A $250 credit was posted twice by mistake
options.why: A credit posted twice would make credits larger, but credits here are smaller than debits, so this does not explain the gap.

options.t: Both sides were recorded using the wrong date
options.why: A wrong date does not change amounts, so debits and credits would still be equal. It could not cause a $500 difference.

options.t: A $500 debit was posted without its credit
options.why: Debits exceed credits by $500, which fits a $500 debit posted without its matching credit, since that leaves the credit side short by that amount.

q: A $450 debit was posted as $540 to one account and the credit was correct. What is the difference in the trial balance?

options.t: The trial balance still balances
options.why: The posted debit was overstated by $90 while the credit was correct, so the two sides will no longer balance.

options.t: Debits exceed credits by $90
options.why: The debit of $540 minus the correct $450 = $90 too much, so debits exceed credits by $90 on the trial balance.

options.t: Debits exceed credits by $450
options.why: $450 is the amount of the original entry. The difference is only the error: $540 - $450 = $90, not the full amount.

options.t: Credits exceed debits by $90
options.why: The overstated amount was on the debit side, so debits exceed credits, not the other way around. The gap is $90.

q: A transposition error occurs when two digits are swapped. Which sign suggests this error?

options.t: The difference is always an odd number
options.why: The difference is not always odd. For example, 63 and 36 differ by 27, but 54 and 45 differ by 9, so no odd rule exists.

options.t: The difference equals an account balance
options.why: A difference equal to an account balance suggests an omitted entry or a one-sided posting, not a transposition error.

options.t: The difference is always exactly $1
options.why: Transposed digits give differences such as 9, 18, 27, and so on, not always $1. The difference is a multiple of 9.

options.t: The difference is evenly divisible by 9
options.why: Swapping two digits changes a number by a multiple of 9, so a trial balance difference divisible by 9 hints at a transposition error.

q: Which transaction increases both assets and owner's equity?

options.t: The owner puts more cash into the business
options.why: The owner investing cash raises cash, an asset, and raises owner's equity by the same amount, so both assets and equity increase.

options.t: The business borrows money from a bank loan
options.why: Borrowing from a bank increases cash and also increases a liability, not equity. Equity stays unchanged in this case.

options.t: The business buys supplies for cash today
options.why: Buying supplies for cash swaps one asset for another. Total assets and equity stay the same.

options.t: The business pays a utility bill in cash
options.why: Paying a utility bill decreases cash and equity through an expense. It reduces both rather than increasing them.

q: Which transaction does NOT change total assets?

options.t: Paying a supplier's invoice
options.why: Paying a supplier's invoice reduces cash and also reduces accounts payable, so total assets fall.

options.t: Buying a computer for cash
options.why: Buying a computer for cash swaps one asset, cash, for another, equipment, so total assets stay the same.

options.t: Receiving cash for services
options.why: Receiving cash for services raises cash and revenue, so total assets increase.

options.t: Borrowing money from a bank
options.why: Borrowing from a bank raises cash and also raises liabilities, so total assets increase.

q: What does the term 'revenue' mean?

options.t: Costs paid to run the business each month
options.why: Costs paid to run the business are expenses. Revenue is the opposite and is the income earned.

options.t: Money borrowed from a bank for a firm
options.why: Money borrowed is a liability, a loan to be repaid. It is not income, so it is not revenue.

options.t: Income from selling goods or services
options.why: Revenue is income earned from selling goods or services to customers and increases owner's equity.

options.t: Money invested by the owner of the firm
options.why: Money invested by the owner is capital, which is part of equity. It is not earned from customers, so it is not revenue.

q: What does the term 'expense' mean?

options.t: A resource the business owns now
options.why: A resource the business owns is an asset, not an expense. Expenses are costs that decrease equity.

options.t: A cost incurred to earn revenue
options.why: An expense is a cost incurred to earn revenue, such as rent, wages, or utilities, and it reduces owner's equity.

options.t: Money earned from customers
options.why: Money earned from customers is revenue, which is the opposite of an expense.

options.t: An amount owed to a supplier
options.why: An amount owed to a supplier is a liability such as accounts payable. An expense is a cost, not a debt.

q: What is net income?

options.t: Cash minus bills owed
options.why: Cash minus bills owed is not net income. Net income is measured from revenue and expenses and not from cash balances.

options.t: Revenue plus expenses
options.why: Adding expenses to revenue would raise profit with every cost. Expenses must be subtracted from revenue.

options.t: Revenue minus expenses
options.why: Net income is revenue minus expenses for a period. A positive result is a profit, and a negative result is a net loss.

options.t: Assets minus liabilities
options.why: Assets minus liabilities gives owner's equity at a point in time, not income earned over a period.

q: If expenses are greater than revenue for a period, the business has a:

options.t: Gross margin
options.why: Gross margin is sales minus cost of goods sold, which is a positive measure. It does not describe expenses exceeding revenue.

options.t: Net profit
options.why: Net profit means revenue exceeds expenses. Here the opposite occurs, so the business does not have a profit.

options.t: Equity gain
options.why: An equity gain is not an accounting term for this result. Expenses above revenue reduce equity as a loss.

options.t: Net loss
options.why: When expenses exceed revenue, the business has a net loss, which reduces owner's equity for the period.

q: What is the accounting cycle's first step?

options.t: Analyze transactions from source documents
options.why: The cycle begins by analyzing transactions from source documents such as receipts and invoices, which supports journalizing and posting.

options.t: Prepare the final financial statements
options.why: Preparing final financial statements comes after journalizing, posting, and adjustments. It is a later step in the cycle.

options.t: Prepare the post-closing trial balance
options.why: The post-closing trial balance is the last step of the cycle. It follows closing the temporary accounts.

options.t: Close the temporary accounts at year end
options.why: Closing temporary accounts is done at the end of the period, after statements, so it is not the first step.

q: Which is a source document?

options.t: A trial balance
options.why: A trial balance is an internal report prepared from ledger balances. It is not evidence of an original transaction.

options.t: A sales receipt
options.why: A sales receipt is original evidence of a transaction, so it is a source document used to record the sale in the books.

options.t: A chart of accounts
options.why: A chart of accounts lists account names and numbers. It is a reference tool, not proof of a transaction.

options.t: A balance sheet
options.why: A balance sheet is a financial statement made at the end of the process. It is not a source document.

q: Where are transactions first recorded in chronological order?

options.t: The ledger
options.why: The ledger holds accounts organized by account, not by date. Transactions are posted to it after being recorded in the journal.

options.t: The sales log
options.why: A sales log is a special record of sales only. It is not the book of original entry for all transactions.

options.t: The trial list
options.why: A trial list is not a standard accounting record. The trial balance lists account balances rather than recording transactions.

options.t: The journal
options.why: The journal is the book of original entry, where transactions are recorded in date order before being posted to ledger accounts.

q: What is posting?

options.t: Moving journal entries to the ledger
options.why: Posting transfers amounts from the journal to the matching ledger accounts, which is how the ledger gets updated with every transaction after it is first recorded in the journal.

options.t: Mailing invoices to customers monthly
options.why: Mailing invoices is a billing and sales task, not an accounting cycle step; invoices are source documents that are later journalized, not the act of posting itself.

options.t: Printing the financial statements
options.why: Printing financial statements happens near the end of the accounting cycle, after posting, the trial balance and adjustments, so it is a reporting step and not posting.

options.t: Writing the first entry from a receipt
options.why: Writing the first entry from a receipt describes journalizing, which comes before posting; posting only begins once the journal entry already exists and is ready to copy.

q: Which is the correct order of the first three steps of the accounting cycle?

options.t: Post, analyze, journalize
options.why: Posting before analyzing makes no sense, because you cannot post a transaction to the ledger until you have analyzed it and journalized it first, so this order fails.

options.t: Journalize, close, post
options.why: Closing happens at the end of the cycle, after adjusting and the statements, so placing close second ahead of post breaks the sequence of the accounting cycle steps.

options.t: Analyze, journalize, post
options.why: The cycle starts by analyzing the source document, then journalizing the transaction, then posting the journal entry to the ledger accounts, so this is the correct order.

options.t: Post, journalize, analyze
options.why: Posting and journalizing come before analyzing here, which is backwards because a transaction must first be analyzed to know which accounts and amounts to record.

q: What is the difference between cash-basis and accrual-basis accounting?

options.t: Cash basis requires double entry of all items
options.why: Double entry is used under both cash and accrual methods, so requiring it is not what separates them; the real difference is timing of recognition for revenue and expenses.

options.t: Accrual records when earned; cash when money moves
options.why: Accrual accounting records revenue when earned and expenses when incurred, while cash basis records them only when cash is received or paid, which is the key timing difference.

options.t: Cash basis records only assets and nothing else overall
options.why: Both methods record assets and other accounts; cash basis is simply less complete and skips receivables and payables, so claiming it records only assets is not accurate.

options.t: Accrual ignores unpaid bills; cash records them
options.why: This reverses the methods: accrual records unpaid bills as payables when incurred, while cash basis ignores them until cash is paid out to the vendor later on.

q: A salon provides a service on March 28 and is paid on April 5. Under accrual accounting, when is the revenue recorded?

options.t: March 28
options.why: Under accrual accounting revenue is recorded when earned, which is when the service was performed on March 28, even though the cash payment did not arrive until April 5.

options.t: April 5
options.why: April 5 is when cash was received, which matters under cash-basis accounting, but accrual accounting records revenue when the service is performed, not when the money arrives.

options.t: Both months
options.why: Revenue is recognized once, in the period it is earned; recording it in both March and April would double count the same $ sale and overstate total income.

options.t: Either month
options.why: Accrual accounting follows the revenue recognition principle, which gives a definite answer; revenue cannot be placed in whichever month is convenient for the business owner.

q: An electric bill arrives on December 28 but is not paid until January 10. Under accrual accounting, the expense belongs to:

options.t: Both months
options.why: An expense is recorded in one period only; splitting one December bill across December and January would double count the cost and overstate expenses overall for the two months.

options.t: No month
options.why: Every expense must land in some period; the bill was incurred, so under accrual accounting it cannot belong to no month and simply be left out of the books.

options.t: January
options.why: January is when the bill is paid in cash, which is the cash-basis answer; accrual accounting records the expense when the service was used or incurred, not when paid.

options.t: December
options.why: Accrual accounting matches expenses to the period in which they are incurred, so the electricity used in December is a December expense even though payment happens in January.

q: What is a compound journal entry?

options.t: An entry that corrects a mistake
options.why: An entry that corrects a mistake is a correcting entry, not a compound entry; compound entries are defined by how many accounts they touch, not by their purpose.

options.t: An entry that is repeated each month
options.why: An entry repeated each month is a recurring entry, such as monthly rent; being repeated does not make an entry compound, which depends on the number of accounts affected.

options.t: An entry with more than two accounts
options.why: A compound journal entry affects more than two accounts, with total debits still equal to total credits, such as a sale paid partly in cash and partly on credit.

options.t: An entry that earns interest each month
options.why: Interest-earning is unrelated to how an entry is structured; a compound entry is simply one that involves three or more accounts, not one that earns anything each month.

q: What is the purpose of a general ledger?

options.t: To record the original source of each transaction
options.why: The original source of each transaction is a source document like an invoice or receipt, while the journal is the book of original entry; the ledger holds summarized accounts.

options.t: To list daily sales only, and nothing else at all
options.why: The ledger holds every account, not just sales, so limiting it to daily sales is wrong; daily sales are typically tracked in a sales journal or register.

options.t: To hold all accounts and their balances in one place
options.why: The general ledger collects every account, such as cash, receivables and revenue, with running balances, so it is the central record used to prepare the trial balance and statements.

options.t: To store customer contact details and addresses
options.why: Customer contact details belong in a customer master file or CRM system; the general ledger holds financial account balances, not names and addresses for mailing purposes.

q: What is a contra account?

options.t: An account that is always zero or negative
options.why: A contra account can carry a normal balance opposite to its parent but is not always zero or negative; for example, Accumulated Depreciation normally has a credit balance of real size.

options.t: An account used only by the auditors
options.why: Contra accounts are used by the company in routine bookkeeping, not only by auditors; examples such as Allowance for Doubtful Accounts appear in the regular ledger and statements.

options.t: An account for owner withdrawals only
options.why: Owner withdrawals go in a Drawing account, which reduces equity, but that is a different equity account type and is not what the term contra account means in general.

options.t: An account that offsets another account
options.why: A contra account has a normal balance opposite its related account and offsets it, like Accumulated Depreciation reducing equipment or Sales Returns reducing sales revenue to a net figure.

q: Which accounts are called temporary accounts?

options.t: Cash and accounts receivable balances
options.why: Cash and accounts receivable are assets, which are permanent accounts whose balances carry forward into the next period rather than being reset to zero by closing entries.

options.t: Revenue, expense and drawing accounts
options.why: Revenue, expense and drawing accounts are temporary because they measure activity for one period, and their balances are closed to zero at period end so the next period starts fresh.

options.t: Any account with a very small balance
options.why: An account is temporary because of its type and function, not because its balance is small; a tiny asset balance still carries over and remains a permanent account.

options.t: Asset, liability and equity accounts
options.why: Asset, liability and equity accounts are permanent (real) accounts because their balances carry over from period to period and appear on the balance sheet, so they are not closed.

q: Why are temporary accounts closed at period end?

options.t: So each new period starts at zero
options.why: Closing resets revenue, expense and drawing accounts to zero so each new period starts with a clean slate and income is measured only for that period, which is the purpose.

options.t: So that they cannot be audited
options.why: Closing has nothing to do with preventing audits; closed accounts remain fully available in the records, and auditors still examine the closing entries along with everything else.

options.t: To increase the cash balance owed
options.why: Closing does not raise any cash balance or create amounts owed; it only transfers temporary balances to equity, and cash is affected by actual receipts and payments instead.

options.t: To remove assets from the ledger
options.why: Closing entries affect temporary accounts and equity, not assets; assets are permanent accounts that stay on the books and are never removed through the closing process.

q: A business has revenue of $52,000 and expenses of $41,500. After closing, what increases by the net income?

options.t: Accounts payable
options.why: Accounts payable is a liability that changes with purchases on credit and payments, not with net income; closing entries do not touch it, so it is unaffected here.

options.t: Owner's capital
options.why: Net income of $52,000 less $41,500 is $10,500, and closing entries transfer that amount to Owner's Capital, increasing owner's equity by exactly the profit earned.

options.t: Total expenses
options.why: Total expenses are temporary account balances that are closed to zero, so they fall to zero after closing rather than increase by net income of $10,500.

options.t: Cash on hand
options.why: Cash changes only through actual receipts and payments; closing entries are bookkeeping transfers between accounts and do not change the cash balance by the net income figure.

q: What is the purpose of adjusting entries?

options.t: To close the revenue accounts to zero first
options.why: Closing entries, not adjusting entries, bring revenue accounts to zero at period end, and they come after adjusting; adjustments exist to update accounts and not to clear them.

options.t: To erase mistakes from the general journal
options.why: Mistakes are fixed with correcting entries, and erasing from the journal is poor practice; adjusting entries instead update accounts for accruals, deferrals and estimates at period end.

options.t: To increase the cash account balance at year end
options.why: Adjusting entries are not meant to raise cash; they usually involve non-cash items like depreciation or accrued wages, and cash changes only when money actually moves.

options.t: To put revenue and expenses in the right period
options.why: Adjusting entries apply the matching principle, recording revenue earned and expenses incurred in the proper period even if cash has not moved, so the statements show accurate results.

q: Which of these is an adjusting entry item?

options.t: Purchasing a truck for cash
options.why: Buying a truck for cash is an ordinary transaction journalized when it happens, exchanging one asset for another, so it needs no period-end adjusting entry afterwards.

options.t: Receiving a customer payment
options.why: Receiving a customer payment is a routine transaction recorded when it occurs; it is not an adjustment made at period end to bring accounts up to date.

options.t: Depreciation of equipment
options.why: Depreciation spreads an asset's cost over its useful life and is recorded by an adjusting entry at period end, since no outside transaction triggers it during the period.

options.t: Paying the owner's draw
options.why: The owner's draw is an ordinary transaction recorded when cash is taken out; it is closed at period end but is not itself an adjusting item for the period.

q: What is a prepaid expense?

options.t: A cost paid ahead that benefits later periods
options.why: A prepaid expense is a cost paid in advance, like insurance or rent, recorded as an asset first and expensed gradually as the benefit is used up over later periods.

options.t: A bill received but not yet paid in full
options.why: A bill received but not yet paid is an account payable or accrued expense, which is a liability; a prepaid expense is the opposite, with cash paid before use.

options.t: Income received long before it is earned
options.why: Income received before it is earned is unearned revenue, a liability for the seller; a prepaid expense involves the business paying out cash, not receiving it.

options.t: A cost that is never paid by the business overall
options.why: A cost that is never paid would not be a prepaid expense; prepaid means the business has already paid cash in advance for a benefit to be received later.

q: What is unearned revenue?

options.t: Profit from the sale of old equipment
options.why: Profit from selling old equipment is a gain, which is reported as income; unearned revenue is a liability for cash received where the work has not yet been done.

options.t: Cash received before service is performed
options.why: Unearned revenue is cash received before the service is performed or goods delivered, so it is a liability until earned, like a prepaid magazine subscription or gift card.

options.t: Revenue earned but not yet collected
options.why: Revenue earned but not yet collected is accrued revenue, an asset (receivable); unearned revenue is the reverse situation, where cash arrives before the work is done.

options.t: Money borrowed from a lender or a bank
options.why: Money borrowed from a lender or bank is a loan, recorded as notes payable; unearned revenue arises from customer prepayments for goods or services, not from borrowing.

q: What is accrued revenue?

options.t: Revenue earned but not yet received or recorded
options.why: Accrued revenue is revenue earned by performing work or delivering goods but not yet received in cash or recorded, so an adjusting entry records it as a receivable and revenue.

options.t: Revenue collected in cash on the day of sale
options.why: Cash collected on the day of sale is ordinary current revenue that is already recorded; accrued revenue is earned but not yet collected, so nothing about it is same day.

options.t: An expense paid in advance of its use by the firm
options.why: An expense paid in advance is a prepaid expense, an asset; accrued revenue concerns income earned and not yet received, not costs paid ahead of use.

options.t: Cash received for work that is not yet done
options.why: Cash received for work not yet done is unearned revenue, a liability; accrued revenue is the opposite, where the work is done but payment has not arrived yet.

q: What is accrued expense?

options.t: Income received early in the period
options.why: Income received early in the period is unearned or deferred revenue, a liability; an accrued expense concerns a cost the business owes, not income the business has received.

options.t: An expense paid before it is used
options.why: An expense paid before it is used is a prepaid expense, an asset; accrued expenses are the reverse, where the cost has been used but cash is still owed.

options.t: A cost permanently written off the books
options.why: A cost written off permanently describes a loss or expiry, not an accrual; an accrued expense is still owed and will be paid in cash at a later date.

options.t: An expense incurred but not yet paid
options.why: An accrued expense is incurred in the period but not yet paid or recorded, such as wages earned by employees at year end, so it is recorded as a payable.

q: On December 31, a business owes employees $1,200 in wages that will be paid in January. What adjusting entry is needed?

options.t: Debit Wages Payable and credit Cash now
options.why: Wages Payable is credited, not debited, when the liability is first recorded; debiting it and crediting Cash would imply cash was paid on December 31, which it was not.

options.t: Debit Cash and credit Wages Expense now
options.why: Debiting Cash would increase cash, but no cash was received; the business owes wages, so the entry must record the expense and the liability, not a cash receipt.

options.t: Debit Wages Expense; credit Wages Payable
options.why: The matching principle requires recording the $1,200 as expense in December, so debit Wages Expense and credit Wages Payable, creating a liability until January payment is made.

options.t: No entry until wages are paid in cash
options.why: Waiting until payment in cash would leave December expenses and liabilities understated; accrual accounting requires the adjusting entry at year end so the expense lands in December.

q: A business paid $2,400 for a year of insurance on October 1. What is the insurance expense for the year ended December 31?

options.why: $1,200 would cover six months of the policy, but only three months (October, November, December) have passed, so this overstates the expense for the year ended December 31.
$200 is one month of insurance ($2,400 divided by 12), but three months have been used by December 31, so this understates the expense for the period by a lot.
$2,400 is the full 12-month cost, which would only be expensed after a whole year; at December 31 just a quarter of the policy has expired and been used.
$2,400 divided by 12 is $200 per month, times 3 months from October 1 to December 31 is $600 of insurance expense, leaving $1,800 as a prepaid asset.

q: A tutor receives $900 in advance on June 1 for six months of lessons. By June 30, how much has been earned?

options.why: $900 divided by six months is $150 per month, and one month of lessons (June) has been completed, so $150 is earned and the remaining $750 stays as unearned revenue.
$900 is the total prepayment for all six months; earning all of it would require the full six months of lessons to be completed, not just the first month.
$450 would be three months of lessons, but only one month (June) has passed, so this would overstate the revenue earned by June 30 by $300.
Cash was received, but revenue is earned as lessons are given; one month of lessons has been delivered by June 30, so earned revenue is $150, not zero.

q: What is the adjusting entry for depreciation?

options.t: Debit Equipment, credit Cash for the cost of the asset as a rule
options.why: Debiting Equipment and crediting Cash is the entry for buying an asset, not for depreciation; depreciation does not involve cash and does not add to the asset's cost.

options.t: Debit Depreciation Expense; credit Accumulated Depreciation
options.why: Depreciation spreads cost over time: debit Depreciation Expense to record the period's cost and credit Accumulated Depreciation, a contra asset, rather than reducing the Equipment account directly.

options.t: Debit Accumulated Depreciation, credit Equipment now
options.why: This debit would reduce a contra account and credit the Equipment account directly, which reverses the proper treatment; depreciation expense must be debited to show the cost used.

options.t: Debit Cash, credit Depreciation Expense for the year
options.why: Depreciation never involves cash; crediting Depreciation Expense would also reduce an expense instead of recording one, so this entry has both sides wrong for the purpose.

q: Which adjusting entry would create a liability on the balance sheet?

options.t: Earning unearned revenue
options.why: Earning unearned revenue reduces a liability by moving it to revenue, so it removes a liability from the balance sheet instead of creating one.

options.t: Using prepaid insurance
options.why: Using prepaid insurance moves cost from an asset to an expense, reducing assets; it does not create a liability on the balance sheet at all.

options.t: Accrued wages expense
options.why: Accrued wages expense records wages owed but unpaid, debiting Wages Expense and crediting Wages Payable, which is a new liability on the balance sheet at period end.

options.t: Depreciation expense
options.why: Depreciation expense is recorded with a credit to Accumulated Depreciation, a contra asset that reduces assets; it does not create any liability on the balance sheet.

q: What is the book value of equipment that cost $9,000 and has accumulated depreciation of $3,500?

options.why: $12,500 adds the depreciation to the cost, but accumulated depreciation is subtracted from cost to get book value, so this is the wrong direction for the arithmetic.
$9,000 is the original cost of the equipment; book value is lower because $3,500 of accumulated depreciation has already been recognized against that asset over time.
$3,500 is only the accumulated depreciation to date, which is the amount already used up, not the remaining book value of the equipment still held on the books.
Book value equals cost minus accumulated depreciation, so $9,000 minus $3,500 equals $5,500, which is the remaining undepreciated cost of the equipment on the books.

q: What is the purpose of the worksheet in the accounting cycle?

options.t: To record transactions as they happen daily
options.why: Daily transactions are recorded in the journal as they happen; the worksheet is a period-end tool and is not part of the day-to-day recording of transactions.

options.t: To replace the general ledger book entirely
options.why: The worksheet is only a working paper and cannot replace the general ledger, which remains the formal permanent record of every account in the accounting system.

options.t: To organize adjustments before the statements
options.why: The worksheet is an informal working paper that lays out the trial balance, adjustments and adjusted balances in columns, making statements easier to prepare accurately afterward.

options.t: To send to the bank as the final report each year
options.why: The worksheet is an internal working paper, not a formal report; the financial statements are what get shared with the bank and outside users, not the worksheet.

q: In which order are the financial statements usually prepared?

options.t: Income statement, owner's equity statement, balance sheet
options.why: The income statement comes first because net income is needed by the owner's equity statement, whose ending capital is then used on the balance sheet, so this order is correct.

options.t: Owner's equity, balance sheet, then income statement
options.why: The balance sheet needs the ending capital from the equity statement, and the equity statement needs net income first, so this order puts the steps out of sequence.

options.t: Balance sheet, owner's equity, then income statement
options.why: The balance sheet cannot be finished until the owner's equity statement gives ending capital, and that depends on net income, so the balance sheet cannot come first.

options.t: Balance sheet first, then income statement, then owner's equity
options.why: Starting with the balance sheet fails because it depends on ending owner's equity, which depends on net income from the income statement; the flow runs in the opposite direction.

q: What is the purpose of closing entries?

options.t: To permanently delete old records of the firm
options.why: Closing entries do not delete anything permanently; they zero out temporary accounts, while old records are kept for audits, taxes and legal reasons for many years afterward.

options.t: To move temporary balances into owner's equity
options.why: Closing entries transfer revenue, expense and drawing balances into owner's equity (capital), resetting those temporary accounts to zero so the next period begins with a fresh start.

options.t: To correct errors in the general journal
options.why: Errors in the journal are fixed with correcting entries, not closing entries; closing is a routine end-of-period step, whether or not any mistakes were found earlier.

options.t: To adjust asset values to match market prices
options.why: Assets are recorded at historical cost and adjusted only by depreciation, never to market prices through closing entries, whose only job is resetting temporary accounts to zero.

q: Which account is used as a temporary clearing account during closing?

options.t: Income Summary
options.why: Income Summary is a temporary account used only during closing: revenues and expenses are moved into it, and its balance, the net income or loss, then goes to capital.

options.t: Contra Asset
options.why: A contra asset account like Accumulated Depreciation is a permanent account that stays on the books; it is not used as the temporary holding account during the closing process.

options.t: Unearned Revenue
options.why: Unearned Revenue is a permanent liability account whose balance carries forward to the next period, so it is not a clearing account used while closing the books.

options.t: Receivables
options.why: Receivables are permanent asset accounts that carry forward; the clearing account used while closing is a temporary account created for the process, which is Income Summary.

q: What is the first closing entry?

options.t: Close the cash account to Income Summary
options.why: Cash is a permanent asset account and is never closed; the closing process only involves temporary accounts such as revenue, expenses and drawing, plus Income Summary.

options.t: Close the liabilities to expense accounts
options.why: Liabilities are permanent accounts that are not closed, and they would never be closed into expense accounts; closing only moves temporary account balances into Income Summary and capital.

options.t: Close revenue accounts to Income Summary
options.why: The first closing entry debits each revenue account for its balance and credits Income Summary, which brings the revenue accounts to zero and starts the transfer to equity.

options.t: Close the owner's capital account first
options.why: Closing the capital account first is incorrect, because capital is permanent and is the final destination; revenue and expense accounts are closed through Income Summary before capital changes.

q: What does a post-closing trial balance contain?

options.t: Every account, even closed
options.why: Closed accounts have zero balances, and only permanent accounts are listed; including every account, even revenue and expenses, would defeat the purpose of the post-closing trial balance.

options.t: Only revenue accounts
options.why: Revenue accounts are temporary and have been closed to zero, so they do not appear with balances on the post-closing trial balance, which lists only permanent accounts.

options.t: Only drawing accounts
options.why: Drawing accounts are temporary and closed to capital during closing, so they have zero balances and do not appear on a post-closing trial balance.

options.t: Only permanent accounts
options.why: After closing, only permanent accounts (assets, liabilities and owner's capital) have balances, so the post-closing trial balance lists just those, proving the ledger is ready for the next period.

q: Why is a post-closing trial balance prepared?

options.t: To calculate net income once more
options.why: Net income is calculated earlier, on the income statement and in the closing process; the post-closing trial balance does not recompute it, only checks account balances after closing.

options.t: To confirm debits equal credits again
options.why: The post-closing trial balance verifies that total debits equal total credits after closing entries have been posted, confirming the ledger is in balance before the next period starts.

options.t: To record the next period's sales
options.why: Next period's sales are recorded as they occur in the new period; the post-closing trial balance is a check on the old period's closing, not a place for new transactions.

options.t: To adjust depreciation at year end
options.why: Depreciation is adjusted before the statements are prepared, using adjusting entries; the post-closing trial balance comes after closing and does not make adjustments of any kind.

q: What is a fiscal year?

options.t: The time between two audits each year
options.why: The time between audits is not what defines a fiscal year; a fiscal year is a 12-month accounting period, whether or not an audit happens at the end of it.

options.t: A period that must start on January 1
options.why: A fiscal year can start on any date, such as July 1 or October 1; only a calendar year must start on January 1, so this is too restrictive.

options.t: A period of exactly six months in length
options.why: Six months is a half-year, and a period of exactly six months would not be a fiscal year, which always covers a full twelve-month span used for reporting.

options.t: Any 12-month period used for accounting
options.why: A fiscal year is any 12-month period a business chooses for reporting, such as July 1 to June 30, which often fits a seasonal business better than the calendar year.

q: After adjusting entries, which account would carry a balance on the post-closing trial balance?

options.t: Accumulated Depreciation
options.why: Accumulated Depreciation is a permanent contra asset account, so its credit balance carries forward and appears on the post-closing trial balance after the temporary accounts are closed.

options.t: Owner's Drawing account
options.why: The Owner's Drawing account is temporary and is closed to capital during the closing process, so it has a zero balance on the post-closing trial balance.

options.t: Depreciation Expense account
options.why: Depreciation Expense is a temporary expense account closed to Income Summary at period end, leaving a zero balance, so it does not appear on the post-closing trial balance.

options.t: Service Revenue account
options.why: Service Revenue is a temporary account that is closed to zero during the closing entries, so it does not carry a balance on the post-closing trial balance.

q: If an adjusting entry for accrued revenue is omitted, how are the statements affected?

options.t: Expenses are overstated and assets too low
options.why: Omitting accrued revenue leaves revenue unrecorded, so revenue is understated rather than expenses overstated; the missing receivable also means assets are too low, not expenses too high.

options.t: Revenue, net income and assets are understated
options.why: Without the entry, revenue earned is not recorded, so revenue and net income are understated, and the missing receivable means assets are understated by the same amount of money.

options.t: Revenue is overstated and liabilities understated
options.why: Leaving out accrued revenue means revenue is understated, not overstated; the unrecorded amount is an asset, so liabilities are not affected by this particular omission.

options.t: Only the cash balance is wrong on the books
options.why: The omission affects revenue, net income, receivables and equity, not just cash; cash is unchanged because the accrued amount has not yet been received from the customer.

q: If the adjusting entry for expired prepaid insurance is omitted, what is the effect?

options.t: Expenses are overstated and assets understated
options.why: Omitting the entry means the insurance expense is never recorded, so expenses are understated rather than overstated, and the prepaid asset stays too high instead of too low.

options.t: Liabilities are understated and revenue too low
options.why: Prepaid insurance is an asset and the omission does not involve liabilities; the unrecorded expense also means revenue is unaffected, so neither of these effects follows from it.

options.t: Expenses are understated and assets are overstated
options.why: Without the adjustment, insurance expense is left out, so expenses are understated and net income is overstated, while the prepaid insurance asset stays too high on the balance sheet.

options.t: Revenue is overstated and equity is too high
options.why: Revenue is unaffected by an unrecorded insurance expense; the actual effect is that expenses are understated, which makes net income and equity too high, but not revenue.

q: A business records $3,000 of rent paid in advance as an expense instead of an asset. What is the effect on the current balance sheet if only part has expired?

options.t: Assets are overstated on the balance sheet
options.why: Assets are understated, not overstated, because the unexpired rent was expensed instead of being kept as a prepaid asset, so the balance sheet shows too little for assets.

options.t: Assets and equity are both understated
options.why: Expensing the full $3,000 removes the unexpired portion from assets and cuts net income too much, so both assets and equity are understated at period end by that unexpired amount.

options.t: Liabilities are overstated at period end
options.why: The rent paid has no effect on liabilities, since no amount is owed; the error involves expensing too much, which understates assets and equity rather than overstating liabilities.

options.t: Equity is overstated on the balance sheet
options.why: Equity is understated, not overstated, because expenses were too high and net income too low; recording rent as an expense instead of an asset reduces equity.

q: The adjusted trial balance shows Supplies of $900. A count shows $350 remaining. What adjusting entry is needed?

options.t: No entry is needed for the supplies on hand
options.why: A count shows only $350 left of $900, so $550 has been used up; no entry would leave supplies and expenses misstated for the period, so an entry is needed.

options.t: Debit Supplies $550, credit Supplies Expense $550
options.why: This entry reverses the right accounts: it would increase Supplies and reduce expense, but $550 was used, so supplies should decrease and Supplies Expense should increase instead.

options.t: Debit Supplies Expense $350, credit Supplies $350
options.why: $350 is the amount still on hand, not the amount used; the entry should record the $550 used ($900 minus $350), not the remaining balance of supplies.

options.t: Debit Supplies Expense $550, credit Supplies $550
options.why: Supplies used equals $900 minus $350, which is $550, so debit Supplies Expense $550 and credit Supplies $550, leaving $350 of supplies on hand as an asset.

q: Which statement best describes the accounting period concept?

options.t: Results are reported for equal time periods
options.why: The accounting period concept divides a business's life into equal time periods, such as months, quarters or years, so results can be reported and compared at regular intervals.

options.t: Only profitable periods are ever reported
options.why: Both profitable and unprofitable periods are reported; reporting only profitable periods would be misleading, and the period concept requires showing results for every period regardless of outcome.

options.t: A business reports only once, at closing
options.why: Businesses report at regular intervals throughout life, not only at closing; the accounting period concept exists so that owners and lenders get timely information in between.

options.t: Periods must always be exactly one year
options.why: Periods can be months, quarters or years, and a fiscal year can run any 12 months; the concept requires equal periods, not periods fixed at exactly one year.

q: What is a reversing entry?

options.t: An entry that closes the revenue accounts at year end
options.why: Closing entries clear revenue and expense accounts at year end; a reversing entry does something different, as it cancels a prior adjusting entry at the start of the next period.

options.t: An entry that cancels a customer's order for goods
options.why: Canceling a customer's order is a sales matter handled outside the journal entries; a reversing entry is an accounting entry that undoes a previous accrual adjustment.

options.t: An optional entry that cancels an earlier accrual
options.why: A reversing entry is optional and made at the start of a new period to cancel an earlier accrual adjustment, which simplifies recording the later cash payment or receipt.

options.t: An entry that corrects the trial balance totals
options.why: Trial balance totals are corrected by finding and fixing errors with correcting entries; reversing entries are unrelated to fixing totals and only undo earlier accruals.

q: Which entry is used to fix a mistake after it has been posted?

options.t: A reversing entry type
options.why: A reversing entry cancels an earlier accrual at the start of a new period; it is an optional bookkeeping step and not the usual way to fix a mistake after posting.

options.t: An opening entry
options.why: An opening entry records the starting balances of a new business or new set of books; it does not fix errors in transactions that were previously posted to the ledger.

options.t: A correcting entry
options.why: A correcting entry fixes an error discovered after posting by reversing the wrong accounts and recording the right ones, leaving a clear audit trail instead of erasing anything.

options.t: A closing entry
options.why: A closing entry transfers temporary account balances to equity at period end; it is part of the routine cycle and not a tool for fixing posted mistakes.

q: A bookkeeper debited Utilities Expense for $180 when the bill was for Telephone Expense. How is it fixed?

options.t: Erase the original entry from the general journal book
options.why: Erasing entries destroys the audit trail and is not acceptable once posted; the proper method is a correcting entry that leaves the original and the fix visible in the journal.

options.t: Debit Cash, credit Utilities Expense for the $180 amount
options.why: Crediting Utilities Expense is partly right, but debiting Cash is wrong because no cash moved; the bill was already recorded, so only the accounts debited need to be corrected.

options.t: Debit Utilities Expense, credit Telephone Expense for $180
options.why: This entry moves in the wrong direction: it would debit Utilities Expense again and credit Telephone Expense, doubling the original error instead of moving the $180 to the right account.

options.t: Debit Telephone Expense, credit Utilities Expense for $180
options.why: The $180 should be in Telephone Expense, so debit Telephone Expense and credit Utilities Expense for $180, which moves the expense to the correct account without touching cash.

q: What does a bank reconciliation compare?

options.t: Revenue with expenses for the whole year to date
options.why: Comparing revenue with expenses is what an income statement does to find profit; a bank reconciliation compares cash figures, not the results of operations for the year.

options.t: The company's cash records and the bank statement
options.why: A bank reconciliation compares the company's cash book balance with the bank statement balance, finding differences like outstanding checks, deposits in transit, fees and errors on either side.

options.t: Assets with liabilities at the year end date
options.why: Comparing assets with liabilities is what a balance sheet does; a bank reconciliation is a cash control that explains the difference between two cash balances at a date.

options.t: Two vendors' price lists, compared before ordering
options.why: Comparing vendors' price lists is a purchasing task; a bank reconciliation has nothing to do with prices and instead matches company cash records against the bank's statement.

q: Which item is added to the bank statement balance in a bank reconciliation?

options.t: Deposits in transit
options.why: Deposits in transit are recorded by the company but not yet by the bank, so they are added to the bank statement balance to reach the true adjusted cash balance.

options.t: Outstanding checks
options.why: Outstanding checks have been written but have not yet cleared the bank, so they are subtracted from the bank statement balance, not added to it.

options.t: Bank service charges
options.why: Bank service charges are deducted by the bank and not yet in the company's books, so they are subtracted from the book balance, not added to the bank balance.

options.t: NSF returned checks
options.why: NSF returned checks are customer checks that bounced, and the bank deducted them, so they are subtracted from the book balance rather than added to the bank statement balance.

q: Which item is subtracted from the bank statement balance in a bank reconciliation?

options.t: Bank collections
options.why: Bank collections, such as notes collected on the company's behalf, increase the book balance side of the reconciliation, not the adjustments made to the bank statement balance.

options.t: Deposits in transit
options.why: Deposits in transit are already in the company's books but not yet at the bank, so they are added to the bank statement balance, not subtracted from it.

options.t: Interest earned
options.why: Interest earned is credited by the bank and is added to the book balance, because the company has not recorded it yet; it is not a subtraction from the bank balance.

options.t: Outstanding checks
options.why: Outstanding checks have been recorded by the company but not yet cleared by the bank, so they are subtracted from the bank balance to match the true available cash.

q: A check you deposited was returned by the bank for insufficient funds. How does the company adjust its books?

options.t: Increase cash by the same amount
options.why: An NSF check does not increase cash; the deposit is reversed because the funds never arrived, so the book balance must decrease, not increase, by the check amount.

options.t: Cash falls and receivables rise
options.why: The bank takes the money back, so the company reduces Cash and re-establishes the customer's Accounts Receivable, because the customer still owes the amount for the sale or invoice.

options.t: Decrease payables by the same sum
options.why: Payables are what the company owes its suppliers and are not affected by a customer's bounced check; the entry involves cash and the customer's receivable instead.

options.t: Decrease revenue by the same amount
options.why: Revenue was already properly earned from the sale, and the bounced check does not undo the sale; the customer still owes the money, so revenue is not reduced by it.

q: What is a petty cash fund used for?

options.t: Repaying bank loans
options.why: Repaying bank loans is done by regular check or bank transfer from the main account, since loan payments are large and need proper records, which petty cash is not designed for.

options.t: Buying large equipment
options.why: Large equipment purchases go through purchase orders and the regular bank account with proper approval; petty cash holds a small sum and is not suited to big purchases.

options.t: Small cash expenses
options.why: A petty cash fund pays small, routine expenses such as postage, coffee or office supplies, avoiding the need to write a formal check for each minor cost.

options.t: Paying staff salaries
options.why: Staff salaries are paid through payroll by check or direct deposit with tax withholdings recorded; petty cash is not meant for such large, regular and documented payments.

q: The petty cash fund holds $200. Receipts total $145 and cash on hand is $52. What is the cash short or over?

options.t: $3 short
options.why: Cash should be $200 minus $145 of receipts, which is $55, but only $52 is on hand, so the fund is $3 short, recorded as a debit to Cash Short and Over.

options.t: $7 short
options.why: A $7 shortage would require only $48 in cash, but the expected cash is $200 minus $145, or $55, and $52 is on hand, so the shortage is $3.

options.t: $3 over
options.why: Over means more cash than expected; expected cash is $55 and only $52 is on hand, which is less, so the fund is short rather than over by $3.

options.t: All correct
options.why: The fund does not balance: receipts of $145 plus cash of $52 equal $197, not the $200 fund, so the $3 difference means the books are not all correct.

q: A business discovers that a purchase of equipment for $4,000 on account was never recorded. What effect does the omission have on the accounting equation?

options.t: Assets and liabilities are both understated by $4,000
options.why: The purchase would add $4,000 to equipment (asset) and $4,000 to accounts payable (liability), so leaving it out understates both assets and liabilities by $4,000 each.

options.t: There is no effect because the equation still balances
options.why: The equation still balances because both sides are understated equally, but that does not mean there is no effect; the totals for assets and liabilities are each wrong.

options.t: Assets are understated, liabilities are overstated
options.why: Liabilities are understated, not overstated, because the unrecorded purchase on account would have added a $4,000 payable; assets are also understated by the missing equipment.

options.t: Assets and equity are both understated by $4,000
options.why: The purchase was on account, so it creates a liability, not a change in equity; equity is unaffected by buying equipment on credit, only assets and liabilities are.

q: Which of the following sequences is correct?

options.t: Prepare statements, journalize, post, then close the books
options.why: Statements cannot be prepared before journalizing and posting, since they draw on ledger balances; closing the books also belongs after the statements, so this order is backwards.

options.t: Close, journalize, post, adjust, then prepare statements
options.why: Closing comes at the end of the cycle, not before journalizing, posting and adjusting; closing first would erase balances before the statements could report them accurately.

options.t: Post, adjust, journalize, close, then prepare statements
options.why: Posting requires journalizing first, since posting transfers journal entries to the ledger; this order puts post before journalize, which is impossible, and closes too early.

options.t: Journalize, post, trial balance, adjust, statements, close
options.why: The cycle runs journalize, post, trial balance, adjust, prepare statements, then close, which follows the logical flow from raw transactions to final reports and a reset of temporary accounts.

q: What is a ledger account balance?

options.t: The number of entries posted to the account
options.why: The number of entries posted is a count and says nothing about the amount in the account; the balance is a dollar figure computed from the debit and credit totals.

options.t: Total debits less total credits in an account
options.why: An account balance is the difference between total debits and total credits; a positive result is a debit balance and a negative result is a credit balance.

options.t: The total of all entries, ignoring the side
options.why: Adding all entries regardless of side would produce a meaningless total, because debits and credits move the balance in opposite directions and must be netted against each other.

options.t: The date of the last entry in the account
options.why: The date of the last entry is just a posting reference; a ledger balance is a dollar amount showing the net of debits and credits in the account.

q: What is a debit?

options.t: Money paid to the owner each period
options.why: Money paid to the owner is called a withdrawal or drawing, which is a specific account; a debit is simply the left side of an account, not a payment to anyone.

options.t: A request for payment sent to a customer
options.why: A request for payment sent to a customer is an invoice or bill; in accounting a debit is not a document but an entry recorded on the left side.

options.t: An entry on the left side of an account
options.why: A debit is an entry on the left side of an account; it increases assets and expenses and decreases liabilities, equity and revenue under double-entry bookkeeping.

options.t: An entry on the right side of an account
options.why: An entry on the right side of an account is a credit, which is the opposite of a debit; debits always go on the left side of the T account.

q: What is a credit?

options.t: A loan from a bank to a customer firm
options.why: A loan from a bank to a customer firm is a type of credit extended, but in bookkeeping a credit is an entry, not a loan, on the right side.

options.t: A discount offered to a buyer by a seller
options.why: A discount offered to a buyer is a sales or cash discount, which is a pricing term; the accounting meaning of credit is the right side of an account entry.

options.t: An entry on the right side of an account
options.why: A credit is an entry on the right side of an account; it increases liabilities, equity and revenue and decreases assets and expenses under double-entry bookkeeping.

options.t: An entry on the left side of an account
options.why: An entry on the left side of an account is a debit, the opposite of a credit; credits always go on the right side of the T account.

q: The Cash account has debits of $12,000 and credits of $8,400. What is its balance?

options.t: $3,600 debit
options.why: The balance is debits minus credits: $12,000 minus $8,400 is $3,600, and because debits exceed credits it is a debit balance, normal for the Cash asset account.

options.t: $8,400 debit
options.why: $8,400 is only the total of the credits, not the balance; the balance is the net of $12,000 debits and $8,400 credits, which is $3,600.

options.t: $3,600 credit
options.why: Debits are larger than credits ($12,000 versus $8,400), so the $3,600 difference is a debit balance, not a credit balance, which would be abnormal for cash.

options.t: $20,400 debit
options.why: $20,400 adds debits and credits together, but a balance nets them against each other by subtracting; $12,000 minus $8,400 gives $3,600 debit, not the sum.

q: What is the purpose of a subsidiary ledger?

options.t: To store old financial statements for audits
options.why: Old financial statements are kept in archives or files for audits; a subsidiary ledger instead holds detailed accounts, such as individual customers, that support a control account in the general ledger.

options.t: To record the owner's personal transactions
options.why: The owner's personal transactions should be kept separate from the business under the separate entity concept, and a subsidiary ledger deals with business details, not personal matters.

options.t: To replace the general journal and ledger
options.why: A subsidiary ledger supports the general ledger and does not replace it, since the general journal and general ledger are still needed for the complete double-entry record.

options.t: To hold the detail behind a control account
options.why: A subsidiary ledger holds the detail, such as each customer's account, behind a control account in the general ledger, whose balance should equal the subsidiary ledger total.

q: The Accounts Receivable control account shows $18,500, but the customer subsidiary ledger totals $18,050. What should the bookkeeper do?

options.t: Delete the customer accounts from the books
options.why: Deleting customer accounts would destroy valid records of amounts owed and not fix anything; the difference should be traced, not wiped out by removing accounts from the books.

options.t: Investigate for a posting or addition error
options.why: The control account and subsidiary ledger should agree, so the $450 difference ($18,500 minus $18,050) signals an error, and the bookkeeper should look for a posting or addition mistake.

options.t: Adjust the control account without checking
options.why: Changing the control account without finding the cause only hides the problem, and the real error would stay in either the subsidiary ledger or the control account postings.

options.t: Ignore it because the difference is small
options.why: Even small differences mean the records disagree and may hide a real posting error or fraud, so a $450 gap between ledgers should never be ignored just because it seems small.

q: What is a journal entry's explanation (narration) for?

options.t: To hide the transaction from auditors
options.why: Hiding transactions from auditors is improper; the explanation actually supports auditors by documenting why each entry was made, which makes the books more transparent and reviewable.

options.t: To calculate the account balance
options.why: Account balances are calculated from the debit and credit amounts in the ledger, not from the narration, which is only a written line of description under the entry.

options.t: To describe the transaction in words
options.why: The explanation briefly describes the transaction in words, making the entry understandable to anyone who reads the journal later and supporting the audit trail for each transaction.

options.t: To check the trial balance totals
options.why: Trial balance totals are checked using the account balances in the ledger; the narration is a text description and has no role in checking whether debits equal credits.

q: What is the effect on the accounting equation of paying $500 for rent?

options.t: No effect on the equation at all
options.why: Paying rent does have an effect: cash decreases and rent expense reduces equity, so the equation changes, even though it stays in balance after the transaction is recorded.

options.t: Liabilities rise by $500, assets stay
options.why: Paying rent does not create a liability; it is a cash payment for an expense, so liabilities stay unchanged while assets and equity decrease together by the payment amount.

options.t: Assets increase by $500 in the period
options.why: Paying $500 reduces cash, so assets decrease rather than increase; there is no new asset received that would offset the payment made in cash for rent.

options.t: Assets and equity both fall by $500
options.why: Cash (an asset) falls $500 and Rent Expense reduces owner's equity by $500, so both sides of the equation decrease equally and the accounting equation stays in balance.

q: A business sells $750 of goods on account. What is the effect on the accounting equation?

options.t: Assets and equity both rise by $750
options.why: A $750 sale on account adds Accounts Receivable (asset) and Sales Revenue (equity), so assets and equity both rise by $750 and the equation remains in balance.

options.t: Assets and liabilities both increase
options.why: Liabilities do not change because nothing is owed by the business; a sale on account creates a receivable owed to the business, and revenue increases equity, not liabilities.

options.t: Cash increases by $750 at the time
options.why: The sale was on account, so no cash came in at the time; the asset that increased is Accounts Receivable, and cash rises only when the customer pays later.

options.t: Assets decrease by $750 in total
options.why: Assets rise by $750, not fall, because a receivable is created from the sale; a decrease in total assets would not match a sale that earns revenue.

q: Which of these is a permanent account?

options.t: Sales Revenue
options.why: Sales Revenue is a temporary account that is closed at the end of every period, so it is not permanent and its balance is reset to zero for the next period.

options.t: Accounts Payable
options.why: Accounts Payable is a liability, a permanent account whose balance carries forward from one period to the next and appears on the balance sheet, so it is not closed.

options.t: Owner's Drawing
options.why: Owner's Drawing is a temporary account, closed to capital at period end, so it starts each new period at zero; it is not permanent like asset or liability accounts.

options.t: Rent Expense
options.why: Rent Expense is a temporary account closed to Income Summary at period end, and it starts the next period at zero, so it is not a permanent account.

q: After closing entries, what is the balance in the Rent Expense account?

options.t: Owed
options.why: Owed describes a liability balance, but Rent Expense is a temporary account that is closed during closing entries, so it does not have any amount owed after closing.

options.t: Prior
options.why: Prior balance does not apply because the closing entry removes the balance; the account starts the new period fresh rather than keeping last period's amount in it.

options.t: Total
options.why: The total of the period's rent is moved to Income Summary during closing and does not stay in the account, so no total remains after the closing entries are posted.

options.t: Zero
options.why: Closing entries credit Rent Expense for its full balance and transfer it to Income Summary, so the temporary account has a zero balance and is ready for the new period.

q: What is accounts receivable?

options.t: Cash kept in the business bank account
options.why: Cash kept in the business bank account is an asset called Cash, not accounts receivable, which is specifically a claim for money owed by customers rather than cash on hand.

options.t: Money the business owes to suppliers
options.why: Money the business owes to suppliers is accounts payable, a liability; accounts receivable is the opposite, representing amounts customers owe to the business.

options.t: Money customers owe for credit sales
options.why: Accounts receivable is money customers owe the business for goods or services sold on credit; it is a current asset that is expected to be collected in cash later.

options.t: Money the owner has invested in it
options.why: Money the owner has invested is owner's capital, an equity account; accounts receivable is an asset arising from customers who bought on credit and have not paid yet.

q: What is accounts payable?

options.t: Money kept for emergencies in a reserve fund
options.why: Money kept for emergencies is a reserve or contingency fund, an asset; accounts payable is a liability, an amount owed rather than money the business has set aside.

options.t: Money the business owes suppliers for credit buys
options.why: Accounts payable is the amount a business owes its suppliers for goods or services bought on credit, a current liability that is paid in cash when the invoice comes due.

options.t: Money customers owe the business for goods sold
options.why: Money customers owe the business for goods sold is accounts receivable, an asset; accounts payable is the opposite, an amount the business itself owes to others.

options.t: Money paid to employees each pay period as wages
options.why: Wages paid to employees are recorded as payroll expense, and unpaid wages as wages payable; accounts payable specifically covers money owed to suppliers for credit purchases.

q: What is an invoice?

options.t: A bill listing goods sold and the amount due
options.why: An invoice is a bill from the seller that lists the goods or services sold, quantities, prices and the total amount due, and it is the basis for the buyer's payable.

options.t: A receipt for cash paid on the spot by a buyer
options.why: A receipt is proof of payment already made, while an invoice requests payment that is still owed, so this describes a receipt and not an invoice.

options.t: A list of the company's assets and values
options.why: A list of the company's assets and values is an asset register or part of a balance sheet, not an invoice, which is a bill sent to a customer.

options.t: A tax form filed by a business each year
options.why: A tax form filed annually is a return, such as the Form 1040 or 1120; an invoice is a commercial document between a seller and a buyer for a sale.

q: What is a purchase order?

options.t: A bill sent by the seller later
options.why: A bill sent by the seller after the sale is an invoice, not a purchase order, which is created by the buyer before the goods are ordered.

options.t: A receipt showing goods arrived
options.why: A receipt showing goods arrived is a receiving report, which documents delivery after the order; a purchase order comes first and is sent by the buyer to the seller.

options.t: A buyer's written request for goods
options.why: A purchase order is the buyer's written request to a supplier for goods or services at agreed prices, authorizing the purchase before delivery and the later invoice.

options.t: A check used to pay a supplier's bill
options.why: A check used to pay a supplier's bill is a payment document made after the invoice; a purchase order is the earlier request placed to order the goods.

q: What is a credit memo?

options.t: A document that reduces the amount a customer owes
options.why: A credit memo is issued by the seller to reduce what a customer owes, for example after a return or pricing error, and it lowers Accounts Receivable.

options.t: A document that raises what a customer owes the seller
options.why: A document that raises what a customer owes is a debit memo, the opposite of a credit memo, which reduces the customer's balance instead of increasing it.

options.t: A reminder of an overdue bill from the seller
options.why: A reminder of an overdue bill is a past-due notice or statement; a credit memo is an adjustment document that lowers the amount owed by the customer.

options.t: A form for applying for a bank loan or credit
options.why: An application for a bank loan or credit is a credit application, a customer or borrower form; a credit memo is the seller's document reducing a balance owed.

q: What does 'net 30' mean on an invoice?

options.t: Payment is due in 30 hours or less
options.why: Net 30 refers to days, not hours; it says the full invoice amount is due within 30 days of the invoice date, with no early payment discount offered.
