options.why: Dividends take assets out of the corporation, so retained earnings go down rather than up; they are a distribution of profit already earned.

options.t: They reduce retained earnings
options.why: Dividends are declared out of profits, which reduces the earnings retained by the corporation, so they are subtracted on the statement of retained earnings.

options.t: They have no effect at all
options.why: Dividends clearly affect retained earnings, because they reduce the profits the corporation keeps in the business instead of paying them to stockholders.

q: In a corporation, what are paid-in capital and retained earnings parts of?

options.t: Stockholders' equity
options.why: Paid-in capital (money invested by shareholders) and retained earnings (profits kept) are the two main components of stockholders' equity on a corporate balance sheet.

options.t: Operating expenses
options.why: Operating expenses are costs of running the business listed on the income statement; capital and earnings are balance sheet equity accounts.

options.t: Cost of goods sold
options.why: Cost of goods sold is the cost of merchandise sold, an income statement item, whereas paid-in capital and retained earnings are owners' equity accounts.

options.t: Short-term liabilities
options.why: Short-term liabilities are debts due within a year; paid-in capital and retained earnings are owners' claims, not debts owed to others.

q: What is a footnote disclosure used for?

options.t: To advertise the company to new customers and buyers
options.why: Footnotes are factual disclosures, not marketing, so they are not used to attract customers; advertising has no place in financial statements.

options.t: To correct arithmetic errors found after printing
options.why: Correcting arithmetic errors is done by revising the statements, not by footnotes; footnotes supply explanation and additional detail beyond the numbers.

options.t: To hide unfavorable results from all the readers
options.why: Footnotes are meant to disclose information, not to conceal it; hiding unfavorable results would violate the full disclosure principle and could be fraud.

options.t: To give readers details that prevent misleading them
options.why: Footnotes provide details, such as accounting policies, debts and pending lawsuits, that are needed so readers are not misled by the numbers on the face of the statements.

q: An audit report that states the statements fairly present financial position is called:

options.t: An adverse opinion
options.why: An adverse opinion says the statements do not fairly present the company's position; it is the opposite of a clean report.

options.t: A qualified opinion
options.why: A qualified opinion says the statements are fair except for a specific issue or limit, so it is not a fully clean opinion.

options.t: A disclaimer of opinion
options.why: A disclaimer of opinion means the auditor could not form an opinion, often because of limits on the work, so it gives no assurance either way.

options.t: An unqualified opinion
options.why: An unqualified (clean) opinion states that the statements fairly present financial position in accordance with GAAP, the best result a company can receive from an auditor.

q: An investor wants to compare the profitability of two companies of different sizes. Which tool is best?

options.t: Common-size statements and ratios
options.why: Common-size statements and ratios turn dollar amounts into percentages, so firms of different sizes can be compared fairly, such as profit margin or return on assets.

options.t: The number of employees hired
options.why: The number of employees hired says nothing about profitability and is not a financial analysis tool; it reflects size, not performance.

options.t: The raw dollar totals of net income
options.why: Raw net income totals favor larger firms; a big company usually earns more dollars, so they cannot fairly compare profitability across different sizes.

options.t: The length of the annual report
options.why: The length of an annual report has no relation to profitability and says nothing about how well a company uses its resources.

q: What does GAAP stand for?

options.t: General Auditing and Accounting Procedures
options.why: GAAP does not stand for auditing procedures; it covers accounting principles used to prepare statements, whereas auditing has its own standards (GAAS).

options.t: Guaranteed Annual Accounting Practices
options.why: GAAP stands for accepted principles, not guaranteed practices; no accounting rule guarantees results, and the word 'Guaranteed' is not in the term.

options.t: Generally Accepted Accounting Principles
options.why: GAAP stands for Generally Accepted Accounting Principles, the common rules and conventions US companies follow so their financial statements are consistent and comparable.

options.t: Government Approved Accounting Policies
options.why: GAAP is not set by government approval of policies; it comes from a private standard-setting body and is described as 'generally accepted'.

q: Which organization sets GAAP for businesses in the United States?

options.t: The Federal Reserve Board system
options.why: The Federal Reserve is the central bank that conducts monetary policy and supervises banks; it does not write GAAP for businesses.

options.t: Financial Accounting Standards Board
options.why: The Financial Accounting Standards Board (FASB) is the independent private body that writes GAAP for US businesses and issues accounting standards updates.

options.t: The Internal Revenue Service (IRS)
options.why: The IRS administers tax law and collects taxes; it does not set GAAP, and tax rules often differ from financial accounting rules.

options.t: The Better Business Bureau (BBB)
options.why: The Better Business Bureau is a nonprofit that rates business practices and handles consumer complaints; it has no role in setting accounting standards.

q: Which agency requires public companies to file financial reports with it?

options.t: The Occupational Safety and Health Administration
options.why: OSHA enforces workplace safety and health rules; it does not collect financial reports from public companies.

options.t: The Federal Trade Commission of the U.S.
options.why: The FTC enforces consumer protection and antitrust laws; it does not require public companies to file financial reports.

options.t: The Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC)
options.why: The SEC requires public companies to file annual (10-K) and quarterly (10-Q) reports so investors get reliable information; it was created in 1934.

options.t: The Environmental Protection Agency (EPA)
options.why: The EPA enforces environmental regulations and does not receive companies' financial reports; its focus is pollution and environmental protection.

q: What is an audit?

options.t: An independent check of financial records
options.why: An audit is an independent examination of a company's financial records and statements by a qualified outside party, giving users confidence that the statements are reliable.

options.t: A tax payment made each quarter by a business
options.why: A quarterly tax payment is an estimated tax payment, not an audit; an audit is an examination, not a payment to the government.

options.t: A sales forecast for the next fiscal year
options.why: A sales forecast looks ahead to expected revenue, whereas an audit examines records of past transactions and statements already prepared.

options.t: A daily entry of transactions in the books
options.why: Daily entry of transactions is bookkeeping, done by the company's own staff; an audit is an independent review carried out afterward.

q: What is an internal control?

options.t: A tax deduction allowed by the IRS each year
options.why: A tax deduction lowers taxable income under IRS rules; internal controls are procedures a company uses to safeguard assets and ensure accurate records.

options.t: A rule that sets the company's goods prices
options.why: Setting prices is a marketing and management decision; internal controls are about safeguarding assets and records, not deciding what goods cost.

options.t: A law passed by Congress for all firms and banks
options.why: Congress passes laws such as Sarbanes-Oxley that require internal controls, but a control is a company procedure, not a law.

options.t: A procedure that protects assets and records
options.why: Internal controls are policies and procedures, like approvals and separation of duties, that protect assets, ensure accurate records and help prevent errors and fraud.

q: What is fraud in a business setting?

options.t: An honest mistake in a calculation
options.why: An honest mistake lacks intent; fraud requires a deliberate act, so an innocent calculation error is an error, not fraud.

options.t: A deliberate deception for gain
options.why: Fraud is intentional deception to gain an unfair or illegal advantage, such as falsifying records or stealing cash; the intent to deceive is what separates it from error.

options.t: A late payment to a vendor firm
options.why: A late payment to a vendor is a breach of payment terms, perhaps poor management, but it involves no deliberate deception, so it is not fraud.

options.t: A legal tax deduction by a business
options.why: A legal tax deduction follows the tax law and is allowed; fraud involves deception, such as claiming false deductions.

q: Which is an example of separation of duties?

options.t: The owner signs checks alone with no review at all
options.why: Having the owner sign checks alone with no review removes oversight, so there is no check on misuse; separation of duties requires a second person.

options.t: One person opens mail, and records and deposits cash
options.why: One person opening mail, recording and depositing cash combines custody and record-keeping, which is the opposite of separation of duties and invites theft.

options.t: Everyone shares the same password for the whole system
options.why: Sharing one password removes accountability, because actions cannot be traced to a person; it weakens control rather than separating duties.

options.t: One person records sales and another handles the cash
options.why: Splitting recording and cash handling between two people means one cannot easily steal and hide it, which is the purpose of separation of duties.

q: Why should checks be prenumbered?

options.t: To make checks harder to cash for outsiders
options.why: Prenumbering does not stop outsiders from cashing checks; security features and endorsements handle that, while the numbers help account for every check.

options.t: To save printing costs for the firm each year
options.why: Printing cost savings are not the reason; prenumbering is an internal control, and the number of checks printed has no bearing on savings.

options.t: So missing or unauthorized checks show up
options.why: Prenumbered checks let the firm account for every check in sequence, so any missing, voided or unauthorized check stands out quickly.

options.t: To meet bank interest rules for savers
options.why: Banks do not set interest rules based on check numbers; prenumbering is a company control and has nothing to do with savers' interest.

q: Why should cash receipts be deposited daily?

options.t: To lower the risk of loss or theft
options.why: Daily deposits keep large amounts of cash from sitting on the premises, which lowers the chance of loss or theft and keeps records current.

options.t: To avoid recording revenue until later
options.why: Revenue is recorded when earned regardless of deposit timing; depositing daily does not delay recording and in fact supports prompt records.

options.t: To avoid paying taxes on the cash
options.why: Depositing cash does not avoid taxes; all cash receipts are income and are reported, so deliberately avoiding tax would be illegal.

options.t: To earn extra interest on the cash
options.why: Extra interest is a minor effect and not the main reason; the principal purpose of daily deposits is safeguarding cash from theft or loss.

q: What does the Sarbanes-Oxley Act (SOX) mainly aim to do?

options.t: Regulate food safety in stores and restaurants
options.why: Food safety is regulated by agencies like the FDA; the Sarbanes-Oxley Act deals with corporate financial reporting, not restaurants.

options.t: Improve the accuracy of public company reports
options.why: SOX, passed in 2002 after the Enron and WorldCom scandals, improves accuracy and reliability of public company reports through stronger controls, audits and executive accountability.

options.t: Set minimum wages for all workers across the nation
options.why: Minimum wages are set by the Fair Labor Standards Act and state laws; SOX concerns financial reporting by public companies.

options.t: Create tax brackets for all income earners
options.why: Tax brackets are created by the Internal Revenue Code; SOX does not set income tax rates and focuses on public company reporting.

q: Under SOX, who must certify the accuracy of financial reports at a public company?

options.t: Only the IRS and its agents in the government
options.why: The IRS collects taxes and does not certify a company's reports; SOX places the responsibility on the company's own senior executives.

options.t: The company's competitors, who check them
options.why: Competitors have no duty or authority to certify a company's reports; SOX assigns that responsibility to the company's own senior officers.

options.t: Only the customers who buy goods from the firm
options.why: Customers are not required to certify statements; SOX places that responsibility on the people who run the company and prepare the reports.

options.t: The chief executive and financial officers
options.why: SOX Section 302 requires the CEO and CFO to personally certify that reports are accurate and complete, with criminal penalties for false certifications.

q: What is a whistleblower?

options.t: A person who builds the budget
options.why: Building the budget is a planning job done by managers or accountants; a whistleblower reports misconduct, not creates budgets.

options.t: Someone who reports wrongdoing
options.why: A whistleblower is someone, often an employee, who reports illegal or unethical conduct such as fraud, and SOX protects them from retaliation.

options.t: A person who audits tax returns
options.why: Auditing tax returns is done by IRS agents; a whistleblower reports wrongdoing rather than examining returns.

options.t: A person who repairs equipment
options.why: Repairing equipment is maintenance work and has nothing to do with reporting wrongdoing, which is what a whistleblower does.

q: What does the AICPA Code of Professional Conduct require of CPAs?

options.t: Lowest possible fees for clients
options.why: The code does not require the lowest fees; it requires professional conduct, and cutting fees below a fair level could harm quality of work.

options.t: Loyalty to the client above all
options.why: CPAs owe their duty to the public as well as clients, so loyalty to the client above all would conflict with the profession's public interest duty.

options.t: Integrity, objectivity and due care
options.why: The AICPA Code requires integrity, objectivity, due care and independence, so CPAs act honestly, impartially and with competence in serving the public interest.

options.t: Secrecy about all client matters
options.why: CPAs must keep client information confidential, but not absolutely; they may have to disclose under legal duty, so secrecy about everything is not required.

q: What does the principle of objectivity require of an accountant?

options.t: Being impartial and free of conflicts
options.why: Objectivity requires being impartial, honest and free of conflicts of interest so that professional judgments are not influenced by bias or outside pressure.

options.t: Keeping opinions secret from clients
options.why: Objectivity is about unbiased judgment, not hiding opinions; an accountant is expected to give honest professional opinions to clients.

options.t: Always choosing the lowest numbers
options.why: Always choosing the lowest numbers is a bias, which is the opposite of objectivity; accountants must report fairly rather than lean one way.

options.t: Agreeing with the client at all times
options.why: Agreeing with the client at all times would compromise independent judgment; objectivity means staying impartial, even when the client disagrees.

q: What does confidentiality require of an accountant?

options.t: Telling friends about client profits and losses
options.why: Telling friends about client profits and losses is a clear breach of confidentiality because the information belongs to the client.

options.t: Posting client results online for the public
options.why: Posting client results online makes private information public, which breaches confidentiality unless the client gives permission.

options.t: Not sharing client data without permission or duty
options.why: Confidentiality means not sharing client information without the client's permission or a legal or professional duty, such as a court order.

options.t: Sharing client data with competitors for a paid fee
options.why: Selling or sharing client data with competitors for a fee is a serious breach of confidentiality, regardless of payment, and may be illegal.

q: An accountant is offered a gift worth $500 by a client being audited. What is the best action?

options.t: Decline the gift to stay independent
options.why: Declining the gift keeps the accountant independent and objective; accepting a $500 gift from an audited client creates a conflict of interest.

options.t: Accept it and give a better opinion
options.why: Accepting a gift in return for a better opinion would be a bribe and would destroy objectivity, which is unethical and likely illegal.

options.t: Accept it only if the client asks
options.why: Accepting the gift because the client asks does not remove the conflict; pressure from the client makes independence even more doubtful.

options.t: Accept it and say nothing to anyone
options.why: Accepting the gift secretly adds concealment to the conflict of interest; hiding it makes the ethical problem worse, not better.

q: A manager asks an accountant to delay recording $15,000 of expenses so a loan application looks better. What should the accountant do?

options.t: Do it because the manager is in charge
options.why: Following the manager's order would mean knowingly misstating expenses; accountants owe a duty to accuracy and the public, not just to superiors.

options.t: Refuse and record them in the proper period
options.why: The accountant should refuse and record the $15,000 of expenses in the period incurred, as the matching principle requires, even if the manager objects.

options.t: Delete the receipts from the books and files
options.why: Deleting receipts destroys evidence and compounds the wrongdoing; it is falsifying records and does not fix the problem of recording expenses.

options.t: Record half of them now and half later on
options.why: Splitting the expenses between periods still misstates results in both periods; the full amount belongs in the period when incurred.

q: Which situation shows a conflict of interest?

options.t: An accountant uses accounting software at work daily
options.why: Using accounting software is a normal part of an accountant's work and creates no competing interest, so it is not a conflict of interest.

options.t: An accountant completes yearly education courses
options.why: Completing education courses is professional development and creates no competing loyalty; it is a requirement for many accountants.

options.t: An accountant meets a filing deadline on time each year
options.why: Meeting a filing deadline is a basic duty and involves no competing interest, so it is not a conflict.

options.t: An accountant approves the books of a spouse's company
options.why: Approving the books of a spouse's company puts personal loyalty against professional impartiality, which creates a conflict of interest and threatens objectivity.

q: How long should businesses generally keep tax records?

options.t: Until the next sale is made at the shop
options.why: Sales activity has no link to how long tax records must be kept; retention is set by tax law, not by the next sale.

options.t: Records need not be kept after filing
options.why: Records must be kept after filing, since the IRS may audit a return later; discarding them could make it impossible to support deductions.

options.t: At least three years, sometimes longer
options.why: The IRS generally has three years from the filing date to audit a return, so records should be kept at least that long, longer in some cases.

options.t: One month at most after the return is filed
options.why: Keeping records for one month would leave the business unable to support its return if audited; the usual audit window is much longer.

q: What is a code of ethics?

options.t: A written set of standards for conduct
options.why: A code of ethics is a written set of principles and standards of conduct that guide employees or professionals in making honest and fair decisions.

options.t: A summary of the financial results
options.why: A summary of financial results is a financial statement; a code of ethics deals with behavior and values rather than numbers.

options.t: A computer program that handles payroll
options.why: Payroll software processes pay; a code of ethics is a document stating rules of conduct, not a computer program.

options.t: A list of tax rules for the state
options.why: Tax rules are set by tax law; a code of ethics is a set of conduct standards adopted by a profession or company.

q: What is the purpose of the materiality concept?

options.t: All items must be reported separately, whatever their size
options.why: Reporting every item separately regardless of size would clutter statements; materiality allows small, insignificant items to be grouped or expensed.

options.t: Only large companies need statements prepared each year
options.why: Materiality does not decide which companies prepare statements; it concerns the significance of individual items, not the size of the company.

options.t: Revenue is reported at market value in all cases of sales
options.why: Reporting at market value is not materiality; revenue is generally recognized under the cost principle and revenue recognition rules, not market value.

options.t: Only items large enough to matter need separate reporting
options.why: The materiality concept says an item needs separate reporting only if it is large enough to influence users' decisions, so small amounts can be handled simply.

q: A $20 stapler bought by a large company is expensed immediately instead of depreciated. Which concept supports this?

options.t: Cost principle
options.why: The cost principle says assets are recorded at purchase cost; it does not explain why a trivial purchase is expensed immediately.

options.t: Materiality
options.why: Materiality allows trivial items like a $20 stapler to be expensed at once, since depreciating it would not change any decision a reader makes.

options.t: Going concern
options.why: Going concern assumes the business will continue operating; it does not tell you how to treat a very small purchase.

options.t: Matching
options.why: Matching links expenses to the revenues they help earn; it does not justify skipping depreciation, which is explained by materiality instead.

q: The conservatism principle says that when in doubt, an accountant should:

options.t: Hide the doubt from users of the statements
options.why: Hiding doubt from users violates full disclosure; conservatism does not allow concealing uncertainty, only choosing cautious estimates.

options.t: Pick the option least likely to overstate results
options.why: Conservatism says when in doubt, choose the option least likely to overstate assets or income, so that financial statements are not overly optimistic.

options.t: Avoid recording any uncertain items at all times
options.why: Conservatism does not mean ignoring uncertain items; likely losses are recorded and disclosed rather than avoided entirely.

options.t: Choose the option that raises income the most
options.why: Choosing the option that raises income the most is the opposite of conservatism, since it overstates results.

q: What does the full disclosure principle require?

options.t: Reporting all information users would need
options.why: Full disclosure requires reporting all information that would be important to users making decisions, usually in the statements or the notes.

options.t: Naming every customer in the financial notes
options.why: Naming every customer is not needed and could expose private details; disclosure only covers information relevant to users' decisions.

options.t: Publishing all internal memos of the firm
options.why: Internal memos are not relevant to outside users and are not published; full disclosure applies to material financial information.

options.t: Reporting only the profitable results of a year
options.why: Reporting only profitable results would hide bad news and violates full disclosure, which requires a balanced picture of the company.

q: A lawsuit against a company is likely to cost $200,000. How should it be reported?

options.t: Ignored until paid, as uncertain
options.why: Ignoring a probable $200,000 loss would understate expenses and liabilities; GAAP requires recording a loss that is likely and can be estimated.

options.t: Recorded as revenue in the period
options.why: A lawsuit cost is not revenue; recording it as revenue would reverse its effect and overstate the company's income.

options.t: Recorded as a loss and disclosed
options.why: When a loss is probable and can be estimated, it is recorded in the period and also disclosed in the notes, following conservatism and full disclosure.

options.t: Hidden from the notes of the report
options.why: Hiding the lawsuit from the notes would mislead users and violate full disclosure; significant contingencies must be reported.

q: What does IFRS stand for?

options.t: International Fiscal Rules for Stocks and Bonds
options.why: IFRS is not about stocks and bonds rules; it is a set of accounting standards used in many countries to prepare financial statements.

options.t: Internal Financial Records System of a firm
options.why: IFRS is not an internal records system for a single firm; it is a set of international rules that many countries use for reporting.

options.t: Independent Federal Revenue Service office
options.why: IFRS is not a revenue service office; tax collection is handled by agencies such as the IRS, while IFRS governs financial reporting.

options.t: International Financial Reporting Standards
options.why: IFRS stands for International Financial Reporting Standards, issued by the International Accounting Standards Board and used in more than 100 countries.

q: Why does the existence of IFRS and GAAP create a challenge for global companies?

options.t: IFRS bans the use of inventory in all countries
options.why: IFRS does not ban inventory; both frameworks allow inventory accounting, though they differ on some methods such as LIFO, which IFRS prohibits.

options.t: Both are identical, so firms compare them easily
options.why: If IFRS and GAAP were identical, there would be no challenge; the difficulty comes from differences between them.

options.t: Rules differ, so statements are harder to compare
options.why: Because US GAAP and IFRS differ in areas such as inventory and development costs, global companies must reconcile statements and investors find them harder to compare.

options.t: Neither one can be used in any country at all
options.why: Both frameworks are used widely; the US uses GAAP and over 100 countries use IFRS, so they are in use rather than unusable.

q: Which tax form do most employers use to report wages paid to an employee at year end?

options.t: Form W-2
options.why: Form W-2 is the Wage and Tax Statement an employer gives each employee by January 31, reporting annual wages and taxes withheld.

options.t: Form I-9
options.why: Form I-9 verifies an employee's identity and work eligibility; it does not report wages paid.

options.t: Form W-4
options.why: Form W-4 is completed by the employee to tell the employer how much tax to withhold; it is not a year end wage report.

options.t: Form 1099
options.why: Form 1099 reports payments to independent contractors and other nonemployee income, not wages paid to employees.

q: Which form reports payments of $600 or more to an independent contractor?

options.t: Form W-4 copy
options.why: Form W-4 is filled out by an employee for withholding and does not report contractor payments.

options.t: Form W-2 copy
options.why: Form W-2 reports wages of employees; independent contractors are not employees and receive a different form.

options.t: Form 941 copy
options.why: Form 941 is the employer's quarterly payroll tax return, not a form that reports payments to contractors.

options.t: Form 1099-NEC
options.why: Form 1099-NEC reports nonemployee compensation of $600 or more paid to an independent contractor during the year.

q: What does an employee complete so the employer knows how much tax to withhold?

options.t: Form 1040
options.why: Form 1040 is the individual income tax return filed with the IRS, not the form that tells the employer how much to withhold.

options.t: Form W-4
options.why: Form W-4 is completed by the employee and tells the employer how much federal income tax to withhold, based on filing status and allowances.

options.t: Form 1099
options.why: Form 1099 reports payments to independent contractors; employees do not complete it, and it does not set withholding.

options.t: Form W-2
options.why: Form W-2 is prepared by the employer after the year ends to report wages and withholding, so the employee does not complete it.

q: What is the purpose of Form I-9?

options.t: To request time off from your boss
options.why: Requesting time off is handled with an internal leave request; Form I-9 is a federal form used for employment eligibility.

options.t: To set tax withholding for the worker
options.why: Tax withholding is set on Form W-4, whereas Form I-9 deals with identity and legal permission to work in the US.

options.t: To report wages paid to the staff yearly
options.why: Yearly wages are reported on Form W-2; Form I-9 does not report any wages or pay information.

options.t: To verify identity and work eligibility
options.why: Employers must complete Form I-9 for each new hire to verify identity and authorization to work in the United States, within three business days of starting.

q: Which statement about independent auditors is true?

options.t: They are employees of the firm that they audit
options.why: An independent auditor must not be an employee of the company audited, because working for it would compromise independence and objectivity.

options.t: They guarantee the company has no fraud at all
options.why: Auditors give reasonable, not absolute, assurance; they do not guarantee the absence of fraud since audits use sampling and cannot detect everything.

options.t: They must be independent of the company they audit
options.why: Independent auditors must be independent in fact and appearance, with no financial or employment ties to the audited company so their opinion is credible.

options.t: They prepare the company's daily entries in books
options.why: Preparing daily entries is the job of the company's own bookkeepers; an auditor who did that would be auditing his or her own work.

q: What is the difference between an internal and an external auditor?

options.t: Internal auditors work for the company; external ones are independent
options.why: Internal auditors are employees who review controls and operations for management, while external auditors are independent outsiders who give an opinion on the statements.

options.t: External auditors work only for the company, and are paid by its own managers
options.why: External auditors do not work only for the company's managers; they are independent and report to outsiders such as shareholders, so independence is key.

options.t: Internal auditors work for the IRS and the state tax office only
options.why: Internal auditors work for their own company, not for the IRS; the IRS has its own agents who examine tax returns.

options.t: There is no difference between internal and external auditors
options.why: The two are different: internal auditors are employees who improve operations, and external auditors are independent professionals who attest to the statements.

q: What is the main goal of a financial audit?

options.t: To prepare the tax return for a client
options.why: Preparing a tax return is tax work, not the aim of a financial audit; an audit examines whether statements are fairly presented.

options.t: To give an opinion on the statements
options.why: The main goal of a financial audit is for an independent CPA to give an opinion on whether the statements fairly present results under GAAP.

options.t: To increase profit by finding customers
options.why: Increasing profit is a management goal; an audit does not find customers or raise earnings but checks the accuracy of reports.

options.t: To find new customers for the firm
options.why: Finding new customers is a marketing function and has nothing to do with auditing, which examines financial records.

q: What does Generally Accepted Auditing Standards (GAAS) guide?

options.t: How auditors carry out examinations
options.why: GAAS are the standards that guide how auditors plan, perform and report their examinations, covering the auditor's qualifications, fieldwork and reporting.

options.t: How companies price their products
options.why: Pricing products is a management and marketing decision; GAAS apply to auditors, not to a company's pricing policy.

options.t: How taxes are collected from firms
options.why: Tax collection is covered by tax law and the IRS, while GAAS guide the conduct of audits.

options.t: How employees are hired by firms
options.why: Hiring employees is governed by employment law and company policy, while GAAS are standards for auditing financial statements.

q: What does 'compliance' mean in accounting?

options.t: Increasing sales every year by a large amount
options.why: Increasing sales is a business goal; compliance is about following rules, not about how much a company sells.

options.t: Hiring more accountants for the firm each year
options.why: Hiring more accountants may help with compliance but is not what the term means; compliance means obeying applicable requirements.

options.t: Choosing the cheapest software available
options.why: Choosing the cheapest software is a purchasing decision; compliance refers to following legal and professional rules.

options.t: Following the laws and standards that apply
options.why: Compliance means following the laws, regulations and standards that apply to the business, such as tax laws, GAAP and SEC rules, to avoid penalties.

q: What can happen if a business fails to comply with tax laws?

options.t: Free audits from the government agency
options.why: Governments do not give free audits as a reward for noncompliance; the IRS audits returns it questions, which can cost the business time and money.

options.t: Penalties, interest and legal action
options.why: Failing to comply with tax laws can bring penalties, interest on unpaid tax and even legal action, including criminal charges in cases of fraud.

options.t: Automatic tax refunds for late payers
options.why: Late payers owe interest and penalties, not refunds; refunds only result from overpaying, and not paying on time never earns one.

options.t: Higher loyalty, as shoppers trust firms
options.why: Noncompliance harms reputation and trust; customers do not reward firms that break tax laws, and there is no loyalty bonus.

q: What does the Foreign Corrupt Practices Act (FCPA) prohibit?

options.t: Selling products overseas to foreign customers
options.why: Selling to foreign customers is legal and common; the FCPA targets bribery, not exports or international sales.

options.t: Paying foreign taxes on time each year
options.why: Paying foreign taxes on time is a lawful obligation; the FCPA does not prohibit it, and it is aimed at corrupt payments.

options.t: Bribing foreign officials to win business
options.why: The FCPA of 1977 makes it illegal for US companies and individuals to bribe foreign officials to win or keep business, and requires accurate books and records.

options.t: Hiring foreign workers for local firms
options.why: Hiring foreign workers is regulated by immigration and labor laws; the FCPA covers bribery and accounting controls, not hiring.

q: The Fair Labor Standards Act sets rules for which accounting-related area?

options.t: Inventory valuation rules
options.why: Inventory valuation is governed by accounting standards such as FIFO and LIFO rules, not by the Fair Labor Standards Act.

options.t: Bank reconciliations rules
options.why: Bank reconciliation is an internal control procedure; the Fair Labor Standards Act does not set rules for it.

options.t: Depreciation methods used
options.why: Depreciation methods come from accounting standards and tax rules; the FLSA covers pay and working conditions.

options.t: Minimum wage and overtime
options.why: The FLSA sets the federal minimum wage, overtime pay at 1.5 times the regular rate after 40 hours, and child labor rules, which affect payroll accounting.

q: An employee is paid $15 per hour and works 46 hours in a week. Overtime is paid at 1.5 times after 40 hours. What is gross pay?

options.why: Regular pay is 40 x $15 = $600; overtime is 6 hours x ($15 x 1.5 = $22.50) = $135; gross pay is $600 + $135 = $735.
$690 pays all 46 hours at the regular rate (46 x $15); it ignores the 1.5 times overtime rate for the 6 hours above 40.
$600 pays only the first 40 hours (40 x $15) and leaves out the 6 overtime hours, which earn $22.50 each, or $135 more.
$1,035 pays all 46 hours at the overtime rate (46 x $22.50); only the 6 hours over 40 get the premium, so most hours stay at $15.

q: What do FICA taxes fund?

options.t: Public schools and libraries
options.why: Schools and libraries are paid mainly from state and local taxes such as property and sales taxes, not from the payroll taxes withheld under FICA.

options.t: National defense spending only
options.why: Defense is funded from general federal revenue, mostly income taxes, and FICA does not go to defense at all, so the word only makes this wrong.

options.t: Social Security and Medicare
options.why: FICA stands for Federal Insurance Contributions Act. Its payroll taxes fund Social Security retirement and disability benefits plus Medicare health coverage, split between employee and employer.

options.t: Highway construction work
options.why: Highway work is paid mainly from fuel excise taxes into the Highway Trust Fund and state budgets, not from the payroll taxes called FICA.

q: An employee earns $2,000 gross. FICA is 7.65% for the employee. How much is withheld for FICA?

options.why: $765 is 7.65% of $10,000, not of $2,000. It uses the wrong wage base, so the decimal is off by a factor of five from the correct amount.
FICA withheld is gross pay times the rate: $2,000 x 0.0765 = $153. This covers 6.2% Social Security plus 1.45% Medicare taken from the employee's pay.
$15.30 is 0.765% of $2,000, so the decimal point is misplaced by one place. The correct calculation $2,000 x 0.0765 gives $153.
$1,530 is 76.5% of $2,000, a decimal slip of one place the other way. The real withholding is $2,000 x 0.0765 = $153.

q: Who pays unemployment taxes (FUTA) in most cases?

options.t: The employee
options.why: Employees do not pay FUTA at all. It is an employer-only payroll tax, so nothing is withheld from the worker's paycheck for federal unemployment.

options.t: The customer
options.why: Customers never pay payroll taxes on a firm's staff. They pay the firm for goods or services, and sales tax if it applies, but not FUTA.

options.t: The IRS office
options.why: The IRS office collects FUTA from employers but does not pay it. It administers the tax and deposits, so the burden falls on the employer.

options.t: The employer
options.why: FUTA is imposed only on employers, usually on the first $7,000 of each employee's wages, and it funds state unemployment programs. It is never deducted from worker pay.

q: What is the difference between an employee and an independent contractor for payroll?

options.t: Employers withhold from employees, not contractors
options.why: Employers must withhold income tax and FICA from employees' pay, while contractors are paid in full and handle their own self-employment taxes. This difference drives payroll treatment.

options.t: Employees pay no taxes on their own wages ever as a rule
options.why: Employees do owe income tax on wages, and the employer withholds it. The claim that they never pay any tax on their wages is false.

options.t: There is no difference between the two groups
options.why: There is a real difference: control over how work is done, who withholds tax, and which forms are filed. Claiming no difference ignores payroll rules.

options.t: Contractors get W-2 forms; employees get 1099s
options.why: This reverses the forms. Employees receive W-2 forms reporting wages and withholding, while independent contractors receive Form 1099-NEC for payments received.

q: A company misclassifies an employee as a contractor to avoid payroll taxes. What is the most likely result?

options.t: A higher credit rating for the firm
options.why: Misclassification does not improve credit ratings. Lenders and agencies view unpaid payroll taxes and legal disputes as negatives, not as a benefit to the firm's credit.

options.t: Back taxes, penalties and legal action
options.why: The IRS and state agencies can assess unpaid payroll taxes, penalties and interest, and the firm may face lawsuits or criminal charges for willful misclassification.

options.t: Lower costs and no risk from the law
options.why: Avoiding payroll taxes may cut costs briefly, but misclassification carries real legal risk. Audits and worker complaints commonly lead to heavy back-tax bills.

options.t: A tax refund from the government agency
options.why: Agencies do not refund tax for misclassifying workers. The authorities pursue the firm for tax it should have withheld, so a refund is the opposite of the outcome.

q: What is data privacy in accounting?

options.t: Deleting all old data every day at the firm
options.why: Data privacy is about protecting information, not erasing it. Records must be kept for legal and tax periods, so deleting everything daily would break record-keeping rules.

options.t: Publishing client records online for anyone to find
options.why: Publishing client records online is the opposite of privacy. It exposes confidential financial data and would violate confidentiality duties and privacy laws.

options.t: Protecting sensitive personal and financial data
options.why: Data privacy means safeguarding sensitive personal and financial information, such as Social Security numbers and account data, from unauthorized access, use or disclosure, as laws and ethics require.

options.t: Sharing passwords between staff members at work
options.why: Sharing passwords between staff weakens security and privacy. Each user should have a unique login so access can be controlled and traced.

q: Which practice best protects accounting data on a computer?

options.t: Sharing one login among all staff
options.why: Sharing one login hides who did what and removes accountability. Unique user accounts are needed so access can be limited and activity traced to a person.

options.t: Turning off software updates for safety
options.why: Software updates patch known security holes. Turning them off leaves the system open to attacks, so it lowers protection instead of raising it.

options.t: Strong passwords and regular backups
options.why: Strong passwords block unauthorized access, and regular backups let the firm restore records after loss, theft or failure. Together they protect confidentiality and availability.

options.t: Keeping the only copy on a flash drive
options.why: A single copy on a flash drive is easily lost, stolen or corrupted. Good practice keeps several copies, including one stored off-site.

q: An accountant finds an error in a prior-year financial statement that is material. What is the proper action?

options.t: Leave it because the year is closed
options.why: A closed year does not excuse a material error. Accounting standards require correcting material misstatements so users of the statements are not misled.

options.t: Correct it and disclose the correction
options.why: A material error in prior statements must be corrected, usually by restating them, and disclosed so readers know what changed. This follows GAAP and ethical duties.

options.t: Wait until someone else finds the error
options.why: Waiting for others to find an error is neglect of professional duty. Accountants must act on known material errors promptly and honestly.

options.t: Remove the evidence of the error entirely
options.why: Removing evidence of an error is concealment and fraud. It violates professional ethics and can bring legal penalties instead of fixing the statements.

q: What is gross income?

options.t: All income before any deductions
options.why: Gross income is total income from all sources before deductions or exemptions. It is the starting point for figuring taxable income on a tax return.

options.t: The amount of tax owed to the state
options.why: Tax owed is calculated from taxable income and the rate schedule. It is a result of the process, not gross income, and it is not specific to the state.

options.t: Income after all taxes are paid
options.why: Income left after taxes are paid is called net or after-tax income, often called take-home pay. Gross income comes before any taxes.

options.t: Only income from wages and salaries
options.why: Gross income includes wages, interest, dividends, business profit, rent and other sources, not only wages and salaries, so this option is too narrow.

q: What is taxable income?

options.t: All money a person has ever received in life
options.why: Taxable income is not everything ever received. It covers income earned in the tax year, minus allowed deductions, and some receipts such as gifts are excluded.

options.t: Income before deductions and exemptions
options.why: Income before deductions and exemptions is gross income. Taxable income is what remains after those subtractions, so this describes the earlier figure.

options.t: The amount of tax withheld from your pay
options.why: Tax withheld is the amount taken from pay during the year as prepayment. It is not the income base on which tax is calculated.

options.t: Income left after deductions and exemptions
options.why: Taxable income equals gross income minus deductions and exemptions. Tax rates are applied to this smaller amount to find the tax owed.

q: What is a tax deduction?

options.t: A refund paid by a bank on request
options.why: A refund is money returned when tax paid exceeds tax owed. A bank does not pay it, and it is not a deduction from income.

options.t: An amount that reduces tax directly
options.why: An amount that reduces tax directly, dollar for dollar, is a tax credit. A deduction reduces the income being taxed, so this describes a credit.

options.t: An amount that reduces taxable income
options.why: A deduction, such as mortgage interest or the standard deduction, subtracts from gross income. The tax is then figured on the smaller taxable income.

options.t: An extra penalty for late filing of tax
options.why: A penalty for filing late is a charge added to the tax bill. A deduction does the opposite and lowers the income that gets taxed.

q: What is a tax credit?

options.t: An amount that cuts tax owed dollar for dollar
options.why: A tax credit directly reduces the tax owed by its full amount, so a $500 credit cuts the bill by $500. It is worth more than a deduction.

options.t: A bank loan for taxes owed to the state agency
options.why: A loan from a bank is borrowed money that must be repaid. A tax credit is not borrowed and is a direct cut in the tax bill.

options.t: An amount that reduces taxable income first
options.why: Reducing taxable income first describes a deduction. A credit instead comes off the final tax owed after the tax has been calculated.

options.t: A penalty for underpaying your tax bill each year
options.why: Underpayment penalties are charges added when too little tax is paid during the year. A credit lowers the bill and is never a penalty.

q: What is a progressive tax?

options.t: A tax with lower rates for higher incomes
options.why: Lower rates for higher incomes would be a regressive pattern. A progressive tax does the reverse, taxing larger incomes at higher rates.

options.t: A tax paid only on purchases of goods
options.why: A tax paid only on purchases of goods is a sales tax or an excise tax. Progressive describes how the rate rises with income.

options.t: A tax with one flat rate for everyone
options.why: One flat rate for everyone is a flat tax. A progressive tax uses brackets, so rates rise as income rises.

options.t: A tax with higher rates for higher incomes
options.why: A progressive tax raises the rate as income rises, as in the US federal income tax brackets. Higher earners pay a larger share of income in tax.

q: What is a sales tax?

options.t: A tax on property owned
options.why: A tax on property owned is a property tax, based on assessed value of real estate. A sales tax is charged on purchases instead.

options.t: A tax added to purchases
options.why: A sales tax is a percentage added to the price of goods and services at the time of purchase. Sellers collect it and send it to the state.

options.t: A tax on wages earned
options.why: A tax on wages earned is an income tax or payroll tax. Sales tax is charged at the register when buying, not on earnings.

options.t: A tax on corporate profits
options.why: A tax on corporate profits is a corporate income tax. Sales tax falls on consumer purchases rather than on business profit.

q: What is property tax based on?

options.t: The price of goods sold by the owner
options.why: A tax on the price of goods sold is a sales tax. Property tax is tied to the owned property itself, not to sales prices.

options.t: Wages earned by the owner each year
options.why: Taxes on wages earned are income taxes or payroll taxes. Property tax does not depend on what the owner earns during the year.

options.t: Dividends received by the owner yearly
options.why: Dividends are taxed under the income tax system. Property tax is a separate tax and does not depend on dividends received.

options.t: The value of real estate or property
options.why: Property tax is based on the assessed value of real estate or other property, such as land and buildings. Local governments use it to fund schools and services.

q: What is withholding?

options.t: Taxes taken from an employee's pay
options.why: Withholding is the part of an employee's pay that the employer takes out and sends to tax authorities, as a prepayment of income tax and FICA.

options.t: A fee paid by customers to firms
options.why: A fee paid by customers to firms is a service charge or price. Withholding concerns amounts taken from wages, not customer payments.

options.t: Pay kept by the employer as profit
options.why: Pay kept by the employer as profit would be wage theft. Withheld taxes belong to the government and must be remitted, not kept.

options.t: A bonus paid at year end to staff
options.why: A year-end bonus is extra pay given to staff. Withholding is a deduction from pay and is not any kind of bonus.

q: What is the usual federal deadline for filing individual income tax returns?

options.t: December 31
options.why: December 31 is the end of the tax year for most people, not the filing deadline. Returns for that year are due in the following spring.

options.t: January 1
options.why: January 1 begins the new tax year and also the time when forms start to arrive. It is far too early to be the filing deadline.

options.t: April 15
options.why: The usual due date for individual federal income tax returns is April 15, or the next business day if it falls on a weekend or holiday.

options.t: June 30
options.why: June 30 is not the usual filing date. Taxpayers needing more time file an extension, which moves the deadline to October 15.

q: Which form do most individuals use to file their federal income tax return?

options.t: Form 1099
options.why: Form 1099 reports non-wage income, such as contractor pay or interest, to the IRS and recipient. It is not the return itself.

options.t: Form 1040
options.why: Form 1040 is the standard US individual income tax return. Taxpayers report income, deductions and credits on it to figure tax owed or a refund.

options.t: Form W-4
options.why: Form W-4 is filled out for an employer to set how much tax is withheld from pay. It is not used to file a return.

options.t: Form W-2
options.why: Form W-2 is the statement an employer gives each employee showing annual wages and taxes withheld. Taxpayers use it to complete Form 1040.

q: What does the standard deduction do?

options.t: Increases taxable income for the whole year
options.why: The standard deduction lowers taxable income, not raises it. Adding to income would increase the tax, which is the opposite of a deduction.

options.t: Pays the tax directly to the government agency
options.why: A deduction never pays tax itself. It only reduces the income on which tax is figured, and taxes are paid through withholding or payments.

options.t: Cuts income by a fixed amount without itemizing
options.why: The standard deduction is a fixed dollar amount, set by filing status, that taxpayers subtract from income without listing or documenting individual expenses.

options.t: Applies only to businesses, which subtract it
options.why: The standard deduction is for individual taxpayers. Businesses deduct their own ordinary and necessary expenses instead and do not use a standard deduction.

q: When might a taxpayer itemize deductions rather than take the standard deduction?

options.t: When their income is zero for the whole year
options.why: With zero income there is nothing to deduct from, so itemizing offers no benefit. Itemizing makes sense only when real expenses are large.

options.t: When allowed expenses exceed the standard amount
options.why: Taxpayers itemize when eligible expenses, such as mortgage interest, state taxes and charitable gifts, add up to more than the standard deduction amount.

options.t: When they want to pay more tax, as itemizing raises it
options.why: Itemizing lowers taxable income, which reduces tax rather than raising it. People choose it only when it saves more than the standard deduction.

options.t: When they have no expenses to claim at all this year
options.why: With no expenses to claim, itemizing gives nothing, so the standard deduction would be better. Itemizing requires qualifying expenses with records.

q: Which of these is an example of an itemized deduction?

options.t: Grocery spending
options.why: Groceries are a personal living cost and are not deductible. The tax code allows itemized deductions only for listed expenses, such as mortgage interest.

options.t: Vacation costs
options.why: Vacation costs are personal spending and cannot be itemized. Only specific categories such as medical costs, taxes, gifts and home interest qualify.

options.t: Clothing purchases
options.why: Clothing for everyday wear is a personal expense. It is not on the list of itemized deductions allowed on Schedule A.

options.t: Mortgage interest
options.why: Mortgage interest on a home loan is a common itemized deduction listed on Schedule A. It can lower taxable income if total itemized items exceed the standard amount.

q: What is an employer's role in income tax withholding?

options.t: Deduct taxes from pay and send them in
options.why: Employers must withhold income tax and FICA from each paycheck and send those amounts to the government on schedule. They hold the money as trustees.

options.t: Keep the taxes as the company profit
options.why: Withheld taxes belong to the government, so an employer cannot keep them as profit. Doing so is illegal and brings serious penalties.

options.t: Pay the employee's taxes from company funds
options.why: Withholding comes out of the employee's pay, not company funds. Paying the tax from company money would be an added expense, not withholding.

options.t: Return the taxes to the employee each week
options.why: Withheld money is sent to the government, not returned weekly. Any difference is settled at filing time with a refund from the IRS.

q: Employees usually receive a refund when:

options.t: They earned no income during the whole year
options.why: With no income, there is typically no tax withheld, so no refund arises. Refunds come from over-withholding and credits, not from zero earnings.

options.t: Their withholding was less than their tax owed overall
options.why: If withholding is less than tax owed, the taxpayer owes the balance at filing time instead of receiving a refund.

options.t: Their withholding was greater than their tax owed
options.why: A refund arises when the tax withheld during the year exceeds the tax actually owed. The IRS returns the difference after the return is filed.

options.t: They filed late and paid a penalty to the IRS
options.why: Filing late with a penalty does not create a refund. Penalties add to the amount due, and refunds come only from overpaid tax.

q: What is a W-2 form?

options.t: A form that sets withholding rules
options.why: The W-4 sets withholding by telling the employer how much to take from pay. The W-2 only reports the totals after the year ends.

options.t: A form used to request a filing extension
options.why: An extension of time to file is requested with Form 4868, not W-2. The W-2 plays no part in requesting extra time.

options.t: A form to claim a refund of tax paid
options.why: A refund of tax paid is claimed by filing a return, such as Form 1040. The W-2 is an input that supports it.

options.t: A form showing wages and taxes withheld
options.why: The W-2 is issued by employers by January 31. It shows an employee's yearly wages and the federal, state, Social Security and Medicare taxes withheld.

q: Who is responsible for paying self-employment tax?

options.t: The government itself
options.why: The government collects taxes but does not pay them. Self-employment tax is owed by the earner on net business income.

options.t: The self-employed person
options.why: Self-employed people owe self-employment tax, 15.3% for Social Security and Medicare, since no employer shares the cost. They pay both halves on net earnings.

options.t: Their customers, who pay it
options.why: Customers pay for goods and services but do not pay the seller's tax. The business owner is responsible for their own self-employment tax.

options.t: Their suppliers or vendors
options.why: Suppliers or vendors are paid for goods they sell and have no duty to pay the owner's self-employment tax. The owner pays it.

q: Why do self-employed people often pay estimated taxes quarterly?

options.t: No employer withholds tax for them
options.why: No employer withholds tax from self-employed income, so they must send estimated payments to the IRS each quarter to cover income and self-employment tax.

options.t: They pay no tax on their income
options.why: Self-employed people do owe tax on their income. Estimated payments exist because that tax is real and must be paid through the year.

options.t: It lowers their tax, as they pay early
options.why: Quarterly payments do not reduce total tax. They only spread payment through the year, and missing them can bring underpayment penalties.

options.t: It is optional for all self-employed
options.why: Estimated payments are generally required when expected tax owed is $1,000 or more. Skipping them can lead to penalties, so they are not just optional.

q: What is a capital gain?

options.t: A loan from a bank to a business owner
options.why: A loan from a bank is borrowed money that must be repaid. It is a liability and not a gain from selling something.

options.t: Wages from a job done each week by a worker
options.why: Wages from a weekly job are ordinary earned income, taxed as such. A capital gain comes from selling something owned at a profit.

options.t: Profit from selling an asset above its cost
options.why: A capital gain is profit when an asset such as stock or real estate is sold for more than its cost basis. It is taxable income.

options.t: Interest on a savings account balance each year
options.why: Interest on savings is ordinary interest income. A capital gain comes only from selling an investment above what was paid for it.

q: Mia bought stock for $1,000 and sold it for $1,600. What is her capital gain?

options.why: $1,000 is Mia's original cost, not her profit. The gain is the sale price minus the cost, not the cost alone.
Capital gain equals selling price minus cost: $1,600 - $1,000 = $600. That profit is what Mia reports for tax.
$1,600 is the sale price, not the profit. Her gain must subtract the $1,000 she paid, leaving $600.
$2,600 adds the cost and the sale price together, which is meaningless. The gain is found by subtracting: $1,600 - $1,000 = $600.

q: What is the difference between a short-term and a long-term capital gain?

options.t: Long-term gains are never taxed at the federal level
options.why: Long-term gains are taxed, though usually at lower rates of 0%, 15% or 20%. They are not exempt from federal tax.

options.t: There is no difference in how the two gains are held
options.why: The two do differ: holding period and tax rate set them apart. Short-term gains are taxed as ordinary income, long-term at lower rates.

options.t: Short-term gains come from assets held for ten years or more
options.why: Short-term gains come from assets held one year or less, not ten years. Ten years is far longer than the one-year dividing line.

options.t: Long-term gains come from assets held more than one year
options.why: Long-term capital gains come from assets held more than one year and get lower tax rates. Short-term gains from assets held a year or less are taxed as ordinary income.

q: What is tax evasion?

options.t: Illegally avoiding tax owed
options.why: Tax evasion is the illegal act of avoiding tax owed, such as hiding income or falsifying deductions. It can lead to fines and prison.

options.t: Filing on time every year
options.why: Filing on time each year is lawful compliance. It is the opposite of evasion, which involves deliberately cheating on taxes owed.

options.t: Paying estimated taxes yearly
options.why: Paying estimated taxes during the year is a lawful requirement for many taxpayers. It meets obligations rather than evading them.

options.t: Using legal deductions to save
options.why: Using legal deductions to save is tax avoidance, which is allowed. Evasion is the illegal form that involves cheating or hiding income.

q: What is tax avoidance?

options.t: Legally lowering tax with allowed deductions
options.why: Tax avoidance means using legal methods, such as deductions, credits and retirement accounts, to reduce the tax owed. It is lawful, unlike evasion.

options.t: Hiding income from the government to avoid tax
options.why: Hiding income from the government is tax evasion, which is illegal. Avoidance uses only methods the law allows.

options.t: Paying taxes late on purpose every single year
options.why: Paying late on purpose is not a tax-saving method and brings penalties and interest. Avoidance is about legally lowering the tax itself.

options.t: Refusing to file a return at all this year
options.why: Refusing to file a return is a violation that can bring penalties or prosecution. It is not a lawful way to lower tax.

q: A business owner deducts a personal vacation as a business expense. This is most likely:

options.t: A tax credit for the owner
options.why: A tax credit is an allowed amount that reduces tax, given by law for specific things. A personal vacation does not qualify as a credit.

options.t: A legal deduction, as the owner
options.why: Personal vacations are not business expenses, so the owner cannot legally deduct them. Only ordinary and necessary business costs are deductible.

options.t: Improper and possibly illegal
options.why: Deducting a personal trip as business is improper and can be tax fraud if intentional. It can bring back taxes, penalties and audits.

options.t: Required by law for all firms
options.why: No law requires firms to deduct personal vacations. Deductions are optional and must be for real business expenses.

q: Which is an ordinary and necessary business expense?

options.t: Owner's groceries
options.why: The owner's groceries are a personal living cost and are not a business expense. Only costs that help the business operate are deductible.

options.t: Rent for a shop
options.why: Rent for a shop is a normal cost of running the business and is both ordinary and necessary. It is deductible against revenue.

options.t: A weekend car
options.why: A car used for weekend personal trips is a personal expense. Only the business-use portion of a vehicle can be deducted.

options.t: A family vacation
options.why: A family vacation is personal spending, not a business cost. It does not meet the ordinary and necessary test for a deduction.

q: A sole proprietor has revenue of $120,000 and deductible business expenses of $78,000. What income is reported for tax before other adjustments?

options.why: $78,000 is only the expenses. Business income is revenue minus expenses, so the expenses alone do not show what is taxed.
$120,000 is revenue before subtracting the $78,000 of deductible expenses. Tax is figured on profit, not on gross revenue.
$198,000 adds revenue and expenses together, which is wrong. Expenses reduce income, so they must be subtracted from revenue.
Net business income is revenue minus deductible expenses: $120,000 - $78,000 = $42,000. The sole proprietor reports this on Schedule C.

q: What type of tax do corporations pay on their profits?

options.t: Estate tax on land
options.why: Estate tax applies to the transfer of property from a deceased person's estate. It is not the tax companies pay on profits.

options.t: Sales tax on goods
options.why: Sales tax is charged on goods bought by consumers and collected by sellers. It is not a tax on corporate profits.

options.t: Corporate income tax
options.why: Corporations pay corporate income tax on their profits. At the federal level the flat rate is 21% under current law.

options.t: Excise tax on gasoline
options.why: An excise tax applies to a specific product such as gasoline. Corporate profits are taxed under the corporate income tax instead.

q: What is double taxation?

options.t: Filing two returns by mistake in the same tax year
options.why: Filing two returns by mistake is an error, not double taxation. Double taxation means the same income is taxed twice, at different levels.

options.t: Paying sales tax twice on the same purchase of goods
options.why: Paying sales tax twice on one purchase is a billing error. Double taxation of corporations refers to taxing profits at two levels.

options.t: Paying two states' income tax on the same earnings
options.why: Paying two states' tax on the same earnings is a multistate issue, usually solved by credits. It differs from corporate double taxation.

options.t: Profits taxed at the company, then again as dividends
options.why: C corporations pay tax on profits, and shareholders pay tax again on dividends received. This two-level taxation is called double taxation.

q: In a partnership, how is business income usually taxed?

options.t: Only the oldest partner is taxed on it
options.why: Business income is not taxed only to the oldest partner. It is split among all partners based on the partnership agreement.

options.t: It passes through to the partners' returns
options.why: A partnership is a pass-through entity. Profits and losses flow to partners' personal returns on Schedule K-1, and each pays tax on their share.

options.t: It is not taxed at all by any government
options.why: Partnership income is taxed, but through the partners. It is not tax-free under any government rules.

options.t: The partnership pays tax and partners pay none
options.why: The partnership itself generally pays no income tax, and the partners pay on their shares. This option has it backward.

q: What is an S corporation?

options.t: A corporation taxed through owners' returns
options.why: An S corporation passes income through to shareholders, who report it on their own returns. This avoids corporate-level tax and double taxation, if IRS rules are met.

options.t: A corporation based in another country
options.why: An S corporation is a US tax election, not a foreign company. A foreign corporation is a different type, based on its country of origin.

options.t: A corporation that pays no taxes ever at all
options.why: S corporations are not tax-free. Owners pay tax on the income through their returns, so the corporation avoids paying only at the entity level.

options.t: A corporation owned only by the government
options.why: Government-owned corporations are a different category. An S corporation is privately owned, limited to 100 eligible shareholders.

q: What is depreciation for tax purposes?

options.t: Adding the asset's cost to revenue each year
options.why: Depreciation is a deduction, so it is subtracted, not added to revenue. Adding cost to revenue would raise taxable income wrongly.

options.t: Deducting the cost of an asset over several years
options.why: Depreciation spreads an asset's cost over its useful life through yearly deductions. This matches the cost to the years the asset is used.

options.t: Deducting the entire cost in the first year always
options.why: Deducting the whole cost in year one is not the general rule. Depreciation spreads it over years, unless a special rule such as Section 179 applies.

options.t: Selling the asset at a loss in its first year
options.why: Selling an asset at a loss is a disposal event. Depreciation is an allocation of cost over time and not a sale.

q: What does MACRS stand for?

options.t: Modified Accelerated Cost Recovery System
options.why: MACRS is the Modified Accelerated Cost Recovery System, the IRS method for depreciating business property, which gives larger deductions in early years.

options.t: Mandatory Accounting Cost Reporting Schedule
options.why: This name sounds plausible but does not exist. MACRS is a tax depreciation method, not a reporting schedule.

options.t: Managed Asset Cost Review Service Plan
options.why: No such review service exists. MACRS stands for the Modified Accelerated Cost Recovery System used for tax depreciation.

options.t: Modern Annual Corporate Revenue Standard
options.why: This invented phrase is not what MACRS stands for. The acronym describes cost recovery of assets, not corporate revenue.

q: Which statement about book depreciation and tax depreciation is true?

options.t: Tax depreciation is never allowed by law
options.why: Tax depreciation is allowed and widely used. The tax code lets businesses deduct the cost of qualifying assets over time.

options.t: They must always be identical in amount
options.why: Book and tax depreciation follow different rules and purposes, so amounts often differ. They do not need to match, and differences create deferred taxes.

options.t: Book depreciation is set by the IRS each year
options.why: The IRS sets rules for tax depreciation, not book depreciation. Book depreciation follows GAAP and the company's own estimates of useful life.

options.t: They can differ because the rules differ
options.why: Book depreciation follows GAAP, while tax depreciation follows IRS rules such as MACRS, so the amounts can differ. Those timing differences create deferred taxes.

q: What is a deferred tax liability?

options.t: Tax already paid in full to the state agency
options.why: Tax already paid in full is not a liability. A deferred tax liability is owed in the future, not settled now.

options.t: A refund due to a company that overpaid its taxes
options.why: A refund due is an asset (a receivable), not a liability. A deferred tax liability is tax the company will owe later.

options.t: Tax owed later because of timing differences
options.why: A deferred tax liability arises when taxable income is lower now than book income, such as from faster tax depreciation. The tax comes due in later periods.

options.t: A late filing penalty charged by the IRS
options.why: A late filing penalty is an expense charged for a violation. A deferred tax liability comes from timing differences, not penalties.

q: Which account records sales tax collected from customers?

options.t: Cash Discounts
options.why: Cash Discounts is not a tax account. It deals with price reductions for early payment, not tax collected from customers.

options.t: Sales Revenue
options.why: Sales Revenue records income from selling goods. Tax collected for the government is not revenue, since it is owed to the state.

options.t: Sales Tax Payable
options.why: Sales tax collected is a liability because it is owed to the government. Sales Tax Payable records it until the business remits it.

options.t: Sales Tax Expense
options.why: Sales Tax Expense would suggest the business bears the tax. Collected sales tax belongs to the state, so it is a payable.

q: A shop sells goods for $400 with 7% sales tax. What is the total the customer pays?

options.why: $407 adds 7 dollars instead of 7 percent. The tax is 7% of $400, which is $28, not $7.
Tax is $400 x 0.07 = $28. The customer pays $400 + $28 = $428 in total.
$468 adds $68, which is far more than the correct tax. Seven percent of $400 is $28, so the total is $428.
$400 is the price before tax. The 7% sales tax of $28 must be added, giving a total of $428.

q: A business collected $1,260 in sales tax. How should it handle this money?

options.t: Send it to the tax authority when due
options.why: Collected sales tax belongs to the government. The business acts as a collector and must send it to the tax authority by the due date.

options.t: Use it to buy equipment for the firm
options.why: Sales tax collected is not the company's money to spend. Using it to buy equipment would leave the firm unable to pay the tax owed.

options.t: Keep it as revenue for the business
options.why: Sales tax is not revenue, because the business owes it to the state. Counting it as revenue would overstate income.

options.t: Give it to the employees as a bonus
options.why: Collected sales tax belongs to the state. Giving it to employees as a bonus would mean the firm cannot remit what it owes.

q: What is payroll tax expense for an employer?

options.t: Sales tax collected from customers on each sale that is made
options.why: Sales tax collected from customers is a liability the business passes on to the state. It is not a payroll tax expense of the employer.

options.t: Property tax on a home that the owner pays to the city each year
options.why: Property tax on a home is a personal tax paid by the owner. It is unrelated to the taxes an employer pays on payroll.

options.t: The employee's income tax withheld and sent to the government
options.why: The employee's income tax withheld is the worker's own tax, held by the employer. It is not an expense of the employer.

options.t: The employer's Social Security, Medicare and unemployment taxes
options.why: Payroll tax expense covers the employer's share: Social Security and Medicare (FICA match) plus federal and state unemployment taxes. It is a cost of employing workers.

q: An employer has gross wages of $10,000 and matches FICA at 7.65%. What is the employer's FICA expense?

options.why: $1,530 is 15.3% of $10,000, which is both halves of FICA. The employer matches only the 7.65% share.
$7,650 is 76.5% of $10,000, which misplaces the decimal. The employer match at 7.65% is $10,000 x 0.0765 = $765.
$76.50 is 0.765% of $10,000, a decimal slip the other way. The correct match is $10,000 x 0.0765 = $765.
The employer matches the employee's FICA at 7.65%: $10,000 x 0.0765 = $765. This is recorded as payroll tax expense.

q: Which of these taxes is an excise tax?

options.t: A tax on a corporation's profit
options.why: A tax on corporate profit is a corporate income tax. An excise tax is aimed at a particular good or activity instead.

options.t: A tax on a house or on a building
options.why: A tax on a house or building is a property tax, based on value. It is not an excise tax on a product.

options.t: A tax on each gallon of gasoline
options.why: An excise tax is charged on a specific product, such as a cents-per-gallon tax on gasoline. It is usually included in the pump price.

options.t: A tax on wages that workers earn
options.why: A tax on wages is an income or payroll tax. Excise taxes target specific goods like fuel, alcohol or tobacco.

q: What is the purpose of an extension of time to file?

options.t: To skip filing forever and ever
options.why: An extension does not let someone skip filing forever. It only moves the filing deadline, often to October 15, and a return is still required.

options.t: More time to file, but not to pay
options.why: An extension gives extra time to file the return, but tax owed is still due by the original date. Interest and late payment penalties apply to unpaid tax.

options.t: To cancel the tax owed for the year
options.why: An extension never cancels tax owed. The full amount remains due, and only the paperwork deadline moves.

options.t: To avoid all penalties and interest
options.why: Penalties and interest on unpaid tax still apply after an extension. It protects against a late-filing penalty, not from payment-related charges.

q: What is an IRS audit?

options.t: A review of a return and records for accuracy
options.why: An audit is an IRS examination of a return and supporting records to check that income, deductions and credits are reported accurately.

options.t: A free tax refund given to all tax filers
options.why: An audit is not a refund, free or otherwise. It is a review that can lead to a refund, additional tax or no change.

options.t: A rule to open a business before taxes are filed
options.why: An audit is not a business-opening rule. It is a check of a return that has already been filed, to verify accuracy.

options.t: A discount for filing a return early in the season
options.why: An audit is not a discount for early filing. It is a review of accuracy, and anyone may be selected, whether they file early or late.

q: What should a taxpayer keep to support deductions in case of an audit?

options.t: Only a note of totals
options.why: A note of totals does not prove the amounts. The IRS can ask for documents showing each deduction, so supporting records are needed.

options.t: Nothing, the IRS checks
options.why: The IRS does not do your record keeping. The taxpayer must prove deductions, so keeping nothing risks having them disallowed.

options.t: Receipts and records
